text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Accumulated deliberate practice explains a minority of variance in sport performance, not the majority: 18% of variance in sports in the pooled estimate.
Effect/estimate: Deliberate practice accounted for 18% of variance in sport performance
Population: Athletes across sports (meta-analysis) | level: Mixed novice to elite | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis | n: See source (sport-domain studies pooled)
Boxing-specific: No - cross-sport, boxing not separately reported | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - cross-sport meta-analytic estimate
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective practice-history designs; 'deliberate practice' operationalised broadly and inconsistently across primary studies; correlational, not causal.
PPBF implication: SHADOW must NOT model development as hours-accumulated. Practice volume is one predictor among many; route logic needs quality, readiness, individual-difference and opportunity variables alongside volume.
Source: Macnamara BN, Moreau D, Hambrick DZ. The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016. (10.1177/1745691616635591 / PMID 27217246)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Among elite-level performers specifically, accumulated deliberate practice accounted for only 1% of performance variance - practice volume does not discriminate within an already-selected elite group.
Effect/estimate: 1% of variance in performance among elite-level performers
Population: Elite athletes subgroup within meta-analysis | level: Elite | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis subgroup | n: Subgroup of the sports meta-analysis
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Range restriction in elite samples mechanically shrinks variance explained; this is a statistical artefact risk, not proof practice is unimportant at elite level. Contested by Ericsson (2016).
PPBF implication: Do not use training-hours totals as a selection or progression gate for advanced PPBF athletes. Rank athletes on demonstrated skill and assessment evidence, not logged hours.
Source: Macnamara BN, Moreau D, Hambrick DZ. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016. (10.1177/1745691616635591 / PMID 27217246)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The claim that deliberate practice largely determines expertise is actively contested: Ericsson argues Macnamara et al. summed hours of any practice type rather than isolating structured, feedback-rich, individually-targeted practice.
Effect/estimate: No pooled estimate - definitional dispute over what counts as deliberate practice
Population: Theoretical/methodological exchange | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Commentary and reply exchange | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: The dispute is definitional as much as empirical. Neither side has boxing-specific longitudinal data.
PPBF implication: SHADOW's practice-log schema must distinguish practice TYPE (coach-targeted, feedback-present, individualised vs general participation) - the two sides of this dispute cannot even be adjudicated without that field. This is a concrete data-model requirement.
Source: Ericsson KA. Summing Up Hours of Any Type of Practice Versus Identifying Optimal Practice Activities. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016; and Macnamara BN, Hambrick DZ, Moreau D. How Important Is Deliberate Practice? Reply to Ericsson. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2016. (10.1177/1745691616635600 (PMID 27217247); 10.1177/1745691616635614 (PMID 27217248))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The original deliberate-practice framework specified individualised tasks with a clear performance goal and immediate informative feedback, supervised by a teacher - not merely repetition volume.
Effect/estimate: No effect size claimed here - definitional
Population: Musicians (original studies) | level: Expert | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Theoretical paper with empirical studies | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No - music domain origin | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing-specific deliberate practice studies not located
LIMITATIONS: Original evidence base is music, not sport; retrospective diary methods.
PPBF implication: PPBF session-quality scoring should encode the four original ingredients as separate observable fields: individualised target, explicit performance goal, feedback present, coach supervision. Maps to Module 196 Session Quality Score.
Source: Ericsson KA, Krampe RT, Tesch-Romer C. The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychol Rev. 1993;100:363-406. (10.1037/0033-295X.100.3.363)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The most comprehensive pro-external-focus meta-analysis reports an external focus outperforms an internal focus for motor performance and for retention and transfer learning.
Effect/estimate: Hedges g = 0.264 (95% CI 0.217-0.310) performance; g = 0.583 (95% CI 0.425-0.741) retention; g = 0.584 (95% CI 0.325-0.842) transfer; age, health status and skill level did not moderate
Population: Mixed lab and applied motor tasks | level: Mixed novice to skilled | sex: Mixed | age: Children to older adults
Design: Systematic review with meta-analyses | n: 73 studies / 1,824 participants (performance); 40 studies / 1,274 participants (learning)
Boxing-specific: No - combat-sport studies not analysed separately | transfer status: Transfer to boxing PARTIAL - a boxing-specific acute trial exists (see A1-008)
LIMITATIONS: Superseded in part by a bias-corrected reanalysis (see A1-006). Predominantly single-session lab tasks; retention intervals typically 24h-1wk, far shorter than a boxing development cycle.
PPBF implication: External-focus cues are a REASONABLE DEFAULT for the PPBF cue library, but the library must not be built on the assumption that this effect is large or settled. Tag every cue with focus_type so PPBF can test it locally.
Source: Chua LK, Jimenez-Diaz J, Lewthwaite R, Kim T, Wulf G. Superiority of external attentional focus for motor performance and learning: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Psychol Bull. 2021;147:618-645. (10.1037/bul0000335 / PMID 34843301)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A robust Bayesian reanalysis of the same external-focus data found moderate-to-strong evidence of publication bias in every analysis; after bias correction the mean effects were negligible.
Effect/estimate: Bias-corrected g = 0.01 (performance), 0.15 (retention), 0.09 (transfer), 0.06 (electromyography), -0.01 (distance effect); Bayes factors favoured the null
Population: Same underlying studies as prior meta-analyses | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review, reanalysis of 7 prior meta-studies | n: Same source data as the 7 prior meta-studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: Bias-correction models are themselves modelling assumptions and can over-correct; this is a reanalysis, not new data. Both this and A1-005 are legitimate readings of a biased literature.
PPBF implication: SHADOW must NOT present 'use external cues' as validated science with a known effect size. Present it as a defensible default with contested evidence, and make the cue library A/B-testable inside PPBF.
Source: McKay B, Corson AE, Seedu J, De Faveri CS, Hasan H, Arnold K, et al. Reporting bias, not external focus: A robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of the external focus of attention literature. Psychol Bull. 2024;150:1347-1362. (10.1037/bul0000451 / PMID 39480294)

[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] OPTIMAL theory proposes enhanced expectancies, autonomy support and external focus jointly improve learning by strengthening goal-action coupling.
Effect/estimate: No pooled estimate - theoretical proposal
Population: Theoretical framework | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Theoretical paper | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: Two of the three OPTIMAL pillars have failed in preregistered tests (see A1-009, A1-010) and the third is bias-contested (A1-006). Treat the integrated theory as unconfirmed.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In trained boxers and kickboxers, external-focus instructions produced faster and more forceful punches than internal-focus instructions in an acute single-session test.
Effect/estimate: External vs internal focus: 4% faster and 5% more forceful (P<0.05); external vs control: 2% faster and 3% more forceful (P<0.05)
Population: Competitive boxers and kickboxers | level: Intermediate (n=8) and expert (n=7) | sex: Not stated in abstract; described as trained combat athletes | age: Adult
Design: Randomised within-subject repeated measures | n: 15 (8 intermediate, 7 expert)
Boxing-specific: YES - boxers and kickboxers, punch outcome measures | transfer status: Boxing-specific ACUTE PERFORMANCE evidence only
LIMITATIONS: ACUTE PERFORMANCE, NOT LEARNING - no retention or transfer test. Small n. Punch integrator, not a live opponent. Effects are single-digit percentages.
PPBF implication: This is the strongest boxing-specific cue evidence available and it is an acute-performance finding. SHADOW may recommend external cues at the point of execution (bag/pad/bout) with an explicit 'acute performance, retention untested' label.
Source: Halperin I, Chapman DW, Martin DT, Abbiss C, Wulf G. The effects of attentional focus instructions on punching velocity and impact forces among trained combat athletes. J Sports Sci. 2016;35:500-507. (10.1080/02640414.2016.1175651 / PMID 27088370)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The self-controlled practice literature shows a moderate naive benefit that does not survive bias assessment: published and unpublished findings differ significantly and the literature lacks evidential value.
Effect/estimate: Naive random-effects g = 0.44 (95% CI 0.31-0.56); significant published/unpublished difference; authors conclude underpowered, biased, lacking evidential value
Population: Motor learning participants | level: Mostly novice | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Meta-analysis with publication-bias assessment | n: k=52 studies, N=2,061
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Bias-correction inference, not new trials. Does not prove autonomy support is useless - it shows the evidence cannot currently support the claim.
PPBF implication: Athlete choice in PPBF (e.g. letting an athlete pick a drill variant) should be justified on engagement, adherence and athlete-voice grounds - which is defensible - NOT as a validated learning accelerator.
Source: McKay B, Yantha ZD, Hussien J, Carter MJ, Ste-Marie DM. Meta-Analytic Findings of the Self-Controlled Motor Learning Literature: Underpowered, Biased, and Lacking Evidential Value. Meta-Psychology. 2022. (10.15626/mp.2021.2803)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A preregistered trial found autonomy-supportive instructional language raised perceived autonomy but produced no group difference in skill acquisition or retention versus controlling language.
Effect/estimate: No group differences in motor performance at acquisition or retention; no differences in perceived competence or intrinsic motivation
Population: Adults learning speed cup stacking | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Preregistered randomised experiment | n: 156
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Single laboratory task (cup stacking); a null on one task does not generalise to all coaching language effects, and coaching language plausibly matters for retention in the sport sense (staying in the gym).
PPBF implication: Separate two SHADOW outcome families: SKILL outcomes and ENGAGEMENT/RETENTION outcomes. Supportive language should be justified and measured against the second, not credited to the first.
Source: St Germain L, McKay B, Barbera L, Tandon C, Seedu J, Carrillo C, et al. Autonomy-supportive instructional language does not enhance skill acquisition compared to controlling instructional language. Psychol Res. 2024. (10.1007/s00426-024-02059-z / PMID 39589568)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The contextual interference effect is a genuine live dispute in the current literature, with two 2023-2024 meta-analyses reaching opposite headline conclusions and a published rebuttal exchange continuing into 2025.
Effect/estimate: Opposite conclusions; no single defensible pooled number for applied sport
Population: Sport and physical education learners | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Children to older adults
Design: Competing systematic reviews with meta-analysis plus commentary exchange | n: See constituent rows A1-012 to A1-014
Boxing-specific: No boxing-specific CI trial located | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Any product that states a single CI recommendation as settled science is misrepresenting the field as of 2026.
PPBF implication: SHADOW's practice-design engine must expose practice-schedule choice as a COACH DECISION with the dispute surfaced, not as an algorithmic recommendation. Maps to Module 061 Practice Design Engine.
Source: Ammar A, et al. Educ Res Rev. 2023;39:100537; Czyz SH, et al. Sci Rep. 2024;14; Ammar A, et al. Educ Psychol Rev. 2024;36; Ammar A, et al. Educ Psychol Rev. 2025;37. (10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100537; 10.1038/s41598-024-65753-3; 10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z; 10.1007/s10648-025-10043-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] One meta-analysis found no evidence supporting contextual interference effects in sport settings: acquisition, retention and transfer performance were unaffected by practice schedule.
Effect/estimate: No significant schedule effect at acquisition, retention or transfer; subgroup analysis identified only constrained conditions where CI appeared
Population: Sport and physical education learners | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: See source (sport-context studies)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Methodology criticised in print by Czyz et al. (2024) for database selection and lack of preregistration; authors responded in 2025.
PPBF implication: Counts as direct evidence AGAINST hard-coding random practice as superior in a gym setting.
Source: Ammar A, Trabelsi K, Boujelbane MA, Boukhris O, Glenn JM, Chtourou H, Schollhorn WI. The myth of contextual interference learning benefit in sports practice: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Educ Res Rev. 2023;39:100537. (10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100537)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A competing meta-analysis found a medium beneficial retention effect of high contextual interference overall, but reported the benefit as almost negligible in APPLIED settings and negligible and non-significant in YOUNG participants.
Effect/estimate: High CI medium beneficial effect overall and statistically significant; effective in laboratory settings; almost negligible in applied settings; large effect in older adults, medium in adults, negligible and non-significant in young participants
Population: Motor learning participants across settings and ages | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Young participants through older adults
Design: Systematic review with three-level mixed model and random-effects meta-analysis | n: 1,255 records; 294 full texts screened; 54 studies in meta-analysis
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Contains a sharply-worded methodological attack on the competing review, answered in print. The applied-setting and young-participant subgroup findings are the operationally relevant ones for PPBF and both point away from a benefit.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL FOR PPBF: even the pro-CI meta-analysis reports the effect is near-zero in applied settings and near-zero in young participants - which is exactly PPBF's population and setting. Do not sell random practice to PPBF coaches as evidence-based for youth.
Source: Czyz SH, Wojcik AM, Solarska P, Kiper P. High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2024;14. (10.1038/s41598-024-65753-3 / PMID 38987617)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A multilevel meta-analysis in physical-education and sport contexts found only 20% of pooled outcomes agreed with the paradoxical CI prediction and no significant pre-to-post difference between blocked and random schedules.
Effect/estimate: 37 of 183 outcomes (20%) agreed with the paradoxical CI effect; delta pre-post low CI 28.9 +/- 59.5% vs high CI 27.9 +/- 52.8%, no significant difference
Population: Physical education and sport learners | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Critical systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis | n: 933 records screened; 36 studies included; 183 pooled outcomes
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Very large SDs on the delta estimates indicate extreme heterogeneity; the percentages are descriptive change scores, not standardised effects.
PPBF implication: Supports a middle path: vary practice for engagement and representativeness reasons, but do not promise a retention dividend from randomisation.
Source: Ammar A, Trabelsi K, Boujelbane MA, Salem A, Boukhris O, Glenn JM, et al. The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. 2024;36. (10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A gradually increasing interference schedule (blocked, then serial, then random) produced better retention than either blocked or random scheduling, and better transfer in the second experiment.
Effect/estimate: Increasing schedule superior on retention (Exp 1, golf putting); superior on retention and transfer vs blocked and random (Exp 2, three basketball passes)
Population: Novices learning golf putting and basketball passes | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Two randomised experiments | n: Two experiments (see source)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - but the progression logic maps naturally onto boxing technical progressions
LIMITATIONS: Small single-lab experiments, novices, closed skills. Not replicated at scale.
PPBF implication: PROPOSED PPBF DESIGN RULE: progress blocked -> serial -> random within a technical block rather than choosing one schedule. This is a reasonable, testable structure for the session builder (Module 007) - label as proposed, not validated in boxing.
Source: Porter JM, Magill RA. Systematically increasing contextual interference is beneficial for learning sport skills. J Sports Sci. 2010;28:1277-1285. (10.1080/02640414.2010.502946 / PMID 20845219)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Serial practice and random practice produce equivalent retention and transfer, so serial is not a lower-interference midpoint on the retention outcome.
Effect/estimate: Serial and random practice showed the same retention and transfer results
Population: Motor learning participants | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analytic review | n: 9 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Only 9 studies; small evidence base.
PPBF implication: If PPBF implements the increasing-CI progression (A1-015), the serial stage should be justified as a coaching scaffold, not as a distinct interference dose.
Source: Lage GM, Faria LO, Ambrosio NFA, Borges AMP, Apolinario-Souza T. What Is the Level of Contextual Interference in Serial Practice? A Meta-Analytic Review. J Mot Learn Dev. 2022;10:224-242. (10.1123/jmld.2021-0020)

text_content:
[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] Differential learning has been evaluated only in an exploratory meta-analytic review with high heterogeneity; it is not established as superior to other methods.
Effect/estimate: High overall heterogeneity reported for the acquisition phase; authors describe the analysis as exploratory and note controversy around DL theory
Population: Mixed motor learning and sport participants | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Exploratory systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 27 studies, 31 experiments
Boxing-specific: No boxing DL trial located | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Small literature concentrated in a limited number of research groups; heterogeneity limits pooling; authors themselves label the analysis exploratory.
PPBF implication: Differential learning must be labelled EXPERIMENTAL in the PPBF constraint library (Module 060). It may be offered to coaches as an option to trial, with mandatory outcome capture - never as a recommended default.
Source: Tassignon B, Verschueren J, Baeyens JP, Benjaminse A, Gokeler A, Serrien B, Clijsen R. An Exploratory Meta-Analytic Review on the Empirical Evidence of Differential Learning as an Enhanced Motor Learning Method. Front Psychol. 2021;12:533033. (10.3389/fpsyg.2021.533033 / PMID 34025487)

[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] The theoretical basis of differential learning is deliberate movement-pattern noise and stochastic perturbation, i.e. never repeating the same movement, which is the direct opposite of technical-model repetition coaching.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate
Population: Theoretical exposition | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Theoretical/review article | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: Author-advocated framework; the same author group co-authored one side of the contextual interference dispute, so independence of the DL evidence base is limited.
PPBF implication: If PPBF trials DL, the boxing safety envelope must be set first: deliberate movement noise near the head, on the inside, or in sparring is a safety question, not just a pedagogy question. Route to Module 003 Safety Gate.
Source: Schollhorn WI, Hegen P, Davids K. The Nonlinear Nature of Learning - A Differential Learning Approach. Open Sports Sci J. 2012;5:100-112. (10.2174/1875399X01205010100)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Representative learning design is the formal requirement that practice tasks preserve the informational variables and action opportunities of competition so that skills transfer.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate - design principle
Population: Sport practitioners and researchers | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: All ages
Design: Conceptual/theoretical paper | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No boxing-specific RLD study located | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED as a validated intervention; the principle itself is widely accepted
LIMITATIONS: It is a design principle, not an intervention with a pooled effect size. Adopting it does not guarantee transfer (see A1-020).
PPBF implication: PPBF drills should carry a representativeness rating field. Shadowboxing, bag work, pads, constrained sparring and open sparring occupy different points on that scale and SHADOW should show it explicitly.
Source: Pinder RA, Davids K, Renshaw I, Araujo D. Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2011;33:146-155. (10.1123/jsep.33.1.146)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Increasing task representativeness does not produce linearly increasing skill gains: in a 6-week tennis serve intervention, different behaviours emerged at different representativeness levels rather than a simple dose-response.
Effect/estimate: Relationship between increasing representativeness and skill acquisition was not linear; groups prioritised serve speed vs placement differently
Population: Junior tennis players (15.4 +/- 1.9 y) | level: Junior competitive | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Adolescent
Design: Three-group intervention with pre/post skill test and in-situ match analysis | n: 33
Boxing-specific: No - tennis | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; other-sport evidence
LIMITATIONS: Small n per group; single sport; no long-term follow-up. Behavioural divergence rather than a clean win for high representativeness.
PPBF implication: SHADOW should not recommend 'make it more like a fight' as a monotonic dial. Higher representativeness changes what the athlete optimises - which for boxing may trade technique quality against competitive expediency. Coach must choose the target behaviour.
Source: Krause L, Farrow D, Pinder R, Buszard T, Kovalchik S, Reid M. Enhancing skill transfer in tennis using representative learning design. J Sports Sci. 2019;37:2560-2568. (10.1080/02640414.2019.1647739 / PMID 31379253)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A coach-usable representativeness rating instrument has been built and consensus-validated in tennis (7 items, each with a task-goal and a competition-relevance sub-question), via a 4-round Delphi with 10 academic and 13 coaching experts.
Effect/estimate: 7-item tool, expert consensus reached; no criterion-validity or reliability effect size reported in the abstract
Population: Tennis coaches and academics | level: N/A | sex: Mixed | age: N/A
Design: Delphi consensus instrument development | n: 23 experts (10 academic, 13 coaching)
Boxing-specific: No - tennis | transfer status: Boxing analogue DOES NOT EXIST - would need to be built
LIMITATIONS: Consensus validity only; predictive validity for actual transfer not established.
PPBF implication: CONCRETE PPBF DELIVERABLE: build a boxing Representative Practice Assessment Tool by the same Delphi method with PPBF and external boxing coaches. This is a fundable, achievable validation project and it gives Module 061 a real input variable.
Source: Krause L, Farrow D, Reid M, Buszard T, Pinder R. Helping coaches apply the principles of representative learning design: validation of a tennis specific practice assessment tool. J Sports Sci. 2017. (10.1080/02640414.2017.1374684 / PMID 28905685)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] The constraints-led approach organises practice design around the interaction of task, environment and performer constraints rather than around a single technical model.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate
Population: Motor development and sport | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: All ages
Design: Theoretical framework chapter | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No boxing-specific CLA trial located | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED as an evaluated intervention
LIMITATIONS: Widely adopted as a framework; comparatively few controlled trials isolating CLA against a matched-dose traditional programme, and none located in boxing.
PPBF implication: PPBF's Coach-Controlled Constraint Engine (Module 045) and Constraint Library (Module 060) already assume this framework. The registry should record that the framework is well-supported conceptually but under-tested as a boxing intervention.
Source: Newell KM. Constraints on the Development of Coordination. In: Motor Development in Children: Aspects of Coordination and Control. 1986. (10.1007/978-94-009-4460-2_19)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A nonlinear pedagogy condition was reported to accommodate individual differences in learning a sports skill better than a linear prescriptive condition.
Effect/estimate: Reported advantage for catering to individual differences; single study
Population: Learners of a sport skill | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Not stated here
Design: Controlled comparison | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Single study; effect not independently replicated at scale; outcome framed as individual-difference accommodation rather than group mean gain.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF's individualised route logic in principle. Insufficient to claim nonlinear pedagogy outperforms traditional boxing instruction.

[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] Formal frameworks now exist for periodising skill acquisition (not just physical load) across a season, including phase-specific manipulation of practice representativeness and coaching input.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate - frameworks not empirically validated against outcomes

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The guidance hypothesis - that 100% feedback aids practice performance but harms learning relative to reduced feedback - originates in a classic study reporting a reduced-frequency retention advantage.
Effect/estimate: Reduced knowledge-of-results frequency enhanced retention relative to 100% frequency
Population: Adults learning a laboratory movement task | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory experiments | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Single-lab, simple laboratory task; superseded by meta-analytic null (A1-026).
PPBF implication: This is the textbook claim PPBF coaches will most likely have been taught. The registry must carry both it and its meta-analytic refutation so SHADOW gives coaches the current picture.
Source: Winstein CJ, Schmidt RA. Reduced frequency of knowledge of results enhances motor skill learning. J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn. 1990;16:677-691. (10.1037/0278-7393.16.4.677)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A large meta-analysis found NO significant effect of reduced feedback frequency at any time point and no significant acquisition-to-delayed-retention reversal; included studies were severely underpowered.
Effect/estimate: No significant effect of reduced feedback frequency at any time point; no significant change in effect from acquisition or immediate retention to delayed retention; substantial heterogeneity; no significant moderators; z-curve indicated severe underpowering
Population: Motor learning participants | level: Mostly novice | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Meta-analysis with multilevel models and z-curve analysis | n: 1,662 articles screened; 61 papers; k=75; N=2,228
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: A null across a heterogeneous, underpowered literature means evidence is lacking, not that feedback frequency is proven irrelevant.
PPBF implication: SHADOW must NOT prescribe a feedback-frequency number (e.g. give feedback on 50% of reps). Any such number in PPBF would be invented. Record feedback events and let PPBF discover its own pattern.
Source: McKay B, Hussien J, Vinh MA, Mir-Orefice A, Brooks H, Ste-Marie DM. Meta-analysis of the reduced relative feedback frequency effect on motor learning and performance. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2022;61:102165. (10.1016/j.psychsport.2022.102165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A factorial trial crossing autonomy support with 100% vs 50%-faded feedback found trivial effects of both on golf-putting learning and performance.
Effect/estimate: Trivial effects for both autonomy support and feedback schedule
Population: Adults learning golf putting | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: 2x2 factorial randomised experiment | n: 56
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Single task, modest n, no vision of results (an unusual constraint).

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Bandwidth knowledge of results (feedback only when error exceeds a tolerance) has been studied since the late 1980s with reported learning advantages in laboratory tasks.
Effect/estimate: Reported learning advantages for bandwidth KR in individual studies; no pooled sport estimate located; the optimal bandwidth width is TBD
Population: Adults on laboratory motor tasks | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory experiments | n: Multiple small laboratory studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Small, old, laboratory-task literature. No meta-analysis in sport located. The bandwidth width itself is arbitrary across studies.
PPBF implication: Bandwidth feedback maps cleanly to a SHADOW threshold field: coach sets an acceptable-error band per technique and only logs/flags outside it. Implement as configurable, not as a fixed evidence-based tolerance.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Observed ringside feedback in competitive amateur boxing is predominantly internal-focus and controlling: excluding neutral statements, coaches gave 15% internal vs 6% external focus feedback, 53% controlling vs 6% autonomy-supportive, and 29% positive vs 12% negative.
Effect/estimate: Internal 15% vs external 6%; controlling 53% vs autonomy-supportive 6%; positive 29% vs negative 12%. In winning bouts: less internal (12% vs 19%), less controlling (48% vs 58%), more positive (36% vs 18%)
Population: Amateur boxing coaches at a national championship | level: Amateur competitive | sex: Coaches not stratified by sex in abstract | age: Adult competition
Design: Systematic observation of competition video/audio | n: 12 boxing coaches at the 2015 Australian Boxing Championships
Boxing-specific: YES - amateur boxing corner feedback | transfer status: Boxing-specific OBSERVATIONAL evidence
LIMITATIONS: OBSERVATIONAL AND CORRELATIONAL. The winning-bout association is not causal - better-performing boxers plausibly elicit more positive corner talk. Single national championship, 12 coaches, one country.
PPBF implication: This is the single most directly relevant study for the PPBF cue library. It establishes (a) a measurable corner-feedback taxonomy PPBF can adopt wholesale, and (b) that real boxing coaches default to internal and controlling language. State the correlation caveat prominently.
Source: Halperin I, Chapman DW, Martin DT, Abbiss C, Wulf G. Coaching cues in amateur boxing: An analysis of ringside feedback provided between rounds of competition. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2016;25:44-50. (10.1016/j.psychsport.2016.04.003)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The gap between motor-learning recommendations and field coaching practice is documented outside boxing too: most instructions athletes reported receiving were internally focused, and only 15% of their own task-related thoughts when fatigued were external.
Effect/estimate: More than half of coach instructions internally focused; 15% of self-reported task-related thoughts external when fatigued
Population: Recreational distance runners | level: Recreational | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional questionnaire | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No - distance running | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED but converges with the boxing observation in A1-029
LIMITATIONS: Self-report questionnaire; recreational sample; recall bias.
PPBF implication: Adoption is the real bottleneck, not the science. If PPBF ships an external-focus cue library, it must measure whether coaches actually use it - an implementation-fidelity metric, not just a content library.
Source: Yamada M, Diekfuss JA, Raisbeck LD. Motor Behavior Literature Fails to Translate: A Preliminary Investigation into Coaching and Focus of Attention in Recreational Distance Runners. Int J Exerc Sci. 2020. (10.70252/MNFI4883 / PMID 32509132)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Systematic observation of coach augmented verbal feedback across 31 studies found no agreement on which feedback types matter most and inconsistent observation instruments.
Effect/estimate: Three themes: variation in observation tools and feedback types; limited evidence base behind observed feedback types; concerns over feedback quality. No pooled effect.
Population: Team sport coaches in developmental and performance contexts | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic review | n: 31 studies
Boxing-specific: No - team sports | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Descriptive review of measurement practice, not of feedback effectiveness.
PPBF implication: PPBF should adopt ONE feedback taxonomy and hold it stable, so its own longitudinal data is comparable over time. Recommend adopting the Halperin boxing taxonomy (A1-029) as the PPBF standard.
Source: Corbett R, Partington M, Ryan L, Cope E. A systematic review of coach augmented verbal feedback during practice and competition in team sports. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2023;19:864-881. (10.1177/17479541231218665)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Learners who acquired a skill with little explicit rule knowledge did not deteriorate under stress, whereas explicitly-instructed learners did - the founding reinvestment finding.
Effect/estimate: Explicit learners' skill degraded under induced stress; implicit learners' did not
Population: Adults learning golf putting | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory experiment with stress manipulation | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - though pressure-induced technical breakdown is a core boxing phenomenon
LIMITATIONS: Small lab study; the implicit group performed articulatory suppression, a confound raised by Hardy et al. (1996).
PPBF implication: Directly relevant to sparring and bout performance. Motivates a PPBF performs-under-pressure assessment distinct from performs-on-pads.
Source: Masters RSW. Knowledge, knerves and know-how: The role of explicit versus implicit knowledge in the breakdown of a complex motor skill under pressure. Br J Psychol. 1992;83:343-358. (10.1111/j.2044-8295.1992.tb02446.x)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The founding implicit-learning result was challenged on methodological grounds: the original implicit group performed articulatory suppression during learning but not during the stress test, so the comparison was confounded.
Effect/estimate: Replication with an additional implicit group performing articulatory suppression in BOTH phases; conclusions of the original study re-examined
Population: Adults learning golf putting | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Replication and extension experiment | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: This is a 1996 challenge to a 1992 study; the wider implicit-learning literature has continued in both directions.
PPBF implication: Register implicit learning as promising-but-contested. Do not build a PPBF pathway that withholds explanation from athletes on the strength of this literature - that has coaching-ethics and athlete-understanding costs.
Source: Hardy L, Mullen R, Jones G. Knowledge and conscious control of motor actions under stress. Br J Psychol. 1996;87:621-636. (10.1111/j.2044-8295.1996.tb02612.x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 25 controlled trials found the claim that implicit learning produces greater automatisation (dual-task resilience) than explicit learning is not clearly supported.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive synthesis of dual-task performance; the automatisation advantage was not clearly established
Population: Sports-related motor task learners | level: Mostly novice | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 25 controlled trials
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Descriptive synthesis rather than pooled meta-analysis; heterogeneous implicit interventions (analogy, errorless, dual-task, external focus grouped together).
PPBF implication: Do not promise coaches that implicit methods produce automaticity. The mechanism claim is weaker than the pressure-performance claim.
Source: Kal E, Prosee R, Winters M, van der Kamp J. Does implicit motor learning lead to greater automatization of motor skills compared to explicit motor learning? A systematic review. PLoS One. 2018;13:e0203591. (10.1371/journal.pone.0203591 / PMID 30183763)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In primary-school children, implicit and explicit learning paradigms were equally effective overall; only 5 of 25 studies were conducted outside the laboratory, and manipulation checks were performed in only 52% of studies.
Effect/estimate: Implicit paradigms as effective as explicit paradigms; the 5 non-lab studies suggested superior implicit efficacy; manipulation checks in 13 of 25 studies (52%)
Population: Typically developing children and children with developmental disorders | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Primary school age
Design: Systematic review | n: 25 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED - relevant to PPBF youth cohort
LIMITATIONS: Methodological quality varied and was often insufficient for firm conclusions; mostly upper-limb aiming tasks, not whole-body sport skills.
PPBF implication: For PPBF's youth programme, implicit methods are not established as superior. Choose instruction style on working-memory and engagement grounds (A1-039), not on a claimed implicit advantage.
Source: van Abswoude F, Mombarg R, de Groot W, Steenbergen B. Implicit motor learning in primary school children: A systematic review. J Sports Sci. 2021. (10.1080/02640414.2021.1947010 / PMID 34219609)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analogy instruction outperformed explicit instruction and control conditions on motor performance in a meta-analysis of 16 RCTs, with children and novices benefiting most.
Effect/estimate: Analogy vs control ES = 0.32 (p=0.03); analogy vs explicit ES = 0.29 (p=0.02); children and novices benefited most (all p<0.01). Retention estimates are reported as ES = 5.72 vs control and ES = 7.25 vs explicit - implausibly large values indicating very few, highly heterogeneous retention comparisons; these must NOT be used as planning numbers.
Population: Motor skill learners | level: Novice to skilled | sex: Mixed | age: Children and adults
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 16 randomised controlled trials
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: The main performance effects are small (~0.3). The retention effect sizes are so extreme they signal instability rather than a large true effect - recorded here only to flag that they should not be quoted as a benefit magnitude. Under-stress effect was only a trend (ES=1.18, p=0.05).
PPBF implication: Analogy is the best-supported instruction TYPE for the PPBF youth cohort. The cue library should carry a substantial analogy set for beginners and youth, tagged cue_type=analogy, with the effect described as small.
Source: Carnero-Diaz A, Pecci J, Calvo-Lluch A, et al. Use your imagination for better performance. Effects of analogy instruction in motor skills. A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2024;102766. (10.1016/j.psychsport.2024.102766 / PMID 39419241)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analogy-taught learners maintained performance under a pressure manipulation while explicitly-taught learners declined, despite equal performance during learning and delayed retention.
Effect/estimate: Analogy and explicit groups equal during learning and delayed retention; explicit group dropped under pressure, analogy group unaffected; probe reaction times showed equal attentional resource allocation
Population: Adults learning a modified basketball shooting task | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Randomised laboratory experiment with pressure transfer test | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Seated, modified task; laboratory pressure manipulation is far weaker than a competitive bout.
PPBF implication: Supports using analogy cues for skills that must survive bout pressure. PPBF should tag which cues are intended for pressure-resilient skills and test them in constrained sparring, not just on pads.
Source: Lam WK, Maxwell JP, Masters RSW. Analogy Learning and the Performance of Motor Skills under Pressure. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2009;31:337-357. (10.1123/jsep.31.3.337)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Children with lower working-memory capacity learned less when given five explicit technical instructions before each practice block - instruction quantity is a real constraint, not a style preference.
Effect/estimate: Lower working-memory capacity limited motor learning under a five-explicit-instruction protocol
Population: Children aged 8-10 learning basketball shooting | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: 8-10 years
Design: Quasi-experimental with WM-capacity grouping, pre/post and 1-week retention | n: 90 children assessed; 24 lower-WM and 24 higher-WM in the motor task
Boxing-specific: No - basketball | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED but the mechanism (verbal instruction load) is domain-general
LIMITATIONS: Extreme-groups design (lowest and highest thirds) inflates apparent group differences; single task.
PPBF implication: DIRECT PRODUCT RULE: cap the number of simultaneous technical cues SHADOW surfaces per drill. One cue at a time for youth and novices. This is a concrete, defensible constraint on the cue library UI.
Source: Buszard T, Farrow D, Verswijveren SJJM, Reid M, Williams J, Polman R, et al. Working Memory Capacity Limits Motor Learning When Implementing Multiple Instructions. Front Psychol. 2017;8:1350. (10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01350 / PMID 28878701)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Observational modelling improves both movement dynamics and movement outcome measures, with effects varying by task constraints.
Effect/estimate: Effects reported separately for movement dynamics and movement outcome across differing task constraints
Population: Motor skill learners | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An applied model for the use of observation specifies the functions, timing and delivery features of observation interventions; a review of 48 studies (2011-2018) affirmed effectiveness and extended it to wider populations and settings.
Effect/estimate: Effectiveness of observation interventions affirmed and extended; 21 of 48 articles addressed the basic effectiveness question

Design: Applied model plus systematic review | n: 48 articles in the 2020 review
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Narrative/structured review, not pooled meta-analysis; heterogeneous interventions.
PPBF implication: PPBF's film-study flow (Module 111 and pilot.shadow_film_study_proposals) should structure clips by observation FUNCTION (skill, strategy, performance) and timing, per this model - not just store clips.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Observing a MIX of expert and novice (error-containing) models produced better learning than observing an expert model alone, replicated across several independent experiments.
Effect/estimate: Mixed expert+novice observation produced more stable movement time, better generalisation and better estimation of model performance than expert-only or novice-only observation
Population: Adults learning timing and surgical tasks | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Multiple randomised experiments | n: Includes a 120-participant randomised study in robotic surgical skills
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Imagery interventions produce measurable benefits in sport in meta-analysis, and the PETTLEP model provides the most-specified delivery framework.
Effect/estimate: Positive pooled effects reported for imagery interventions in sport; PETTLEP reviewed as the dominant structured approach. No boxing-specific estimate exists.
Population: Athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analyses and systematic reviews | n: See sources
Boxing-specific: No boxing-specific imagery trial located | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Imagery literatures are prone to expectancy and allocation-concealment problems; blinding is essentially impossible. The PETTLEP functional-equivalence mechanism has itself been critically reflected on in print.
PPBF implication: Imagery is a low-risk, low-cost PPBF addition (at-home homework modules 085-092). Specify it via PETTLEP elements so what is delivered is auditable, and measure adherence.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Experts differ systematically from non-experts on perceptual-cognitive measures: 42 studies and 388 effect sizes showed superior response accuracy and response time plus distinct visual search behaviour (fewer, longer fixations).
Effect/estimate: Experts superior on response accuracy and response time; experts used fewer fixations of longer duration
Population: Athletes across sports | level: Expert vs non-expert | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis | n: 42 studies, 388 effect sizes
Boxing-specific: No - cross-sport | transfer status: Transfer to boxing PARTIAL - a combat-sport-specific meta-analysis exists (A1-045)
LIMITATIONS: EXPERT-NOVICE DIFFERENCE, NOT A TRAINING EFFECT. Shows what expertise looks like, not that training these measures creates expertise.
PPBF implication: Perceptual measures are candidate PPBF ASSESSMENT variables (Module 058 Cue Recognition Engine). They are not, on this evidence, candidate training targets.
Source: Mann DTY, Williams AM, Ward P, Janelle CM. Perceptual-Cognitive Expertise in Sport: A Meta-Analysis. J Sport Exerc Psychol. 2007;29:457-478. (10.1123/jsep.29.4.457)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In combat sports specifically, experts outperformed non-experts on perceptual anticipation with large effect sizes for response accuracy and reaction time across 27 studies and 233 datasets.
Effect/estimate: Response accuracy 1.51 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.87); reaction time -0.91 (95% CI -1.08 to -0.73). A visual-fixation result is reported with an apparent sign inconsistency between point estimate and confidence interval in the published abstract, so no fixation number is carried forward here.
Population: Combat sport athletes (multiple combat sports) | level: Expert vs non-expert | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 27 studies, 233 datasets
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - combat sports including but not limited to boxing; boxing not separately pooled in the abstract | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence; within-boxing estimate NOT AVAILABLE
LIMITATIONS: EXPERT-NOVICE DIFFERENCE, NOT A TRAINING EFFECT. Cross-sectional. Heterogeneous paradigms across English- and Chinese-language databases. The fixation-duration reporting inconsistency reduces confidence in that detail.
PPBF implication: Justifies building a boxing anticipation assessment into PPBF (occlusion-style video test) as a DISCRIMINATIVE measure. Does not justify selling anticipation training as a proven route to expertise.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 12-session implicit perceptual-motor training programme improved decision-making accuracy and changed gaze behaviour in highly-skilled junior female karate fighters relative to matched-motor-training and control groups.
Effect/estimate: Only the implicit perceptual-motor group significantly improved decision-making accuracy; that group also fixated on fewer locations for longer; no significant session-by-session improvement except at the final session
Population: Highly skilled junior female karate fighters (M age 15.7 +/- 1.2 y) | level: Highly skilled junior | sex: Female | age: Adolescent
Design: Randomised three-group intervention with video-based and on-mat tests | n: 18 total (6 implicit, 6 placebo motor training, 6 control)
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - karate, a striking combat sport, but not boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence; boxing transfer UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: VERY SMALL n (6 per group). Single sport, single sex, elite juniors. Improvement appeared only at the final session, which is consistent with a late-emerging effect or with noise.
PPBF implication: Closest existing analogue to a PPBF decision-training module (Module 057). Cite it as a design template and an explicit power warning: n=6 per arm is not a basis for a product claim.
Source: Milazzo N, Farrow D, Ruffault A, Fournier JF. Effect of Implicit Perceptual-Motor Training on Decision-Making Skills and Underpinning Gaze Behavior in Combat Athletes. Percept Mot Skills. 2016;123:300-323. (10.1177/0031512516656816 / PMID 27371637)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Quiet eye duration discriminates experts from novices and successful from unsuccessful attempts, and quiet-eye training interventions show large effects in meta-analysis.
Effect/estimate: Expert vs novice quiet eye d = 1.04; successful vs unsuccessful within-individual d = 0.58; intervention effects d = 1.53 (quiet eye period) and d = 0.84 (performance)
Population: Athletes, largely in aiming and targeting tasks | level: Expert and novice | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Meta-analysis (two syntheses) | n: Synthesis 1: 27 studies, 38 effect sizes. Synthesis 2: 9 articles
Boxing-specific: No - dominated by golf, shooting and basketball free throws | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED and questionable: quiet eye is best established in self-paced aiming tasks, not in reactive striking exchanges
LIMITATIONS: Small intervention literature (9 articles). Aiming-task dominance limits generalisation to open, reactive boxing skills.
PPBF implication: Do NOT port quiet-eye training into boxing on this evidence. Flag as a research question for PPBF: does a quiet-eye analogue exist for a reactive striking sport?

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Interventions to counteract choking under pressure show small-to-moderate pooled benefits, with larger and more consistent effects in closed-skill contexts than in open-skill contexts.
Effect/estimate: Motor accuracy g = 0.660; executional success g = 0.444; target deviation g = 0.301; closed-skill contexts g = 0.455 with larger and more consistent effects than open-skill contexts
Population: Athletes under pressure | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis of interventions | n: 21 studies
Boxing-specific: No - boxing not separately analysed | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing is an OPEN skill, the context where these effects were weaker
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous interventions pooled (quiet eye training, pre-performance routines, mindfulness, left-hand contraction, self-talk, rational emotive behaviour therapy). The open-skill subgroup is the relevant one for boxing and is the weaker one.
PPBF implication: PPBF pressure-management support is defensible, but the effect should be expected to be SMALLER in boxing than the headline numbers because boxing is an open skill. State that in any coach-facing summary.
Source: Zeng Z, Yan W, Mohammadi A, et al. Counteracting choking under pressure in sport: A meta-analysis of interventions. Psychol Sport Exerc. 2026;103130. (10.1016/j.psychsport.2026.103130 / PMID 41951087)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of whole and part practice generally supported textbook recommendations based on task complexity/organisation and skill classification, but several analyses were compromised by too few studies.
Effect/estimate: Mean effect sizes generally supported textbook recommendations; authors concluded more studies are needed to verify empirical validity
Population: Motor skill learners | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Meta-analysis | n: 44 articles located; 20 provided sufficient information for effect size calculation
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Thin evidence base (20 usable studies); published 2009; underpowered subgroup analyses.
PPBF implication: PPBF can use the complexity/organisation heuristic to decide when to break a combination into parts, but must label it a HEURISTIC. Combination punching (high organisation) is the case where part practice is least supported.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Performance during practice is an unreliable index of learning: manipulations that improve practice performance can impair long-term retention and transfer, and vice versa.
Effect/estimate: No single effect size - the learning/performance dissociation is the finding
Population: General learning and motor skills | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Integrative reviews | n: N/A - review of decades of evidence
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Domain-general principle; applies to boxing by construction
LIMITATIONS: The dissociation is well-established in principle; several specific manipulations claimed to produce it (contextual interference, reduced feedback) are the ones now failing meta-analysis (A1-011, A1-026).
PPBF implication: SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT PRINCIPLE FOR SHADOW'S MEASUREMENT MODEL. Any PPBF skill score taken during or immediately after a coached drill is a PERFORMANCE observation, not a LEARNING observation. pilot.shadow_formula_observations must carry an observation-context field distinguishing them.
Source: Schmidt RA, Bjork RA. New Conceptualizations of Practice: Common Principles in Three Paradigms Suggest New Concepts for Training. Psychol Sci. 1992;3:207-218; Soderstrom NC, Bjork RA. Learning Versus Performance: An Integrative Review. Perspect Psychol Sci. 2015;10:176-199. (10.1111/j.1467-9280.1992.tb00029.x; 10.1177/1745691615569000)

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Establishing that learning has occurred requires a delayed retention test and a transfer test administered without the practice-condition supports, not an end-of-session measure.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate - methodological requirement. No consensus-validated retention interval for boxing skills exists: TBD.
Population: Motor learning research methodology | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Methodological convention grounded in the learning/performance literature | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No boxing-specific retention protocol located | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: Retention intervals in the literature are typically 24 hours to one week - far shorter than a boxing development cycle. The correct interval for a boxing technique is unknown.
PPBF implication: PPBF VALIDATION REQUIREMENT: Module 055 Retention Tracking Engine must implement a no-cue, no-coach-prompt retest at a defined delay. The delay value is TBD and must be set from PPBF pilot data, not assumed.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Individual differences in motor learning are substantial and largely unpredictable from current predictor variables; a 20-year critical review found serious methodological problems with published prediction claims.
Effect/estimate: Large variation in predictors used, prediction strength and sample size; authors raise concerns about the quality of evidence for prediction of individual learning differences
Population: Motor learning participants | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Critical review (2000-2020 literature) and companion review | n: 20 years of literature reviewed
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: A critique of a prediction literature, not a demonstration that prediction is impossible.
PPBF implication: Direct warning to SHADOW's forecasting modules (178 Development Forecasting, 181 Risk Forecasting): individual learning-rate prediction is not a solved problem. Any PPBF forecast must ship with wide uncertainty and mandatory coach override.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Scaling equipment and play area to children improves aspects of motor skill acquisition and is preferred by children, based on 25 studies with 989 participants.
Effect/estimate: Children preferred scaled equipment; benefits reported across psychological, skill-acquisition, biomechanical and cognitive-processing factors. Boxing scaling values are TBD - none published.
Population: Children under 18 | level: Novice to junior | sex: Mixed | age: Under 18
Design: Systematic review | n: 25 studies, 989 children
Boxing-specific: No - dominated by tennis and other ball sports | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED; boxing scaling analogues (glove weight, bag size, ring dimensions, round length, target size) are UNSTUDIED
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous outcomes; risk-of-bias assessment reported but effect sizes not pooled into a single estimate.
PPBF implication: STRONG CANDIDATE FOR A PPBF RESEARCH PROJECT: define and test boxing scaling parameters for youth (glove weight, bag size, round length, target size). No published boxing values exist - any number PPBF adopts must be labelled PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER - ASSUMPTION, REQUIRES VALIDATION.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Mental fatigue degrades sport-specific technical performance, established by meta-analysis in soccer, with a separate meta-analysis of counteractive interventions.
Effect/estimate: Mental fatigue impairs offensive and defensive technical skills in soccer; counteractive interventions pooled across 13 papers. No boxing-specific threshold exists: TBD.
Population: Soccer players (technical performance meta-analysis); athletes across sports (intervention meta-analysis) | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic reviews with meta-analysis | n: Intervention review: 13 qualified papers
Boxing-specific: No - soccer-dominated | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory mental-fatigue induction protocols (e.g. Stroop tasks) may not represent the cognitive load of a competitive boxing week (school, weight management, travel).
PPBF implication: PPBF's Readiness-to-Learn Score (Module 197) should include a mental-fatigue/cognitive-load input, not only physical readiness. Threshold values are TBD and must come from PPBF pilot data.
Source: Sun H, Soh KG, Roslan S, Wazir MRWN, Soh KL. Effects of mental fatigue on technical performance in soccer players: A systematic review with a meta-analysis. Front Public Health. 2022;10:922630; Sun H, Soh KG, Mohammadi A, et al. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Physical fatigue measurably degrades punch output in amateur boxers: after a lower-body fatigue circuit, punch force declined significantly across all punch types.
Effect/estimate: Pre-fatigue the cross produced the highest punch force (1475.42 N), ground reaction force (947.54 N) and rate of force development (3973.38 N/s). Post-fatigue punch force declined across all punches by -4.26% (p = 0.027), with the greatest reductions in the cross and left hook. RFD responses were variable.
Population: Male amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Repeated-measures pre/post fatigue protocol with force plates and a boxing force sensor | n: 10 male amateur boxers
Boxing-specific: YES - amateur boxers, boxing punches | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=10, male only, single laboratory, a 9.5-minute lower-body circuit rather than sparring-induced fatigue. The absolute newton values are lab- and equipment-specific and must not be used as PPBF benchmarks.
PPBF implication: Supports a PPBF fatigue-breakdown flag (Module 081) using punch-quality decrement as an observable. Do NOT import 1475 N or -4.26% as PPBF thresholds - they come from 10 laboratory boxers.
Source: Stewart C, Cornett R, Baker JS, et al. The Role of Lower Limb Kinetics in Boxing Punches and the Impact of Fatigue on Biomechanical Performance. Bioengineering (Basel). 2025;12:1355. (10.3390/bioengineering12121355 / PMID 41463652)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Wearable accelerometry fused with videography has been demonstrated as a method for monitoring fatigue effects on punching performance in elite boxers.
Effect/estimate: Computational framework demonstrated; laterality effects analysed via statistical parametric mapping. No validated fatigue threshold produced.
Population: Elite male boxers | level: Elite | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Method-development study with a boxing-specific punch fatigue protocol | n: 6 elite male boxers
Boxing-specific: YES - elite boxers | transfer status: Boxing-specific methods evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=6; a feasibility and methods paper, not a validated monitoring product. Custom IMUs embedded in gloves are not off-the-shelf equipment.
PPBF implication: If PPBF ever adds punch sensors, this is the closest published methodology. Feasibility, cost and youth-appropriateness are unaddressed. Treat as a research direction, not a roadmap item.

[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] The influence of sleep on motor skill acquisition in children remains controversial; a systematic review found the evidence unsettled.
Effect/estimate: No reliable pooled estimate; effects of sleep on procedural memory consolidation in children described as controversial
Population: Children aged 12 and under | level: Novice | sex: Mixed | age: Up to 12 years
Design: Systematic review (PROSPERO-registered) | n: See source
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer to boxing UNTESTED

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In novice-level amateur bouts, winners landed more punches than losers, driven by lead-hand punches, total head punches, block-and-counter combinations and punching combinations.
Effect/estimate: Winners landed 18 +/- 11 more punches. Lead-hand punches in round 1: 34.2 +/- 10.9 vs 26.5 +/- 9.4. Total punches to the head: 121.3 +/- 10.2 vs 96.0 +/- 9.8. Block-and-counterpunch combinations: 2.8 +/- 1.1 vs 0.1 +/- 0.2. Punching combinations in rounds 1 and 3: 44.3 +/- 6.4 vs 28.8 +/- 6.7. All P < .05. Peak post-bout blood lactate 11.8 +/- 1.6 mmol/L irrespective of result.
Population: Novice-level male amateur boxers | level: Novice amateur | sex: Male | age: 19.3 +/- 1.4 years
Design: Observational activity profile from competition video with post-bout blood lactate | n: 32 male boxers (blood lactate measured in 16)
Boxing-specific: YES - amateur boxing competition | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: CORRELATIONAL AND OBSERVATIONAL - these are correlates of winning, not proven causes, and judging criteria partly define the outcome. 3x2-min novice format, male only, 32 boxers, single competition context. Modern amateur formats and judging criteria differ by jurisdiction and era.
PPBF implication: Gives PPBF an evidence-anchored (if correlational) short list of trainable behaviours: lead-hand activity, head-target accuracy, block-and-counter linkage, and combination punching. These should be first-class skill dimensions in Module 038 Boxing Skill Tracking and in the cue library.
Source: Davis P, Wittekind A, Beneke R. Amateur Boxing: Activity Profile of Winners and Losers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2013;8:84-92. (10.1123/ijspp.8.1.84 / PMID 22869640)

Design: Critical narrative review | n: N/A - review
Boxing-specific: YES - amateur boxing | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review; limited somatotype data; female evidence base thinner than male; published 2015.
PPBF implication: Frames the physical qualities PPBF's skill work sits on top of. Flags a real equity gap: female-specific boxing evidence is thinner, so SHADOW must not present male-derived profiles as universal.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Amateur boxing produces a large acute physiological, endocrine and biochemical response, with greater alterations in competitive bouts than in sparring, and greater in sparring than in boxing-specific simulations.
Effect/estimate: Pre-post standardised mean differences: blood lactate 4.62, cortisol 1.33, myoglobin 1.43, aspartate transaminase 1.37, alanine aminotransferase 0.97, creatine kinase 0.65. Small increase in countermovement jump height (SMD 0.33). Responses consistently greatest in competitive bouts, then sparring, least in simulations.
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Predominantly male in the included literature | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 25 studies
Boxing-specific: YES - amateur boxing | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: Methodological quality assessed with a modified checklist; heterogeneous protocols; female representation limited. Authors note task-specific performance may NOT deteriorate despite the biochemical response.
PPBF implication: Provides a verified ORDERING for PPBF practice-intensity classification: simulation < sparring < competition. SHADOW can use this ordering in session-load and representativeness logic without inventing numbers.
Source: Finlay MJ, Greig M, Page RM, Bridge CA. Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci. 2022. (10.1080/17461391.2022.2063072 / PMID 35380916)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A shared phase structure has been defined for four boxing punches (lead punches, rear straight and hook) using ground reaction force, EMG and kinematics in experienced competitive boxers.
Effect/estimate: Phase definitions established for four punch types; no performance-outcome effect size
Population: Experienced competitive boxers | level: Experienced competitive | sex: Not stated as mixed in abstract | age: 25.6 +/- 5.97 years
Design: Mixed-method biomechanical study | n: 10 experienced competitive boxers
Boxing-specific: YES - boxing punch biomechanics | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=10; heavier-than-typical sample (body mass 95.66 +/- 21.82 kg); descriptive taxonomy rather than a performance model.
PPBF implication: Gives PPBF a published, citable phase vocabulary for punch technique so coach observations and cue targets align to the same movement segments. Use for the technique_target field in the cue library.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In expert boxers throwing a rear-hand straight punch at a head-mass movable target, reduction in arm-segment momentum explained approximately 95% of the impact impulse, distributed 40% upper arm, 35% forearm and 20% fist plus glove.
Effect/estimate: Arm momentum reduction explained ~95% of the impulse (upper arm 40%, forearm 35%, fist plus glove 20%); Pearson r = 0.902 between peak impact force and impulse
Population: Male expert collegiate boxers | level: Expert collegiate | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory biomechanics with motion capture and target accelerometry | n: 9 male expert collegiate boxers
Boxing-specific: YES - expert boxers, straight punch | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=9, male, single punch type, laboratory target rather than an opponent. Says nothing about whether coaching cues can change this distribution.
PPBF implication: Grounds cue design for the straight punch: proximal segments dominate the impulse, which argues against cues that fixate the athlete on the fist. Note this is a mechanical inference, not a validated cue test.
Source: Nakano G, Iino Y, Imura A, Kojima T. Transfer of momentum from different arm segments to a light movable target during a straight punch thrown by expert boxers. J Sports Sci. 2014;32:517-523. (10.1080/02640414.2013.843014 / PMID 24404907)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] False-performance feedback (positive, negative or neutral) produced no meaningful change in punching force, pacing or RPE in elite amateur boxers - a null that challenges generalising novice feedback findings to trained athletes.
Effect/estimate: No statistical or meaningful differences in punching force, pacing or RPE between conditions (P > 0.05; differences <= 2%)
Population: Elite amateur male boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Randomised within-subject crossover across four days | n: 15 elite amateur male boxers
Boxing-specific: YES - elite amateur boxers | transfer status: Boxing-specific evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=15, male, simulated bout on a punch integrator (84 maximal punches over three rounds), not live competition. A null with modest n cannot rule out small effects.
PPBF implication: GOVERNANCE ANCHOR: SHADOW must never manipulate feedback content to influence an athlete, and this study indicates it would not work in elite boxers anyway. Feedback surfaced by PPBF must be truthful and traceable to the underlying observation.
Source: Halperin I, Chapman DW, Thompson KG, Abbiss C. False-performance feedback does not affect punching forces and pacing of elite boxers. J Sports Sci. 2018. (10.1080/02640414.2018.1482526 / PMID 29863966)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] External-focus instructions improved kicking performance only among LESS skilled youth competitors in a combat sport, indicating cue effectiveness may depend on skill level in young athletes.
Effect/estimate: Improved kicking performance with external versus internal focus instructions only among the less skilled participants
Population: Taekwondo competitors aged 10-15 | level: Higher and lower skilled youth | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: 10-15 years
Design: Controlled comparison with pre/post instruction | n: 40 taekwondo competitors
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - taekwondo, a striking combat sport, not boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence; boxing transfer UNTESTED
LIMITATIONS: Small n per cell; acute performance not learning; sits in tension with the Chua et al. meta-regression finding that skill level did not moderate (A1-005).
PPBF implication: The cue library must carry an athlete_level field, and PPBF should test whether cue effectiveness differs by level in its own athletes rather than assuming one cue set fits all.
Source: Siltanen S, Bottas R. Instructions for External Focus of Attention Improved Taekwondo Kicking Performance Only Among Less Skilled Youth. Percept Mot Skills. 2022;129. (10.1177/00315125221083748 / PMID 35400230)

Population: Boxers (amateur and professional); athletes generally for the consensus statement | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: All ages
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis; international consensus statement | n: See sources
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - boxing-specific for the head-trauma review; general sport for the consensus statement | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: An older systematic review of amateur boxing and chronic traumatic brain injury described the observational evidence base as limited in quality; this remains an evolving clinical field with jurisdictional differences in rules and medical oversight.
PPBF implication: HARD BOUNDARY. SHADOW performs NO concussion assessment, NO return-to-play clearance and NO contact/sparring medical clearance. Those decisions are owned by a qualified physician or licensed medical officer under the relevant governing body, with the head coach and safeguarding lead executing the resulting restriction. SHADOW's only role is to surface the restriction status a human has set (pilot.shadow_medical_administrative_status) and block conflicting training assignments.

Design: Systematic review of RCTs | n: 52 RCTs

Effect/estimate: Highest reported mean force 3427 N for straight punch; palm strike lower velocity than reverse/straight/junzuki punch
Population: Combat-sport athletes across disciplines | level: mixed elite/trained | sex: predominantly male, not fully disaggregated | age: adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (28 studies, 9 strike types) | n: 28 studies
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - pooled across boxing, karate, taekwondo, self-defence | transfer status: MIXED-COMBAT-SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Pools heterogeneous measurement devices and populations; device differences alone can shift absolute force; not a boxing-only estimate
PPBF implication: SHADOW must NOT treat any absolute punch-force number as a cross-device benchmark. Force fields require a device_id and are only comparable within device.
Source: pooled review: 'Force and velocity of impact during upper limb strikes in combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis', Sports Biomechanics (10.1080/14763141.2020.1778075)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In Olympic boxers striking an instrumented dummy head, mean punch force was 3427 (SD 811) N, hand velocity 9.14 (SD 2.06) m/s and effective punch mass 2.9 (SD 2.0) kg; force was higher in heavier weight classes primarily via higher effective mass, not higher hand speed.
Effect/estimate: Force 3427±811 N; velocity 9.14±2.06 m/s; effective mass 2.9±2.0 kg; jaw load 876±288 N; peak translational acceleration 58±13 g
Population: Olympic boxers from five weight classes | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Laboratory biomechanics, Hybrid III instrumented dummy | n: 7 boxers, 18 punches
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=7; straight punches to a dummy face only; laboratory target is not a moving opponent; wide SD on effective mass
PPBF implication: Supports coaching emphasis on whole-body linkage (effective mass) over pure hand speed. Justifies a curriculum prerequisite that weight transfer and trunk linkage precede power-punch instruction.
Source: Walilko et al., 'Biomechanics of the head for Olympic boxer punches to the face', British Journal of Sports Medicine (10.1136/bjsm.2004.014126)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] During a rear-hand straight punch to a movable head-mass target, reduction in momentum of the punching arm accounted for approximately 95% of the impact impulse, apportioned as roughly 40% upper arm, 35% forearm and 20% fist plus glove.
Effect/estimate: Arm-segment momentum reduction explained ~95% of impulse (40/35/20 split); r=0.902 between peak and impulse of impact force
Population: Expert collegiate boxers | level: trained/collegiate | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Laboratory 3D motion capture plus target-mounted accelerometer | n: 9 expert boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=9; single punch type; describes the ARM segment partition of impulse at impact and does not by itself quantify how much of that arm momentum was generated by the legs and trunk upstream
PPBF implication: Use as the evidence anchor for the 'proximal segments matter' teaching point while explicitly refusing to publish a numeric 'legs contribute X%' figure.
Source: 'Transfer of momentum from different arm segments to a light movable target during a straight punch thrown by expert boxers', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2013.843014)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The specific quantified coaching claim that a stated percentage of punch power 'comes from the legs' is not supported by a single verifiable boxing biomechanics estimate. Lower-limb kinetics do measurably contribute (dual force-plate GRF and RFD covary with punch output) and lower-body strength/power correlate with punch impact force, but no validated partition of punch force into leg/trunk/arm percentages exists in the boxing literature retrieved.
Effect/estimate: Cross punch pre-fatigue peak punch force 1475.42 N, GRF 947.54 N, RFD 3973.38 N/s (n=10); lower-body maximal and explosive strength associated with punch impact force in elite amateurs. NO validated percentage partition exists
Population: Amateur and highly trained boxers | level: amateur to elite amateur | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: Synthesis of force-plate kinetics study, strength-correlation study and review | n: 10 amateur boxers (force plate study); 28 highly trained (strength study)
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Correlational: strength-punch associations are not causal. Absolute forces are device-specific. The colloquial percentage claim is a coaching heuristic, not a measured quantity
PPBF implication: SHADOW cue library must carry 'drive from the floor' as COACHING HEURISTIC with a biomechanical rationale flag, never as a quantified claim. Block any generated text asserting a leg-contribution percentage.
Source: 'The Role of Lower Limb Kinetics in Boxing Punches and the Impact of Fatigue on Biomechanical Performance' (Bioengineering) and Beattie & Ruddock, 'The Role of Strength on Punch Impact Force in Boxing' (J Strength Cond Res) (10.3390/bioengineering12121355 ; 10.1519/JSC.0000000000004252)
