Effect/estimate: Rear hook 2624±581 N (vertically mounted force plate); cross 1475.42 N (boxing force sensor + dual force plates)
Population: Senior elite amateur boxers; amateur boxers | level: elite amateur and amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Two independent laboratory reliability/kinetics studies | n: 10 senior elite amateurs; 10 amateurs
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Different devices, mounting, target compliance and populations. The discrepancy is most parsimoniously explained by measurement method, not by a true reversal of punch mechanics
PPBF implication: Rubrics must score punch QUALITY behaviourally, not by force ranking. Any force-based punch comparison in the app must be within-athlete, within-device, within-session.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Lead-hand and rear-hand straight punches differ measurably in kinematics and kinetics in elite boxers, and bilateral asymmetry is a describable, trainable characteristic rather than an error to be eliminated.

Population: Elite male orthodox right-handed boxers | level: elite | sex: male | age: adult (height 175.25±7.81 cm, mass 66.06±2.77 kg)
Design: Laboratory 3D motion capture (Vicon) plus two Kistler force plates | n: 17 male boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Single stance (orthodox) and single handedness; no southpaw comparison; no female sample
PPBF implication: Rubrics must score lead and rear straights on SEPARATE criteria. SHADOW asymmetry flags must not treat lead/rear force difference as a defect.
Source: 'Kinematic and kinetic differences between lead and rear straight punches in elite boxers: bilateral asymmetry and training implications', BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation (10.1186/s13102-026-01738-1)

Effect/estimate: Elite 4800±227 N; intermediate 3722±133 N; novice 2381±116 N (rear hand, simulated boxing)
Population: Elite, intermediate and novice boxers | level: mixed levels | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A shared phase structure for four boxing punches (lead and rear straight and hook punches) has been defined using synchronised ground reaction force, EMG, high-speed video and striking dynamometry.
Effect/estimate: Phase definitions established for 4 punch types
Population: Experienced competitive boxers | level: experienced/competitive | sex: male (mass 95.66±21.82 kg) | age: adult (25.6±5.97 y)
Design: Mixed-method laboratory phase-definition study | n: 10 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC

Source: 'Is effective mass in combat sports punching above its weight?', Human Movement Science (10.1016/j.humov.2014.11.016)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Lower-body fatigue reduces punch force. After a 9.5-minute lower-body circuit, punch force declined significantly across all punch types by 4.26% on average, with the largest reductions in the cross and left hook; RFD responses were variable with compensatory increases in some punches.
Effect/estimate: -4.26% punch force overall (p=0.027); largest decrements in cross and left hook
Population: Amateur boxers | level: amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Within-subject pre/post fatigue laboratory study | n: 10 male amateur boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=10; artificial circuit rather than sparring-induced fatigue; single session
PPBF implication: Every technical rubric needs a fatigued-state observation context. A skill scored only when fresh is not evidence the skill survives round 3.
Source: 'The Role of Lower Limb Kinetics in Boxing Punches and the Impact of Fatigue on Biomechanical Performance', Bioengineering (10.3390/bioengineering12121355)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An independent study in 28 highly trained amateur boxers found intense intermittent lower-body and trunk exercise (rowing) altered punch force and force-time variables across jab, cross, and lead- and rear-hand hooks.
Effect/estimate: Significant (p<0.05) differences between non-fatigued and fatigued states across punch types; effect sizes reported
Population: Highly trained amateur boxers | level: highly trained amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Within-subject repeated-measures crossover | n: 28 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Rowing is not boxing-specific fatigue; direction and magnitude by punch type not extractable from abstract
PPBF implication: Supports mandatory 'late-round' rubric variants; two independent samples now show fatigue degrades punch output.
Source: 'The effect of fatiguing lower-body exercise on punch forces in highly-trained boxers', European Journal of Sport Science (10.1080/17461391.2021.1916085)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Maximal lower-body strength and explosive strength of both upper and lower body are largely associated with punch impact force in elite amateur boxers; separately, upper- and lower-body strength and power variables relate to punch force-time characteristics in highly trained amateurs.
Effect/estimate: Associations reported between CMJ / bench throw / isometric measures and punch peak force, impulse and RFD
Population: Elite and highly trained amateur boxers | level: elite/highly trained amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Narrative review plus cross-sectional correlational study | n: review; 28 highly trained male amateurs
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Correlational, not causal. Being strong is associated with punching hard; it does not follow that strength training alone raises punch force without technical work
PPBF implication: Physical-quality track (A-other) owns strength prescription. Track 2 only records that technique rubrics must not be confounded with strength: a stronger athlete can score high on force and low on technique.
Source: Beattie & Ruddock (J Strength Cond Res) and Dunn et al. (J Strength Cond Res) (10.1519/JSC.0000000000004252 ; 10.1519/JSC.0000000000003585)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Body height and arm span explained about 36% of the variance in straight punch impact power and 30-34% for other punch categories in 69 boxing practitioners.
Effect/estimate: BH and AS explained ~36% of straight punch impact power variance; 30-34% for other categories
Population: Boxing practitioners | level: mixed/recreational to trained | sex: not disaggregated in abstract | age: adult (27.0±6.1 y)
Design: Cross-sectional correlational/regression | n: 69 practitioners
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional; 'boxing practitioners' is a heterogeneous competitive level; device-specific (PowerKube)
PPBF implication: Any SHADOW punch-power metric must be interpreted alongside height/arm span or it will systematically rank taller athletes as more skilled. Flag as a fairness risk in the youth cohort where growth confounds everything.
Source: 'Influence of Anthropometric Characteristics and Muscle Performance on Punch Impact', Sports (10.3390/sports13080281)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a randomised-signal backward straight punch task, the boxing group produced the highest impact force at 3.96 +/- 0.45 times body weight, above Tao Lu (Chinese Wushu), Karate and physical-education control groups, with a moderate positive correlation between impact and muscle activation patterns.
Effect/estimate: Boxing 3.96±0.45 x body weight, highest of four groups
Population: Boxing, Tao Lu, Karate athletes and PE-student controls | level: mixed trained | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional pendulum impact plus 16-channel sEMG | n: 28 participants total
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (comparative)
LIMITATIONS: Small per-group n (28 total across 4 groups); pendulum target; body-weight normalisation is device- and protocol-specific
PPBF implication: Evidence that boxing technique is not interchangeable with other striking styles — supports refusing cross-discipline technical transfer claims in the curriculum without explicit flagging.
Source: 'Analysis of the impact force and key technique of backward straight punch in different combat sports', Scientific Reports (10.1038/s41598-025-96264-4)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Competitive boxers showed measurable long-term baropodometric asymmetry versus non-athlete controls, including greater total foot load on the right foot, greater rearfoot load on the left foot, and an inversion of the rearfoot-to-forefoot load ratio between feet.
Effect/estimate: TFL right p=0.022; RfL left p=0.011; FfL right vs left p=0.001; ratio inversion p=0.001
Population: Competitive boxers vs non-sportsmen | level: competitive | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional baropodometry | n: 20 boxers, 20 controls
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional: cannot distinguish training-induced adaptation from self-selection. No injury or performance outcome measured. Stance side not reported in the abstract
PPBF implication: Do NOT build a SHADOW rule that flags boxing stance asymmetry as pathology. Route asymmetry concerns to a qualified clinician; the app records the observation only.
Source: 'Long-term effects of asymmetrical posture in boxing assessed by baropodometry', The Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness (10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12040-7)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Fighters (boxing/muay thai) differed from non-fighter controls in lower-limb muscle responses evoked by electrical vestibular stimulation, indicating altered vestibular balance reflexes.

Population: Combat sport athletes vs controls | level: trained/competitive | sex: not disaggregated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional laboratory neurophysiology | n: not stated in abstract

Source: 'Altered Vestibular Balance Function in Combat Sport Athletes', Journal of Neurotrauma (10.1089/neu.2020.7432)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A vertically mounted force plate showed excellent within-day and good-to-excellent between-day reliability for peak punch impact force and RFD in senior elite amateur boxers (ICC 0.89-0.99, CV 3-10%), with SEM and smallest worthwhile change permitting detection of small-to-moderate changes.
Effect/estimate: ICC 0.89-0.99; CV 3-9% day 1, 4-10% day 2
Population: Senior elite amateur boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Test-retest reliability study over two days | n: 10 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=10, all senior elite male; reliability in novices and youth is unknown and likely worse
PPBF implication: If PPBF ever acquires force instrumentation, this is the reliability protocol template (two separate days, ICC + CV + SEM + SWC). Reliability MUST be re-established in PPBF's own youth/novice population.
Source: 'Test-retest reliability and sensitivity of senior elite amateur boxers maximal punch force, as quantified by a vertically mounted force plate', PLoS ONE (10.1371/journal.pone.0289791)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Intrasession and intersession variability and reliability of punching impact kinetics (impulse, peak and mean force) have been quantified separately for untrained participants and experienced boxers across four punch types using CV and ICC.
Effect/estimate: CV and ICC reported by cohort and punch type (jab, cross, lead and rear hook)
Population: Untrained participants and experienced boxers | level: untrained and experienced | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Reliability study (striking dynamometry) | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Abstract does not give the numeric split; reliability differs between cohorts, which is the substantive point
PPBF implication: Reliability is population-specific. A rubric or device validated on experienced boxers cannot be assumed reliable on PPBF beginners. This is the single most important measurement caveat for Track 2.
Source: Lenetsky et al., 'Variability and Reliability of Punching Impact Kinetics in Untrained Participants and Experienced Boxers', Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research (10.1519/JSC.0000000000002352)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Commercially available punch trackers (three consumer devices tested) showed no strong correlations with gold-standard force-plate peak force or with 3D-tracked peak and mean punch velocity during full-contact punches.
Effect/estimate: No strong correlations; MAPE and MPE reported per device variable
Population: Male participants performing rear straights, hooks and uppercuts | level: not competitive-level specified | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Criterion-validity study vs force plate and Qualisys 3D | n: 20 subjects, 6 punches each type
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Three specific 2023-era devices; firmware and models change; does not test every product on the market
PPBF implication: HARD PRODUCT RULE: SHADOW must not ingest consumer punch-tracker force/velocity as a validated performance measure. If ingested at all, tag source_quality as LOW and exclude from progression decisions. Vendor claims are low-authority.
Source: Omcirk et al., 'Validity of Commercially Available Punch Trackers', Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research (10.1519/JSC.0000000000004535)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A low-cost accelerometer/smartphone system for punch and kick velocity showed only moderate reliability (ICC(3,1) 0.746-0.786; SEM 0.488-0.921 m/s), comparable to commercial systems.
Effect/estimate: ICC(3,1) 0.746-0.786; SEM 0.488-0.921 m/s
Population: Combat athletes | level: not specified | sex: not specified | age: adult
Design: Instrument reliability study | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - punches and kicks | transfer status: MIXED-COMBAT-SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Low sampling frequency acknowledged by authors; moderate not excellent reliability
PPBF implication: A ~0.5-0.9 m/s SEM is larger than most plausible within-athlete weekly change. Any SHADOW trend line built on such a device would be mostly noise. Set a minimum-detectable-change gate before plotting trends.
Source: 'Reliability of a Low-Cost Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) to Measure Punch and Kick Velocity', Sensors (10.3390/s25020307)

Population: Mechanical/simulated strikes in a laboratory | level: NOT APPLICABLE | sex: NOT APPLICABLE | age: NOT APPLICABLE

Effect/estimate: 74% of reviewed studies had n<30; ~1/3 with insufficient description
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: mixed | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Systematic review with methodological quality appraisal | n: 39 studies
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - includes boxing among six sports | transfer status: MIXED-COMBAT-SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Review of validation quality rather than of any single test
PPBF implication: Foundational justification for the honest reliability_status='UNVALIDATED - PPBF MUST ESTABLISH' on every rubric row. The field has not solved this; PPBF must not pretend it has.
Source: 'Tests for the Assessment of Sport-Specific Performance in Olympic Combat Sports: A Systematic Review With Practical Recommendations', Frontiers in Physiology (10.3389/fphys.2018.00386)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Observational movement-rating instruments reach usable inter-rater reliability only with defined criteria and rater training: an FMS-style tool scored by generalist primary-school teachers achieved good inter-rater reliability by ICC for overall movement competence, whereas the Functional Movement Screen scored by 20 qualified physiotherapists acting as untrained raters was studied precisely because untrained-rater agreement is a known problem.
Effect/estimate: Good inter-rater reliability (ICC, two-way mixed, absolute agreement) for overall movement competence in the teacher study
Population: School teachers rating children; physiotherapists rating athletes | level: n/a (raters) | sex: mixed | age: children 10-13 y; adult raters
Design: Two inter-rater reliability studies | n: 246 children/10 teachers; 20 physiotherapists
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT/GENERAL TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Neither instrument is a boxing instrument. Transfer of the reliability figures to boxing rubrics is NOT justified; only the METHOD transfers
PPBF implication: PPBF's inter-rater study must report ICC (two-way mixed, absolute agreement) for ordinal totals and weighted kappa for individual criteria, and must test the raters who will actually score: volunteer and assistant coaches, not only the head coach.
Source: 'Inter-rater reliability of the FMS assessment tool among generalist primary-school teachers' (JSAMS) and Elias, 'The Inter-rater Reliability of the Functional Movement Screen Within an Athletic Population Using Untrained Raters' (JSCR) (10.1016/j.jsams.2025.07.008 ; 10.1519/JSC.0b013e3182a1ff1d)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Canadian Agility and Movement Skill Assessment demonstrates that a criterion-referenced observational movement assessment can be built with documented feasibility, objectivity and reliability evidence, using expert Delphi face validity followed by field testing in children.
Effect/estimate: Feasibility, objectivity and reliability evidence established
Population: Children 8-12 years | level: n/a - general population | sex: mixed | age: 8-12 years
Design: Instrument development with Delphi expert review and field reliability testing | n: Delphi panel n=19; field sample of children
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT/GENERAL TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing; not combat sport; the transferable element is the development pathway, not the content
PPBF implication: Adopt this sequence for PPBF rubrics: Delphi with coaches for content validity, then video-based inter-rater study, then live-scoring feasibility, then longitudinal sensitivity to change.
Source: 'Canadian Agility and Movement Skill Assessment (CAMSA): Validity, objectivity, and reliability evidence for children 8-12 years of age', Journal of Sport and Health Science (10.1016/j.jshs.2015.11.004)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Inter-rater reliability of an observational alignment scale was successfully established using standardised instructions and lateral video recordings of standardised poses, demonstrating a feasible protocol design for video-based scoring of postural criteria.
Effect/estimate: Inter-rater reliability of a 3-pose observational scale assessed from lateral video
Population: Adults performing standardised poses | level: NOT APPLICABLE | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional inter-rater reliability study | n: 38 individuals rated
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-DOMAIN TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Yoga poses are static; boxing skills are dynamic and interactive. Only the video-protocol design transfers
PPBF implication: PPBF should run the reliability study on VIDEO first (fixed stimulus, all raters see the same performance), then test live-scoring agreement separately. These are two different reliability questions.
Source: 'Interrater Reliability of an Observational Rating Scale and Video Analysis of Yoga Poses', Journal of Sport Rehabilitation (10.1123/jsr.2021-0056)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sport-specific classification systems can achieve excellent inter-rater reliability when built on defined test batteries: all three classifier teams agreed on overall class allocation for all athletes in a Para Va'a system, with almost perfect agreement in 14 individual tests.
Effect/estimate: 100% agreement on class allocation; excellent ICC for trunk, leg and on-water batteries; Fleiss kappa almost perfect in 14 tests
Population: Para Va'a athletes | level: international para athletes | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Inter-rater reliability study | n: 12 athletes, 3 classifier teams
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: PARA-SPORT / OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Different sport and purpose (eligibility classification not skill development); small athlete n
PPBF implication: Directly relevant to PPBF's adaptive lane: it is possible to reach near-perfect agreement on banding decisions, but only with explicit test batteries and trained rater teams. Reports Fleiss kappa for multi-rater categorical agreement — the correct statistic when >2 raters assign a band.
Source: 'Interrater Reliability of the New Sport-Specific Evidence-Based Classification System for Para Va'a', Adapted Physical Activity Quarterly (10.1123/apaq.2019-0141)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] High contextual interference (random/varied practice order) improves RETENTION in motor learning relative to low interference, confirmed in a meta-analysis of 54 studies using both three-level mixed and random-effects models.
Effect/estimate: High CI favours retention (both models concordant)
Population: Mixed human learners across laboratory and applied tasks | level: mostly non-elite/novice | sex: mixed | age: mixed, mostly adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 54 studies in meta-analysis (294 full texts screened)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Dominated by laboratory tasks and novice learners; effects in expert athletes on complex interactive skills are less established; boxing-specific CI trials were not found in this search
PPBF implication: CORE CURRICULUM PRINCIPLE. Blocked practice flatters the session scorecard; random practice produces the learning. SHADOW session logic must schedule blocked practice only in the introduction phase and switch to randomised/varied order for consolidation, and must never treat within-session improvement as evidence of learning.
Source: 'High contextual interference improves retention in motor learning: systematic review and meta-analysis', Scientific Reports (10.1038/s41598-024-65753-3)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Contextual interference produced a medium overall benefit for TRANSFER in motor learning (SMD = 0.55) favouring random practice, across 34 studies in the quantitative synthesis.
Effect/estimate: SMD = 0.55 favouring random practice for transfer
Population: Laboratory and applied settings, multiple age groups | level: mostly non-elite | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 42 studies reviewed, 34 meta-analysed
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Same laboratory-dominance caveat; moderators by age and setting were examined but boxing was not a represented sport
PPBF implication: Justifies the mandatory transfer_test_variant column in the rubric CSV: transfer is the outcome the practice schedule is chosen to produce, so it must be the outcome measured.
Source: 'The effect of contextual interference on transfer in motor learning - a systematic review and meta-analysis', Frontiers in Psychology (10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1377122)

Population: Theoretical framework for motor learners generally | level: all levels | sex: NOT APPLICABLE | age: NOT APPLICABLE
Design: Theoretical framework paper with testable hypotheses | n: NOT APPLICABLE

Source: Guadagnoli & Lee, 'Challenge point: a framework for conceptualizing the effects of various practice conditions in motor learning', Journal of Motor Behavior (10.3200/JMBR.36.2.212-224)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Practice with variations of a criterion task produced better retention than practice on the criterion task alone in a force-production task, contradicting a strict specificity-of-learning interpretation.
Effect/estimate: Variable acquisition practice produced superior retention vs constant practice
Population: Adult learners in a laboratory force-production task | level: novice | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Two laboratory experiments | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: 1990 laboratory force task; considerable distance from interactive boxing skill; specificity vs variability remains a live debate
PPBF implication: Supports building variability into every drill specification (target height, distance, angle, tempo) rather than fixed-repetition prescription.
Source: 'Specificity and variability of practice', Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport (10.1080/02701367.1990.10608671)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A robust Bayesian reanalysis of the external-focus literature, incorporating several plausible models of publication bias, found moderate to strong evidence of publication bias and concluded that the apparent external-focus superiority is substantially attributable to reporting bias.
Effect/estimate: Moderate-to-strong evidence of publication bias; external-focus advantage not robust to bias-adjusted models
Population: Same underlying literature as the prior meta-analyses | level: mostly novice | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of seven prior meta-studies | n: reanalysis of prior meta-analytic datasets
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: A reanalysis, not new primary data; bias-adjusted models involve modelling assumptions of their own
PPBF implication: MUST-RECONCILE FOR SYNTHESIS. SHADOW's cue library cannot state 'external cues are better' as settled fact. Present both cue types, record which was used and the athlete response, and let PPBF's own data accumulate. This is a genuine live scientific dispute in 2026.
Source: 'Reporting bias, not external focus: A robust Bayesian meta-analysis and systematic review of the external focus of attention literature', Psychological Bulletin (10.1037/bul0000451)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A network meta-analysis of attentional foci (external, internal, holistic, switching) on the acquisition of SPORT-SPECIFIC motor tasks in healthy adults was conducted following PRISMA and Cochrane methods, extending the focus question beyond laboratory tasks.
Effect/estimate: Network comparison of four focus types
Population: Healthy adults learning sport-specific tasks | level: mixed, mostly non-elite | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Systematic review with network meta-analysis of RCTs | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL/SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Healthy adults; heterogeneous sports; does not include boxing-specific trials in the abstract
PPBF implication: Supports offering holistic and switching cue options in the SHADOW cue library rather than a binary external/internal toggle.
Source: 'The effectiveness of different attentional foci on the acquisition of sport-specific motor skills in healthy adults: a systematic review with network meta-analysis', PeerJ (10.7717/peerj.17799)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Reduced relative frequency of augmented feedback benefits learning relative to constant feedback in classic experiments supporting the guidance hypothesis: high-frequency physical guidance produced the poorest retention and both high-frequency feedback conditions produced the least learning.
Effect/estimate: High-frequency physical guidance produced poorest retention
Population: Adult laboratory learners | level: novice | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Controlled experiment crossing feedback type and relative frequency | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: 1994 laboratory movement task; later work (see A2-041) shows the guidance effect is not universal, so this is a principle with boundary conditions rather than a law
PPBF implication: Coach-facing guidance: constant correction during pad work inflates in-drill performance and may suppress learning. SHADOW should prompt coaches to fade feedback across a skill's introduction-to-consolidation arc.
Source: 'Effects of physical guidance and knowledge of results on motor learning: support for the guidance hypothesis', Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport (10.1080/02701367.1994.10607635)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The reduced-feedback principle has documented exceptions: augmented kinematic feedback in rifle shooting produced group differences only at delayed no-feedback retention tests rather than during acquisition, and separate work reports conditions under which continuous feedback benefits learning of a novel coordination pattern.
Effect/estimate: No between-group differences during acquisition; differences emerged at retention
Population: Rifle shooters; adults learning novel coordination patterns | level: novice to intermediate | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: RCT with 2- and 10-day retention tests (n=40, 480 shots); plus separate experimental work on continuous auditory feedback | n: 40 participants (shooting study)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT / GENERAL TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Different tasks; the exceptions do not overturn the guidance hypothesis but bound it
PPBF implication: Reinforces the central Track 2 message: acquisition-phase performance is a poor predictor of learning. The rifle study is the cleanest demonstration that groups can look identical during practice and differ at retention.
Source: 'The effects of augmented kinematic feedback on motor skill learning in rifle shooting' (J Sports Sci) and 'More Feedback Is Better than Less: Learning a Novel Upper Limb Joint Coordination Pattern with Augmented Auditory Feedback' (Front Neurosci) (10.1080/0264041031000101944 ; PMID 27375414)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Meta-analysis of 29 studies (1,147 participants) found self-controlled feedback gave no significant advantage during acquisition but facilitated motor skill learning in both retention and transfer phases compared with passively received and yoked feedback.
Effect/estimate: Null in acquisition; positive in retention and transfer
Population: Mixed learners | level: mostly novice | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 29 studies, 1,147 participants
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Effects on autonomy-support are debated: a separate meta-analysis reported reduced feedback frequency and autonomy support had trivial effects on a golf putting task, and a preregistered study found choice failed to enhance retention
PPBF implication: Athlete-requested feedback ('ask for the replay') is a low-cost, evidence-supported feature. Note it is exactly the pattern where acquisition and learning diverge — build it and measure it at retention.
Source: 'Self-Controlled Feedback and Behavioral Outcomes in Motor Skill Learning: A Meta-Analysis', Behavioral Sciences (10.3390/bs15091291)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] Autonomy-support effects are not robust: a study of a golf putting task found autonomy support and reduced feedback frequency had trivial effects on learning and performance, and a preregistered manipulation found increased perceptions of autonomy through choice failed to enhance motor skill retention.
Effect/estimate: Trivial effects; failure to replicate retention benefit of choice
Population: Adult learners, golf putting and cup-stacking | level: novice | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Controlled experiments including one preregistered study | n: not stated in abstracts
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Task-specific; does not negate the meta-analytic retention finding but bounds it
PPBF implication: Do not over-engineer autonomy features on the assumption they are proven. Log usage and outcome; treat as a hypothesis PPBF can test.
Source: 'Autonomy support and reduced feedback frequency have trivial effects on learning and performance of a golf putting task' (Human Movement Science) and 'Increased perceptions of autonomy through choice fail to enhance motor skill retention' (J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform) (10.1016/j.humov.2020.102592 ; 10.1037/xhp0000992)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Self-controlled video feedback facilitated the learning of TACTICAL skills in tennis in intermediately skilled players, and self-control over combined video feedback and expert modelling facilitated motor learning of a golf chip shot with retention and transfer tests administered.
Effect/estimate: Self-controlled group outperformed yoked group on tactical performance measured by a custom tool
Population: Intermediate tennis players; adult golf learners | level: intermediate and novice | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Two controlled studies with yoked control groups | n: 23 tennis players; golf study n not in abstract
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Tennis and golf, not boxing; small samples; coach-delivered attentional cueing was bundled with the video in the tennis study
PPBF implication: Supports SHADOW's film-study lane for TACTICAL learning specifically, with athlete-initiated replay. Note the tennis effect was on tactical, not technical, performance.
Source: 'Self-Controlled Video Feedback Facilitates the Learning of Tactical Skills in Tennis' (RQES) and 'Self-control over combined video feedback and modeling facilitates motor learning' (Human Movement Science) (10.1080/02701367.2023.2275801 ; 10.1016/j.humov.2016.01.014)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In an early controlled trial, video-feedback training of the tennis service was compared against traditional training and a no-training control over five weeks in players with at least two years' experience, establishing the design template for sport video-feedback trials.
Effect/estimate: Three-arm comparison over 5 weeks, twice weekly, 40 min sessions
Population: Intermediate tennis players | level: intermediate | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Randomised three-group training study | n: 66 participants (22 per group)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: 1989 study; effect direction not extractable from the abstract text retrieved
PPBF implication: Design template only: three arms, matched contact time, a genuine no-intervention control.
Source: 'The effect of video-feedback on the learning of the tennis service by intermediate players', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640418908729833)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A six-week tennis serving intervention manipulating task representativeness (serve only vs serve-return vs serve+3) directly tested whether higher representativeness improves transfer of serving skill, using a validated representative practice assessment tool to classify task representativeness.
Effect/estimate: 56 serves twice weekly for 6 weeks across three representativeness levels
Population: Junior tennis players (15.4 +/- 1.9 y) | level: junior/development | sex: mixed | age: adolescent
Design: Six-week three-group intervention with pre/post skill testing | n: 33 participants
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Tennis serve is self-paced; boxing skills are opposed and reactive, arguably making representativeness MORE important, but that is inference
PPBF implication: The core justification for the PPBF constrained-sparring ladder: skills practised without an opponent's information are being practised in a non-representative environment and may not transfer.
Source: 'Enhancing skill transfer in tennis using representative learning design', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2019.1647739)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A consensus-based tool for coaches to rapidly assess the representativeness of practice tasks was developed via a four-round Delphi process with 10 academic and 13 coaching experts, reaching consensus on seven items each with two sub-questions.
Effect/estimate: Seven-item consensus tool
Population: Tennis coaches and academics | level: NOT APPLICABLE | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Delphi consensus tool development | n: 23 experts (10 academic, 13 coaching)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Tennis-specific item wording; requires re-specification for boxing
PPBF implication: DIRECTLY ACTIONABLE: PPBF should build a boxing Representative Practice Assessment Tool by the same Delphi method, so SHADOW can score every drill for representativeness and surface 'this route is all non-representative practice' to the coach.
Source: 'Helping coaches apply the principles of representative learning design: validation of a tennis specific practice assessment tool', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2017.1374684)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Match simulation practice may not represent competitive match play: analysis in professional Australian football found constraint interactions and their frequencies in training tasks differed from competition, and a separate study concluded match simulations did not reproduce competitive demands.
Effect/estimate: Differences in pressure and time-in-possession constraint interactions between competition, match simulations and small-sided games
Population: Elite Australian football players | level: elite | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Observational comparison of training vs competition constraint profiles | n: elite squad data
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Team invasion sport; boxing has a different constraint structure
PPBF implication: Even coaches who believe they are simulating competition frequently are not. SHADOW should compare the constraint profile of assigned drills against the recorded profile of sparring/competition and flag the gap.
Source: 'Applications of a working framework for the measurement of representative learning design in Australian football' (PLoS ONE) and 'Match simulation practice may not represent competitive match play in professional Australian football' (J Sports Sci) (10.1371/journal.pone.0242336 ; 10.1080/02640414.2021.1993622)

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Reviews of perceptual-cognitive skill training conclude that retention and transfer to the field is the outcome that matters and remains the key unresolved design problem, and a classification framework has been proposed to predict which modified perceptual training tasks will transfer.
Effect/estimate: No pooled effect; both papers frame transfer as the open question
Population: Athletes across sports | level: mixed | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Two narrative/framework reviews | n: review
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Opinion/framework pieces rather than meta-analyses
PPBF implication: Treat any generic 'sports vision' or reaction-light product as unproven for boxing transfer. Vendor claims are low-authority under the source-priority rule.
Source: 'Perceptual-cognitive skill training and its transfer to expert performance in the field: future research directions' (Eur J Sport Sci) and 'Modified perceptual training in sport: A new classification framework' (JSAMS) (10.1080/17461391.2014.957727 ; 10.1016/j.jsams.2018.01.011)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Video/point-light temporal-occlusion anticipation training COMBINED with motor practice of the observed movement pattern improved anticipation in emerging expert cricket batsmen relative to a control group, with transfer tests to different bowlers.
Effect/estimate: Intervention group improved anticipation to significantly above chance; control did not
Population: Emerging expert cricket batsmen from a state squad | level: sub-elite/emerging expert | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult/late adolescent
Design: Randomised controlled intervention with transfer tests | n: 12 batsmen (6 per group)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: n=12; striking sport but ball-based; the coupling of perception with action is the transferable design principle
PPBF implication: If PPBF builds anticipation training, it must keep perception coupled to a movement response (slip, step, parry) rather than a button press or a screen tap.
Source: 'Visual-perceptual training with motor practice of the observed movement pattern improves anticipation in emerging expert cricket batsmen', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2019.1621510)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 12-session implicit perceptual-motor training programme improved decision-making accuracy in highly skilled junior female karate fighters on a video-based test, where a matched motor-training placebo group did not.
Effect/estimate: Only the implicit perceptual-motor group improved video-based decision accuracy
Population: Highly skilled junior female karate fighters (mean age 15.7 y) | level: highly skilled junior | sex: female | age: adolescent
Design: Controlled intervention with placebo group and gaze tracking | n: 18 participants (6 per group)
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - karate, a striking combat sport | transfer status: OTHER-COMBAT-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Very small groups (n=6); improvement demonstrated on a video-based test with on-mat testing also conducted; single squad
PPBF implication: Closest available evidence that decision training works in a striking combat sport, and it is thin (n=18, karate, female juniors). Any PPBF decision-training claim must carry that caveat explicitly.
Source: 'Effect of Implicit Perceptual-Motor Training on Decision-Making Skills and Underpinning Gaze Behavior in Combat Athletes', Perceptual and Motor Skills (10.1177/0031512516656816)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Expert karate fighters were more accurate and faster than less-skilled counterparts at blocking and counterattacking, and picked up a repeating attack pattern after the fifth repetition where novices did not.
Effect/estimate: Experts detected the repeating pattern by the fifth repetition; novices did not
Population: Expert and novice karate fighters | level: expert vs novice | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: In situ decision-making experiment with manipulated attack probability | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - karate | transfer status: OTHER-COMBAT-SPORT TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Karate rules and distances differ from boxing; cross-sectional expert-novice design cannot show trainability
PPBF implication: Grounds the 'pattern reading' competency in the tactical curriculum as an observable, testable behaviour: does the athlete adjust after a repeated opponent action?
Source: 'Do karate fighters use situational probability information to improve decision-making performance during on-mat tasks?', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2015.1122824)

Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - karate performers, non-boxing stimuli | transfer status: OTHER-COMBAT-SPORT TRANSFER

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a boxing-specific Simon-like task, expert boxers' incidental responses resembled counterattacks, beginner boxers' resembled defensive responses, and non-athletes showed no punch-direction influence — indicating experience shapes automatic response tendencies to punch stimuli.
Effect/estimate: Distinct response patterns by expertise level despite no instruction to attend to punch direction
Population: Expert boxers, beginner boxers, non-boxers | level: expert, beginner, none | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional cognitive experiment | n: three groups, n not in abstract
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory key-press task, not ring behaviour; cross-sectional
PPBF implication: Rare boxing-specific perceptual evidence, and it maps to a curriculum ordering hypothesis: defensive response tendencies appear before counter tendencies. Testable in PPBF's own cohort.
Source: 'What boxing-related stimuli reveal about response behaviour', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2014.977939)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a boxing-specific spatial attention task mimicking feint-punch combinations, boxers and non-boxers showed significantly longer reaction times to a punch thrown on the same side as a preceding cue, consistent with inhibition-of-return effects operating on feint-punch timing.
Effect/estimate: Longer RT to same-side punch following a cue
Population: Boxers and non-boxers | level: trained boxers vs untrained | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional experimental spatial-attention task | n: 20 boxers, 20 non-boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Screen-based task; cue-target intervals fixed by the experiment, not by a live opponent
PPBF implication: Gives feint instruction a mechanistic rationale (attentional cueing and its time course) rather than pure tradition, while stopping well short of prescribing feint timings in seconds.
Source: 'Timing a fake punch: Inhibitory effects in a boxing-specific spatial attention task', Human Movement Science (10.1016/j.humov.2023.103092)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Elite male amateur boxing (3x3 min) requires maintaining approximately 1.4 actions per second, comprising about 20 punches, 2.5 defensive movements and 47 vertical hip movements per minute across three rounds of about 200 s.
Effect/estimate: ~1.4 actions/s; ~20 punches, ~2.5 defensive movements, ~47 vertical hip movements per minute
Population: Elite male amateur boxers in Olympic semifinal and final bouts | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult (25.1±3.6 y)
Design: Notational analysis of competition video | n: 29 bouts, 39 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Pre-2013-rules Olympic footage; elite ceiling values, not youth or novice targets
PPBF implication: Defines the observable action vocabulary SHADOW should count (punches, defensive movements, vertical hip movements). These are ELITE reference values, never youth targets.
Source: 'The activity profile of elite male amateur boxing', International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance (10.1123/ijspp.2013-0474)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite male amateur bouts, winners had higher total punches landed and a lower thrown-to-landed ratio than losers in round 3, higher rear-hand hook landed in rounds 2 and 3, and used fewer defensive movements; the authors note technical discrimination between winners and losers is limited.
Effect/estimate: Punches landed p=0.041; thrown:landed ratio p=0.027; rear-hand hook landed p=0.038 (R2) and p=0.016 (R3); defensive movements p=0.036
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Notational analysis of competition video | n: 29 bouts, 39 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Judging is subjective, so 'winning' is partly a judging artefact (see A2-063). Authors explicitly caution the discrimination is limited. Association, not causation: throwing more accurate punches may reflect winning rather than cause it
PPBF implication: Accuracy (landed/thrown) is the most defensible single performance ratio SHADOW can track. Do not build a 'win probability' model on these coefficients.
Source: 'The activity profile of elite male amateur boxing', IJSPP (10.1123/ijspp.2013-0474)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In novice-level amateur bouts (3x2 min), winners landed 18 +/- 11 more punches than losers, applying more lead-hand punches in round 1 (34.2 +/- 10.9 vs 26.5 +/- 9.4), more total punches to the head (121.3 +/- 10.2 vs 96.0 +/- 9.8), more block-and-counterpunch combinations across all rounds (2.8 +/- 1.1 vs 0.1 +/- 0.2) and more punching combinations in rounds 1 and 3 (44.3 +/- 6.4 vs 28.8 +/- 6.7).
Effect/estimate: Block-and-counter combinations 2.8±1.1 vs 0.1±0.2 (all p<0.05); peak post-bout [La] 11.8±1.6 mmol/L in 16 boxers
Population: Novice-level male amateur boxers | level: novice | sex: male | age: 19.3±1.4 y
Design: Notational analysis with post-bout blood lactate | n: 32 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (NOVICE)
LIMITATIONS: Observational and correlational; small n; single competition context; 3x2 min format
PPBF implication: MOST IMPORTANT CURRICULUM FINDING FOR NOVICES. Lead-hand volume and the block-counter unit distinguish novice winners; the 2.8 vs 0.1 gap for block-and-counter is the largest behavioural separation in the retrieved literature. Prioritise lead hand and block-counter in the novice route — flagged as association, not proof of causation.
Source: 'Amateur boxing: activity profile of winners and losers', International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance (10.1123/ijspp.8.1.84)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Notational analysis of 26 elite male competitors under the Ten Point Must System found winners punched more accurately, with behavioural measures including guard-drop time, movement style, clinch time and interaction time recorded alongside technical measures.
Effect/estimate: Winners punched more accurately; behavioural and technical measures compared
Population: Elite male competitors at a national championship | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Notational analysis with self-reported effort and fatigue | n: 26 competitors
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Subjective judging system defines the outcome; self-report used for effort and fatigue
PPBF implication: GUARD-DROP TIME is a directly observable, countable variable with a competition-behaviour basis. Adopt it as a rubric criterion for the guard skill instead of the aesthetic 'keeps hands up'.
Source: 'Human behaviours associated with dominance in elite amateur boxing bouts: A comparison of winners and losers under the Ten Point Must-System', PLoS ONE (10.1371/journal.pone.0188675)

Effect/estimate: ~1.6 actions/s; ~16 punches/min; ~3.3 defensive movements/min; ~63 vertical hip movements/min
Population: Elite female amateur boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: female | age: adult (26.4±4.6 y)
Design: Notational analysis of competition video | n: 18 bouts
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (FEMALE)

Source: 'Performance Analysis of Elite Female Amateur Boxers and Comparison With Their Male Counterparts', IJSPP (10.1123/ijspp.2014-0133)

Effect/estimate: OER and DER computed per boxer
Population: Elite female boxers at world championship finals | level: elite | sex: female | age: adult
Design: Notational analysis with a defined offensive-defensive interaction cycle framework | n: 12 bouts, 2,779 actions coded
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (FEMALE, CURRENT FORMAT)
LIMITATIONS: Finals only (a selected, high-quality subsample); 12 bouts; single championship

Source: 'Notational Analysis of the Final Matches of the 2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships', Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology (10.3390/jfmk10030350)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Boxing outcomes are partly a product of subjective officiating: bouts ending in points decisions had a significantly higher proportion of home wins than those decided by knockout in European championship boxing, and an experimental study found a scoring discrepancy attributable to referees' visual access to one ring zone.
Effect/estimate: Higher home-win proportion for points decisions vs knockouts; significant Zone D scoring discrepancy under traditional ropes (F(5,90)=2.442, p=.040)
Population: European championship boxing; certified international referees | level: elite/professional and officials | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Archival analysis of bout outcomes; counterbalanced experimental officiating study | n: archival dataset; 25 certified officials
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Home advantage has multiple causes; the officiating study is small and single-context
PPBF implication: CRITICAL FOR THE DATA MODEL: bout result is a NOISY, partly biased label. SHADOW must never train a skill model on win/loss as ground truth. Use coded technical behaviour as the outcome, with result recorded separately as context.
Source: 'Do judges enhance home advantage in European championship boxing?' (J Sports Sci) and 'Ergonomic Solutions for Referee Mistakes: A Visual Assessment of the Environment in Boxing Competitions' (Percept Mot Skills) (10.1080/02640410400021583 ; 10.1177/00315125251379145)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 2013 amateur rules change measurably altered boxing technique: post-2013 elite bouts showed fewer total punches thrown, fewer rear-hand punches and rear-hand hooks, fewer punches landed, fewer uppercuts and fewer body punches, with more ring movement and more defensive movements.
Effect/estimate: All listed technique reductions p<0.05; movement and defensive movement increases p<0.004
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: adult (24.3±3.2 y)
Design: Comparative notational analysis pre- vs post-rule change | n: 29 Olympic + 50 World Championship bouts, 99 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Observational comparison across different competitions and eras; headguard removal and scoring changes are confounded
PPBF implication: GOVERNANCE-CRITICAL: technical norms are rule-dependent and therefore have expiry dates. Every SHADOW technical reference value must carry the ruleset and year it was derived under, and be re-validated when rules change.
Source: 'Comparison of amateur boxing before and after the 2013 rules change and the impact on boxers' safety', British Journal of Sports Medicine (10.1136/bjsports-2017-097667)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Reaction time of the rear straight lengthened during sparring load in the precompetition period after the third round (to 390 ms) compared with the competition period (310 ms), and lead-straight reaction time lengthened between rounds 1 and 3 during precompetition with no such change during the competition period.
Effect/estimate: Rear straight RT 390 ms (precompetition R3) vs 310 ms (competition period); lead straight lengthened R1 to R3 in precompetition (p<=0.05)
Population: National-level boxers | level: national level | sex: male | age: 20.3±2.7 y
Design: Repeated-measures sparring study across two training periods | n: 7 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=7; training-period comparison is confounded with training state, taper and motivation
PPBF implication: Supports round-3 skill degradation as a real, measurable phenomenon and justifies the fatigued-state rubric variant. n=7 means these millisecond values are illustrative, not normative.
Source: 'Effects of Sparring Load on Reaction Speed and Punch Force During the Precompetition and Competition Periods in Boxing', Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research (10.1519/JSC.0000000000001885)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sports visual abilities measured on a commercial sensory station correlated with in-competition punching accuracy in 26 highly trained male amateur boxers, with a parallel study conducted in female amateur boxers.
Effect/estimate: Correlations between visual ability measures and competition punch accuracy
Population: Highly trained amateur boxers | level: highly trained amateur | sex: male study and separate female study | age: adult
Design: Cross-sectional correlation and regression | n: 26 male boxers (plus separate female cohort)
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional and correlational; commercial test battery; does not show visual training improves boxing
PPBF implication: Correlation is not a training rationale. Do NOT let SHADOW recommend commercial vision training on the basis of these associations; log as a research backlog item.

Effect/estimate: Effects of mental fatigue on RT and accuracy across technique types and occlusion windows
Population: Expert and novice boxers | level: expert and novice | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Mixed-design experimental study with induced mental fatigue | n: 20 expert boxers plus novice group
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory Stroop-induced fatigue rather than training- or school-induced fatigue; video-based recognition task
PPBF implication: Justifies capturing a mental-state/mental-fatigue context field on every technical assessment. A youth athlete assessed after a school exam day is not being assessed on skill alone.
Source: 'Mental Fatigue Impairs Temporal Perceptual Prediction: A Study on Boxing Performance Across Skill Levels', Sports (10.3390/sports13050154)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A short-term structured boxing programme in novice female university students produced significant improvements in stance, straight punches, hooks and uppercuts from baseline to four weeks, assessed under both static and dynamic conditions with a two-month follow-up retention assessment.
Effect/estimate: Significant improvement in all technical skills at 4 weeks (T2 vs T1); two-month follow-up (T3) conducted
Population: Novice female university students | level: novice | sex: female | age: university-age adults
Design: Pre/post/follow-up intervention study with a customised scoring system | n: not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (NOVICE, FEMALE)
LIMITATIONS: Custom scoring system with no reported reliability or validity evidence; no control group in the abstract; single cohort
PPBF implication: The closest existing analogue to what PPBF is building, and it illustrates the field's core weakness: a customised technical scoring system used without published reliability. PPBF must not repeat that. Also a rare study with a genuine delayed retention timepoint — copy that design.
Source: 'Short-Term Effects of a Structured Boxing Program on Technical Skill Acquisition in Novice Female Students', Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology (10.3390/jfmk11010026)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The hand is the most frequently injured body location in elite amateur boxing: five-year prospective surveillance of the Great Britain squad found more injuries affected the hand than any other body location.
Effect/estimate: Hand was the most frequently injured location
Population: Great Britain elite amateur boxing squad | level: elite amateur | sex: mixed (squad) | age: adult
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance, 2005-2009 | n: 66 boxers over 5 years
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Single national squad; elite training volumes; medically diagnosed injuries only
PPBF implication: DIRECT CURRICULUM CONSEQUENCE: fist formation, wrist alignment and hand-wrapping competency must be a HARD PREREQUISITE gate before any full-power bag work, not a footnote. This is the strongest evidence-based prerequisite in the entire Track 2 graph.
Source: 'Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome', British Journal of Sports Medicine (10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Pooled competition injury incidence in amateur boxing was estimated at 54.7 (95% CI 33.8-88.4) injuries per 1000 athlete-exposures in a meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies, with separate per-minute and training-hour estimates modelled.
Effect/estimate: Competition IIR 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4)
Population: Amateur boxers in competition and training | level: amateur | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Wide confidence interval; heterogeneous injury definitions across included studies despite IOC consensus guidance
PPBF implication: Baseline for PPBF's own surveillance. PPBF must record exposure (athlete-exposures and training hours), not just injury counts, or its rates will be uninterpretable.
Source: 'Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis', Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are highly effective at reducing facial lacerations in amateur boxers and appropriate for avoiding auricular injury, but should not be relied upon to reduce concussion or other traumatic brain injury risk.
Effect/estimate: Effective for lacerations and auricular injury; not established for concussion reduction
Population: Combat sport athletes | level: all levels | sex: all | age: all
Design: Position statement of a professional physician body | n: expert panel
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC (and other striking sports)
LIMITATIONS: Position statement synthesising limited evidence; a related Current Opinion argues insufficient evidence supports headguard BANS, so the policy debate remains live
PPBF implication: SHADOW must never present headgear as concussion protection in any coach, athlete or parent-facing text. Equipment gating logic should state the actual protective claim (lacerations, ears) and nothing more.
Source: 'Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians', The Physician and Sportsmedicine (10.1080/00913847.2023.2242415)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Laboratory punch-machine and drop testing show headguards alter head impact dynamics but with performance varying by test condition: peak contact forces of 1.9-5.9 kN were recorded across impact speeds of 4.1-8.3 m/s, with differences between an AIBA-approved headguard and a bare headform depending on impact location.
Effect/estimate: Peak contact forces 1.9-5.9 kN; performance varied by test condition and location
Population: Instrumented Hybrid III headform and ISO rigid headform | level: n/a laboratory | sex: NOT APPLICABLE | age: NOT APPLICABLE
Design: Laboratory impact testing | n: 7 headguard models tested across studies
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC EQUIPMENT
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory headforms are not human heads; linear impactor and drop tests do not reproduce rotational injury mechanisms of real punches
PPBF implication: Reinforces A2-073: bench performance under linear impact does not license a concussion-protection claim to parents.
Source: 'Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests' and 'The impact performance of headguards for combat sports', British Journal of Sports Medicine (10.1136/bjsports-2015-095094 ; 10.1136/bjsports-2015-095093)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The evidence base for the IBA/AIBA headguard ban is contested: a Current Opinion argues headguards are effective against cuts and lacerations and that there is insufficient evidence supporting headguard bans, while a systematic review of head trauma in boxing assessed headguard efficiency alongside concussion ratios.
Effect/estimate: Insufficient evidence characterised as supporting the ban; effectiveness against cuts affirmed
Population: Amateur boxers | level: amateur/elite amateur | sex: mixed | age: adult and youth
Design: Current Opinion article plus systematic reviews | n: reviews
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Policy debate with governing-body and scientific positions not aligned; jurisdictional variation

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Head impacts occur routinely in boxing sparring at measurable rates: an average of 27.63 +/- 17.87 impacts above a 9.6 g threshold per boxer were recorded across two 2-minute sparring rounds in collegiate boxers, with average peak linear acceleration 23.48 +/- 15.20 g.
Effect/estimate: 27.63±17.87 impacts >9.6 g per boxer in two 2-min rounds; peak linear acceleration 23.48±15.20 g; peak rotational 1761.40±1064.34 rad/s^2
Population: Intercollegiate male boxers | level: collegiate amateur | sex: male | age: adult
Design: Instrumented headgear measurement with pre/post neurocognitive testing | n: 27 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Instrumented headgear sensors have known accuracy limitations (see A2-077); single short sparring exposure; 'small but measurable' neurocognitive changes reported
PPBF implication: Head-impact exposure is the reason the curriculum's sparring ladder exists. Every rung that can be taught without head contact should be, and the gating layer must make that the default.
Source: 'Quantifying head impacts and neurocognitive performance in collegiate boxers', Journal of Sports Sciences (10.1080/02640414.2021.2001175)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Wearable head-impact sensors substantially over- or under-count events in boxing: against 5,168 video-verified events across 115 sparring rounds, an instrumented mouthguard recorded 695 events while a skin patch recorded 1,579 and a headgear patch 1,690; a companion study found a large proportion of kinematic traces were of questionable or low quality.
Effect/estimate: Event counts 695 / 1,579 / 1,690 against 5,168 video-verified contacts; trace quality categorised as high, questionable or low
Population: Boxers in sparring | level: competitive | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Video-referenced sensor validation with sensitivity, specificity and PPV | n: 7 boxers, 115 rounds, 5,168 video-identified events
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Seven boxers; specific sensor models and firmware; video identification of contacts is itself imperfect
PPBF implication: HARD PRODUCT RULE: SHADOW must not ingest wearable head-impact counts as a safety signal or exposure metric. A device disagreeing with video by a factor of two cannot underwrite a gating decision. Coach-observed and video-verified contact counts are the only defensible input.
Source: 'Capturing Head Impacts in Boxing: A Video-Based Comparison of Three Wearable Sensors' and 'Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing', Annals of Biomedical Engineering (10.1007/s10439-023-03369-w ; 10.1007/s10439-024-03647-1)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] The acute dose-response relationship between head impact exposure and concussion remains unresolved; an exploratory cohort in seven competitive boxers tracked SCAT5 symptom-scale changes before, immediately after and 48 h after sparring against instrumented-mouthguard impact data.
Effect/estimate: Exploratory; the authors state the acute dose-response relationship remains elusive
Population: Competitive boxers | level: competitive | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adult
Design: Exploratory observational cohort | n: 7 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: n=7; exploratory; sensor limitations per A2-077
PPBF implication: There is NO validated sparring-volume threshold. Any PPBF sparring dose limit is a PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER requiring validation, and the decision owner is a qualified coach plus medical oversight, never SHADOW.
Source: 'Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring', Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport (10.1016/j.jsams.2026.01.018)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Concussion recognition, management and return-to-play decisions are governed by the 6th International Consensus Statement on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam 2022), with paediatric-specific recommendations issued separately; SCAT tools show best diagnostic discrimination within the first 72 hours and subacute evaluation beyond 72 hours requires a multimodal assessment.
Effect/estimate: SCAT best diagnostic discrimination within 72 h post-injury; multimodal tool required subacutely
Population: Athletes including children (5-12) and adolescents (13-18) | level: all levels | sex: all | age: 5 years to adult
Design: International consensus statement informed by 10 systematic reviews | n: expert consensus over 3.5 years
Boxing-specific: NO - cross-sport, applies to boxing | transfer status: CROSS-SPORT CONSENSUS
LIMITATIONS: Consensus statements reflect expert synthesis and are periodically superseded
PPBF implication: HARD BOUNDARY: SHADOW performs NO concussion assessment, no symptom interpretation and no RTP decision. It routes to a qualified healthcare professional and records that a human decision is pending. Decision owner: licensed medical provider; PPBF role: escalate and document.
Source: 'Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022' (BJSM) and 'Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023' (Pediatrics) (10.1136/bjsports-2023-106898 ; 10.1542/peds.2023-063489)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of observational studies concluded on the risk of chronic traumatic brain injury from amateur boxing across 36 papers with extractable data, and a subsequent systematic review examined later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts.
Effect/estimate: Chronic traumatic brain injury defined by clinical neurological examination, psychometric testing, neuroimaging and EEG abnormality
Population: Amateur boxers; athletes with RHI exposure across sports | level: amateur and mixed | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Systematic reviews of observational studies | n: 36 papers (boxing review)
Boxing-specific: PARTIAL - one boxing-specific, one cross-sport | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC and CROSS-SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Observational study designs with substantial methodological heterogeneity and selection bias; causal inference is limited
PPBF implication: The ethical basis for PPBF's no-contact-first curriculum design and for maximising the proportion of technical development achievable without head contact. This is a programme-design consequence, not a medical claim.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Biological maturation, not chronological age, drives major physiological and structural change through childhood and adolescence, and selection in youth sport follows a maturity-related gradient; several non-invasive methods for estimating maturity status and timing exist but require further validation in athletes.
Effect/estimate: Methods described: skeletal age, secondary sex characteristics, age at peak height velocity, percentage of predicted near-adult height, predicted maturity offset
Population: Youth athletes | level: youth/development | sex: male and female | age: childhood through adolescence
Design: Authoritative reviews | n: reviews
Boxing-specific: NO - cross-sport | transfer status: CROSS-SPORT YOUTH DEVELOPMENT
LIMITATIONS: Maturity-estimation methods carry their own error and the anthropometric methods are explicitly flagged as needing further athlete validation
PPBF implication: Rubric age_band fields must be treated as CONTEXT, not as gates. Progression must key on demonstrated competency plus safety clearance, never on birthday alone. Note: maturity assessment involving secondary sex characteristics is a safeguarding-sensitive procedure PPBF should NOT perform.
Source: Malina et al., 'Biological maturation of youth athletes: assessment and implications' (BJSM) and 'Chronological age vs. biological maturation: implications for exercise programming in youth' (JSCR) (10.1136/bjsports-2015-094623 ; 10.1519/JSC.0000000000000391)

Population: English amateur boxers aged 10 to under 16 | level: development/novice youth | sex: male and female | age: 10 to under 16 years
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook | n: NOT APPLICABLE

Source: England Boxing Technical and Competition Rules; England Boxing Rule Book (Skills Bouts annex) (no DOI - governing body document)

Population: Fencers and elite interactive individual sport athletes | level: elite | sex: male and female | age: adult

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Errorless learning — constraining early practice to promote success and minimise errors — has an active evidence base including a registered systematic review and meta-analysis across the lifespan, and interacts with practice-schedule manipulations in ways tested directly against contextual interference in a dart-throwing paradigm.
Effect/estimate: Combined effects of random/blocked practice with errorless/errorful conditions examined at retention
Population: Mixed learners including children with neurodevelopmental conditions | level: novice | sex: mixed | age: children to adults
Design: Systematic review/meta-analysis (registered) plus controlled experiment | n: 120 participants across 8 groups in the CI/errorless experiment
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Errorless learning and high contextual interference pull in partly opposite directions, so their combination is not settled; the meta-analysis was identified at protocol/publication stage in this search
PPBF implication: Directly relevant to PPBF's adaptive and beginner lanes, where early success matters for retention in the programme (not just skill retention). Reconcile with the CI finding: errorless-first for the introduction phase, high CI for consolidation, is a coherent but UNTESTED sequencing hypothesis.
Source: 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of errorless motor learning on movement outcomes' (Front Psychol) and 'An Examination of the Contextual Interference Effect and the Errorless Learning Model during Motor Learning' (J Motor Behav) (10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1722743 ; 10.1080/00222895.2022.2072265)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Multiple independent lines of evidence show that within-practice performance and durable learning dissociate: high contextual interference depresses acquisition while improving retention and transfer; self-controlled feedback shows no acquisition advantage but retention and transfer benefits; and augmented kinematic feedback produced no group differences during acquisition with differences emerging only at delayed retention tests.
Effect/estimate: Consistent direction across independent literatures: acquisition performance is a biased estimator of learning
Population: Motor learners across laboratory and sport settings | level: novice to intermediate | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Convergence of three meta-analyses and one RCT with delayed retention testing | n: 54 studies (CI retention); 34 studies (CI transfer); 29 studies (self-controlled); 40 participants (shooting RCT)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: GENERAL MOTOR LEARNING TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Boxing-specific confirmation is absent; the principle is imported
PPBF implication: THE governing principle of the A2 deliverable. Every rubric carries a retention_test_variant and a transfer_test_variant because a score taken inside the teaching drill measures acquisition, and acquisition is a biased proxy for learning. SHADOW must not mark a skill 'achieved' on same-session evidence.
Source: Scientific Reports PMID 38987617; Frontiers in Psychology PMID 39205981; Behavioral Sciences PMID 41009321; Journal of Sports Sciences PMID 14620030 (10.1038/s41598-024-65753-3 ; 10.3389/fpsyg.2024.1377122 ; 10.3390/bs15091291 ; 10.1080/0264041031000101944)

Design: government regulation | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - Ontario, Canada
LIMITATIONS: Ontario-specific; other jurisdictions grade differently.
PPBF implication: Round duration is an age-graded safety control in real regulation. PPBF session templates for youth and masters should mirror the same downward grading.
Source: Government of Ontario, Amateur Combative Sport Rules - Boxing, Parts IV and V (n/a)

PPBF implication: Hard block in the app. A stoppage sets an end-dated restriction that no coach and no SHADOW output can shorten.

Effect/estimate: Sparring prohibition co-extensive with the competition suspension
Population: professional boxers licensed in Louisiana | level: professional | sex: all | age: 18+
Design: state administrative code | n: n/a

Source: Louisiana Administrative Code Title 46, Part XI, Section 126, Medical Suspensions (n/a)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Elite male amateur boxing at 3x3-min requires sustaining an activity rate of approximately 1.4 actions per second, comprising about 20 punches, 2.5 defensive movements and 47 vertical hip movements per minute, across three rounds of about 200 s.
Effect/estimate: ~1.4 actions/s; ~20 punches/min; ~47 vertical hip movements/min
Population: Olympic final and semifinal bouts | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: 25.1 +/- 3.6 y
Design: observational video notational analysis | n: 29 bouts, 39 boxers
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - elite male amateur only
LIMITATIONS: Elite male only; pre-2013 rule set; authors note technical discrimination between winners and losers is difficult.
PPBF implication: Session work blocks must sustain a high action rate with a large vertical leg component; flat-footed bag work does not reproduce the demand.
Source: The activity profile of elite male amateur boxing. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2014. (PMID 24912199; DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2013-0474)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] After the 2013 rule changes, elite male amateur boxing required an activity rate of about 1.55 actions per second, comprising about 21 punches, 3.6 defensive movements and 56 vertical hip movements per minute.
Effect/estimate: ~1.55 actions/s; ~21 punches/min; ~56 vertical hip movements/min
Population: World Championship bouts | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: 23.5 +/- 2.8 y
Design: observational video notational analysis | n: 50 bouts, 60 boxers
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - elite male amateur only
LIMITATIONS: Elite male only; rule-set specific; winners differed mainly in straight punches and accuracy.
PPBF implication: Movement and defensive volume rose after the rule change - ring movement and long-range straights need real session time.
Source: The Activity Profile of Elite Male Amateur Boxing After the 2013 Rule Changes. J Strength Cond Res 2018. (PMID 30480653; DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000001864)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In novice-level 3x2-min amateur boxing, winners landed 18 +/- 11 more punches than losers and applied more lead-hand punches, more total punches to the head and more block-and-counterpunch combinations; peak post-bout blood lactate was 11.8 +/- 1.6 mmol/L in 16 boxers irrespective of result.
Effect/estimate: Winners +18 +/- 11 punches landed; post-bout BLa 11.8 +/- 1.6 mmol/L
Population: novice male amateur boxers | level: novice amateur | sex: male | age: 19.3 +/- 1.4 y
Design: observational video analysis with post-bout blood lactate | n: 32 boxers (16 for lactate)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - NOVICE level, which is rarer and more relevant to PPBF than elite data
LIMITATIONS: Male only; 3x2-min format; single competition context.
PPBF implication: Novice-specific benchmark. The winning pattern at novice level emphasises lead-hand volume to the head and counterpunching off defence - directly coachable at S04.
Source: Amateur boxing: activity profile of winners and losers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2012. (PMID 22869640; DOI 10.1123/ijspp.8.1.84)
