text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Comparing pre- and post-2013 elite male amateur bouts, many previously dominant techniques were used less post-2013 (total punches thrown, rear-hand punches, rear hook, punches landed, uppercuts, body punches) while ring movement and defensive movements increased, with boxers increasing foot movement by 20%; rounds in which standing counts were issued fell from 9% to 3%.
Effect/estimate: Foot movement +20%; standing-count rounds 9% -> 3%
Population: Olympic (pre-2013) and World Championship (post-2013) bouts | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: 24.3 +/- 3.2 y
Design: observational comparative video analysis | n: 79 bouts, 99 boxers
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - elite male amateur
LIMITATIONS: Observational; the rule change is confounded with scoring-system change and headguard removal, so single-cause attribution is not possible.
PPBF implication: Rule sets materially change the sport's demands. Any PPBF technical model must record the rule set it was derived under.
Source: Comparison of amateur boxing before and after the 2013 rules change and the impact on boxers' safety. Br J Sports Med 2017. (PMID 28954796; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-097667)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a 3x2-min semicontact amateur boxing bout, total metabolic cost was approximately 680 kJ with relative energy-system contributions of 77% aerobic, 19% anaerobic alactic and 4% anaerobic lactic; roughly 70 kJ of the aerobic expenditure reflected rephosphorylation of high-energy phosphates during between-round breaks.
Effect/estimate: 77% aerobic / 19% alactic / 4% lactic; Wtot ~680 kJ
Population: amateur boxers performing a semicontact bout against handheld pads | level: amateur | sex: male | age: 23.7 +/- 4.1 y
Design: laboratory measurement of respiratory gases and blood lactate | n: 10
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - but pad-based semicontact simulation, not a full-contact bout
LIMITATIONS: n=10, male, semicontact against pads; 3x2-min format, not the current 3x3-min elite format.
PPBF implication: Justifies a substantial aerobic base in every conditioning plan, including for coaches who describe boxing as purely anaerobic.
Source: The energetics of semicontact 3 x 2-min amateur boxing. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2014. (PMID 24572964; DOI 10.1123/IJSPP.2013-0006)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In full-contact 3x3-min fights in highly trained amateur boxers, blood lactate exceeded 15 mmol/L (range 12-18), heart rate reached above 93% of maximum in rounds 1 and 2 and above 97% in the final round, and average calculated oxygen uptake during the fight was 89% of VO2max.
Effect/estimate: BLa 12-18 mmol/L; HR >93-97% HRmax; VO2 ~89% VO2max
Population: highly trained amateur boxers | level: highly trained amateur | sex: male | age: not stated in abstract
Design: laboratory tests plus competitive-fight measurement | n: 10
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - male highly trained amateur
LIMITATIONS: n=10, male; gas analysis was not performed during the fight, so fight VO2 was calculated rather than measured.
PPBF implication: Competition runs at near-maximal cardiovascular strain on top of a predominantly aerobic supply. Train both.
Source: Metabolic and physiological demands of 3×3-min-round boxing fights in highly trained amateur boxers. J Sports Med Phys Fitness 2022. (PMID 35415997; DOI 10.23736/S0022-4707.22.13661-3)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] During a simulated Olympic boxing match (3x2 min with 1-minute recovery), heart rate and oxygen uptake were above ventilatory threshold 2 for 219.8 +/- 67.4 seconds, increasing across rounds; group mean VO2max was 52.2 +/- 7.2 mL/kg/min.
Effect/estimate: ~220 s above VT2; VO2max 52.2 +/- 7.2 mL/kg/min
Population: highly trained Olympic boxing athletes | level: elite amateur | sex: mixed (6 men, 4 women) | age: not stated in abstract
Design: cross-sectional simulated match with treadmill-derived thresholds | n: 10 (6 male, 4 female)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - includes female athletes, which is unusual and valuable
LIMITATIONS: n=10; simulated match, not competition; 3x2-min format.
PPBF implication: Conditioning should target sustained work above the second ventilatory threshold, not just VO2max.
Source: Heart rate response during a simulated Olympic boxing match is predominantly above ventilatory threshold 2: a cross sectional study. Open Access J Sports Med 2013. (PMID 24379723; DOI 10.2147/OAJSM.S44807)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite Olympic boxers (4 female, 10 male), a 3x3-min free-contact combat simulation produced mean heart rates of 92%, 94% and 95% of maximal across rounds 1-3 and blood chemistry indicative of acidosis after round 3 (pH 7.21 +/- 0.08, lactate 15.1 +/- 3.8 mmol/L); body fat was 17.2% in females and 4.6% in males, with VO2max 50.0 +/- 2.5 and 56.2 +/- 5.2 mL/kg/min respectively.
Effect/estimate: HR 92/94/95% HRmax by round; post-R3 pH 7.21; lactate 15.1 mmol/L
Population: elite Olympic boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male and female | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional laboratory characterisation plus combat simulation | n: 14 (10 male, 4 female)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - one of the few datasets including elite female boxers
LIMITATIONS: Only 4 female participants; simulation rather than competition; body-fat values are unusually low and single-method.
PPBF implication: Provides sex-disaggregated reference values, but n=4 for women. PPBF must not treat female reference values as established.
Source: Physical Capacities and Combat Performance Characteristics of Male and Female Olympic Boxers. Res Q Exerc Sport 2024. (PMID 38787600; DOI 10.1080/02701367.2024.2325683)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In the same boxing-specific 3x3-min protocol performed by elite amateur boxers, pad work produced higher blood lactate (2.7 +/- 0.8 vs 2.3 +/- 0.9 mmol/L), higher average heart rate (160 +/- 9 vs 150 +/- 16 b/min) and higher average oxygen uptake than bag work.
Effect/estimate: Pad vs bag: BLa 2.7 vs 2.3 mmol/L; HRave 160 vs 150 b/min
Population: elite male amateur boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male | age: 22 +/- 2 y
Design: within-subject comparison of two training modalities | n: 14
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - male elite amateur
LIMITATIONS: n=14, male; differences are modest; acute response measured, not adaptation.
PPBF implication: When the goal is internal load choose pads; when it is punch volume at lower coach cost choose the bag. Neither requires head contact.
Source: Physical Response to Pad- and Bag-Based Boxing-Specific Training Modalities. J Strength Cond Res 2020. (PMID 30358696; DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000002928)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In professional boxers completing 6x3-min rounds of pad, bag or sparring training, significantly fewer punches were thrown in sparring than in the other training modalities.
Effect/estimate: Significantly lower punch count in sparring (p < 0.001)
Population: male professional boxers | level: professional | sex: male | age: 26 +/- 5 y
Design: observational within-subject comparison with near-infrared spectroscopy and heart rate | n: 10
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - male professional
LIMITATIONS: n=10, male, observational; punch count is one dimension of stimulus and sparring has tactical value pads cannot replicate.
PPBF implication: Directly undercuts 'spar for fitness': sparring buys head-impact exposure for LESS punch volume than pads or bag. Central to PPBF sparring policy.
Source: Use of NIRS to explore skeletal muscle oxygenation during different training sessions in professional boxing. Eur J Appl Physiol 2023. (PMID 37656280; DOI 10.1007/s00421-023-05305-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A critical review of amateur boxers' physical and physiological attributes reports high-level boxers of both sexes show low body fat, elite males are characterised by higher mesomorphy with well-developed muscle mass, high cardiorespiratory fitness supports metabolic demand and between-round recovery, and upper- and lower-limb muscle strength and power are central to performance.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive physical/physiological profile
Population: amateur boxers | level: amateur, mostly high-level | sex: male and female (male-dominated evidence) | age: adult
Design: critical narrative review | n: n/a (review)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Narrative not systematic; authors note limited somatotype and isometric-strength studies; female data sparse.
PPBF implication: Supports an assessment battery covering aerobic fitness, anaerobic power, and upper/lower-body strength and power.
Source: Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes. Sports Med 2015. (PMID 25358529; DOI 10.1007/s40279-014-0274-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review with meta-analysis of acute responses to amateur boxing activity (25 studies) found large pre-post increases in blood lactate (SMD 4.62), cortisol (1.33), myoglobin (1.43), aspartate transaminase (1.37) and alanine aminotransferase (0.97), moderate increases in creatine kinase (0.65) and small increases in countermovement jump height (0.33), with consistently greater alterations in competitive bouts, followed by sparring, and less in boxing-specific simulations.
Effect/estimate: BLa SMD 4.62; cortisol 1.33; Mb 1.43; AST 1.37; ALT 0.97; CK 0.65; CMJ 0.33
Population: amateur boxers | level: amateur | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 25 studies
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Quality assessed with a modified Downs and Black checklist; heterogeneous protocols; predominantly male.
PPBF implication: Competition > sparring > simulation in physiological disturbance. Simulations are a legitimate lower-exposure substitute for many training goals.
Source: Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci 2022. (PMID 35380916; DOI 10.1080/17461391.2022.2063072)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of the role of strength on punch impact force found lower-body maximal strength and upper- and lower-body explosive strength qualities are largely associated with punch impact force in elite amateur boxers, whereas upper-body maximal strength is not associated with punch impact force and does not differentiate boxers.
Effect/estimate: Lower-body maximal and explosive strength associated with punch force; upper-body maximal strength not
Population: amateur and professional boxers | level: amateur and professional | sex: male and female (male-dominated) | age: adult
Design: critical review | n: n/a (review)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Underlying evidence is largely cross-sectional; association not causation; technique is acknowledged as a major contributor.
PPBF implication: Prioritise lower-body maximal and explosive strength in S&C. Do not sell upper-body maximal strength as a punching-power intervention.
Source: The Role of Strength on Punch Impact Force in Boxing. J Strength Cond Res 2022. (PMID 35836314; DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000004252)

text_content:
[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] In 12 boxers from the Lithuanian national team, running speed at the first and second ventilatory thresholds, VO2max and maximal oxygen pulse showed moderate to strong correlations with sport-mastery ranking.
Effect/estimate: Moderate-to-strong correlations with ranking; group mean VO2max 58.03 +/- 3.00 mL/kg/min
Population: Lithuanian national-team boxers | level: national elite amateur | sex: not specified in abstract | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional correlational | n: 12
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct but very small sample
LIMITATIONS: n=12, cross-sectional, correlational. CORRELATION IS NOT CAUSATION - no training intervention was tested.
PPBF implication: Supports measuring aerobic capacity; does NOT support promising that raising VO2max raises competitive ranking.
Source: Aerobic capacity is correlated with the ranking of boxers. Percept Mot Skills 2014. (PMID 25153738; DOI 10.2466/30.29.PMS.119c12z9)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In seven national-level male boxers, reaction time of the rear straight punch lengthened after round three during sparring in the precompetition period (to 390 ms) compared with the competition period (310 ms), and both rear and lead straight punch forces were greater at all measurement points during precompetition than during competition.
Effect/estimate: Rear-straight reaction time 390 ms (precompetition R3) vs 310 ms (competition R3)
Population: national-level male boxers | level: national amateur | sex: male | age: 20.3 +/- 2.7 y
Design: repeated-measures observational across two training periods | n: 7
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - male national amateur
LIMITATIONS: n=7. Period effects are confounded with overall training load, taper and fatigue; no control condition.
PPBF implication: Sparring performance markers change with training phase, so they can be MONITORED rather than assumed - a candidate low-cost readiness measure.
Source: Effects of Sparring Load on Reaction Speed and Punch Force During the Precompetition and Competition Periods in Boxing. J Strength Cond Res 2017. (PMID 28538306; DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000001885)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguard data from 23 boxing and mixed martial arts athletes across 53 amateur training sessions and 6 competitions identified 896 video-verified head impacts, of which 827 occurred in practice and 69 in competition; men experienced a greater number of impacts than women per practice session but there was no significant sex difference in impact magnitude.
Effect/estimate: 827 of 896 verified head impacts occurred in PRACTICE, 69 in competition
Population: amateur boxing and MMA athletes | level: amateur | sex: male and female (4 women of 23) | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification | n: 23 athletes; 896 verified impacts
Boxing-specific: partly - boxing and MMA combined | transfer status: direct for boxing plus MMA
LIMITATIONS: n=23 with only 4 women; sensor-derived counts have known validity limits (see A3-035/036); combining boxing and MMA complicates sport-specific inference.
PPBF implication: THE central exposure finding for PPBF: practice is where head-impact exposure is spent, and practice is the part a club controls. Exposure reduction is a training-design lever, not a competition-policy lever.
Source: Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts. Orthop J Sports Med 2021. (PMID 34901294; DOI 10.1177/23259671211059815)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Across 115 boxing sparring rounds with 5,168 video-identified contact events, an instrumented mouthguard, skin patch and headgear patch recorded 695, 1,579 and 1,690 events with sensitivities of 35%, 86% and 78% and specificities of 90%, 76% and 75% respectively.
Effect/estimate: Sensitivity 35% / 86% / 78%; specificity 90% / 76% / 75% for mouthguard / skin patch / headgear patch
Population: boxers in sparring | level: amateur | sex: not specified in abstract | age: adult
Design: validation study against video reference | n: 7 boxers, 115 sparring rounds, 5,168 video-identified events
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: n=7 boxers; sensor performance is device- and fit-specific.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT buy a head-impact sensor and treat its count as ground truth. Video-verified coach logging is the practical exposure record.
Source: Capturing Head Impacts in Boxing: A Video-Based Comparison of Three Wearable Sensors. Ann Biomed Eng 2023. (PMID 37728812; DOI 10.1007/s10439-023-03369-w)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Assessing the quality of kinematic traces from three head impact sensors during boxing sparring against pre-defined objective criteria, high-quality criteria were met in only 53%, 20% and 26% of events for the instrumented mouthguard, skin patch and headgear patch respectively.
Effect/estimate: High-quality traces: 53% mouthguard, 20% skin patch, 26% headgear patch
Population: boxers in sparring | level: amateur | sex: not specified in abstract | age: adult
Design: signal-quality assessment study | n: 442 events per sensor
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Device-specific; quality criteria are the authors' own.
PPBF implication: Reinforces A3-035: sensor-derived exposure magnitudes are unreliable in boxing. Any PPBF exposure metric must be countable by a human.
Source: Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment. Ann Biomed Eng 2024. (PMID 39625630; DOI 10.1007/s10439-024-03647-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 237 professional boxers competing in Maryland between 2003 and 2008, higher scores on a Cumulative Sparring Index were associated with poorer performance on both a cognitive test (Symbol Digit Modalities Test) and a balance test (Sharpened Romberg Test), with a threshold effect noted whereby those reporting index values above about 150 experienced a decline in cognition.
Effect/estimate: Threshold effect at Cumulative Sparring Index above approximately 150
Population: professional boxers | level: professional | sex: not specified in abstract | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional association study using self-reported exposure | n: 237
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - PROFESSIONAL boxers; does NOT transfer to youth or novice amateur
LIMITATIONS: CROSS-SECTIONAL AND ASSOCIATIONAL - does not establish causation. Exposure was self-reported. The index is a composite; the '150' threshold is specific to that index and is not a rounds-per-week number.
PPBF implication: Supports monitoring CUMULATIVE sparring exposure, not weekly counts alone. Does NOT license PPBF to publish a safe dose. The threshold value must never be quoted as a PPBF limit.
Source: Sparring and neurological function in professional boxers. Front Public Health 2014. (PMID 25101253; DOI 10.3389/fpubh.2014.00069)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 42 volunteer professional boxers, neuropsychological test performance was not associated with age, boxing record, career length or history of knockout or technical knockout, but the amount of sparring was inversely associated with performance on several tests, with impairments in attention, concentration and memory.
Effect/estimate: Inverse association between sparring amount and several neuropsychological test scores
Population: professional boxers | level: professional | sex: not specified in abstract | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional volunteer cohort with neuropsychological testing | n: 42
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - professional
LIMITATIONS: n=42, volunteer sample, cross-sectional, 1996. Self-reported exposure. No causal claim possible.
PPBF implication: A second, independent associational signal pointing the same direction as A3-037. Two associational studies are still not a dose-response finding.
Source: Sparring and cognitive function in professional boxers. Phys Sportsmed 1996. (PMID 20086991; DOI 10.3810/psm.1996.05.1358)

Effect/estimate: NFL 845 vs 208 ng/L (p=.008); total tau 449 vs 306 ng/L (p=.006)
Population: amateur boxers (11 men, 3 women) and 10 non-athletic male controls | level: amateur | sex: male and female | age: adult
Design: longitudinal study with cerebrospinal-fluid biomarkers | n: 14 boxers, 10 controls
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct

PPBF implication: Supports the principle that rest after competition is biologically warranted, and supports the regulated post-stoppage restriction periods.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies in amateur boxing produced pooled competition injury incidence estimates of 54.7 per 1,000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1,000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and a training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1,000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0); the most commonly injured regions were head and neck in competition (median 72%, range 46-100%) and upper limb in training (median 49%, range from 40%).
Effect/estimate: Competition 54.7/1000 AE and 6.8/1000 min; training 1.3/1000 h; head/neck 72% of competition injuries
Population: amateur boxers | level: amateur | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Wide confidence intervals, especially for training injuries (0.2-7.0), indicating substantial heterogeneity. Population-level rates cannot be converted into an individual's risk or a safe bout number.
PPBF implication: Two design consequences: head and neck dominate competition injury (exposure control), upper limb dominates training injury (hand/wrist conditioning is not optional in the warm-up).
Source: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport 2022. (PMID 36195527; DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology studies (14 studies) produced pooled injury incidence rates of 223.9 per 1,000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4), 233.3 per 1,000 competition exposures (95% CI 161.3-305.2) and 13.0 per 1,000 minutes of competition (95% CI 8.9-17.1).
Effect/estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers; 233.3/1000 competition exposures; 13.0/1000 competition minutes
Population: boxers across organised boxing activities worldwide | level: amateur and professional | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: systematic review with single-arm meta-analyses | n: 14 studies
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Most included studies were of moderate quality (11 of 14); estimates differ substantially from A3-042 because of different denominators and inclusion criteria - the two syntheses are not directly comparable.
PPBF implication: Cite alongside A3-042 and show both. Presenting one injury rate as THE rate would misrepresent the literature.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of head trauma in boxing (35 of 84 articles included) reported that boxers have a significantly elevated risk of sustaining a concussion compared with other combat sports, and that among the boxers analysed 147 of 631 (23.3%) had cavum septum pellucidum and 125 of 411 (30.4%) presented with some form of brain atrophy.
Effect/estimate: Cavum septum pellucidum 23.3%; brain atrophy 30.4%
Population: amateur and professional boxers | level: amateur and professional | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 35 included articles; 631 and 411 boxers for the imaging findings
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Pooling heterogeneous imaging studies with varying definitions and eras; selection into imaging studies may not be representative; no comparable non-boxing control prevalence is given in the abstract.
PPBF implication: PPBF must present head-trauma risk honestly in guardian and athlete informed consent. Not a SHADOW output; a governance and disclosure requirement.
Source: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med 2023. (PMID 37862081; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001195)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of observational studies on chronic traumatic brain injury in amateur boxing found the quality of evidence was generally poor, and that the best-quality studies - cohort designs and those using psychometric tests - yielded the most negative results, with only four of 17 (24%) better-quality studies finding any indication of chronic traumatic brain injury.
Effect/estimate: 4 of 17 (24%) better-quality studies found any indication of chronic traumatic brain injury
Population: amateur boxers | level: AMATEUR - not professional | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: systematic review of observational studies (MOOSE protocol) | n: 36 papers with extractable data from 93 evaluated
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - AMATEUR specifically
LIMITATIONS: Published 2007 - predates much modern imaging and biomarker work. Poor underlying evidence quality means absence of a finding is not strong evidence of absence.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL FOR HONEST COMMUNICATION: the amateur-boxing chronic-injury literature is weaker and more equivocal than the professional literature. PPBF must not import professional-boxing risk estimates into an amateur or youth context.
Source: Amateur boxing and risk of chronic traumatic brain injury: systematic review of observational studies. BMJ 2007. (PMID 17916811; DOI 10.1136/bmj.39342.690220.55)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In the Caerphilly Prospective Study of 1,123 men aged 45-59 at baseline followed for 35 years, a self-report of having boxed 'seriously' when younger was associated with a two-fold increase in cognitive impairment (odds ratio 2.27, 95% CI 1.18-4.38), rising to 2.78 (95% CI 1.37-5.65) for amnestic impairment, and with an advancement in dementia onset of 4.8 years (95% CI 0.9-8.8).
Effect/estimate: Cognitive impairment OR 2.27 (1.18-4.38); amnestic OR 2.78 (1.37-5.65); onset advanced 4.8 y (0.9-8.8)
Population: men in a representative population cohort | level: amateur (self-reported) | sex: male | age: 45-59 at baseline, followed 35 years
Design: prospective population cohort | n: 1,123
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - male amateur; historical exposure era
LIMITATIONS: Exposure was self-reported at a single examination with no dose measure; 'boxed seriously' is undefined; confounding by era, occupation and other exposures is plausible; wide confidence intervals.
PPBF implication: Sits in direct tension with A3-046. Both must be presented. This is the strongest single argument for PPBF minimising unnecessary head contact even in amateur and recreational settings.
Source: Amateur Boxing and Dementia: Cognitive Impairment Within the 35-Year Caerphilly Cohort Study. Clin J Sport Med 2021. (PMID 35470341; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000976)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review informing the Amsterdam consensus examined later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion or exposure to repetitive head impacts, including ten studies of former amateur athletes and 18 of former professional athletes; depression was examined in five studies of former amateurs with none identifying an increased risk, and nine studies examining suicidality or suicide as manner of death found no association with increased risk.
Effect/estimate: No increased depression or suicidality risk identified in former amateur athletes in the included studies; some professional-vs-general-population associations reported for dementia and ALS
Population: former amateur and professional athletes across sports | level: amateur and professional | sex: predominantly male | age: adult, later life
Design: systematic review of case-control and cohort studies | n: 28 studies
Boxing-specific: no - multi-sport | transfer status: OTHER SPORTS - multi-sport review, boxing is not the focus
LIMITATIONS: No post-mortem neuropathology or neuroimaging studies met inclusion criteria. Absence of an identified association in a limited set of studies is not evidence of safety.
PPBF implication: Use to keep PPBF's risk communication calibrated: the amateur-level later-life picture is less alarming than public discourse assumes, and less reassuring than the absence of findings suggests.
Source: Examining later-in-life health risks associated with sport-related concussion and repetitive head impacts: a systematic review of case-control and cohort studies. Br J Sports Med 2023. (PMID 37316187; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106890)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam, October 2022) produced a consensus statement supported by ten systematic reviews, together with revised tools including the Concussion Recognition Tool 6, Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 and Child SCAT6, and a new Sport Concussion Office Assessment Tool 6.
Effect/estimate: Consensus process outputs: CRT6, SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, Child SCOAT6
Population: athletes across sports | level: all | sex: all | age: child and adult
Design: international consensus statement informed by systematic reviews | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no - all sport | transfer status: general sport consensus applied to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, not a trial. Boxing is a sport where head impact is intentional, which differs from the sports that dominate the evidence base.
PPBF implication: PPBF should adopt the current consensus tools rather than invent its own. Recognition and removal is a coach responsibility; assessment and clearance are clinician responsibilities. SHADOW does neither.
Source: Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med 2023. (PMID 37316210; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106898)

Effect/estimate: Categorical position: opposition to youth boxing
Population: children and adolescents under 19 in North America | level: youth amateur | sex: all | age: under 19
Design: professional body policy statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - North America
LIMITATIONS: A policy position weighing risk against acknowledged benefits (exercise, self-discipline, self-confidence), not a new empirical finding. Published 2011.
PPBF implication: MUST be disclosed to guardians at intake. A youth boxing programme that does not surface the paediatric position is not operating with informed consent. Governance decision for Jason and the board.
Source: Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics 2011. (PMID 21873697; DOI 10.1542/peds.2011-1165)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are highly effective at reducing facial lacerations in studies of amateur boxers and are appropriate especially in sparring prior to competition where avoidance of laceration and blood-borne pathogen exposure matters, but that headguards should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, since they have not been shown to prevent these injuries in combat sports and human studies on their effect on concussive injury are lacking.
Effect/estimate: Effective for lacerations and auricular injury; NOT demonstrated for concussion prevention
Population: combat sport athletes | level: amateur and professional | sex: all | age: all
Design: professional body position statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: partly - combat sports including boxing | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Position statement. The statement notes biomechanical studies suggest reduced linear and rotational cranial acceleration, but also raises behavioural risk compensation when wearing headguards.
PPBF implication: PPBF must never present headgear as concussion protection to athletes or guardians. Headgear is laceration and ear protection with an unproven brain-injury effect.
Source: Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed 2023. (PMID 37559553; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2023.2242415)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A cross-sectional observational study comparing World Series of Boxing (without head guards) to other AIBA competitions (with head guards), and comparing the 2009 and 2011 world championships (with head guards) to 2013 (without), found that the number of stoppages due to head blows was significantly decreased without head guards, alongside a notable increase in cuts.
Effect/estimate: Significantly fewer stoppages due to head blows without head guards; increase in cuts
Population: AIBA-competition boxers | level: elite amateur | sex: male (competitions concerned) | age: adult
Design: prospective cross-sectional observational, data recorded by ringside physicians | n: stoppages per 10,000 rounds across the compared competitions
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - elite male amateur
LIMITATIONS: CONTESTED. Stoppages are a proxy for acute brain injury, not a measure of it. Behaviour, refereeing and boxer style all changed simultaneously. A published response letter exists (PMID 27740948; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000401, Clin J Sport Med 2018) and a 2025 Sports Med Open opinion argues the evidence does not support headguard bans.
PPBF implication: Do not present headguard removal as settled science in either direction. This is the clearest example in the file of a CONTESTED PRACTICE claim.
Source: Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments-A Cross-Sectional Observational Study. Clin J Sport Med 2017. (PMID 27116592; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000322)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of 29,357 Olympic-style boxing bouts from 1952 to 2011 examined how rule changes altered verdict rates, reporting an increase in referee-stopped-contest-injury rate (0.72% to 2.42%) after the introduction of the standing-count rule, and changes in RSC-Head rates associated with subsequent rule modifications.
Effect/estimate: RSC-Injury 0.72% to 2.42% after the standing-count rule (p<0.03)
Population: Olympic-style boxing bouts 1952-2011 | level: amateur | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: retrospective analysis of competition records | n: 29,357 bouts
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective; verdict coding changed over the period; era confounds are substantial; rule changes did not occur in isolation.
PPBF implication: Historical evidence that rule changes shift injury-relevant outcomes in measurable ways - supports treating rule sets as a variable in PPBF's data model, not a constant.
Source: Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health. Br J Sports Med 2013. (PMID 23314931; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2012-091771)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians identifies criteria for combat sports athletes at significantly increased risk of injury and mortality: age younger than 13 or older than 35; three consecutive losses, particularly by KO/TKO (professional) or referee-stops-contest (amateur); inactivity exceeding one year (professional); no prior wins; significant mismatches in record, experience, age or physical conditioning; history of concussion, lack of full recovery and clearance from the most recent concussion, or other significant neurological injury; severe pre-bout hypertension (systolic above 160 or diastolic above 100 mmHg in adults, or stage 2 hypertension in paediatric athletes); and any medical condition identified at licensing or pre-bout examination that compromises defensive abilities.
Effect/estimate: Eight named risk criteria; most graded LOE V (expert opinion), concussion history graded LOE II, three-consecutive-losses LOE III
Population: combat sports athletes | level: amateur and professional | sex: all | age: all, with explicit under-13 and over-35 markers
Design: professional body position statement with graded levels of evidence per criterion (LOE II-V) | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: partly - combat sports including boxing | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: MOST CRITERIA ARE LEVEL V EVIDENCE, i.e. expert opinion. The authors label the levels honestly and PPBF should too.
PPBF implication: The single most directly implementable safety artefact found in this track. Encode as coach-facing FLAGS with the LOE shown, never as an automated block or clearance.
Source: Identifying High-Risk Combat Sport Athletes: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Clin J Sport Med 2025. (PMID 41413937; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001403)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians defines Older Fighters as combat sports athletes older than 35 and states that age-related changes to the neurological, cardiopulmonary, endocrinological, thermoregulatory, osmoregulatory and musculoskeletal systems increase injury risk and may prolong recovery, warranting special considerations for competition, licensure, pre-fight clearance, in-fight supervision, post-fight examination and retirement counselling, including more comprehensive neurological evaluation and neuroimaging, careful cardiac assessment, and individualised post-injury clearance.
Effect/estimate: Age threshold 35 for enhanced medical consideration
Population: combat sports athletes over 35 | level: amateur and professional | sex: all | age: over 35
Design: professional body position statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: partly - combat sports | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Position statement based on general age-related physiology rather than combat-sport-specific trials.
PPBF implication: Directly drives the S11 Masters stage design: enhanced medical clearance is a hard gate, recovery is the planning variable, and clearance is individualised by a clinician.
Source: Care of The Older Fighter: Position Statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed 2024. (PMID 38708547; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2024.2344227)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of participation patterns found that predictors of junior versus senior elite performance are opposite: compared with national-class counterparts, adult world-class athletes had MORE childhood/adolescent multi-sport coach-led practice, a LATER main-sport start, LESS main-sport practice and SLOWER initial progress, whereas higher-performing juniors had an earlier main-sport start, more main-sport practice, less other-sports practice and faster initial progress; peer-led play had negligible effects.
Effect/estimate: Cohen's d between |0.23| and |0.50| for adult world-class predictors, |0.23| to |0.61| for junior predictors, all p<0.001; GRADE moderate to high except peer-led play (low)
Population: athletes from local to Olympic level across diverse sports | level: junior and adult, national-class to world-class | sex: mixed | age: childhood through adult
Design: systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 71 study reports, 262 athlete samples, 685 effect sizes, 9,241 athletes
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: OTHER SPORTS - diverse sports, results reported robust across sport types; boxing not separately analysed
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective participation data are subject to recall bias. Results robust across sport types but boxing is not identified as a separate stratum.
PPBF implication: THE key youth-policy finding. A programme optimised to produce good 15-year-old boxers is, on this evidence, not the programme that produces good 25-year-old boxers. PPBF should encourage multi-sport participation and resist early main-sport concentration.
Source: Predictors of Junior Versus Senior Elite Performance are Opposite: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Participation Patterns. Sports Med 2022. (PMID 35038142; DOI 10.1007/s40279-021-01625-4)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A critical review of the Long-Term Athlete Development model found a number of problems not necessarily transparent to coaches: the model is one-dimensional and primarily physiological, there is a lack of empirical evidence on which it is based, interpretations are restricted because the underlying data rely on questionable assumptions and erroneous methodologies, and it is a generic model rather than an individualised plan; the authors argue it should be seen as a work in progress.
Effect/estimate: Categorical critique; the 'windows of opportunity' construct specifically identified as under-evidenced
Population: youth athletes in systems that adopted LTAD | level: youth development | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: critical review | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport - directly applicable because LTAD is adopted by boxing federations
LIMITATIONS: A critique, not an empirical test. LTAD's general principles (individualise, account for maturation) remain defensible.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT build progression gates that assume a closing developmental window. Say openly in any LTAD-referencing material that the evidence base is contested.
Source: The long-term athlete development model: physiological evidence and application. J Sports Sci 2011. (PMID 21259156; DOI 10.1080/02640414.2010.536849)

Design: review/commentary | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport
LIMITATIONS: Commentary rather than empirical study.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF designing around the barriers it actually faces (transport, attendance, deconditioning) - already partly modelled in pilot.transportation/attendance barrier tracking (Module 096).

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed-methods survey of 236 practitioners found that they recognised responsibility for delivering long-term athletic development, were familiar with existing models and reported high adherence focused on health and wellbeing, but that practices associated with growth and maturity, monitoring and assessment, and systematic progression and individualisation were weaker.
Effect/estimate: Self-reported adherence high on health/wellbeing; weaker on maturation, monitoring and individualisation
Population: practitioners delivering youth athletic development (sport coaches, PE teachers) | level: youth development | sex: n/a (practitioners) | age: adult practitioners
Design: mixed-methods survey | n: 236 practitioners
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; no observation of actual practice; sampling not representative of boxing coaches specifically.
PPBF implication: The gap this study names - maturation, monitoring, individualisation - is precisely what a well-designed SHADOW could support. That is a defensible product rationale.
Source: Optimising long-term athletic development: An investigation of practitioners' knowledge, adherence, practices and challenges. PLoS One 2022. (PMID 35077515; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0262995)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 23 sport-organisation guidelines across soccer, basketball, ice hockey and swimming found consensus on only 2 of 15 framework items - emphasis on early skill development and access to well-trained coaches - with volume recommendations inconsistent between and within sports and no group proposing methods to monitor athlete wellbeing.
Effect/estimate: Consensus on 2 of 15 framework items; volume recommendations inconsistent
Population: youth sport governing-body guidelines | level: youth | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: systematic review of published guidelines | n: 23 guidelines (5 general, 18 sport-specific)
Boxing-specific: no - soccer, basketball, ice hockey, swimming | transfer status: OTHER SPORTS
LIMITATIONS: Guidelines published 2000-2018; boxing not among the sports reviewed.
PPBF implication: There is NO agreed youth training-volume number in sport governance. Anyone quoting one to PPBF must produce its source. PPBF should not invent one either.
Source: Current Sport Organization Guidelines From the AMSSM 2019 Youth Early Sport Specialization Research Summit. Sports Health 2021. (PMID 34668454; DOI 10.1177/19417381211051383)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of health organisation guidelines and position statements on youth sport specialisation (11 of 56 articles meeting criteria) synthesised recommendations across a 15-item framework covering psychological development, physical development and load, facilities and resources, and timing and monitoring of specialisation.
Effect/estimate: Framework synthesis; detailed consensus levels not extracted
Population: youth athletes | level: youth | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: systematic review | n: 11 included articles
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport
LIMITATIONS: Guideline synthesis rather than primary evidence.
PPBF implication: Use the 15-item framework as the checklist against which PPBF's own youth policy is written and audited.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A multidisciplinary scoping systematic review of youth sport specialisation (40 empirical publications from 906 screened) concluded that a thorough understanding of the phenomenon is still lacking and that the lack of synthesis makes existing practical recommendations potentially tenuous.
Effect/estimate: Categorical: recommendations described as potentially tenuous
Population: youth athletes | level: youth | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: scoping systematic review | n: 40 empirical publications
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport
LIMITATIONS: Scoping review; heterogeneous definitions of specialisation across the literature.
PPBF implication: Reinforces caution: PPBF should describe its youth policy as a reasoned position with stated uncertainty, not as evidence-based prescription.
Source: Youth sport specialization: a multidisciplinary scoping systematic review. J Sports Sci 2019. (PMID 31135271; DOI 10.1080/02640414.2019.1621476)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A scoping review of 82 articles on multisport engagement in early athlete development found that different terms are used to describe the multisport pathway, most studies are empirical retrospective questionnaire studies aimed at the pathway to sporting excellence, and there is little investigation of when multisport engagement occurs or at what intensity.
Effect/estimate: Definitional inconsistency; timing and intensity of multisport engagement under-investigated
Population: developing athletes | level: youth to elite | sex: mixed | age: childhood and adolescence
Design: scoping review | n: 82 articles from 1,974 abstracts screened
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general sport
LIMITATIONS: Terminology heterogeneity is the finding.
PPBF implication: If PPBF records multi-sport participation (recommended, see A3-062), it must define its own terms precisely and record dose, not just a yes/no flag.
Source: Is There Just One Type of Multisport Pathway? A Scoping Review of Multisport Engagement in Early Athlete Development. Sports Med Open 2023. (PMID 37851177; DOI 10.1186/s40798-023-00644-x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC consensus statement on youth athletic development critically evaluated the state of science and practice and presented recommendations for developing healthy, resilient and capable youth athletes while providing opportunities for all levels of sport participation and success, challenging youth sport governing bodies to implement the guiding principles.
Effect/estimate: Consensus principles
Population: youth athletes | level: all youth levels | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: international consensus statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, 2015; principles rather than prescriptions.
PPBF implication: The authoritative anchor for PPBF's youth development philosophy. Align PPBF's stated principles with it explicitly.
Source: International Olympic Committee consensus statement on youth athletic development. Br J Sports Med 2015. (PMID 26084524; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2015-094962)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 2024 IOC consensus statement on elite youth athletes competing at the Olympic Games notes adolescence is a vulnerable period of development that is inherently dynamic with non-linear and asynchronous progression of physical, physiological, psychological and social attributes, that age-based criteria and conventional pathways for youth Olympic candidates are not well or consistently defined, and that policies and practices vary widely across International Federations.
Effect/estimate: Consensus position on non-linearity and inconsistent age criteria
Population: elite youth athletes | level: elite youth | sex: all | age: adolescent
Design: international consensus statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: Consensus; focused on the elite Olympic context, which most PPBF athletes will not enter.
PPBF implication: Any PPBF plan spanning a minor's growth period must surface maturation context rather than assume linear progression. Directly supports Module 109.
Source: IOC consensus statement on elite youth athletes competing at the Olympic Games: essentials to a healthy, safe and sustainable paradigm. Br J Sports Med 2024. (PMID 39197945; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2024-108186)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A review of bio-banding - grouping youth athletes by maturity status, most commonly percentage of predicted young adult height, rather than chronological age - reports several applications in youth soccer with positive responses from players and coaches, and notes that bio-banding reduces but does not eliminate maturity-associated variation.
Effect/estimate: Reduces but does not eliminate maturity-associated variation
Population: youth athletes, primarily soccer | level: youth academy | sex: predominantly male | age: pubertal
Design: narrative review of concept and applications | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no - soccer | transfer status: OTHER SPORT - soccer; boxing application untested
LIMITATIONS: Predominantly male soccer; prediction of adult height carries its own error; no boxing studies.
PPBF implication: In boxing, matching is governed by weight and age under the rulebooks, so bio-banding could only be a TRAINING-GROUP tool, never a matchmaking tool. PPBF cannot override governing-body matching rules.
Source: Bio-Banding in Youth Sports: Background, Concept, and Application. Sports Med 2019. (PMID 31429034; DOI 10.1007/s40279-019-01166-x)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The National Strength and Conditioning Association updated position statement holds that research increasingly indicates resistance training can offer unique benefits for children and adolescents when appropriately prescribed and supervised, and that qualified acceptance of youth resistance training by medical, fitness and sport organisations is becoming universal.
Effect/estimate: Categorical endorsement conditional on appropriate prescription and supervision
Population: school-aged children and adolescents | level: all | sex: all | age: child and adolescent
Design: professional body position statement | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general youth
LIMITATIONS: Position statement, 2009. 'Appropriately prescribed and supervised' is the load-bearing qualifier.
PPBF implication: Supervised youth resistance training is defensible in PPBF's youth stages. The supervision requirement is a coach-qualification requirement.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis found neuromuscular training injury prevention strategies are effective in youth sport.
Effect/estimate: Effect sizes not extracted from the retrieved record - see the paper before quoting a number

Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: OTHER SPORTS - predominantly team sports

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of deliberate practice and performance across music, games, sports, education and professions found that deliberate practice explained a minority of the variance in performance.
Effect/estimate: Deliberate practice explained a minority of performance variance
Population: performers across multiple domains | level: all | sex: all | age: all
Design: meta-analysis | n: not extracted (multi-domain)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: CROSS-DOMAIN
LIMITATIONS: Contested by Ericsson and colleagues; the sport-specific companion analysis (PMID 27217246) is the more relevant one for PPBF.
PPBF implication: Volume of structured practice matters but does not determine outcome. A development route must not imply that accumulating hours guarantees progression.
Source: Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis. Psychol Sci 2014. (PMID 24986855; DOI 10.1177/0956797614535810)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A meta-analysis of the relationship between deliberate practice and performance specifically in sports was published in Perspectives on Psychological Science in 2016, alongside a published reply and commentary reflecting active scientific disagreement.
Effect/estimate: Effect magnitude not extracted; the existence of a formal published dispute is the recorded finding
Population: athletes | level: all | sex: all | age: all
Design: meta-analysis with published reply and commentary | n: not extracted
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: general sport
LIMITATIONS: An active academic dispute. PPBF should not adopt either extreme position.
PPBF implication: Practice volume is one input among many. SHADOW should not treat accumulated hours as a progression criterion on its own.
Source: The Relationship Between Deliberate Practice and Performance in Sports: A Meta-Analysis. Perspect Psychol Sci 2016. (PMID 27217246; DOI 10.1177/1745691616635591)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of the contextual interference effect produced 139 effect-size estimates from 61 studies with an average overall effect size of 0.38, but with a significantly larger effect for basic research (0.57) than applied research (0.19), and for adults (0.50) than younger learners (0.10); the overall mean statistical power of the reviewed studies was 0.43.
Effect/estimate: Overall d = 0.38; basic 0.57 vs applied 0.19; adults 0.50 vs younger learners 0.10; mean power 0.43
Population: motor learners across settings | level: mostly laboratory and applied practice contexts | sex: mixed | age: children and adults
Design: meta-analysis | n: 61 studies, 139 effect sizes
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: MOTOR LEARNING LABORATORY AND APPLIED - not boxing
LIMITATIONS: Low mean statistical power (0.43) across the included studies. The applied effect (0.19) and the youth effect (0.10) are small.
PPBF implication: Interleaved practice is defensible for adult learners but the applied and youth effects are SMALL. Do not promise a large benefit from interleaving, and do not assume it transfers to children.
Source: Contextual interference: a meta-analytic study. Percept Mot Skills 2004. (PMID 15446636; DOI 10.2466/pms.99.1.116-126)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of tapering in endurance athletes (14 studies) found significant improvement from pre- to post-taper in time-trial performance (SMD -0.45) and time to exhaustion (SMD 1.28) with no significant improvement in VO2max or economy of movement; subgroup analysis found tapering combined with pre-taper overload had a greater effect than conventional tapering, and that reducing training volume by 41-60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over durations of up to 7, 8-14 or 15-21 days using a progressive or step taper, significantly improved time-trial performance.
Effect/estimate: Time trial SMD -0.45; TTE SMD 1.28; volume reduction 41-60% with intensity and frequency maintained
Population: endurance athletes | level: competitive endurance | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 14 studies
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: OTHER SPORT - ENDURANCE ATHLETES. No boxing taper trial was found.
LIMITATIONS: Endurance performance outcomes, not combat-sport outcomes. Transfer to a technical, intermittent, weight-category combat sport is an assumption.
PPBF implication: The basis for PPBF's proposed taper template (40-60% volume reduction, intensity and frequency maintained, 7-14 days). MUST be labelled as transferred from endurance athletes and validated within PPBF.
Source: Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One 2023. (PMID 37163550; DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0282838)

Effect/estimate: ES 0.47-1.04 across strength, jump, change-of-direction and sport-specific outcomes; 4-12 weeks at 2-3 sessions/week

PPBF implication: Provides a defensible plyometric dose range (4-12 weeks, 2-3 sessions/week) but PPBF must state that the evidence comes from other combat sports, not boxing.
Source: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Plyometric-Jump Training on the Physical Fitness of Combat Sport Athletes. Sports (Basel) 2023. (PMID 36828318; DOI 10.3390/sports11020033)

Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: GENERAL EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGY - endurance-dominated evidence

Effect/estimate: Sprint d=1.72; jump d=0.61; agility d=1.40 after 5 min jogging + 7 min dynamic exercise
Population: team sport athletes | level: mixed | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: systematic review | n: not extracted
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: OTHER SPORTS - team sport
LIMITATIONS: Team sport, not boxing. Outcomes are sprint, jump and agility, not punch force or boxing performance.
PPBF implication: The basis for PPBF's proposed 8-minute warm-up floor. That floor is an ASSUMPTION compressed from team-sport evidence and requires validation in boxing.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In ten senior elite amateur boxers, punch-specific isometric and elastic-resistance conditioning activities produced small to moderate worthwhile increases in punch force and rate of force development, with the isometric punch condition appearing superior, and no meaningful change in countermovement jump performance.

Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - senior elite amateur
LIMITATIONS: n=10. Acute effect only; no evidence it improves competition outcome. The effect was localised (no CMJ change).

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A survey of pre-conditioning and recovery strategies in senior elite and non-elite amateur boxing found post-activation performance enhancement was used in the pre-competition warm-up by 31% of senior elite boxers versus 2% of senior development boxers, and that massage (59% vs 29%) and cold-water immersion (47% vs 29%) were more commonly used by senior elite boxers.
Effect/estimate: PAPE use 31% vs 2%; massage 59% vs 29%; cold-water immersion 47% vs 29%
Population: senior elite and senior development amateur boxers | level: senior elite and senior development amateur | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional survey | n: not extracted from the retrieved record
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported practice, not efficacy. Differences likely reflect ACCESS to support staff and facilities as much as informed choice.
PPBF implication: Describes what elite boxers do, not what works. PPBF should not adopt a practice merely because elite boxers report using it.
Source: The prevalence of pre-conditioning and recovery strategies in senior elite and non-elite amateur boxing. Phys Sportsmed 2021. (PMID 34003715; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2021.1931525)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A study of the physical preparation practices of amateur boxers by competitor level found that 56% of senior elite boxers versus 26% of senior development boxers had their physical preparation managed by a strength and conditioning coach or sport scientist.
Effect/estimate: S&C/sport-science management: 56% senior elite vs 26% senior development
Population: amateur boxers across competitor levels | level: senior elite and senior development amateur | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional survey | n: not extracted from the retrieved record
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; the level difference confounds resources with expertise.
PPBF implication: Most development-level boxers have no qualified physical-preparation support. This is exactly the gap a coach-support tool addresses - and it is why coach S&C literacy is a PPBF priority.

Effect/estimate: 78% without professional S&C or sport-science accreditation
Population: boxing coaches and practitioners | level: all | sex: n/a (practitioners) | age: adult
Design: cross-sectional survey | n: not extracted from the retrieved record
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct
LIMITATIONS: Self-report survey; sampling frame not extracted.
PPBF implication: Coach capability, not athlete motivation, is the binding constraint on programme quality. Justifies prioritising the S12 coach pathway as a first-class PPBF workstream.
Source: Strength Training Practices in Amateur and Professional Boxing. J Strength Cond Res 2025. (PMID 40403184; DOI 10.1519/JSC.0000000000005088)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A systematic review of the acute:chronic workload ratio and time-loss injury in adult elite team sports included studies covering 2,375 injuries in 1,234 athletes and found methodological heterogeneity and inconsistent risk estimates across studies.

Effect/estimate: Categorical: causal claims not supported by the available designs
Population: n/a - methodological | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: methodological critique | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: methodological - applies to any sport
LIMITATIONS: A critique; proponents dispute it.
PPBF implication: Directly relevant to the project charter's prohibition on false precision. Log load, show trends, do not compute a ratio implying a risk threshold.

Effect/estimate: Onset in the teenage years; typically 2-3 weight-loss episodes per year
Population: combat sport athletes | level: mixed | sex: mixed | age: teenage and adult
Design: review | n: 26 studies, 3,994 participants, 14 combat sports
Boxing-specific: partly - one of 14 combat sports | transfer status: combat sports

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An analysis of 71 IBF title fights, using the IBF-mandated second weigh-in 12 hours before the contest, found average weight gain between weigh-ins of 2.52 +/- 1.37 kg (3.8 +/- 2.2% of initial body weight), with neither the amount of weight gained nor the between-opponent weight discrepancy affecting the match outcome.
Effect/estimate: Weight gain 2.52 +/- 1.37 kg (3.8 +/- 2.2% of body weight); no effect on outcome
Population: professional championship boxers | level: professional championship | sex: predominantly male | age: adult
Design: retrospective analysis of official weigh-in records | n: 71 title fights
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: direct - professional championship boxing only
LIMITATIONS: Championship-level professionals only; the 12-hour window is IBF-specific; weight regain is a proxy for rapid weight loss, not a direct measure.
PPBF implication: Notable finding for coaching conversations: the competitive advantage assumed to come from cutting and regaining weight was NOT observed in this dataset. Do not extend to youth in any form.
Source: Rapid weight gain in professional boxing and correlation with fight decisions: analysis from 71 title fights. Phys Sportsmed 2016. (PMID 27564844; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2016.1228421)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In highly trained male amateur boxers, a full-contact 3x3-min bout produced post-fight blood lactate >15 mmol/L (range 12-18), heart rate >93% HRmax in rounds 1-2 and >97% in round 3, and mean oxygen uptake ~89% of VO2max; calculated energy provision was 73% aerobic, 19% anaerobic alactic, 8% anaerobic glycolytic.
Effect/estimate: BLa >15 mmol/L; HR >97% HRmax final round; VO2 ~89% VO2max; 73/19/8% aerobic/alactic/glycolytic
Population: Highly trained amateur boxers | level: Amateur (highly trained) | sex: Male | age: Adult (senior)
Design: Cross-over laboratory + competitive bout measurement | n: n=10
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Very small sample (n=10); male only; VO2 during the fight was calculated, not directly measured; single format.
PPBF implication: Conditioning must develop BOTH a high aerobic ceiling and repeated near-maximal alactic output. SHADOW conditioning templates should not treat boxing as a purely anaerobic sport.
Source: Bruzas et al. (2022). Metabolic and physiological demands of 3x3-min-round boxing fights in highly trained amateur boxers. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. (doi:10.23736/S0022-4707.22.13661-3)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a 3x2-min semicontact amateur boxing bout against handheld pads, relative energy contributions were approximately 77% aerobic, 19% anaerobic alactic and 4% anaerobic lactic, with authors highlighting aerobic capacity as a prerequisite for high activity rate and inter-round phosphagen resynthesis.
Effect/estimate: ~77% aerobic / 19% alactic / 4% lactic; Wtot ~680 kJ
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult (mean ~24 y)
Design: Laboratory-controlled simulated bout with gas analysis and blood lactate | n: n=10
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Semicontact against pads, not a live opponent — lower emotional/defensive load than competition; n=10; male only; 3x2 format is no longer the elite adult format.
PPBF implication: Justifies an aerobic base block in PPBF conditioning as a recovery-enabler, not as 'cardio for weight loss'. Frame aerobic work as between-round recovery capacity.
Source: Davis et al. (2014). The energetics of semicontact 3 x 2-min amateur boxing. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/IJSPP.2013-0006)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In competitive bouts among senior national-level boxers, pooled mean heart rate was approximately 178 beats/min and mean blood lactate approximately 8.24 mmol/L, with no consistent difference between weight categories.
Effect/estimate: Mean HR ~178 b/min; mean BLa ~8.24 mmol/L
Population: Senior national-level amateur boxers (India) | level: Amateur (national) | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Field measurement during competitive bouts | n: n=26
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: 1995 study — bout format and rules have changed since; single-nation cohort; older lactate assay methods; magnitudes differ substantially from more recent 3x3 full-contact data (A5-001).
PPBF implication: Illustrates that lactate values are format- and era-dependent. SHADOW must never store a lactate or HR threshold as a fixed constant; store format context alongside any physiological value.
Source: Ghosh et al. (1995). Heart rate & blood lactate response in amateur competitive boxing. Indian J Med Res. (PMID:8543363)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of male amateur boxing competition reported activity-to-rest ratios higher in elite (about 18:1) than novice (about 9:1) boxers, with ratios changing across rounds in novices (round 1 about 16:1, round 2 about 8:1, round 3 about 6:1) and increasing total stop-time across rounds.
Effect/estimate: Activity:rest ~18:1 elite vs ~9:1 novice; novice degradation across rounds
Population: Male amateur boxers, novice and elite | level: Amateur — novice and elite | sex: Male | age: Any age category (as reviewed)
Design: Narrative/brief review of time-motion and physiological studies | n: Multiple studies pooled narratively
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Brief review, not a systematic review/meta-analysis; male only; heterogeneous methods across the underlying time-motion studies; ratio definitions vary between studies.
PPBF implication: Work:rest densities in PPBF conditioning must be LEVEL-SCALED. A novice should not be prescribed elite work:rest densities. SHADOW should attach a level band to every conditioning template.
Source: Slimani et al. (2017). Performance Aspects and Physiological Responses in Male Amateur Boxing Competitions: A Brief Review. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001643)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Time-motion analysis of the 12 finals of the IBA 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships (3x3-min format) found significant differences across rounds in punching, clinching, no-fighting and arbitral-interruption phases, and different fighting/no-fighting ratios by weight category, with heavyweight categories relying more on clinching.
Effect/estimate: Round and weight-category differences in phase frequency/duration (p<0.001 to p=0.007 across phases)
Population: Elite female boxers | level: Elite amateur (world championship finals) | sex: Female | age: Adult (senior)
Design: Observational video time-motion analysis | n: 12 finals bouts
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Finals only — a selected, non-representative subset of bouts; no physiological measures; descriptive design; conclusions about strategy are interpretive.
PPBF implication: Conditioning and tactical prescriptions should be weight-category aware, and PPBF should not assume women's demands mirror men's. Store weight category as a first-class conditioning context field.
Source: Martusciello et al. (2025). Time-Motion Analysis of the 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships Finals. Sports (Basel). (doi:10.3390/sports13060187)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review with meta-analysis of acute responses to amateur boxing-specific activity found large increases in blood lactate (SMD 4.62), cortisol (SMD 1.33), myoglobin (SMD 1.43), AST (1.37), ALT (0.97) and moderate creatine kinase increases (0.65), with only small pre-post increases in countermovement jump height (SMD 0.33); responses were consistently greatest in competitive bouts, then sparring, then simulations.
Effect/estimate: BLa SMD 4.62; cortisol 1.33; Mb 1.43; CK 0.65; CMJ +0.33
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Predominantly male (as reported in included studies) | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 25 studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous included studies; methodological quality assessed with a modified Downs and Black checklist; female representation limited; biochemical markers are not themselves outcomes coaches can act on.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL for PPBF load model: competition > sparring > simulation in physiological cost. This ordering is the defensible basis for weighting sparring more heavily than pad/bag work in a session load index. Also: CMJ may NOT drop after boxing activity, so jump height is a weak same-day fatigue marker in this sport.
Source: Finlay et al. (2022). Acute physiological, endocrine, biochemical and performance responses associated with amateur boxing: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci. (doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2063072)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A review of amateur boxers' physical and physiological attributes reports low body fat, a mesomorphic tendency in elite males, high peak and mean anaerobic power in international boxers, and describes upper- and lower-limb muscle strength and power as central to performance, with isometric strength linked to higher-level performance.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive; no pooled effect estimate
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur, incl. international | sex: Male and female (data sparser for female) | age: Adult
Design: Narrative review | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Narrative (non-systematic) review; the authors explicitly note limited studies, particularly on somatotype and on female boxers; cross-sectional associations cannot establish that training these qualities causes performance gains.
PPBF implication: Supports a multi-quality PPBF test battery (strength, power, anaerobic capacity, body composition) rather than a single 'fitness score'. Note the female data gap explicitly in SHADOW confidence output.
Source: Chaabène et al. (2015). Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0274-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Using a validated striking dynamometry method, intra-session variability of punch impact kinetics (impulse, peak force, mean force across jab, cross, lead and rear hook) in untrained participants and experienced boxers was mostly small (ICC >0.67, CV <10%), while between-session measures in the untrained cohort were mostly of moderate variability.
Effect/estimate: Intra-session mostly ICC >0.67 / CV <10%; inter-session mostly moderate variability
Population: Untrained participants and experienced boxers | level: Mixed (untrained and experienced) | sex: Male (as reported) | age: Adult
Design: Reliability study | n: Two cohorts (small)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Small cohorts; between-session reliability established only in the untrained group; device-specific — results do not transfer automatically to other dynamometers or commercial bags.
PPBF implication: Punch force can be logged as a tracked metric BUT PPBF must establish its own device-specific typical error before calling a change real. Do not compare across devices.
Source: Lenetsky et al. (2018). Variability and Reliability of Punching Impact Kinetics in Untrained Participants and Experienced Boxers. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002352)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Laboratory testing of a commercial punch/kick impact device found peak power reductions ranging from 15.9% to 41.4% when strikes were off-centre and/or inclined relative to level centred strikes, and the authors advise videoing strikes to ensure consistent impact orientation.
Effect/estimate: Peak power reduced 15.9%-41.4% with off-centre/inclined impacts
Population: Simulated mechanical strikes (laboratory) | level: N/A (device validation) | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Laboratory device reliability study | n: Mechanical trials
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific device
LIMITATIONS: Mechanical simulation rather than human strikes; single commercial device; does not establish what a real athlete's technique variation contributes.
PPBF implication: Treat gym punch-power readings as LOW source quality unless strike orientation is standardised. SHADOW should tag any commercial-device punch power with a source_quality flag and never trend it without a standardised protocol note.
Source: Del Vecchio et al. (2022). Reliability and Practical Use of a Commercial Device for Measuring Punch and Kick Impact Kinetics. Sports (Basel). (doi:10.3390/sports10120206)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A custom wall-mounted punch force dynamometer built from two S-type load cells showed excellent reliability in mechanical trials (ICC >0.90) and good-to-excellent reliability in a sport-specific condition with experienced striking athletes (ICC 0.75-0.90), with standard error of measurement consistently below the smallest worthwhile change.
Effect/estimate: ICC 0.75-0.90 in sport-specific condition; SEM < SWC
Population: Experienced striking combat-sport athletes | level: Experienced (non-elite specified) | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Device development and reliability study | n: n=11 athletes, two lab visits
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific (striking sports)
LIMITATIONS: Very small athlete sample (n=11); 'partial' ecological validity by the authors' own framing; single custom device.
PPBF implication: Demonstrates the SEM-vs-SWC standard PPBF should adopt for every physical test: a change is only reportable when it exceeds the measured typical error.
Source: Meireles et al. (2026). Development and Measurement Properties of a Custom-Built Punch Force Dynamometer Based on S-Type Load Cells. Percept Mot Skills. (doi:10.1177/00315125261464714)

text_content:
[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] A survey of 72 trainers/support staff in amateur and professional boxing found that most practitioners (72-88%) implemented strength training to improve punching power and muscular endurance and to reduce injury likelihood.
Effect/estimate: 72-88% reported these rationales
Population: Boxing trainers and support staff | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Not applicable (practitioners) | age: Adult practitioners
Design: Cross-sectional practitioner survey | n: n=72 practitioners
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: This documents what coaches DO, not whether it works. Survey responses are self-reported and subject to social desirability; no performance or injury outcomes measured.
PPBF implication: Useful as the baseline 'current practice' layer in the PPBF doctrine engine. Must be labelled PRACTICE, not EVIDENCE, in the SHADOW source hierarchy.
Source: Beattie et al. (2025). Strength Training Practices in Amateur and Professional Boxing. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000005088)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 24 high-school amateur boxers aged 12-18 with 3-5 years of experience, both an 8-week plyometric programme and an 8-week jump-rope programme (30 min, 3 days/week) improved countermovement jump rate of force development, punch reaction time, rear-leg peak ground reaction force during the jab, and jab velocity, with no differences between groups.
Effect/estimate: Both groups improved RFD, punch reaction time, rear-leg peak GRF, jab velocity; no between-group difference
Population: Junior amateur boxers | level: Junior/high-school amateur | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: 12-18 y
Design: Two-arm comparative training intervention (8 weeks) | n: n=24
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: No true (non-training) control group — improvements cannot be fully separated from ongoing boxing training or maturation over 8 weeks in a growing population; small n; sex not reported in abstract.
PPBF implication: PPBF youth programming: rope work is a defensible low-cost stimulus for junior boxers and is not inferior to plyometrics in this trial. Supports keeping equipment demands low for a nonprofit gym.
Source: Chottidao et al. (2022). A Comparison of Plyometric and Jump Rope Training Programs for Improving Punching Performance in Junior Amateur Boxers. Front Bioeng Biotechnol. (doi:10.3389/fbioe.2022.878527)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 8 experienced male amateur boxers, 12 sessions of plyometric training with external weights over 4 weeks did not change single-punch force or punch frequency within a series (except increased power in the rear-hand low punch), but did increase summative force/energy output over 3 s and 8 s efforts and across a series of eight 8-s tests.
Effect/estimate: No change in single-punch force; increases in 3 s/8 s summative force and energy output (p<0.05)
Population: Experienced male amateur boxers | level: Amateur, >=7 years experience | sex: Male | age: Adult (~22 y)
Design: Single-group pre-post training study (4 weeks) | n: n=8
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: No control group; n=8; 4 weeks is short for a strength-power adaptation; single-device outcome measure; pre-post design cannot exclude learning/familiarisation effects.
PPBF implication: Important nuance for SHADOW: repeated-effort punch output and single-punch force are DIFFERENT qualities that respond differently. Do not collapse them into one 'punch power' score.
Source: Bruzas et al. (2016). Effects of plyometric exercise training with external weights on punching ability of experienced amateur boxers. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. (doi:10.23736/S0022-4707.16.06674-3)
