text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of PAPE in combat sports (13 studies, 176 athletes) on sport-specific outcomes found a profound moderating effect of training status: on the Frequency Speed of Kick Test, amateurs showed large significant improvement (g=1.28, p<0.001) while elite athletes showed trivial non-significant change (g=0.11, p=0.357); athletes with under 6 years' experience showed larger enhancements than those with more.
Effect/estimate: FSKT-10: amateur g=1.28 vs elite g=0.11; <6 y experience g=1.60 vs >6 y g=0.42
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: Amateur and elite | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis (Hedges' g, random effects) | n: 13 studies, 176 athletes
Boxing-specific: Partly (combat sports, sport-specific tests are predominantly taekwondo-based) | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: The primary sport-specific outcomes (FSKT-10, TSAT) are taekwondo tests, not boxing tests — transfer to punching is an assumption. Small total sample; combat-sport heterogeneity.
PPBF implication: PPBF should NOT assume warm-up potentiation protocols generalise across levels. If SHADOW ever proposes a PAPE warm-up, it must condition the suggestion on training level and flag it as transfer evidence.
Source: Terbalyan et al. (2026). Effect of Post-Activation Performance Enhancement in Combat Sports: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis-Part II: Specific Performance Indicators. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. (doi:10.3390/jfmk11020157)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 10 male senior elite amateur boxers, isometric punch and elastic-resistance punch conditioning activities (but not the control trial) produced small worthwhile increases (effect size >=0.20, at or above the smallest worthwhile change) in punch force during a boxing-specific simulated bout.
Effect/estimate: ES >= 0.20 (>= SWC) for punch force with both conditioning activities
Population: Senior elite amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Repeated-measures cross-over trial | n: n=10
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: n=10, male only; 'small worthwhile' is a modest magnitude; simulation rather than competition; individual responsiveness varied, which the authors themselves emphasise.
PPBF implication: Any PPBF warm-up potentiation protocol must be INDIVIDUALLY tested and coach-reviewed, not applied squad-wide. SHADOW may log the protocol and observed response; it must not auto-prescribe.
Source: Finlay et al. (2024). Post-Activation Performance Enhancement of Punch Force and Neuromuscular Performance in Amateur Boxing: Toward a More Individualized and "Real-World" Approach. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004740)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a randomised trial of 30 elite male amateur boxers, 8 weeks of thrice-weekly upper-body resistance training at 20-30% 1RM with 40-50% limb occlusion pressure produced significantly greater dominant-arm strength gains than a control group training at 50-60% 1RM (e.g. 1RM elbow flexion +3.3 kg, p<0.001, d=3.20), alongside punch force outcomes.
Effect/estimate: 1RM elbow flexion +3.3 kg (p<0.001, d=3.20) favouring BFRT
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur (>=3 y competitive experience) | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Randomised controlled trial (8 weeks) | n: n=30
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Implausibly large effect sizes for a strength trial warrant caution; the comparator trained at a different (lower-than-typical) intensity; male only; single-site; BFR requires trained supervision and cuff pressure control that a volunteer-staffed nonprofit gym may not have.
PPBF implication: DO NOT adopt BFR at PPBF without qualified supervision and a medical screen. Record as a research-watch item, not a programme component. Occlusion training on minors is out of scope.
Source: Awana et al. (2025). Blood flow restriction training enhances punching force and upper body strength in elite boxers: a randomized trial. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1693271)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A systematic review of core strength training in striking combat sports (karate, taekwondo, boxing, Chinese martial arts, Muay Thai) examined effects on kick count, striking force and impact speed.
Effect/estimate: No single pooled effect estimate reported in the abstract
Population: Striking combat-sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic review (PRISMA) | n: Multiple studies across five striking sports
Boxing-specific: Partly | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer, partly boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Systematic review without meta-analysis in the reported abstract; included sports differ substantially in the striking task; 'core strength training' is a heterogeneous, poorly standardised intervention category; CNKI inclusion introduces language/indexing heterogeneity.
PPBF implication: Trunk/rotational work is defensible in a PPBF programme, but SHADOW must not attach a numeric expected punch-force gain to it. TBD: PPBF-specific dose-response.
Source: Zhang et al. (2025). Effects of core strength training on the technical skill performance of striking combat sport players: a systematic review. PeerJ. (doi:10.7717/peerj.19615)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 14 boxers, three landmine-punch-throw variations (seated without trunk rotation, seated with rotation, standing whole body) at 20, 22.5 and 25.0 kg were mostly highly reliable within session (ICC >0.91), with the non-dominant hand as reliable or more reliable than the dominant hand, and very strong linear group-average load-velocity relationships.
Effect/estimate: ICC >0.91 for most variation x load x hand combinations
Population: Boxers | level: Not specified beyond 'boxers' (mean 24.1 y, 72.6 kg) | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Reliability and load-velocity profiling study | n: n=14
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Intra-session reliability only (no between-session data); small n; requires a linear position transducer, which many community gyms lack.
PPBF implication: A candidate PPBF upper-body power test IF a velocity device is available. Otherwise use as a training exercise, not a test. Between-session reliability is unestablished — a TBD for PPBF.
Source: Omcirk et al. (2024). Reliability of Three Landmine-Punch-Throw Variations and Their Load-Velocity Relationships Performed With the Dominant and Nondominant Hands. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2023-0235)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Force-plate-derived measures of the countermovement push-up were assessed for test-retest reliability in 18 elite Olympic boxers across two sessions 7 days apart, with the authors noting no gold-standard test currently exists for upper-limb force development performance.
Effect/estimate: Reliability across peak force, mean force, flight time, RFD, impulse, vertical stiffness
Population: Elite Olympic boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult (~23 y)
Design: Test-retest reliability study | n: n=18
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Requires dual force platforms — not feasible in most community gyms; n=18; elite population may not generalise to novice/youth.
PPBF implication: Confirms there is NO gold-standard upper-limb power test in boxing. PPBF should choose a feasible proxy and validate it locally rather than claim a validated standard exists.
Source: Parry et al. (2021). The Test-Retest Reliability of Bilateral and Unilateral Force Plate-Derived Parameters of the Countermovement Push-Up in Elite Boxers. J Sport Rehabil. (doi:10.1123/jsr.2020-0340)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 18 experienced male amateur boxers, 4 weeks of sport-specific sprint interval training (3 rounds of 14 sets of 3-s all-out bag punching with 10-s rests, 3x/week) improved punching ability and upper-body aerobic power compared with the same rounds performed at low intensity.
Effect/estimate: Improved punch characteristics and upper-body aerobic power vs low-intensity control
Population: Experienced male amateur boxers | level: Amateur (experienced) | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Controlled training intervention (4 weeks) | n: n=18 (9 per group)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Small n; 4-week duration; male only; the control group performed the same drill at low intensity, so the contrast is intensity rather than modality; single laboratory.
PPBF implication: STRONG candidate for PPBF conditioning: the intervention uses only a heavy bag and a timer, which fits a $0-cost nonprofit constraint. Structure is loggable as rounds x sets in the session model.
Source: Kamandulis et al. (2018). Sport-Specific Repeated Sprint Training Improves Punching Ability and Upper-Body Aerobic Power in Experienced Amateur Boxers. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002056)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 16 elite male boxers, 4 weeks of boxing-specific repeated sprint training (14 sets of 3-s maximal heavy-bag punches, 10-s rest, 1-min between rounds, 3x/week) produced large within-group improvements in upper-body Wingate peak power (d=1.10, +16.7%) and mean power alongside conventional training.
Effect/estimate: Wingate peak power d=1.10, +16.7%
Population: Elite male boxers | level: Elite | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Randomised controlled training intervention (4 weeks) | n: n=16 (8 per group)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Very small n (8 per group); 4 weeks; male only; replication of a similar protocol by an overlapping methodological approach rather than a fully independent design.
PPBF implication: Second independent-cohort support for bag-based repeated-sprint conditioning. Elevates confidence that this is a defensible PPBF conditioning template for experienced boxers (NOT for novices without technique screening).
Source: Tian et al. (2026). The effects of 4 weeks of sport-specific repeated sprint training on upper-body strength quality, anaerobic capacity and punching ability of elite male boxers. Front Sports Act Living. (doi:10.3389/fspor.2026.1839505)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies found a significant moderate-magnitude advantage of high-intensity interval training over control conditions for maximal oxygen uptake in Olympic combat sport athletes, with study quality assessed by PEDro and certainty by GRADE.
Effect/estimate: Moderate effect size favouring HIIT for VO2max
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Trained athletes | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 20 studies
Boxing-specific: Partly (Olympic combat sports incl. boxing) | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer, partly boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Pooled across combat sports with different demands; interventions heterogeneous in work:rest and duration; the comparator ('active control') varies across studies.
PPBF implication: Supports including HIIT in PPBF conditioning blocks. Do NOT specify a single optimal work:rest — the literature is heterogeneous. Set the parameter as a coach-adjustable template field.
Source: Yue et al. (2025). Effects of high-intensity interval training on aerobic and anaerobic capacity in olympic combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1576676)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 12 male Olympic boxers completing 30-s Wingate cycling, arm cranking, bag punching, uphill treadmill running to exhaustion and a progressive VO2max test, performance indices of the different anaerobic tests were largely NOT closely correlated, and punches landed on a bag in 30 s correlated only with relative Wingate power.
Effect/estimate: Most inter-test correlations weak; 30-s bag punch count associated only with relative Wingate power
Population: Elite amateur (Olympic) boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional test-battery comparison | n: n=12
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: n=12; male only; single session per test in some cases; correlation-based design cannot establish which test best predicts competitive success.
PPBF implication: MAJOR implication: PPBF cannot substitute one anaerobic test for another. If the battery drops a test, the quality is no longer measured. SHADOW must model qualities and tests as separate entities with explicit, non-interchangeable mappings.
Source: Venckunas et al. (2024). Anaerobic Performance Profiling in Elite Amateur Boxers. Sports (Basel). (doi:10.3390/sports12090231)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 3-week integrative neuromuscular training programme in 18 male Chinese national-team boxers improved bench press (ES=1.13), squat (ES=1.72), countermovement jump (ES=1.14), 400-m sprint (ES=1.26), 1-min hexagon jump (ES=1.73) and 3-min double-unders (ES=1.73), with NO significant change in 30-m sprint (p=0.593) or 3000-m run.
Effect/estimate: Large ES for strength/jump/400 m; no change in 30 m sprint or 3000 m run
Population: Elite male national-team boxers | level: Elite amateur (international) | sex: Male | age: Adult (~22.5 y)
Design: Single-group pre-post intervention (3 weeks) | n: n=18
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: No control group — 3-week pre-post gains of this magnitude in elite athletes are likely inflated by learning and testing familiarisation; male only; concurrent normal training uncontrolled.
PPBF implication: Note the null results are as informative as the positives: general endurance running (3000 m) did NOT improve and short sprint did NOT improve. Do not promise transfer to qualities the intervention did not move.
Source: Zhang et al. (2026). The effect of integrative neuromuscular training on physical fitness and punching performance in highly-trained male boxers. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2026.1810393)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A before-and-after controlled experiment in 37 elite Chinese female boxers applied integrative neuromuscular training 11 times per week for 3 weeks and reported significant improvements in baseline physical fitness measures including squat and bench press 1RM.
Effect/estimate: Significant pre-post improvements in fitness and striking tests
Population: Elite female boxers | level: Elite amateur (international) | sex: Female | age: Adult (~26 y)
Design: Before-and-after controlled experiment (3 weeks) | n: n=37
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: 11 sessions/week for 3 weeks is an extreme dose not transferable to a community programme; short duration; pre-post design; potential testing familiarisation.
PPBF implication: One of the few boxing physical-preparation studies in FEMALE athletes. Cite it when noting the female evidence gap — but the dose is not replicable at PPBF and must not be copied.
Source: Niu et al. (2024). Impact of three weeks of integrative neuromuscular training on the athletic performance of elite female boxers. PeerJ. (doi:10.7717/peerj.18311)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 20 studies (504 participants; 428 male, 76 female) found significant improvements in maximal dynamic and isometric strength, muscle power, flexibility and balance following strength training in Olympic combat sport athletes, with improvements also in sport-specific actions in judo, karate, fencing and boxing.
Effect/estimate: Significant improvements in strength, power, flexibility, balance
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: 428 male / 76 female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review (PRISMA, TESTEX quality appraisal) | n: 20 studies, 504 participants
Boxing-specific: Partly | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer, partly boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Only 15% of participants were female — the female evidence base is thin; heterogeneous protocols; no pooled effect size reported in the abstract; positive-result publication bias likely.
PPBF implication: Provides the evidentiary basis for including resistance training in PPBF programming at all levels — this directly contradicts the 'weights make you slow/muscle-bound' gym tradition.
Source: Cid-Calfucura et al. (2023). Effects of Strength Training on Physical Fitness of Olympic Combat Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review. Int J Environ Res Public Health. (doi:10.3390/ijerph20043516)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 18 amateur boxers (9 elite, 9 non-elite), peak torque of knee flexors and extensors was higher in the elite group at all angular velocities, with differences also in unilateral and bilateral ratios.
Effect/estimate: Elite > non-elite peak torque at 60, 180, 240 deg/s
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Elite vs non-elite amateur | sex: Both (5M/4F per group) | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional isokinetic comparison | n: n=18
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION: elite boxers being stronger does not show that getting stronger makes a boxer elite. Very small groups (n=9 per group); requires an isokinetic dynamometer unavailable to community gyms.
PPBF implication: Illustrates the discriminative-validity trap. SHADOW must not present cross-sectional level differences as development targets or as evidence that training a quality causes advancement.
Source: Zhou et al. (2022). Lower extremity isokinetic strength characteristics of amateur boxers. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2022.898126)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A parallel-group study in 29 right-handed orthodox-stance adolescent boxers compared 8 weeks of unilateral, bilateral and hybrid complex resistance training on straight-punch performance and dominant/non-dominant side adaptations.
Effect/estimate: Between-modality comparison of straight-punch performance and side-specific adaptation
Population: Adolescent boxers | level: Adolescent (level not fully specified) | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adolescent
Design: Three-arm parallel group training intervention (8 weeks) | n: n=29 (10/9/10)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Very small groups (~10 each) for a three-arm comparison; adolescent population with concurrent maturation; loads were set from bilateral 1RM, which complicates the unilateral-load comparison.
PPBF implication: Relevant to PPBF's adolescent lane and to the bilateral-asymmetry question inherent in orthodox/southpaw stance. Underpowered — treat as hypothesis-generating for a PPBF asymmetry study.
Source: Liu et al. (2025). Comparative effects of unilateral, bilateral, and hybrid combined resistance training on straight punch performance in adolescent boxers: a focus on dominant and non-dominant-side adaptations. Eur J Appl Physiol. (doi:10.1007/s00421-025-05913-z)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of 21 studies (422 effect sizes) reported mean effect sizes for strength development of 1.76 for strength training alone versus 1.44 for concurrent training, and for power 0.91 versus a lower concurrent value, indicating attenuation rather than abolition of strength/power adaptation when endurance training is added.
Effect/estimate: Strength ES: 1.76 (strength only) vs 1.44 (concurrent); hypertrophy 1.23 vs 0.85
Population: Trained and untrained adults | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Meta-analysis | n: 21 studies, 422 effect sizes
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / general-population transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing-specific; predominantly male; the modality, duration and frequency of endurance training moderate the effect and are heterogeneous; older meta-analysis.
PPBF implication: Directly addresses the 'roadwork kills your power' claim: interference is measurable but partial. PPBF should sequence rather than eliminate — schedule high-quality strength/power work away from high-volume aerobic sessions.
Source: Wilson et al. (2012). Concurrent training: a meta-analysis examining interference of aerobic and resistance exercises. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31823a3e2d)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis examined sex-specific and training-status differences in strength, power, hypertrophy and VO2max adaptations to concurrent strength and endurance training in healthy adults aged 18-50.
Effect/estimate: Sex- and training-status-moderated adaptations
Population: Healthy trained and untrained adults | level: Mixed | sex: Male and female (explicit comparison) | age: 18-50 y
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis (Cochrane risk of bias) | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / general-population transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing-specific; the female evidence base within concurrent-training research is smaller than the male; heterogeneous interventions.
PPBF implication: SHADOW must not apply one concurrent-training rule to all athletes. Sex and training status are moderators that belong in the programming context model.
Source: Huiberts et al. (2023). Concurrent Strength and Endurance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on the Impact of Sex and Training Status. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01943-9)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of combining endurance training with heavy or explosive strength training reports that running economy is improved by combined training with either heavy or explosive strength training, and that concurrent endurance and heavy strength training can increase velocity/power at VO2max or time to exhaustion at those intensities.
Effect/estimate: Improved running economy; increased Vmax/Wmax or time to exhaustion
Population: Endurance-trained runners and cyclists | level: Trained endurance athletes | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Review of intervention studies | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (endurance athletes, not boxers)
LIMITATIONS: Endurance-athlete population, not boxers; the outcome (running economy) is not a boxing performance outcome; transfer to a 9-minute intermittent striking task is an inference.
PPBF implication: Evidence-vs-tradition entry: strength training does not degrade endurance qualities in endurance athletes. FLAG: this rests on transfer from a non-boxing population.
Source: Rønnestad et al. (2013). Optimizing strength training for running and cycling endurance performance: A review. Scand J Med Sci Sports. (doi:10.1111/sms.12104)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of weighted-vest sprint training (11 studies) found vest loads of 5-40% body mass acutely increased sprint times (4.1-16.9%) and decreased velocity, horizontal force, maximal power and flight times while increasing contact times; longitudinal studies (5.6-18.9% body mass, 3-7 weeks) showed small improvements in velocity (1.2-1.3%) and times, with the authors noting optimum load and volume remain to be established.
Effect/estimate: Acute: sprint times +4.1-16.9%; longitudinal: velocity +1.2-1.3%
Population: Sprint-trained and athletic populations | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 11 studies (6 acute, 5 longitudinal)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (sprint running, not boxing)
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing; not footwear; the acute effects are large and negative; longitudinal effects are small and the optimum dose is explicitly unestablished; loading distribution of a vest differs from that of heavy boots.
PPBF implication: Closest available evidence for 'running in heavy boots'. It shows external loading acutely degrades movement quality with only small, uncertain longitudinal gain — and NO study addresses distal (foot) loading in boxing. Classify boots as tradition with an evidence-transfer caveat.
Source: Macadam et al. (2019). Acute and longitudinal effects of weighted vest training on sprint-running performance: a systematic review. Sports Biomech. (doi:10.1080/14763141.2019.1607542)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review, meta-analysis and multivariate meta-regression of 189 studies representing 6654 adults examined the frequency, intensity and volume of static stretching required to maximise flexibility, and whether this is moderated by muscle group, age, sex, training status and baseline flexibility.
Effect/estimate: Dose-response for flexibility established across acute and chronic protocols
Population: Adults | level: General and trained adults | sex: 61% male | age: Adults (mean ~27 y)
Design: Systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression | n: 189 studies, 6654 adults
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General-population transfer
LIMITATIONS: Flexibility is the outcome — NOT performance and NOT injury prevention; not boxing-specific; the moderator analyses are observational within the meta-regression.
PPBF implication: PPBF may prescribe static stretching to increase range of motion with a good evidence base, but must NOT claim it prevents injury or improves punching. Separate the mobility goal from the performance goal in the app.
Source: Ingram et al. (2024). Optimising the Dose of Static Stretching to Improve Flexibility: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Multivariate Meta-regression. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02143-9)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression (28 studies) found cold-water immersion superior to other recovery methods for recovery from muscle soreness and similar to other methods for recovery of muscular power and flexibility in physically active populations.
Effect/estimate: CWI superior for soreness; similar to other methods for power and flexibility recovery
Population: Physically active participants | level: Physically active / athletes | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression | n: 28 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / general transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing-specific; the outcomes are short-term recovery markers, not competitive performance; long-term interference with strength adaptation was not the focus; predominantly male.
PPBF implication: If PPBF offers cold exposure it should be framed as soreness management around competition, not as a routine training adjunct. Ice baths for minors require guardian consent and supervision — route to the safety lane.
Source: Moore et al. (2022). Effects of Cold-Water Immersion Compared with Other Recovery Modalities on Athletic Performance Following Acute Strenuous Exercise in Physically Active Participants: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01800-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A separate systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression compared cold-water immersion with passive recovery on athletic performance, perceptual measures and creatine kinase after a single bout of strenuous exercise, dividing studies into eccentric-exercise and high-intensity-exercise subgroups.
Effect/estimate: Subgroup-dependent effects on performance, perception and CK
Population: Physically active participants | level: Physically active / athletes | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / general transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing; heterogeneous protocols (temperature, duration, immersion depth); single-bout designs cannot address chronic adaptation.
PPBF implication: Second source confirming cold-water immersion evidence is context-dependent. SHADOW should present recovery modalities with their evidence class visible, not as a checklist.
Source: Moore et al. (2022). text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review located 36 studies examining the validity and reliability of the session-RPE method using the modified CR-10, and reported that these studies confirmed the validity, good reliability and internal consistency of session-RPE across several sports.
Effect/estimate: Validity and reliability confirmed across sports; influencing factors identified
Population: Athletes across multiple sports | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Male and female | age: Youth to adult
Design: Review of validation studies | n: 36 validation studies
Boxing-specific: No (multi-sport, includes combat sports elsewhere in the literature) | transfer status: Other-sport transfer with combat-sport support
LIMITATIONS: A review rather than a meta-analysis; session-RPE is influenced by factors including exercise mode, intensity distribution and individual characteristics, which the review itself flags; correlations with objective load vary by modality.
PPBF implication: FOUNDATION of the PPBF internal load model: sRPE x duration is the defensible primary internal load metric. It is cheap, requires no hardware, and fits a nonprofit budget.
Source: Haddad et al. (2017). Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring: Validity, Ecological Usefulness, and Influencing Factors. Front Neurosci. (doi:10.3389/fnins.2017.00612)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A study comparing player and coach ratings concluded that player session-RPE is a more valid tool than coaches' ratings for monitoring internal training load.
Effect/estimate: Player sRPE outperformed coach rating
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Trained athletes | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adolescent/adult
Design: Validation comparison study | n: Single-cohort study
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Single study in a team-sport context; boxing has a different coach-athlete observation relationship (one-on-one padwork gives coaches better visibility than a team field session).
PPBF implication: PPBF should collect sRPE FROM THE ATHLETE, not have the coach estimate it. This is a concrete app requirement: an athlete-entered RPE field, with coach observation stored separately as a different data type.
Source: Lupo et al. (2019). Player Session Rating of Perceived Exertion: A More Valid Tool Than Coaches' Ratings to Monitor Internal Training Load in Elite Youth Female Basketball. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2019-0248)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Session rating of perceived exertion has been validated for quantifying internal training load in adolescent athletes, with a separate study also supporting the validity of retrospective session-RPE in youth athletes.
Effect/estimate: Acceptable validity for internal load quantification in youth
Population: Adolescent athletes | level: Youth/adolescent | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent
Design: Validation study | n: Adolescent cohort
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth
LIMITATIONS: Youth comprehension of RPE scales varies with age and cognitive development; scale choice and anchoring instructions matter; rating timing affects the value; not boxing-specific.
PPBF implication: PPBF may use sRPE with adolescents but must standardise the scale, anchoring script and collection timing (consistent post-session delay). Youngest bands may need a pictorial scale.
Source: Mann et al. (2019). The Validation of Session Rating of Perceived Exertion for Quantifying Internal Training Load in Adolescent Distance Runners. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2018-0120)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Session-RPE has been validated for quantifying training load in karate athletes and used to quantify the load of different youth taekwondo training sessions.
Effect/estimate: Acceptable validity/reliability in combat-sport sessions
Population: Karate and youth taekwondo athletes | level: Trained combat athletes | sex: Mixed | age: Youth and adult
Design: Validation studies | n: Small combat-sport cohorts
Boxing-specific: Partly (combat sports, not boxing) | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Karate and taekwondo differ from boxing in session structure and contact; small samples; no boxing-specific sRPE validation study was located in this search.
PPBF implication: Closest combat-sport validation available. GAP: no boxing-specific sRPE validation was found — this is a concrete PPBF validation study opportunity.
Source: Tabben et al. (2015). Validity and reliability of the session-RPE method for quantifying training load in karate athletes. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. (PMID:25908242)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 56 original studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being found that subjective and objective measures generally did NOT correlate, and that subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.
Effect/estimate: Subjective measures superior in sensitivity and consistency to objective measures
Population: Athletes | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Male and female | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 56 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / general athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not boxing-specific; 'superior' refers to sensitivity to load, not to predicting injury or performance; subjective measures are vulnerable to reporting bias, especially where athletes fear being withheld from sparring or selection.
PPBF implication: Strongly supports a low-cost PPBF wellness questionnaire as a primary monitoring tool over expensive objective kit. BUT the app must protect against athletes gaming reports to secure sparring — see governance section of the load model.
Source: Saw et al. (2015). Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094758)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An international consensus statement arising from the 2016 Doha conference on monitoring athlete training loads set out a shared conceptual framework for internal and external load monitoring for coaches, sport-science and sport-medicine staff.
Effect/estimate: Framework, not an effect estimate
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: All
Design: Consensus statement | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete framework
LIMITATIONS: Consensus statements reflect expert agreement rather than pooled data; the field has moved on since 2017, particularly regarding ACWR criticism; not boxing-specific.
PPBF implication: Adopt the internal/external load distinction as the PPBF data-model backbone: external = what was done (rounds, sets, minutes, punches counted); internal = how it was experienced (sRPE, wellness).
Source: Bourdon et al. (2017). Monitoring Athlete Training Loads: Consensus Statement. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/IJSPP.2017-0208)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of methods for monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes surveyed the available internal and external load monitoring tools and their interpretation.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive synthesis
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Review | n: Multiple tools reviewed
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete framework
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review; tool availability and validity have both changed since publication; not boxing-specific.
PPBF implication: Background reference for the PPBF monitoring rationale. Not a source of thresholds.
Source: Halson (2014). Monitoring training load to understand fatigue in athletes. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-014-0253-z)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 25 experienced athletes, illnesses and minor injuries were related to indices of training load, monotony (daily mean divided by standard deviation) and strain (load multiplied by monotony), with a high percentage of illnesses accounted for when individuals exceeded INDIVIDUALLY identifiable training thresholds, mostly related to strain.
Effect/estimate: Illness incidence related to individually identified strain thresholds
Population: Experienced athletes | level: Trained | sex: Not specified | age: Adult
Design: Observational study | n: n=25
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Small n; observational; the thresholds were INDIVIDUAL, not population thresholds — a critical caveat routinely lost in secondary citation; illness is self- or coach-reported; 1998 study.
PPBF implication: PPBF may compute monotony and strain as DESCRIPTIVE trend variables. It must NOT apply a population monotony/strain cut-off: the original evidence is explicitly individual-threshold based. Any PPBF threshold is an ASSUMPTION requiring local validation.
Source: Foster (1998). Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1097/00005768-199807000-00023)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Studies tracking training load, monotony and strain across seasons in team-sport athletes have described variations across the competitive year and examined dose-response relationships with aerobic fitness.
Effect/estimate: Seasonal variation in monotony and strain described
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Trained/professional | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Longitudinal observational | n: Season-long cohorts
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Observational; team-sport calendars differ fundamentally from boxing's bout-driven calendar; no causal claim supported.
PPBF implication: PPBF should baseline its OWN monotony distribution across a season before interpreting any value as high or low.
Source: Clemente et al. (2019). Variations of training load, monotony, and strain and dose-response relationships with maximal aerobic speed, maximal oxygen uptake, and isokinetic strength in professional soccer players. PLoS One. (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0225522)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine argued that mathematical coupling inherent in the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculation causes spurious correlation, because the acute load appears in both the numerator and the denominator of the chronic load.
Effect/estimate: Demonstration of spurious correlation arising from coupling
Population: Methodological (statistical critique) | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Statistical/methodological critique | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Methodological — applies to any sport
LIMITATIONS: A methodological argument rather than an empirical outcome study; the practical magnitude of the resulting bias is itself debated (see A5-046).
PPBF implication: PPBF MUST NOT ship a coupled ACWR as a risk indicator. If any ratio is displayed at all it must be uncoupled and labelled CONTESTED, with no threshold-based action attached.
Source: Lolli et al. (2017). Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098110)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Using training and competition workload data from international-level basketball and weightlifting athletes before Olympic qualifying tournaments, a commentary found that although some differences existed between coupled and uncoupled chronic load and ACWR data, the effect sizes of those differences were almost all trivial (g=0.04-0.21), with ACWR-to-uncoupled-ACWR correlations of r=0.88-0.99.
Effect/estimate: Coupled vs uncoupled differences g=0.04-0.21; r=0.88-0.99
Population: International-level basketball and weightlifting athletes | level: International | sex: Not specified | age: Adult
Design: Case-study commentary using real monitoring data | n: Two athlete groups
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: A case study from two sports, not a general proof; being numerically similar does not resolve the underlying inferential problem the coupling critique raises; the debate remains unresolved.
PPBF implication: Present BOTH sides in the PPBF evidence ledger. The existence of an active methodological dispute is itself the reason SHADOW must not automate any ACWR-driven decision.
Source: Coyne et al. (2019). Does Mathematical Coupling Matter to the Acute to Chronic Workload Ratio? A Case Study From Elite Sport. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2018-0874)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Systematic reviews of the acute:chronic workload ratio and injury risk report substantial heterogeneity between studies in the variables studied (e.g. total distance vs high-speed running), the ratio cut-offs analysed (1.50-1.80 vs >=1.50), and the reference groups used (0.80-1.20 vs <=0.85), leading to caution about utilising ACWR for external load.
Effect/estimate: High between-study variability in variables, ratios and reference groups
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Professional/elite team sports | sex: Almost exclusively male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 27 studies (quality scores 48.2-64.3%)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (team sports)
LIMITATIONS: Study quality scores were modest (48.2-64.3%); no boxing or combat-sport data; the heterogeneity means no single threshold is supportable.
PPBF implication: DEFINITIVE for PPBF: there is NO validated ACWR threshold to hand the product. Any number in a PPBF UI would be invented. Do not ship a 'danger zone'.
Source: Maupin et al. (2020). The Relationship Between Acute: Chronic Workload Ratios and Injury Risk in Sports: A Systematic Review. Open Access J Sports Med. (doi:10.2147/OAJSM.S231405)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 20 studies comprising 2375 injuries from 1234 athletes examining the ACWR and time-loss injury risk in adult elite team sports reported that all participants were male, with a mean age of 24 years.
Effect/estimate: Population characteristic: 100% male, mean age 24
Population: Adult elite team-sport athletes | level: Professional/elite | sex: ALL MALE | age: Adult (mean 24 y)
Design: Systematic review (modified Downs and Black appraisal) | n: 20 studies; 1234 athletes; 2375 injuries
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (male adult team sport only)
LIMITATIONS: The entire evidence base underpinning ACWR in this review is male, adult and professional team sport. There is no female, no youth and no combat-sport evidence in it.
PPBF implication: This single fact disqualifies ACWR for a PPBF population that includes youth, women, novices and adaptive athletes. State it explicitly in the app's methods note if ACWR is ever discussed.
Source: Andrade et al. (2020). Is the Acute: Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR) Associated with Risk of Time-Loss Injury in Professional Team Sports? A Systematic Review of Methodology, Variables and Injury Risk in Practical Situations. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01308-6)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 22 articles (median Newcastle-Ottawa Scale score 8, range 5-9) examining the association between injury occurrence and the ACWR, using rolling-average and exponentially weighted moving-average models, reported findings supporting an association between the ACWR and injury in team sports.
Effect/estimate: Reported association supported; best application method not resolved
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Professional/elite team sports | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 22 articles
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Reports association, NOT causation; even this supportive review did not resolve which calculation method should be used; observational designs throughout; the coupling critique (A5-045) applies to the underlying studies.
PPBF implication: CONTESTED PRACTICE: reviews disagree. PPBF's position must be to log the inputs (acute and chronic load) and let a qualified human interpret, rather than to compute a ratio verdict.
Source: Griffin et al. (2020). The Association Between the Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio and Injury and its Application in Team Sports: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01218-2)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of methodological variation in ACWR research in elite male football players found twelve eligible articles, judged all studies to be of poor quality, and documented heterogeneity in workload measures, running-intensity zone thresholds, exposure type, data collection timing, ratio windows (1:2, 1:3, 1:4 weeks) and statistical analysis.
Effect/estimate: All studies rated poor quality; extensive methodological heterogeneity
Population: Elite male football players | level: Elite professional | sex: Male only | age: Adult
Design: Systematic methodological review | n: 12 articles
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Single-sport (football) review; 'poor quality' is the reviewers' own overall appraisal; does not itself test the ACWR-injury relationship.
PPBF implication: Closes the case for PPBF: even within one well-resourced sport the ACWR literature is of poor quality and non-comparable. ACWR is CONTESTED PRACTICE and must be labelled as such wherever it appears.
Source: Wang et al. (2020). A systematic review on methodological variation in acute:chronic workload research in elite male football players. Sci Med Footb. (doi:10.1080/24733938.2020.1765007)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] An influential British Journal of Sports Medicine paper framed a training-injury prevention paradox, arguing that appropriately high chronic training loads may be protective and that rapid load spikes are the risk, popularising load-ratio thinking in applied sport.
Effect/estimate: Conceptual framing
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Elite/professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Narrative/position paper | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: This is a conceptual/position paper, not primary evidence; it has been extensively criticised in the subsequent methodological literature (A5-045, A5-047, A5-050); widely cited in ways that overstate its evidentiary weight.
PPBF implication: Include in the PPBF ledger explicitly as a HIGH-CITATION, CONTESTED source so that SHADOW's source-reliability engine does not treat citation count as authority.
Source: Gabbett (2016). The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder?. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095788)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The International Olympic Committee convened an expert group and published a consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury, providing guidelines for the prescription of training and competition load and for the monitoring of training, competition and psychological load, athlete well-being and injury.
Effect/estimate: Guidelines, not effect estimates
Population: Elite athletes | level: Elite | sex: Male and female | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Consensus statement | n: IOC expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: Consensus reflects expert judgement; published 2016 and predates much of the ACWR methodological critique; the guidance is general rather than sport-specific.
PPBF implication: Authoritative anchor for the PPBF load-monitoring policy. Cite for the PRINCIPLE (monitor load, well-being and injury together) not for any numeric threshold.
Source: Soligard et al. (2016). How much is too much? (Part 1) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of injury. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096581)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A companion IOC consensus statement addressed the relationship between load — including rapid changes in training and competition load, calendar congestion, psychological load and travel — and the risk of illness and overtraining, with practical guidelines for load management.
Effect/estimate: Guidelines, not effect estimates
Population: Elite athletes | level: Elite | sex: Male and female | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Consensus statement | n: IOC expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: Consensus-level evidence; 2016 publication; general rather than boxing-specific; the authors themselves identified urgent research priorities, indicating the evidence base was incomplete.
PPBF implication: Supports logging illness alongside injury in the PPBF model. Illness is an under-collected but cheap and informative monitoring signal.
Source: Schwellnus et al. (2016). How much is too much? (Part 2) International Olympic Committee consensus statement on load in sport and risk of illness. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096572)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The joint European College of Sport Science / American College of Sports Medicine consensus statement distinguishes functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome, notes that the distinction between non-functional overreaching and overtraining syndrome is very difficult and depends on clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis, and states there is no scientific evidence to confirm or refute the suggestion that overtraining-syndrome symptoms are more severe.
Effect/estimate: No validated diagnostic marker; exclusion diagnosis required
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Joint consensus statement (ECSS/ACSM) | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: Consensus level; explicitly acknowledges the absence of a validated diagnostic marker; the boundary between overreaching and overtraining syndrome is not measurable by any field tool.
PPBF implication: HARD BOUNDARY: SHADOW must NEVER output 'overtrained' or 'overtraining syndrome'. That is an exclusion diagnosis requiring a physician. SHADOW may only surface descriptive patterns (e.g. 'load rising while wellness declines for N sessions') and route to a qualified human.
Source: Meeusen et al. (2013). Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1249/MSS.0b013e318279a10a)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A narrative review and 2021 expert consensus reported that elite athletes are particularly susceptible to sleep inadequacies characterised by habitual short sleep (under 7 hours/night) and poor sleep quality, that performance is reduced by a night or more without sleep while the effect of partial sleep restriction over 1-3 nights remains unclear, and that habitually sleeping under 7 hours/night increases susceptibility to respiratory infection in the wider population.
Effect/estimate: Habitual short sleep <7 h/night; respiratory infection susceptibility (general population evidence)
Population: Elite athletes | level: Elite | sex: Male and female (authors note a lack of females in the literature) | age: Adult
Design: Narrative review with expert consensus | n: Expert panel + literature review
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus; infection evidence transferred from general population
LIMITATIONS: The authors explicitly note inadequate experimental control, a lack of female participants and questions about sleep-assessment tool validity in the athlete sleep literature; the infection link is transferred from non-athlete populations.
PPBF implication: Sleep is a high-yield, zero-cost PPBF monitoring target. Collect self-reported sleep duration and quality. Do NOT set a PPBF-specific sleep threshold beyond flagging habitual short sleep for coach conversation.
Source: Walsh et al. (2020). Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102025)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic and meta-analytical review of 227 outcome measures classified performance tasks into anaerobic power, speed/power endurance, high-intensity interval exercise, strength, endurance, strength-endurance and skill categories, comparing normal sleep (over 6 h in any 24 h) with sleep loss (6 h or less), and examined sleep-loss protocol, time of day and upper- versus lower-body strength as moderators.
Effect/estimate: Impairments varied by exercise category and by time of day
Population: Adults including athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression | n: 227 outcome measures
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General / other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory sleep-restriction protocols do not replicate real athlete sleep patterns; predominantly male; effects differ by task type, so a single 'sleep loss harms performance' statement oversimplifies.
PPBF implication: Supports flagging acute sleep loss before high-skill or high-contact sessions. PPBF coaching translation: consider reducing sparring intensity after reported poor sleep — as a coach decision, not an automated gate.
Source: Craven et al. (2022). Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01706-y)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 11 male collegiate basketball players, a 5-7 week sleep extension period targeting a minimum 10 hours in bed increased objective nightly sleep by 110.9 minutes and produced faster timed sprints and improved shooting accuracy compared with baseline.
Effect/estimate: Sleep +110.9 ± 79.7 min; faster sprint; improved shooting accuracy
Population: Collegiate basketball players | level: Collegiate | sex: Male | age: Young adult (~19 y)
Design: Single-group extended baseline-then-intervention study | n: n=11
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: n=11, male, single sport, no control group over a long study period during which normal training progression could account for gains; 10 h in bed is not achievable for most working or school-attending athletes.
PPBF implication: Frequently over-cited. PPBF may encourage sleep opportunity but MUST NOT promise a performance gain from a specific sleep duration. Do not put a sleep-hours target in the app as if validated.
Source: Mah et al. (2011). The effects of sleep extension on the athletic performance of collegiate basketball players. Sleep. (doi:10.5665/SLEEP.1132)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a survey of 112 adolescent athletes (mean age 15 y) with retrospective injury-record review, multivariate analysis found hours of sleep per night and school grade to be the best independent predictors of injury, with athletes sleeping under 8 hours per night 1.7 times (95% CI 1.0-3.0, p=0.04) more likely to have had an injury.
Effect/estimate: OR 1.7 (95% CI 1.0-3.0) for <8 h sleep
Population: Adolescent athletes | level: School athletes | sex: 54 male / 58 female | age: 12-18 y (mean 15)
Design: Cross-sectional survey with retrospective record review | n: n=112
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth
LIMITATIONS: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION — cross-sectional with retrospective injury recall; the confidence interval's lower bound touches 1.0, so the association is marginal; self-reported sleep; single school.
PPBF implication: Cite carefully. PPBF may raise sleep as a modifiable factor with adolescents and guardians, but must not tell a family that short sleep caused an injury.
Source: Milewski et al. (2014). Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes. J Pediatr Orthop. (doi:10.1097/BPO.0000000000000151)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of sleep in teenage athletes (13-19 y) concluded that few studies exist on the effects of disordered sleep in this population and noted a paucity of evidence-based recommendations to promote sleep quantity and quality in athletes of this age.
Effect/estimate: No pooled estimate; explicit evidence paucity
Population: Teenage athletes | level: Youth | sex: Mixed | age: 13-19 y
Design: Narrative review (level 4 evidence) | n: Literature review
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth
LIMITATIONS: The review itself is level 4; it documents an evidence gap rather than filling it.
PPBF implication: Honest position for PPBF's guardian-facing material: sleep matters, the youth-specific evidence base is thin, and PPBF should not present numeric sleep prescriptions to families as established science.
Source: Coel et al. (2022). Sleep and the Young Athlete. Sports Health. (doi:10.1177/19417381221108732)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 25 intervention studies published 2011-2021 examined sleep hygiene, naps and other sleep interventions in athletes, requiring at least one objective performance or recovery outcome.
Effect/estimate: Heterogeneous interventions and outcomes
Population: Athletes (individual and team sports) | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 25 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous interventions prevent pooling; short intervention durations; adherence rarely reported; not boxing-specific.
PPBF implication: Sleep hygiene education is a low-risk, low-cost PPBF intervention worth piloting with a defined outcome, but the expected effect size is not established.
Source: Cunha et al. (2023). The Impact of Sleep Interventions on Athletic Performance: A Systematic Review. Sports Med Open. (doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00599-z)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review and consensus statement by 26 researchers and clinicians on travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes concluded that evidence on optimal assessment and management is lacking, which restricted the strength of the recommendations possible, and provided fundamental principles and travel toolboxes for pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight strategies.
Effect/estimate: Principles only; the panel explicitly noted weak evidence
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Review and consensus statement | n: 26-member expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus
LIMITATIONS: The consensus panel states directly that the lack of evidence restricts recommendation strength; no combat-sport-specific data.
PPBF implication: For PPBF, travel is mostly regional (short trips). Log travel as a context flag on session and competition records rather than applying an unvalidated jet-lag adjustment.
Source: Janse van Rensburg et al. (2021). Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01502-0)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of 27 studies in competitive athletes found the optimal strategy to be a taper of 2 weeks' duration (overall effect 0.59 ± 0.33, p<0.001) achieved by decreasing training volume while examining intensity, frequency, taper pattern and duration as independent variables.
Effect/estimate: Overall taper effect 0.59 ± 0.33 (p<0.001); 2-week duration optimal
Population: Competitive athletes | level: Competitive | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Meta-analysis | n: 27 of 182 screened studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (predominantly endurance and swimming)
LIMITATIONS: The underlying studies are predominantly endurance sports, NOT intermittent combat sports; predominantly male; 2007 publication; a 2-week taper conflicts with the frequent, short-notice matchmaking common in amateur boxing.
PPBF implication: PPBF should implement a taper TEMPLATE (reduce volume, maintain intensity) and NOT a fixed 2-week rule, because amateur boxing bout notice is often shorter. Flag as transfer from endurance sport.
Source: Bosquet et al. (2007). Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1249/mss.0b013e31806010e0)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies in team-sport athletes found limited evidence of a moderate taper-induced improvement in repeated sprint ability (SMD 0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.55, I2=0%) and moderate evidence of moderate increases in maximal power (SMD 0.44, 95% CI 0.32-0.56, I2=15%), change-of-direction speed (SMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.60, I2=28%) and maximal oxygen uptake.
Effect/estimate: RSA SMD 0.41; max power SMD 0.44; COD SMD 0.38
Population: Team-sport athletes | level: Competitive team sport | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 14 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (team sports, intermittent — closer to boxing than endurance)
LIMITATIONS: Team sports, not combat sports; predominantly male; only 14 studies; the authors themselves describe the RSA evidence as limited.
PPBF implication: Better transfer anchor than the endurance taper literature because the sports are intermittent. Supports maintaining power qualities through a PPBF fight-week taper.
Source: Vachon et al. (2020). Effects of tapering on neuromuscular and metabolic fitness in team sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Sport Sci. (doi:10.1080/17461391.2020.1736183)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies in endurance athletes found significant improvements in time-trial performance (SMD -0.45) and time to exhaustion (SMD 1.28) but no improvement in maximal oxygen consumption or movement economy, with subgroup analysis showing that reducing training volume by 41-60% while maintaining intensity and frequency, over durations of up to 7 days, 8-14 days or 15-21 days, significantly improved time-trial performance.
Effect/estimate: TT SMD -0.45; TTE SMD 1.28; volume reduction 41-60% effective
Population: Endurance athletes | level: Competitive endurance | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 14 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (endurance, not boxing)
LIMITATIONS: Endurance sport outcomes (time trial, time to exhaustion) are not boxing performance; the 41-60% volume reduction figure comes from endurance protocols and has NOT been tested in boxing.
PPBF implication: The 41-60% volume reduction is the only published range with meta-analytic support, but transferring it to boxing is an ASSUMPTION. If PPBF uses it, label it: PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER — ASSUMPTION, REQUIRES VALIDATION.
Source: Wang et al. (2023). Effects of tapering on performance in endurance athletes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One. (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0282838)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies produced pooled amateur boxing competition injury incidence estimates of 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and a training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0); the most commonly injured region was the head and neck in competition (median 72%) and the upper limb in training (median 49%).
Effect/estimate: Competition 54.7/1000 AE (95% CI 33.8-88.4); 6.8/1000 min (4.2-10.9); training 1.3/1000 h (0.2-7.0)
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Male and female (studies vary) | age: Adult predominantly
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Confidence intervals are very wide, especially for training (0.2-7.0), reflecting between-study heterogeneity in injury definitions and exposure recording; female data sparse; underlying studies span decades and rule eras.
PPBF implication: PRIMARY reference incidence for the PPBF injury model. Note that competition is where head/neck injury concentrates and training is where upper-limb injury concentrates — different prevention targets for different contexts.
Source: Alevras et al. (2022). Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. (doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 epidemiology studies published 2000-2021 calculated a pooled overall injury incidence rate of 223.9 per 1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4) and 13.0 per 1000 minutes (95% CI 8.9-17.1), with professional boxing showing a higher rate than the pooled figure.
Effect/estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers (157.5-290.4); 13.0/1000 min (8.9-17.1); professional rate higher
Population: Amateur and professional boxers | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 14 studies (11/14 moderate quality)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Only moderate study quality in most included studies; incidence denominators (per 1000 boxers vs per 1000 minutes) are not interchangeable and are frequently confused in secondary citation; heterogeneous injury definitions.
PPBF implication: Establishes that professional injury rates exceed amateur. Supports PPBF treating the professional lane as a distinct risk context requiring different documentation.
Source: Mao et al. (2023). Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. Orthop J Sports Med. (doi:10.1177/23259671221127669)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Five-year prospective surveillance of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad (66 boxers, 2005-2009) with injuries recorded by the team doctor and physiotherapist found the hand was the most-injured location overall, in training and in competition; the total competition injury rate was 828 per 1000 hours, hand injury rate in competition was 302 per 1000 hours, more injuries occurred in training than competition, and the incidence of concussion was comparatively low.
Effect/estimate: Total competition 828/1000 h; hand 302/1000 h; concussion comparatively low
Population: Elite amateur boxers (GB squad) | level: Elite amateur | sex: Both (squad composition) | age: Adult
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance (5 years) | n: 66 boxers
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Single national squad — an elite, well-medically-supported population that may under-represent community-gym risk; medically diagnosed injuries only, so self-managed injuries are missed; per-1000-hour competition rates look alarming but competition hours are very small denominators.
PPBF implication: MOST ACTIONABLE injury finding for PPBF: hands and wrists are the dominant injury target, and MORE injuries occur in training than competition. Prioritise hand/wrist protection, wrapping quality and bag-work technique in the prevention lane.
Source: Loosemore et al. (2015). Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Longitudinal prospective surveillance of the Great Britain boxing squad from 2005 to 2012 found finger carpometacarpal instability and metacarpophalangeal joint extensor hood/capsule sprain ('boxer's knuckle') significantly more common than other diagnoses; the competition hand/wrist injury rate was 347 per 1000 hours while the estimated training rate was under 0.5 per 1000 hours, with a similar absolute number of injuries occurring in training and competition despite far greater training hours.
Effect/estimate: Competition hand/wrist 347/1000 h; training <0.5/1000 h; similar absolute counts
Population: Elite amateur boxers (GB squad) | level: Elite amateur | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance (2005-2012) | n: GB squad
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Single elite squad; estimated (not directly measured) training exposure hours; specialist diagnosis may not be available in a community setting.
PPBF implication: Concrete PPBF prevention target: boxer's knuckle and CMC instability. Build a hand/wrist symptom flag into the observation intake, routed to a clinician — never self-diagnosed by the app.
Source: Loosemore et al. (2016). Hand and Wrist Injuries in Elite Boxing: A Longitudinal Prospective Study (2005-2012) of the Great Britain Olympic Boxing Squad. Hand (N Y). (doi:10.1177/1558944716642756)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A one-year prospective cohort of 33 amateur and 14 professional boxers in Victoria, Australia found 21 injuries, most to the head region (71%) with concussion the most common individual injury (33%), and an overall injury rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing, with the authors concluding that boxing's acute injury rates were comparable to and often lower than other contact and non-contact sports given the high training exposure.
Effect/estimate: 2.0 injuries/1000 h overall; 71% head region; 33% of injuries were concussion
Population: Amateur and professional boxers | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: 18+
Design: Prospective cohort (1 year) | n: 47 boxers; 21 injuries
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Very small cohort (21 injuries total) producing a wide underlying uncertainty; the 'comparable to other sports' conclusion applies to ACUTE injury rate per hour only and says nothing about cumulative head-impact exposure; single Australian state.
PPBF implication: Important nuance: per-hour acute injury rate is not the main safety concern in boxing — cumulative head impact is. PPBF messaging to guardians must not use the low per-hour rate to imply overall low risk.
Source: Zazryn et al. (2006). A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsm.2006.025924)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective cohort of 545 professional boxers across 907 fights over 8.5 years recorded 214 injuries, corresponding to 23.6 injuries per 100 professional fights, with the majority being lacerations to the head and face, and with increasing age and increasing number of fights both significant predictors of injury.
Effect/estimate: 23.6 injuries per 100 fights; age and bout count predicted injury
Population: Professional boxers | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male (gender examined as a variable) | age: 18-43 y
Design: Retrospective cohort (8.5 years) | n: 545 boxers; 907 fights; 214 injuries
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective, based on a commission fight-statistics database with possible incomplete data entry (the authors note this); physician-reported bout injuries only, so training injuries are absent; single jurisdiction (Victoria, Australia) — rules and reporting differ elsewhere.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF tracking cumulative career bout count as a persistent athlete-record field. Age and accumulated bouts are administrative facts SHADOW can surface — the medical implication remains a physician's call.
Source: Zazryn et al. (2009). Injury rates and risk factors in competitive professional boxing. Clin J Sport Med. (doi:10.1097/JSM.0b013e31818f1582)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A prospective cohort using IOC injury surveillance across Beijing 2008, London 2012 and Rio 2016 (7712 athlete exposures) found an overall competition injury incidence of 7.8 per 1000 minutes (95% CI 7.0-8.7), with boxing at 9.2 (95% CI 7.6-10.9) significantly higher than wrestling at 4.8 (3.6-6.2); the proportion of injuries causing more than 7 days' absence was LOWER in boxing (21.0%) than wrestling (39.6%), judo (35.9%) or taekwondo (32.5%); there was no difference in injury risk by sex, weight category or tournament round, but losing athletes had a rate ratio of 3.59 (95% CI 2.68-4.79) versus their winning opponents.
Effect/estimate: Boxing 9.2/1000 min; no sex difference; losers RR 3.59 (2.68-4.79)
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Olympic elite | sex: Male and female (sex compared explicitly) | age: Adult
Design: Prospective cohort using standardised IOC surveillance | n: 7712 athlete exposures across 3 Games
Boxing-specific: Yes (boxing is a comparison arm) | transfer status: Boxing-specific within a multi-sport study
LIMITATIONS: Competition injuries only — training injuries not captured; Olympic-level athletes; the loser/winner rate ratio is associational and confounded by the fact that being outclassed both causes injury and causes losing.
PPBF implication: Two PPBF-relevant facts: (1) no sex difference in competition injury risk at this level, and (2) boxing injuries are frequent but comparatively LESS time-loss severe than other combat sports. Use both to counter over- and under-statement of risk to guardians.
Source: Lystad et al. (2020). Injury incidence, severity and profile in Olympic combat sports: a comparative analysis of 7712 athlete exposures from three consecutive Olympic Games. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2020-102958)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research in Olympic combat sport (9 studies, most at moderate risk of bias) provided level 1/2b evidence that the most frequently injured areas in boxing were the head/face (45.8%), wrist (12.0%) and lower back (7.8%), and noted that heterogeneity in injury severity classification and inconsistency in exposure measures prevented direct cross-sport comparison of severity or incidence.
Effect/estimate: Boxing: head/face 45.8%, wrist 12.0%, lower back 7.8%
Population: Elite combat athletes | level: Elite | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review of prospective studies | n: 9 studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific within multi-sport review
LIMITATIONS: Most included studies had moderate risk of bias; the authors state that heterogeneous definitions prevented cross-sport comparison; body-region proportions are not incidence rates.
PPBF implication: Adds LOWER BACK to the PPBF prevention target list alongside hand/wrist and head/face — a region often ignored in boxing conditioning.
Source: Bromley et al. (2017). A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-097313)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Injury surveillance at the 4th Elite Women's National Boxing Championship in India (235 female boxers) recorded an injury rate of 43.98 per 1000 athlete bouts (95% CI 33.71-54.07) and 293.21 per 1000 athlete hours of competition (95% CI 225.94-360.47), with head, face and neck the most commonly injured sites, mostly bruises/contusions followed by cuts and epistaxis, and NO concussions reported.
Effect/estimate: 43.98/1000 bouts (33.71-54.07); 293.21/1000 h (225.94-360.47); zero concussions recorded
Population: Elite female boxers | level: Elite amateur (national championship) | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Prospective competition injury surveillance | n: 235 boxers
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific, female
LIMITATIONS: Zero reported concussions in a striking tournament almost certainly reflects under-detection or a reporting threshold rather than true absence — treat the null concussion count with strong scepticism; single tournament; single nation; the authors' conclusion that women are less injury-prone than men is not supported by this design.
PPBF implication: Illustrates why PPBF must define concussion RECOGNITION and reporting procedure explicitly. An absence of recorded concussions in a log is evidence about the log, not about the athletes.
Source: Dande et al. (2021). Injury surveillance during elite women's national boxing championship in India. Med J Armed Forces India. (doi:10.1016/j.mjafi.2021.03.016)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A prospective study of injuries in competitive boxing documented injury patterns across training and competition contexts.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive injury profile
Population: Competitive boxers | level: Competitive amateur | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Prospective study | n: Single cohort
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Limited detail available from the abstract; single cohort; adds to but does not change the pooled estimates in A5-065.
PPBF implication: Supporting reference for the PPBF training-injury context. Pooled estimates (A5-065) should take precedence.
Source: Siewe et al. (2014). Injuries in competitive boxing. A prospective study. Int J Sports Med. (doi:10.1055/s-0034-1387764)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Multiple ophthalmology reports and reviews have documented ocular complications of boxing including retinal and other eye injuries in boxers.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive prevalence of ocular pathology
Population: Boxers | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Predominantly male in older series | age: Adult
Design: Clinical case series and reviews | n: Multiple clinical series
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Older clinical literature; case-series designs without denominators; screening practice and glove/rules eras have changed; prevalence figures from these series should not be applied to current amateur populations.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF requiring documented eye examination as part of medical clearance where the governing body requires it. SHADOW surfaces whether the document EXISTS; it never interprets an eye exam.
Source: Bianco et al. (2005). Ocular complications of boxing. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsm.2003.006643)
