text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective analysis of Australian news media reports 1832-2020 identified 163 boxing-related fatalities (122 professional, 40 amateur), of which traumatic brain injury was the most common cause (n=121, 74.2%) followed by cardiac arrest (11, 6.7%); the fatality rate declined precipitously from the 1930s to the 1980s, with eleven deaths since regulatory legislation began in the mid-1970s and no discernible further reduction after that legislation.
Effect/estimate: 74.2% traumatic brain injury; 6.7% cardiac arrest; steep pre-legislation decline
Population: Boxers (Australia) | level: Professional and amateur | sex: Predominantly male | age: All
Design: Retrospective media-report analysis (188 years) | n: 163 fatalities
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: News media reports are an incomplete and biased ascertainment source with no denominator, so no rate can be computed; single country; the finding that decline preceded legislation is descriptive, not causal.
PPBF implication: Establishes that catastrophic outcomes in boxing are real but rare and dominated by traumatic brain injury. Grounds honest, non-alarmist guardian communication. Death is a governing-body and medical matter, never a SHADOW computation.
Source: Alevras et al. (2021). Boxing-related fatalities in Australia: A retrospective analysis of news media reports. J Sci Med Sport. (doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2021.08.002)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians issued a consensus statement on neuroimaging in professional combat sports, noting that deaths in the ring are usually the result of an acute catastrophic neurological event such as acute subdural haematoma, and that although neuroimaging is included in licensing in some jurisdictions, required imaging specifics and frequency vary with no consensus guidelines.
Effect/estimate: Explicit statement that imaging requirements vary by jurisdiction with no consensus
Population: Professional combat sport athletes | level: Professional | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Consensus statement (Association of Ringside Physicians) | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing/combat-sport-specific
LIMITATIONS: Consensus level; addresses professional combat sports and does not automatically apply to amateur or community programmes; jurisdictional variation is explicitly acknowledged.
PPBF implication: JURISDICTION IS A DATA FIELD. PPBF must store which sanctioning body and jurisdiction applies to each athlete, because imaging and clearance requirements differ. SHADOW surfaces the requirement and whether documentation is on file; it never determines clearance.
Source: Sethi et al. (2022). Neuroimaging in professional combat sports: consensus statement from the association of ringside physicians. Phys Sportsmed. (doi:10.1080/00913847.2022.2083922)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A cross-sectional study using custom-fit instrumented mouthguards in 23 boxing and MMA athletes (4 women) collected data from 53 amateur training sessions and 6 competitions with video verification of true-positive impacts, characterising peak linear and peak angular acceleration by sport, activity type, sex and impact location.
Effect/estimate: Impact counts and accelerations characterised by sport/activity/sex
Population: Boxing and MMA athletes | level: Amateur | sex: 19 male / 4 female | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification | n: 23 athletes; 896+ impacts across 53 training sessions and 6 competitions
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific (with MMA)
LIMITATIONS: Only 4 female participants, so sex comparisons are underpowered; sensor accuracy issues affect this class of measurement (see A5-081); training sessions vastly outnumbered competitions.
PPBF implication: Confirms training/sparring is where the bulk of head-impact exposure accrues by count. Directly justifies the PPBF proxy model: count SPARRING rounds, not just bouts.
Source: Jansen et al. (2021). Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts. Orthop J Sports Med. (doi:10.1177/23259671211059815)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguards worn by 22 male US Military Academy cadets during a compulsory introductory boxing course recorded 809 video-verified impacts across 205 analysed player-bouts, averaging 3.9 impacts per player-bout, with mean peak linear acceleration 16.5 ± 7.1 g (maximum 70.8 g) and a right-skewed distribution in which 640 of 809 events (79.1%) fell between 10 and 20 g, and mean peak angular acceleration 1.52 ± 0.96 krad/s2 (maximum 8.85 krad/s2).
Effect/estimate: 3.9 impacts per player-bout; mean PLA 16.5 ± 7.1 g; 79.1% between 10-20 g; max 70.8 g
Population: Novice boxers (military cadets) | level: Novice / introductory | sex: Male | age: Young adult (~19.9 y)
Design: Prospective instrumented-mouthguard study | n: 22 subjects; 205 player-bouts; 809 impacts
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific, novice population
LIMITATIONS: Male only; military cadets in a compulsory course are not volunteer community boxers; a single course; sensor quality issues apply (A5-081); impacts per bout will differ with sparring intensity and rules.
PPBF implication: The most directly relevant head-impact data for a BEGINNER boxing programme like PPBF's entry lane. Note most impacts are low magnitude — but the count accumulates. This supports counting exposure rather than only reacting to visible events.
Source: Fetchko et al. (2023). Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets. Mil Med. (doi:10.1093/milmed/usad249)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In an exploratory observational cohort of 7 competitive boxers monitored with instrumented mouthguards and SCAT5 symptom scales before, immediately after and 48 hours after sparring, group analyses showed no difference in symptom scores pre versus post sparring (median change in total symptom severity score -1, p=0.85), symptoms were significantly LOWER at 48 hours than pre-sparring (p=0.02), and 4 of 16 sessions (25%) from three participants showed a symptom-severity increase greater than 5, with no strong relationship found between exposure metrics and symptom change.
Effect/estimate: No group-level pre/post symptom change; 25% of sessions showed individual increase >5; no strong exposure-symptom relationship
Population: Competitive boxers | level: Competitive amateur | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Exploratory observational cohort | n: n=7; 16 sessions
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Only 7 participants and 16 sessions — exploratory by the authors' own framing; symptom scales are subjective and may be under-reported by athletes wanting to keep sparring; the null result is as likely to reflect insufficient power as a true absence of relationship.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL for PPBF: symptom checklists after sparring have low signal at the group level but flagged individual sessions. Symptom reporting must be treated as a routing trigger to a qualified human, NEVER as a computed clearance or all-clear.
Source: Le Flao et al. (2026). Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring. J Sci Med Sport. (doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2026.01.018)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Comparing instrumented mouthguards, skin patches and headgear patches across 442 boxing sparring events each, predefined quality criteria were met in only 53%, 20% and 26% of events respectively; high-quality recordings were less frequent for impacts near the sensor (30% vs 61% for the mouthguard) and showed LOWER peak kinematics than low-quality recordings (p<0.001), and even among carefully selected simultaneous high-quality recordings there was little to no association between sensors.
Effect/estimate: Mouthguard 53%, skin patch 20%, headgear patch 26% high-quality; little to no inter-sensor agreement
Population: Boxers during sparring | level: Sparring cohort | sex: Not specified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Sensor validation / comparison study | n: 442 events per sensor type
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Single study; the quality criteria are the authors' own predefined objective criteria; does not address whether any sensor is 'correct' in absolute terms.
PPBF implication: DECISIVE for the PPBF monitoring architecture: even instrumented sensors produce largely low-quality, non-agreeing data in boxing. This REMOVES the argument that PPBF is disadvantaged by using proxies. Proxies (counted rounds, intensity category, coach-observed impacts) are honest and cheap; sensors would be expensive and still unreliable.
Source: Le Flao et al. (2024). Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing: Prevalence, Effects, and Implications for Exposure Assessment. Ann Biomed Eng. (doi:10.1007/s10439-024-03647-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 included articles reported that boxers have a significantly elevated risk of sustaining a concussion compared with other combat sports (risk ratio 0.253 vs 0.065, p<0.001); among 631 amateur and professional boxers analysed, 147 (23.30%) had cavum septum pellucidum, and 125 of 411 (30.41%) presented with some form of brain atrophy.
Effect/estimate: Concussion RR 0.253 vs 0.065 other combat sports; CSP 23.30%; brain atrophy 30.41%
Population: Amateur and professional boxers | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 35 articles; 631 boxers imaged
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: The imaging findings pool studies across eras, exposure levels and imaging methods; cavum septum pellucidum occurs in non-boxers too, so a prevalence figure without a matched control group cannot establish attribution; heavily weighted toward professional and historically high-exposure boxers; publication bias likely toward positive imaging findings.
PPBF implication: Report to guardians as: structural imaging abnormalities are found in a substantial minority of studied boxers, chiefly professionals with high cumulative exposure, and the amateur/community picture is far less established. Do not extrapolate professional imaging prevalence to youth non-contact or light-contact programmes.
Source: Donnelly et al. (2023). A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med. (doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000001195)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A consensus paper on neuropathological diagnostic criteria describes chronic traumatic encephalopathy pathology as unique, characterised by a pathognomonic lesion of perivascular neuronal phosphorylated tau accumulation with variable astrocytic aggregates at the depths of cortical sulci and a distinctive molecular structural configuration of p-tau fibrils unlike ageing, Alzheimer's disease or other tauopathies; CTE has been reported in boxers among many other contact-sport participants, and can currently be definitively diagnosed ONLY by postmortem neuropathological examination, with the corresponding clinical condition termed traumatic encephalopathy syndrome.
Effect/estimate: Pathognomonic perivascular p-tau lesion at sulcal depths; postmortem diagnosis only
Population: Deceased contact-sport athletes including boxers | level: Amateur and professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult / deceased
Design: Consensus neuropathological criteria paper | n: Hundreds of postmortem cases
Boxing-specific: Partly (boxing among many sports) | transfer status: Boxing included; much of the case series is American football
LIMITATIONS: Postmortem case series are subject to profound ascertainment bias — brains are donated because of symptoms — so prevalence cannot be estimated from them; the pathology-to-symptom relationship is not established; no in-life diagnosis exists.
PPBF implication: PPBF position: the PATHOLOGY is established; the RISK MAGNITUDE for a given athlete and the dose-response are not. SHADOW must never estimate an individual's CTE risk. This is a physician and researcher domain.
Source: McKee et al. (2023). Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE): criteria for neuropathological diagnosis and relationship to repetitive head impacts. Acta Neuropathol. (doi:10.1007/s00401-023-02540-w)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A published commentary argued that chronic traumatic encephalopathy does not rise to the level of a verifiable disease and remains at the level of case report, citing arguments that traumatic brain injury does not cause neurodegeneration, that protein deposits in the brain poorly predict behavioural symptoms, and that p-tau is not necessarily toxic or self-propagating.
Effect/estimate: Argumentative, no new data
Population: N/A (conceptual argument) | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Commentary / position paper | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Partly (references the boxing 'dementia pugilistica' debate directly) | transfer status: Conceptual
LIMITATIONS: A single-author opinion piece, not primary evidence; contested by the neuropathology consensus (A5-083); included here for honest representation of the state of debate, not as an endorsement.
PPBF implication: Include in the PPBF evidence ledger to demonstrate that SHADOW represents scientific disagreement rather than a single narrative. Neither minimise nor alarm: the honest statement is that pathology is established, causal dose-response in living amateurs is not.
Source: Randolph (2018). Chronic traumatic encephalopathy is not a real disease. Arch Clin Neuropsychol. (doi:10.1093/arclin/acy063)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Professional Fighters Brain Health Study is a longitudinal study of active professional fighters (boxers and mixed martial artists), retired professional fighters and matched controls, designed over 5 years with anticipated enrolment of more than 400 boxers and MMA athletes, using annual 3-tesla MRI, computerised cognitive assessment, speech analysis, mood and impulsivity surveys and blood sampling, with a composite fight exposure index developed as a summary measure of cumulative traumatic exposure.
Effect/estimate: Composite fight exposure index as predictor
Population: Active and retired professional fighters plus controls | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult (34+ in some analyses)
Design: Prospective longitudinal cohort study protocol | n: 400+ anticipated enrolment
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific (with MMA)
LIMITATIONS: Professional fighters only — not amateur, not youth, not community participants; volunteer cohort; the composite exposure index is study-specific and not a validated general tool.
PPBF implication: The strongest available longitudinal design in combat sports. PPBF should track its outputs rather than attempt its own neuro-imaging research. Note explicitly: findings apply to PROFESSIONALS.
Source: Bernick et al. (2013). Professional fighters brain health study: rationale and methods. Am J Epidemiol. (doi:10.1093/aje/kws456)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 94 active professional MMA fighters from the Professional Fighters Brain Health Study, adjusted multivariable regression found that a HIGHER number of weekly sparring rounds during typical training was significantly associated with LARGER left (beta=13.5 microlitres/round, 95% CI 2.26-24.8) and right (beta=14.9, 95% CI 3.64-26.2) caudate volumes, with no significant association with thalamus, putamen, hippocampus or amygdala volumes; more weekly sparring rounds was NOT significantly associated with smaller volumes.
Effect/estimate: Caudate: +13.5 and +14.9 microlitres per weekly sparring round; null for other regions
Population: Active professional MMA fighters | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional analysis within a longitudinal cohort | n: n=94
Boxing-specific: Partly (MMA, not boxing; sparring is the exposure) | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: CROSS-SECTIONAL and CORRELATIONAL — cannot establish direction of causation; MMA sparring differs from boxing sparring; self-reported sparring rounds; larger caudate volume is not established as beneficial or harmful; survivorship bias is plausible (fighters who tolerate high sparring keep fighting); confounded by motor-skill training effects the authors themselves raise.
PPBF implication: IMPORTANT ANTI-ALARMISM ENTRY: the simple assumption 'more sparring equals visible brain atrophy' was not supported in this cohort. PPBF should still minimise unnecessary head-impact exposure on precautionary grounds, but must not cite atrophy as an established consequence of sparring volume in this population.
Source: Esagoff et al. (2023). Sparring and the Brain: The Associations between Sparring and Regional Brain Volumes in Professional Mixed Martial Arts Fighters. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01838-9)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In the Professional Fighters Brain Health Study with plasma samples from 471 participants, baseline neurofilament light differed across groups with active boxers having the highest levels, higher baseline NF-L correlated with lower baseline MRI regional volumes and lower cognitive scores, and the number of sparring rounds completed by active fighters correlated with NF-L (95% CI 0.0116-0.4053, p=0.0381) but not with tau.
Effect/estimate: Sparring rounds correlated with NF-L (95% CI 0.0116-0.4053, p=0.0381); active boxers highest baseline NF-L
Population: Active and retired professional fighters and controls | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Longitudinal biomarker cohort | n: 471 plasma samples; 126 with multiple yearly samples
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific (with MMA)
LIMITATIONS: Correlational; the confidence interval nearly touches zero and the p-value is marginal; NF-L is a non-specific marker of axonal injury with many causes; professional population only; blood biomarkers are not clinically actionable for individual athletes at present.
PPBF implication: Provides the strongest single justification for treating COUNTED SPARRING ROUNDS as the key modifiable exposure variable in PPBF. Sparring rounds is a number a coach can log for free — and it is the exposure variable that correlated with a biological marker.
Source: Bernick et al. (2018). Longitudinal Performance of Plasma Neurofilament Light and Tau in Professional Fighters: The Professional Fighters Brain Health Study. J Neurotrauma. (doi:10.1089/neu.2017.5553)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a secondary analysis of 130 active and retired professional fighters older than 34 from the Professional Athletes Brain Health Study, 52 (40%) were adjudicated as traumatic encephalopathy syndrome positive under 2021 clinical criteria; TES-positive athletes were older with significantly lower education, and showed statistically significant between-group differences and interactions across all MRI volumetric measurements, with greater increases in lateral and inferior lateral ventricles and a decrease in the hippocampus.
Effect/estimate: 40% TES+; significant volumetric divergence including ventricular enlargement and hippocampal decrease
Population: Professional fighters older than 34 | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Over 34 y
Design: Secondary longitudinal analysis | n: n=130 (52 TES+)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific (with MMA)
LIMITATIONS: TES-positive athletes were older and less educated, both established confounders for cognitive and volumetric outcomes; TES criteria are clinical and evolving; selected older professional cohort; observational.
PPBF implication: Establishes that measurable divergence exists in older professionals with clinical syndrome. Does NOT establish risk for amateur or youth participants. PPBF's amateur/community messaging must not import this finding.
Source: Conway Kleven et al. (2023). Longitudinal Changes in Regional Brain Volumes and Cognition of Professional Fighters With Traumatic Encephalopathy Syndrome. Neurology. (doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000207594)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of published studies and analysis of active professional boxer data found that since the 1930s the average duration of a professional boxer's career dropped from 19 years to 5 years and the mean number of career bouts fell from 336 to 13, despite no significant decline in participation rates from 1931 to 2002.
Effect/estimate: Career length 19 y to 5 y; career bouts 336 to 13
Population: Professional boxers (UK and Australia) | level: Professional | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Literature review with exposure-data analysis | n: Historical and contemporary cohorts
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: The inference that CTBI incidence will therefore diminish is a projection, not an observed outcome; bout count omits sparring exposure, which may not have fallen proportionately; two-country data.
PPBF implication: Crucial context for honest guardian communication: the historical 'punch-drunk' literature reflects exposure levels (300+ bouts, 19-year careers) that no contemporary amateur or community participant approaches. Anchoring modern risk to that literature overstates it.
Source: Clausen et al. (2005). The risk of chronic traumatic brain injury in professional boxing: change in exposure variables over the past century. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsm.2004.017046)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review with meta-analysis found six moderate- to high-quality retrospective studies including 41,699 athletes in contact sports (boxing, basketball, ice hockey, American football and soccer), of which three studies comprising 37,065 male professional soccer players could be meta-analysed, reporting no differences in risk of all-cause (p=0.138), cardiovascular (p=0.085) or cancer mortality.
Effect/estimate: No difference in all-cause, cardiovascular or cancer mortality in the meta-analysable subset
Population: Professional contact-sport athletes | level: Professional | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 6 studies, 41,699 athletes; 3 studies meta-analysed (37,065 soccer players)
Boxing-specific: Partly (boxing included in the review but the meta-analysis was soccer) | transfer status: Other-sport transfer for the pooled estimate
LIMITATIONS: The pooled analysis is soccer players, NOT boxers — a critical distinction usually lost in citation; retrospective designs; described by the authors as preliminary findings; mortality is a blunt outcome that misses morbidity.
PPBF implication: Do NOT cite this as evidence about boxing mortality. It is included in the PPBF ledger specifically as an example of a finding that is routinely mis-transferred across sports.
Source: Morales et al. (2021). Mortality Risk from Neurodegenerative Disease in Sports Associated with Repetitive Head Impacts: Preliminary Findings from a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-021-01580-0)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A review examined the consequences of repetitive subconcussive head impacts in sport, covering brain changes and associated measurement approaches.
Effect/estimate: Mechanistic synthesis; no pooled estimate
Population: Contact-sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Narrative review | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: Partly | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review; the subconcussive literature uses heterogeneous exposure metrics and short-term outcome measures whose clinical meaning is unestablished.
PPBF implication: Background support for the precautionary principle in PPBF sparring policy: minimise unnecessary head contact even in the absence of diagnosed concussion, without claiming a quantified harm.
Source: Di Virgilio et al. (2019). Understanding the Consequences of Repetitive Subconcussive Head Impacts in Sport: Brain Changes and Dampened Motor Control Are Seen After Boxing Practice. Front Hum Neurosci. (doi:10.3389/fnhum.2019.00294)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review examined the use of biofluid markers to evaluate the consequences of sport-related subconcussive head impact exposure.
Effect/estimate: Marker responses reviewed; no clinical decision threshold established
Population: Contact-sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic/scoping review | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: Partly | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Biofluid markers are research tools with no established clinical decision threshold for individual athletes; assays and timing vary; not available or appropriate in a community gym.
PPBF implication: Out of scope for PPBF operations. Recorded so the research backlog reflects that biomarker monitoring is not a currently deployable option.
Source: Lember et al. (2024). The Use of Biofluid Markers to Evaluate the Consequences of Sport-Related Subconcussive Head Impact Exposure: A Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. (doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00665-6)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport (Amsterdam, October 2022) consensus statement, informed by 10 systematic reviews conducted over three and a half years, produced revised tools including the Concussion Recognition Tool 6 and Sport Concussion Assessment Tool 6 (and child versions) plus the new Sport Concussion Office Assessment Tool 6, and integrated a focus on para athletes, the athlete's perspective, concussion-specific medical ethics, athlete retirement and potential long-term effects including neurodegenerative disease.
Effect/estimate: Tools: CRT6, SCAT6, Child SCAT6, SCOAT6, Child SCOAT6
Population: Athletes in all sports | level: All levels | sex: Male and female, including para athletes | age: Child to adult
Design: International consensus statement informed by 10 systematic reviews | n: Expert panel + 10 systematic reviews
Boxing-specific: No (all sports, includes combat sports) | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus applicable to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus process reflects expert interpretation; the Concussion in Sport Group process has itself attracted criticism regarding scope and conflicts; the tools are screening and assessment aids for appropriately trained users, not diagnostic instruments for lay coaches.
PPBF implication: AUTHORITY ANCHOR. PPBF adopts CRT6 as the RECOGNITION tool coaches may use to remove an athlete and escalate. SCAT6/SCOAT6 are for trained clinicians. SHADOW must never compute, score or interpret these instruments toward a clearance decision.
Source: Patricios et al. (2023). Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport-Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106898)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis registered on PROSPERO evaluated prevention strategies, unintended consequences and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussion and head impacts, screening eight databases and including 192 of 220 eligible studies based on SIGN methodological quality ratings of high or acceptable.
Effect/estimate: Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors evaluated across sports
Population: Athletes across sports | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: Youth to adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 192 included studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Boxing-specific prevention evidence within this review is limited; the strongest prevention evidence in sport generally relates to rule changes and contact restriction, which are governing-body decisions rather than gym-level programming.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF prioritising EXPOSURE REDUCTION (contact policy, sparring rules) over equipment or strength interventions as the primary head-impact mitigation lever.
Source: Eliason et al. (2023). Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2022-106656)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement concludes that headguards are highly effective in reducing facial lacerations in amateur boxers and appropriate where avoidance of laceration or auricular injury matters, but explicitly states that headguards should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, have not been shown to prevent these injuries in combat sports, and that although biomechanical studies suggest reduced linear and rotational cranial acceleration, changes in athlete behaviour toward more risk-taking when wearing headguards may offset any risk reduction.
Effect/estimate: Effective for lacerations; NOT shown to prevent concussion; behavioural compensation flagged
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: All ages
Design: Position statement (Association of Ringside Physicians) | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing/combat-sport-specific
LIMITATIONS: Position statement rather than pooled data; the authors themselves call for further research; the behavioural-compensation mechanism is hypothesised rather than demonstrated in combat sports.
PPBF implication: PPBF POLICY-CRITICAL: headguards may be required for laceration protection in sparring, but must never be described to athletes, coaches or guardians as concussion protection. Write this into the sparring policy text verbatim in meaning.
Source: deWeber et al. (2023). Headguard use in combat sports: position statement of the Association of Ringside Physicians. Phys Sportsmed. (doi:10.1080/00913847.2023.2242415)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a laboratory linear-impactor study using an instrumented Hybrid III head and neck system with a semirigid fist-and-glove interface at impact speeds of 4.1-8.3 m/s, peak contact forces were 1.9-5.9 kN; in 8.3 m/s fist-glove impacts mean peak resultant headform acceleration was approximately 130 g bare versus approximately 85 g in forehead impacts with an AIBA-approved headguard, and in 6.85 m/s bare impacts mean peak resultant angular accelerations of 5200-5600 rad/s2 were almost halved by the headguard.
Effect/estimate: Bare ~130 g vs headguard ~85 g at 8.3 m/s; angular acceleration ~5200-5600 rad/s2 roughly halved
Population: Laboratory headform (Hybrid III) | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Laboratory impact biomechanics study | n: Mechanical impactor trials
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific equipment testing
LIMITATIONS: LABORATORY HEADFORM, NOT HUMANS — reduced headform acceleration has not translated into demonstrated concussion reduction in athletes (see A5-095); a rigid impactor differs from a live punch; single headguard model; no behavioural compensation is modelled in a laboratory.
PPBF implication: Textbook case of lab evidence not equalling field outcome. PPBF's evidence engine should carry both this and A5-095 linked, so SHADOW never surfaces the biomechanics finding alone as proof of protection.
Source: McIntosh et al. (2015). Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095094)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A Current Opinion article argued that the International Boxing Association's prohibition of headguards has generated controversy, demonstrated headguard effectiveness against cuts and lacerations, and stated there is insufficient evidence supporting headguard bans, while highlighting a gap in collaboration and communication between the IBA and smaller representative bodies for future policy reform.
Effect/estimate: Argues insufficient evidence for headguard bans
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Male and female | age: All ages
Design: Current Opinion / position article | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: An opinion article, not a systematic review; policy differs by governing body and age category — headguard requirements for junior and youth categories differ from elite senior rules in many jurisdictions.
PPBF implication: PPBF must store headguard policy as a per-jurisdiction, per-age-category RULE FIELD sourced from the applicable governing body, not as a global setting. Never present one nation's or one body's rule as universal.
Source: Le et al. (2025). The Case for Protective Headguards in Amateur Boxing and Implications for International Policy on Headguard Bans. Sports Med Open. (doi:10.1186/s40798-025-00871-4)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis identified five eligible articles and, across five planes of motion (flexion, extension, right and left flexion, and total), found NO statistically significant differences in neck strength between concussed and non-concussed athletes; some studies reported a positive trend toward concussion risk reduction with greater neck strength, and the authors concluded the evidence remains inconclusive and that further large randomised controlled trials are needed before neck strength can be recommended as a preventive strategy.
Effect/estimate: No statistically significant differences across five planes of motion
Population: Athletes in contact sports | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 5 articles
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (no boxing-specific concussion outcome data)
LIMITATIONS: Only 5 eligible studies; heterogeneous neck-strength measurement methods; no boxing data; absence of evidence given small numbers is not evidence of absence.
PPBF implication: DEFINITIVE PPBF POSITION on the popular neck-strength claim: the concussion-prevention benefit is NOT established. Neck training may be programmed for other reasons, but PPBF must not market or log it as concussion prevention.
Source: Postula et al. (2026). Evaluation of Neck Strength and Concussion Risk: A Systematic Review. Curr Sports Med Rep. (doi:10.1249/JSR.0000000000001313)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a study collecting preseason anthropometric measurements from 6704 high school athletes in boys' and girls' soccer, basketball and lacrosse across 51 high schools in 25 states, smaller mean neck circumference, smaller mean neck-to-head circumference ratio and weaker mean overall neck strength were significantly associated with concussion incidence.
Effect/estimate: Smaller neck circumference, smaller neck:head ratio and weaker neck strength associated with concussion
Population: High school athletes | level: High school | sex: Boys and girls | age: Adolescent
Design: Prospective observational pilot with tool validation | n: 6704 athletes; 51 schools
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (soccer, basketball, lacrosse — NOT boxing)
LIMITATIONS: CORRELATION NOT CAUSATION — observational; described by the authors as a pilot study; no boxing or combat-sport athletes; neck strength is confounded with body size, sport, sex and playing experience; strengthening the neck was not tested as an intervention.
PPBF implication: This is the study most often cited to justify neck training for concussion prevention. PPBF must represent it accurately: an observational association in non-combat high school sports, not an intervention trial, and contradicted by the pooled analysis in A5-098.
Source: Collins et al. (2014). Neck strength: a protective factor reducing risk for concussion in high school sports. J Prim Prev. (doi:10.1007/s10935-014-0355-2)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review searching four databases and screening 2462 articles found only THREE papers eligible for inclusion on neck strengthening and injury outcomes in adult collision-sport athletes; all reported only male participants (two rugby union, one American football), two found significant isometric neck strength improvement following intervention, and NONE reported any impact of neck strengthening exercises on cervical spine injuries, leading the authors to conclude there is currently a lack of evidence supporting neck strengthening interventions for reducing impact injury risk.
Effect/estimate: 2 of 3 improved isometric neck strength; ZERO reported an injury-outcome effect
Population: Adult collision-sport athletes | level: Amateur to professional | sex: MALE ONLY | age: Adult (18+)
Design: Systematic review | n: 3 eligible papers from 2462 screened
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (rugby, American football)
LIMITATIONS: Only three eligible studies from 2462 screened — an extremely thin base; male only; no combat-sport data; adults only.
PPBF implication: Second independent confirmation that neck training's INJURY-PREVENTION claim is unsupported. Neck training CAN increase neck strength; that is the only defensible claim PPBF may make.
Source: Daly et al. (2021). A Systematic Review of Strength and Conditioning Protocols for Improving Neck Strength and Reducing Concussion Incidence and Impact Injury Risk in Collision Sports; Is There Evidence?. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. (doi:10.3390/jfmk6010008)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A two-part systematic review and expert Delphi consensus study searched four databases to September 2024 on neck training interventions in sport, applying PRISMA, a modified Downs and Black quality assessment and GRADE, and then established expert consensus on best practices for implementing neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in collision, combat and motor sport.
Effect/estimate: Consensus implementation guidance; GRADE-assessed underlying evidence
Population: Collision, combat and motor sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adult predominantly
Design: Systematic review plus expert Delphi consensus | n: Systematic search plus expert panel
Boxing-specific: Partly (combat sport explicitly included) | transfer status: Partly transferable to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Delphi consensus reflects expert opinion where trial evidence is insufficient; the target outcome is head acceleration events, not concussion incidence; GRADE assessment of the underlying literature indicates limited certainty.
PPBF implication: The most defensible position PPBF can take: if neck training is included, follow published consensus implementation practice, target head ACCELERATION as the hypothesised mechanism, and state that concussion reduction is unproven.
Source: Fownes-Walpole et al. (2025). Combining evidence and practice to optimise neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport: a systematic review and Delphi-consensus study. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2024-108847)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of five cross-sectional studies found that higher neck strength is associated with lower head acceleration during purposeful heading in soccer (p<0.05, r<-0.5), and concluded that further research is needed to determine the most effective method of strengthening the neck musculature.
Effect/estimate: Higher neck strength associated with lower head acceleration (p<0.05, r<-0.5)
Population: Soccer players | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review of cross-sectional studies | n: 5 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (soccer heading, an ANTICIPATED self-initiated impact)
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional only; soccer heading is a self-initiated, anticipated impact with neck pre-activation, which is mechanically very different from an unanticipated punch — this limits transfer to boxing severely.
PPBF implication: The mechanism (stronger neck, lower head acceleration) has support ONLY in anticipated impacts. A boxer is often struck unanticipated. Flag this transfer limitation explicitly wherever PPBF discusses neck training.
Source: Peek et al. (2019). Higher neck strength is associated with lower head acceleration during purposeful heading in soccer: A systematic review. J Sci Med Sport. (doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2019.11.004)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 49 high school and collegiate American football players with preseason cervical testing and season-long Head Impact Telemetry System data, linemen with stronger lateral flexors and greater composite cervical strength had about 1.75 times INCREASED odds of sustaining moderate rather than mild linear head impacts compared with weaker linemen.
Effect/estimate: Stronger linemen: ~1.75x increased odds of moderate vs mild impacts
Population: High school and collegiate American football players | level: High school and collegiate | sex: Male | age: Adolescent to young adult
Design: Prospective cohort with instrumented helmets | n: n=49
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (American football)
LIMITATIONS: Observational; helmet-based sensors have known accuracy limitations; a plausible behavioural explanation is that stronger players engage more aggressively; football linemen contact is unlike boxing.
PPBF implication: Included deliberately: a finding in the OPPOSITE direction to the popular claim. PPBF's evidence ledger must retain disconfirming results so SHADOW's synthesis is not one-sided.
Source: Schmidt et al. (2014). The influence of cervical muscle characteristics on head impact biomechanics in football. Am J Sports Med. (doi:10.1177/0363546514536685)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 37 youth ice hockey players (mean age 15.0 y) wearing accelerometer-instrumented helmets across a full season with preseason isometric cervical strength measured for multiple muscle groups and categorised into tertiles, NO differences were observed in linear or rotational head acceleration across strength groups for anterior neck flexors, anterolateral neck flexors, cervical rotators or posterolateral extensors.
Effect/estimate: Null across all measured muscle groups (all p>0.05 for linear; rotational p=0.060-0.579)
Population: Youth ice hockey players | level: Youth | sex: Male (as reported) | age: ~15 y
Design: Prospective cohort with instrumented helmets | n: n=37
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (youth ice hockey)
LIMITATIONS: Small n=37; helmet sensor limitations; youth population with maturational variation in strength; single season.
PPBF implication: Third independent null/contrary result in the neck-strength question, and in a YOUTH population directly relevant to PPBF's age range.
Source: Mihalik et al. (2011). Does cervical muscle strength in youth ice hockey players affect head impact biomechanics?. Clin J Sport Med. (doi:10.1097/JSM.0B013E31822C8A5C)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a prospective observational study of 28 civilian law enforcement cadets (9 female) undergoing occupational combat training with isometric neck strength measured by handheld dynamometer and head acceleration events over 5 g recorded by instrumented mouthguards, principal component analysis and adjusted regression demonstrated NO significant effect of neck characteristics on head acceleration events per exposure, median peak linear acceleration or median peak rotational velocity when controlling for sex.
Effect/estimate: No significant effect of neck strength or girth on HAE quantity or magnitude
Population: Law enforcement cadets in combat training | level: Occupational trainees (novice) | sex: 19 male / 9 female | age: Adult (~28 y)
Design: Prospective observational study with instrumented mouthguards | n: n=28
Boxing-specific: Partly (combat/striking training, not competitive boxing) | transfer status: Close transfer — combat training population
LIMITATIONS: Small n=28; a training rather than competitive context; single cohort; mouthguard sensor limitations apply.
PPBF implication: The closest population to PPBF's beginner boxing lane (novices in supervised combat training, mixed sex) and the result is NULL. Strongest single reason PPBF should not sell neck training as head-impact mitigation.
Source: Smith et al. (2025). Neck Strength Is Not a Protective Factor for Lower Repetitive Head Impact Exposure in Law Enforcement Cadets. Mil Med. (doi:10.1093/milmed/usaf150)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A review of neck muscular strength, training, performance and sport injury risk found differences in neck strength between playing positions, sexes and ages, that neck strength training programmes were generally effective for both untrained and trained participants using dynamic or isometric actions with various resistance devices, with a wide range of reported strength increases and the smallest gains from lower-intensity or lower-frequency programmes, limited evidence associating greater isometric strength or dynamic training with better head stabilisation during low-level force application, and a retrospective analysis of professional rugby union players indicating isometric training reduced match-related cervical spine injuries.
Effect/estimate: Neck training reliably increases neck strength; head-stabilisation evidence limited to low-level force
Population: Athletes across sports | level: Mixed | sex: Male and female | age: Youth to adult
Design: Narrative review | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review; the cervical-spine injury finding is from a RETROSPECTIVE analysis in rugby, not a trial; head stabilisation evidence applies to LOW-LEVEL force application, not punch-magnitude impacts.
PPBF implication: Defensible PPBF claim set: neck training increases neck strength (well supported); may aid head stabilisation at low force (limited); concussion prevention (NOT supported). Encode these three claims separately with different confidence levels.
Source: Hrysomallis (2016). Neck Muscular Strength, Training, Performance and Sport Injury Risk: A Review. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0490-4)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sex-specific multiple regression equations predicting years from peak height velocity from height, sitting height, leg length and chronological age were developed in 152 Canadian children aged 8-16 and cross-validated in Canadian and Flemish samples, with coefficients of determination of 0.92 (boys) and 0.91 (girls) and standard errors of estimate of 0.49 and 0.50 years.
Effect/estimate: R2 0.92 (boys) / 0.91 (girls); SEE 0.49 / 0.50 years
Population: Children and adolescents | level: General youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: 8-16 y
Design: Regression development and cross-validation study | n: 152 development; 209 cross-validation
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: Developed in non-athlete Canadian/Flemish samples decades ago; accuracy degrades away from the time of peak height velocity and in early/late maturers; requires a sitting-height measurement many gyms do not take accurately.
PPBF implication: PPBF may estimate maturity offset non-invasively, but must display the estimation error and never treat a predicted age at PHV as a fact. Store as an estimate with uncertainty, per the SHADOW confidence model.
Source: Mirwald et al. (2002). An assessment of maturity from anthropometric measurements. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1097/00005768-200204000-00020)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A validation of modified maturity offset prediction equations in independent longitudinal samples (193 boys aged 8-18, 198 girls aged 8-16) from the Wroclaw Growth Study found that predicted ages at peak height velocity approximated observed ages only in AVERAGE-maturing boys NEAR the time of peak height velocity, with a corresponding narrow window in girls, and noted that validation studies of the original equations had indicated major limitations.
Effect/estimate: Accurate only for average maturers near PHV
Population: Children and adolescents | level: General youth | sex: 391 boys and girls | age: 8-18 y
Design: Independent longitudinal validation | n: 193 boys; 198 girls
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: The equations are systematically biased for early and late maturers — precisely the athletes for whom maturity information matters most; non-athlete samples.
PPBF implication: HARD CONSTRAINT: PPBF must NOT use predicted maturity offset to group, match or restrict individual youth athletes, because the method is least accurate for the outliers. Use it only as a squad-level descriptive context, with the limitation surfaced.
Source: Kozieł et al. (2018). Modified Maturity Offset Prediction Equations: Validation in Independent Longitudinal Samples of Boys and Girls. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-017-0750-y)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of methods for assessing maturity status (skeletal age, secondary sex characteristics) and estimating timing (age at peak height velocity, age at menarche) plus two non-invasive anthropometric methods noted that the latter need further validation with athletes, and described how selection and exclusion in many sports follows a maturity-related gradient largely during puberty and the growth spurt.
Effect/estimate: Maturity-related selection gradient described; anthropometric methods need athlete validation
Population: Youth athletes | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Pubertal ages
Design: Review | n: Multiple methods reviewed
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Skeletal age requires radiographic imaging, which is inappropriate for routine screening; secondary sex characteristic assessment raises safeguarding concerns and should not be performed by coaches.
PPBF implication: SAFEGUARDING BOUNDARY: PPBF must NOT collect pubertal-stage or secondary-sex-characteristic data. Restrict to height, sitting height and weight, collected by trained staff under a documented youth-measurement protocol with guardian consent.
Source: Malina et al. (2015). Biological maturation of youth athletes: assessment and implications. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094623)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A scoping review of 30 eligible studies found that injury incidence and burden generally increased with maturity status, that growth-related injuries peaked during the adolescent growth spurt, that more rapid growth in stature and of the lower limbs was associated with greater injury incidence and burden, and that while maturity TIMING did not show a clear or consistent association with injury it may contribute to risk and burden through variation in maturity status.
Effect/estimate: Injury burden rises with maturity status; growth-related injuries peak at the growth spurt; rapid growth associated with higher burden
Population: Elite-pathway youth athletes | level: Elite youth pathways | sex: Mixed (male-dominated in included studies) | age: Adolescent
Design: Scoping review | n: 30 studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth (no boxing-specific data located)
LIMITATIONS: The authors note significant heterogeneity across samples and in how growth, maturation and injury were operationalised and measured; elite-pathway athletes only; predominantly male; no boxing data.
PPBF implication: PPBF should track growth RATE (change in stature over time) as a low-cost monitoring variable and reduce high-impact loading during rapid growth phases — as a coach-reviewed adjustment, not an automated restriction.
Source: Parry et al. (2024). Associations between growth, maturation and injury in youth athletes engaged in elite pathways: a scoping review. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2024-108233)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A review of maturity-associated considerations for training load, injury risk and physical performance in youth soccer described how maturity-related changes in anthropometric and physical fitness characteristics are diverse among individuals particularly around peak height velocity, that players are at increased risk of overuse or growth-related injury during this time, and that implementing training interventions is consequently challenging.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive; individual variability emphasised
Population: Youth soccer players | level: Youth pathway | sex: Male (soccer context) | age: Adolescent
Design: Review with practical tools | n: Literature review plus estimation tools
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth
LIMITATIONS: Youth soccer, not boxing; the practical estimation tools inherit the accuracy limits of maturity-offset prediction (A5-108); male-focused.
PPBF implication: Supports PPBF's principle of individualising youth load around growth rather than chronological age — with the explicit caveat that maturity estimation is imprecise.
Source: Towlson et al. (2020). Maturity-associated considerations for training load, injury risk, and physical performance in youth soccer: One size does not fit all. J Sport Health Sci. (doi:10.1016/j.jshs.2020.09.003)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The National Strength and Conditioning Association position statement on long-term athletic development argues that children and adolescents should engage in appropriately prescribed exercise programmes promoting physical development to prevent injury and enhance lifelong fitness behaviours, and that a structured, logical and evidence-based approach to developing athleticism is needed irrespective of whether the child participates in organised sport.
Effect/estimate: Principles and recommendations
Population: Children and adolescents | level: All youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Childhood to adolescence
Design: Position statement (NSCA) | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth-development framework
LIMITATIONS: Position statements reflect expert consensus rather than pooled trial data; many long-term athletic development models remain largely untested longitudinally.
PPBF implication: Provides the professional-body anchor for PPBF's youth development pathway. Cite for PRINCIPLES (broad athletic development, appropriate prescription) not for specific volumes.
Source: Lloyd et al. (2016). National Strength and Conditioning Association Position Statement on Long-Term Athletic Development. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001387)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The National Strength and Conditioning Association's updated position statement on youth resistance training, and a separate American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report on resistance training for children and adolescents, support appropriately designed and competently supervised resistance training for young people.
Effect/estimate: Supported with supervision and appropriate design
Population: Children and adolescents | level: All youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Childhood to adolescence
Design: Position statement and clinical report | n: Professional-body panels
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: Safety conclusions are conditional on competent supervision and appropriate progression — conditions a volunteer-staffed community gym must actively meet, not assume.
PPBF implication: Removes the 'weights stunt growth' myth from PPBF doctrine. BUT the supervision condition is a real operational requirement: PPBF must document coach qualification for youth resistance sessions.
Source: Faigenbaum et al. (2009). Youth resistance training: updated position statement paper from the national strength and conditioning association. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31819df407)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A clinical review defined sports specialisation as year-round training exceeding 8 months per year, choosing a single main sport and/or quitting other sports, and reported that specialised training in young athletes carries risks of injury and burnout with the degree of specialisation positively correlated with increased serious overuse injury risk; risk factors identified included year-round single-sport training, more competition, decreased age-appropriate play and individual sports requiring early technical skill development.
Effect/estimate: Degree of specialisation positively correlated with serious overuse injury risk
Population: Young athletes | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Childhood to adolescence
Design: Non-systematic clinical review (level 4) | n: Literature review
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth
LIMITATIONS: Level 4 non-systematic review; the underlying evidence is largely cross-sectional and correlational; a separate review notes there is a limited number of comprehensive long-term outcome studies linking early specialisation to injury or burnout.
PPBF implication: Boxing is an individual sport requiring early technical skill — one of the listed risk factors. PPBF should actively encourage multi-sport participation in its youth lane and log other-sport participation as a load context field.
Source: Myer et al. (2015). Sport Specialization, Part I: Does Early Sports Specialization Increase Negative Outcomes and Reduce the Opportunity for Success in Young Athletes?. Sports Health. (doi:10.1177/1941738115598747)

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A review of early sport specialisation noted there is no universally agreed terminology or definition for early sport specialisation, that there is a limited number of comprehensive long-term outcome studies identifying a potential link between early specialisation and musculoskeletal injury or burnout, and that methodologically sound prospective research is needed.
Effect/estimate: Definitional inconsistency; limited long-term outcome evidence
Population: Young athletes | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Preteen to adolescent
Design: Review | n: Literature review
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: Highlights that the early-specialisation literature suffers from definitional inconsistency, making pooled conclusions unreliable.
PPBF implication: Balances A5-114. PPBF's position should be 'encourage varied movement' framed as a development principle, not 'specialisation causes injury' framed as established fact.
Source: Agel et al. (2021). Early Sport Specialization. J Bone Joint Surg Am. (doi:10.2106/JBJS.21.00018)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report described how imbalances of training load and recovery can produce overuse injuries from repetitive stress without sufficient recovery, that extended periods of training load exceeding recovery can produce systemic consequences including overtraining syndrome with decreased performance, increased injury and illness risk and endocrine, neurologic, cardiovascular and psychological derangement, and that burnout — physical or mental exhaustion with a reduced sense of accomplishment leading to devaluation of sport — is a primary reason for attrition in youth sports.
Effect/estimate: Descriptive clinical framework
Population: Young athletes | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Childhood to adolescence
Design: Clinical report (American Academy of Pediatrics) | n: Professional-body panel
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: Clinical report reflecting professional consensus; no quantified load thresholds are supplied because none are validated for youth.
PPBF implication: Authoritative basis for PPBF logging BURNOUT/attrition signals (engagement, enjoyment, attendance drop) alongside physical load in the youth lane. Attrition is a program outcome PPBF's grant reporting already needs.
Source: Brenner et al. (2024). Overuse Injuries, Overtraining, and Burnout in Young Athletes. Pediatrics. (doi:10.1542/peds.2023-065129)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis using multilevel Bayesian models pooled pairwise effect sizes comparing exercise performance in the early follicular phase against all other menstrual cycle phases in eumenorrheic women, with the authors noting that data are conflicting and that no consensus exists on whether exercise performance is affected by cycle phase.
Effect/estimate: Conflicting data; no consensus on cycle-phase effect
Population: Eumenorrheic women | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Bayesian multilevel) | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female transfer (no boxing-specific data)
LIMITATIONS: The underlying study quality is the central problem — see A5-119; small samples; poor cycle-phase verification in most primary studies; no boxing data.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT build cycle-phase-based training prescriptions. The evidence does not support them. Log cycle information only if the athlete chooses to, under strict privacy tiering, and use it for athlete-led self-management.
Source: McNulty et al. (2020). The Effects of Menstrual Cycle Phase on Exercise Performance in Eumenorrheic Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01319-3)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of menstrual cycle verification methods in recent exercise-science literature (2008-2018) found that only 44% of the selected studies measured actual concentrations of oestrogen and progesterone, that the likely inclusion of participants with anovulatory or luteal-phase-deficient cycles combined with small participant numbers has affected results, and recommended a combination of three verification methods for future research.
Effect/estimate: Only 44% of studies measured hormone concentrations
Population: Female research participants | level: Research populations | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Methodological review | n: Literature 2008-2018
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Methodological — applies across sports
LIMITATIONS: Documents a methodological problem rather than resolving the underlying physiological question.
PPBF implication: THE key citation for PPBF's honest statement that menstrual cycle evidence quality is LOW. Any SHADOW output touching cycle phase must carry this caveat.
Source: Janse DE Jonge et al. (2019). Methodological Recommendations for Menstrual Cycle Research in Sports and Exercise. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002073)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review examined the prevalence of menstrual cycle disorders and cycle-related symptoms — including amenorrhoea, anovulation, dysmenorrhoea, heavy menstrual bleeding, luteal phase deficiency, oligomenorrhoea and premenstrual syndrome — among female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives, and evaluated the assessment methods used to identify them.
Effect/estimate: Prevalence of a range of MC disorders and symptoms
Population: Female athletes not using hormonal contraceptives | level: Mixed | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review (PRISMA) | n: Multiple studies to September 2022
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female-athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Definitions of each disorder varied across studies; self-reported symptoms; no combat-sport-specific data; excludes hormonal contraceptive users, a large group.
PPBF implication: Distinguishes SYMPTOM BURDEN (real and prevalent, worth an athlete-initiated conversation) from PERFORMANCE PHASE EFFECTS (unsupported). PPBF should support the former and avoid claiming the latter. Amenorrhoea is a medical matter for a clinician.
Source: Taim et al. (2023). The Prevalence of Menstrual Cycle Disorders and Menstrual Cycle-Related Symptoms in Female Athletes: A Systematic Literature Review. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01871-8)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of oral contraceptive effects on exercise performance compared performance in OCP users against naturally menstruating women (phase-matched two ways) and compared OCP consumption against withdrawal phases.
Effect/estimate: Between- and within-group comparisons performed
Population: Women using and not using oral contraceptives | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female transfer
LIMITATIONS: OCP formulations vary widely and are frequently not reported; study quality assessed but heterogeneous; no combat-sport data.
PPBF implication: PPBF must not make contraceptive-status-based training recommendations. Contraceptive use is sensitive health data requiring the highest privacy tier and is not needed for coaching decisions.
Source: Elliott-Sale et al. (2020). The Effects of Oral Contraceptives on Exercise Performance in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01317-5)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis of the effect of hormonal contraceptive use on skeletal muscle hypertrophy, power and strength adaptations to resistance exercise training identified only 8 eligible articles (54 effects, 325 participants) from 4669 screened.
Effect/estimate: Very small eligible evidence base
Population: Women undertaking resistance training | level: Mixed | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with multilevel meta-analysis | n: 8 articles; 325 participants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female transfer
LIMITATIONS: Only 8 studies from 4669 screened — an extremely thin base; heterogeneous contraceptive formulations; no combat-sport data.
PPBF implication: Reinforces that PPBF should program resistance training for female boxers on the same principles as male boxers, because no evidence supports differentiating by contraceptive status.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 2023 International Olympic Committee consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport updated the 2018 statement following more than 170 original research publications, described emerging data on low carbohydrate availability and the interplay between mental health and REDs, presented updated Health and Performance Conceptual Models and a novel Physiological Model, and outlined guidelines for safe and effective body composition assessment to help prevent REDs.
Effect/estimate: Conceptual and physiological models; body composition assessment guidance
Population: Male and female athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: International consensus statement (IOC) | n: Expert panel; 170+ publications reviewed
Boxing-specific: No (all sports; highly relevant to weight-category sports) | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus, high relevance to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus level; energy availability is difficult to measure accurately in the field, which the consensus itself acknowledges; diagnosis requires clinical assessment.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL for a weight-category sport with youth participants. PPBF must have a RED-S awareness and referral pathway. SHADOW may surface risk-context flags (rapid weight change, missed sessions, reported fatigue) and route to a clinician. It must NEVER diagnose REDs or issue nutrition prescriptions.
Source: Mountjoy et al. (2023). 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A critical review challenged the REDs construct, noting that the IOC 2023 consensus itself concludes energy availability is impossible to measure accurately enough in the field, that consequently the only apparent way to diagnose an athlete with REDs is by symptom presentation and risk factors, that the symptoms are rather generic and the causes likely multifactorial, and that it is very difficult to isolate the effects of low energy availability from other potential causes of the same symptoms.
Effect/estimate: Argues the diagnostic construct is not field-measurable
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Critical review | n: Conceptual analysis
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: A critique rather than new data; does not dispute that low energy availability causes harm, only the diagnostic construct and its application.
PPBF implication: Reinforces the operational rule: PPBF flags RISK CONTEXT and refers. It does not diagnose. The diagnostic uncertainty is exactly why the decision belongs to a clinician.
Source: Jeukendrup et al. (2024). Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist?. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02108-y)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An analysis of 972 original research articles from three journals in 1991 and 2021 found that although the average percentage of women per article as participants increased from 21.9% to 36.3%, in 2021 studies with smaller datasets (under roughly 3000 participants) still included fewer women (35.6%), and that greater representation of women as editors and authors was associated with more women participants.
Effect/estimate: Women participants 21.9% (1991) to 36.3% (2021); 35.6% in smaller studies
Population: Exercise science research participants | level: Research populations | sex: Analysis of male/female representation | age: All
Design: Bibliometric analysis | n: 972 articles; 2,984,883 participants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Methodological — applies across sport science
LIMITATIONS: Three journals only; gender/sex terminology conflation is acknowledged in this literature; does not itself quantify the consequence for recommendation validity.
PPBF implication: PPBF must attach a female-evidence-quality flag to any recommendation derived from predominantly male samples. This is implementable: a boolean plus a note on each evidence-ledger row — this registry does it in the 'sex' column.
Source: James et al. (2023). Underrepresentation of women in exercise science and physiology research is associated with authorship gender. J Appl Physiol (1985). (doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.00377.2023)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An audit-based review of 11 resistance-training consensus statements and position stands encompassing 104,251,363 participants found that youth guidelines comprised 69% male participants, and identified 287 studies that included both sexes.
Effect/estimate: Youth resistance-training guidelines 69% male
Population: Participants in studies informing RT guidelines | level: All levels | sex: 69% male in youth guidelines | age: Youth to older adult
Design: Audit-based review | n: 11 guidelines; 104,251,363 participants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Methodological — applies across strength and conditioning
LIMITATIONS: An audit of representation, not of whether recommendations are actually invalid for women; participant totals are dominated by very large epidemiological datasets.
PPBF implication: Directly relevant: PPBF's youth resistance-training guidance inherits a 69%-male evidence base. State this in the framework rather than presenting guidelines as sex-neutral.
Source: Pandit et al. (2023). Data Informing Governing Body Resistance-Training Guidelines Exhibit Sex Bias: An Audit-Based Review. Sports Med. (doi:10.1007/s40279-023-01878-1)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An analysis using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data evaluated whether typical recruitment and participant characterisation practices in sport and exercise science — under-representing cisgender females, small sample sizes and misgendering — cause incorrect statistical decisions, using sample sizes common in the field (mean N=187, median N=20).
Effect/estimate: Effects of imbalance, small n and misgendering on statistical decisions
Population: Simulated from population survey data | level: N/A | sex: Sex/gender representation analysis | age: Adult
Design: Simulation study using survey data | n: N=3645 source dataset
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Methodological
LIMITATIONS: A simulation using a general health survey rather than sport performance data; findings depend on the modelled effect structure.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of rapid weight loss in youth Olympic combat sports found RWL is highly prevalent in children and adolescent combat athletes, ranging from 25% to 94% depending on the combat sport, age and level of competition, that these athletes regularly prompt RWL by increasing exercise frequency and intensity, decreasing fluid and food intake, training in impermeable suits and using sauna frequently, and that the magnitude of RWL ranged from approximately 1% to 6.3 ± 3.7% body mass.
Effect/estimate: RWL prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3 ± 3.7% body mass
Population: Youth combat sport athletes | level: Youth, various competitive levels | sex: Boys and girls | age: Children and adolescents
Design: Systematic review | n: Multiple studies across combat sports
Boxing-specific: Partly (Olympic combat sports incl. boxing) | transfer status: Other-combat-sport with boxing relevance
LIMITATIONS: Prevalence varies enormously by sport and level; self-reported questionnaire data; retrospective recall; the health consequences in youth are not quantified by this review.
PPBF implication: SAFETY-CRITICAL for PPBF: youth weight cutting is common and the listed methods (impermeable suits, sauna, fluid restriction) are dangerous. PPBF must have an explicit NO YOUTH WEIGHT CUTTING policy. SHADOW must flag rapid body-mass change and route to a clinician and safeguarding lead — never advise a cut.
Source: Lakicevic et al. (2022). Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review. J Eat Disord. (doi:10.1186/s40337-022-00595-w)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 14-month study across 24 combat sports events collecting weight-management questionnaires one day post-competition and injury questionnaires seven days post-competition obtained 172 responses from 155 athletes (37 female, 118 male), of whom 88 (51%) reported no injury and 84 (49%) reported injury; rapid weight loss 7 days before weigh-in averaged 4.9 ± 3.4% (female) and 6.1 ± 3.2% (male), and 24 hours before weigh-in averaged 2.6 ± 2.1% and 3.0 ± 1.9% respectively.
Effect/estimate: RWL -7 days: 4.9 ± 3.4% (F), 6.1 ± 3.2% (M); -24 h: 2.6 ± 2.1% (F), 3.0 ± 1.9% (M)
Population: Adult combat sports competitors | level: Competitive amateur/professional | sex: 37 female / 118 male | age: Adult
Design: Prospective questionnaire study across 24 events | n: 172 responses from 155 athletes
Boxing-specific: Partly (combat sports incl. boxing) | transfer status: Combat-sport specific
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported injury with no clinical verification; 49% injury self-report rate suggests a very broad injury definition; response bias likely; adults only.
PPBF implication: These percentages describe what ADULT competitors DO — they are NOT recommendations and must never be presented as targets. PPBF logs body mass trend as an observation; weight-making advice belongs to a registered dietitian and physician.
Source: Doherty et al. (2025). Is there a relationship between rapid weight changes and self-reported injury in combat sports athletes? A 14-month study of 24 combat sports events. J Sci Med Sport. (doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2025.01.007)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on nutrition and weight-cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports comprises 16 approved points, including that as match duration increases beyond 4 minutes the aerobic contribution can rise to over 70% while anaerobic alactic and glycolytic pathways support high-output bursts, and that during the off-camp/general preparation phase athletes should maintain a weight ranging 12% to 15% above the weight division requirement.
Effect/estimate: Aerobic contribution >70% beyond 4 min; off-camp weight 12-15% above division
Population: Combat sport athletes | level: Adult competitive | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (International Society of Sports Nutrition) | n: Professional-body review
Boxing-specific: Partly (MMA-centred, covers other combat sports) | transfer status: Combat-sport specific with MMA emphasis
LIMITATIONS: The 12-15% off-camp figure is a professional-body recommendation for ADULT competitive athletes and is not derived from a randomised trial; MMA-centred; explicitly NOT applicable to youth; nutrition societies have a different evidence standard from medical consensus bodies.
PPBF implication: PPBF may reference this for ADULT athletes only, and only through a qualified nutrition professional. It must be excluded entirely from youth-facing material. SHADOW must not surface any weight-cut figure to an athlete or guardian.
Source: Ricci et al. (2025). International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrition and weight cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. (doi:10.1080/15502783.2025.2467909)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of acute weight loss strategies for combat sports and applications to Olympic success summarised the performance effects of weight-making practices, the physiological nature of body-mass losses, and provided practical recommendations in the form of a decision tree for achieving acute body-mass loss while minimising performance decrement.
Effect/estimate: Decision-tree guidance; no single numeric prescription
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Elite adult | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Review with practical decision tree | n: Literature review
Boxing-specific: Partly | transfer status: Combat-sport specific
LIMITATIONS: Elite adult context with professional support staff; the review addresses minimising performance decrement, not health protection in unsupervised settings; not applicable to youth.
PPBF implication: Reference for the adult competitive lane only, under professional supervision. PPBF's default for all youth and novice athletes is: compete at natural weight.
Source: Reale et al. (2016). Acute-Weight-Loss Strategies for Combat Sports and Applications to Olympic Success. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2016-0211)
