text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 16 national-champion male youth boxers (17 ± 1 y) measured on three occasions during the 30 days before competition, urine osmolality and urine specific gravity increased from day 3 to day 10 by 16% and 0.4% respectively despite athletes being in their weight-stability period and consuming fluid ad libitum, and hypohydration was universally prevalent among all athletes on both test days (USG 1.027 ± 0.003; UOSM 1035 ± 108 mOsmol/kg).
Effect/estimate: USG 1.027 ± 0.003; UOSM 1035 ± 108 mOsmol/kg; hypohydration universally prevalent
Population: Elite youth boxers | level: Elite amateur youth | sex: Male | age: 17 ± 1 y
Design: Repeated-measures observational study | n: n=16
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific, youth
LIMITATIONS: Small n=16; male only; single national squad; urinary markers have known limitations as hydration indices; 'weight-stable phase' still occurred within a competition preparation period.
PPBF implication: Striking finding for PPBF's youth lane: chronic hypohydration was universal even WITHOUT deliberate weight cutting. Fluid availability and education are cheap, high-value interventions. Do not require athletes to hit a urine-colour target — see A5-133.
Source: Zubac et al. (2016). Fluid balance and hydration assessment during the weight-stable preparation phase in elite youth boxers. J Sports Sci. (doi:10.1080/02640414.2016.1184302)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of 69 daily urine samples from 23 elite adolescent amateur boxers (17.3 ± 1.9 y) during the weight-stable phase evaluated the reliability and diagnostic accuracy of non-invasive urinary dehydration markers in field-based settings, finding uniform increments in urine osmolality of 11.2 ± 12.8% (lightweight) and 19.9 ± 22.7% (heavyweight) over the study, despite stable body mass and ad libitum fluid intake.
Effect/estimate: Osmolality increments 11.2 ± 12.8% and 19.9 ± 22.7%; very large variability
Population: Elite adolescent amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur youth | sex: Male (as reported) | age: 17.3 ± 1.9 y
Design: Field reliability study | n: 23 athletes; 69 samples
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific, youth
LIMITATIONS: The standard deviations exceed or approach the means, indicating very poor day-to-day precision; small sample; single squad.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT use a single urinary hydration reading to gate participation. The measurement is too noisy day to day. Use fluid-availability policy and education instead of a measurement gate.
Source: Zubac et al. (2018). Reliability of Urinary Dehydration Markers in Elite Youth Boxers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (doi:10.1123/ijspp.2016-0621)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Assessment of 94 Olympic combat sport athletes (56 male, 38 female) by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry within 7-21 days of competition found that most athletes were heavier than their weight division and that sport had a significant effect on physique traits including lean mass, lean mass distribution, stature and BMI, with the study also investigating the appropriateness of athletes' self-selected weight classes against the NCAA minimum wrestling weight scheme.
Effect/estimate: Most athletes heavier than their declared division; sport-specific physique differences
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Elite | sex: 56 male / 38 female | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional DXA study | n: n=94
Boxing-specific: Partly (boxing among four Olympic combat sports) | transfer status: Combat-sport specific
LIMITATIONS: DXA is not available to community gyms; elite adults only; cross-sectional; the minimum-weight scheme referenced was developed for wrestling, not boxing.
PPBF implication: Confirms most elite combat athletes compete below their off-season mass. Relevant context, but body composition assessment in youth carries eating-disorder risk — PPBF should follow the IOC body-composition guidance (A5-123) and restrict such assessment.
Source: Reale et al. (2019). Body composition of elite Olympic combat sport athletes. Eur J Sport Sci. (doi:10.1080/17461391.2019.1616826)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of endurance exercise performance in masters athletes reported that peak endurance performance is maintained until approximately 35 years of age, followed by modest decreases until 50-60 years of age with progressively steeper declines thereafter, and identified a progressive reduction in maximal oxygen consumption as the primary mechanism, with lactate threshold reduction contributing while exercise economy is comparatively preserved.
Effect/estimate: Plateau to ~35 y; modest decline to 50-60 y; steeper thereafter; VO2max the primary mechanism
Population: Masters endurance athletes | level: Masters/recreational to competitive | sex: Predominantly male in the underlying data | age: 35-80+ y
Design: Review | n: Multiple cross-sectional and longitudinal studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (endurance, not boxing)
LIMITATIONS: Endurance athletes, not combat athletes; predominantly male data; cross-sectional age comparisons confound ageing with cohort and training-history effects.
PPBF implication: PPBF's masters lane (World Boxing categorises boxers over 40 as Masters, regulated by national federations) should expect aerobic decline but not assume proportional decline in skill or technique. Log age band as a programming context.
Source: Tanaka et al. (2007). Endurance exercise performance in Masters athletes: age-associated changes and underlying physiological mechanisms. J Physiol. (doi:10.1113/jphysiol.2007.141879)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A scoping review of exercise-induced muscle damage and recovery from resistance exercise in adults aged 65 and over identified current knowledge gaps and noted that little is known about recovery from resistance exercise in older adults, which may have implications for exercise prescription.
Effect/estimate: Documents an evidence gap
Population: Adults aged 65+ | level: General older adults | sex: Mixed | age: 65+ y
Design: Scoping review | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General older-adult transfer
LIMITATIONS: Age 65+ is older than most masters boxers; not athletes in most included studies; scoping review documents gaps rather than providing prescriptions.
PPBF implication: PPBF should allow longer between-session recovery for masters athletes as a precautionary default, and label the specific interval as an assumption requiring local observation.
Source: Hayes et al. (2023). Recovery from Resistance Exercise in Older Adults: A Systematic Scoping Review. Sports Med Open. (doi:10.1186/s40798-023-00597-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of sport-specific performance assessment in Olympic combat sports including amateur boxing found 39 eligible studies, of which the majority (74%) had sample sizes under 30 subjects, nearly one third lacked sufficient description of participants (anthropometrics, age, expertise level), 72% did not sufficiently report participant inclusion/exclusion criteria, and in 62% the description or inclusion of familiarisation sessions was incomplete or absent.
Effect/estimate: 74% n<30; ~33% insufficient participant description; 72% insufficient inclusion criteria; 62% incomplete familiarisation reporting
Population: Combat sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Systematic review with methodological appraisal | n: 39 studies
Boxing-specific: Yes (includes amateur boxing) | transfer status: Boxing-specific within combat sports
LIMITATIONS: The review's finding IS the limitation: the combat-sport test-validation literature is methodologically weak across the board.
PPBF implication: FOUNDATIONAL for the PPBF test battery: sport-specific combat tests are largely under-validated. PPBF should favour general tests with strong validation plus locally established reliability, and be explicit that boxing-specific normative data mostly does not exist.
Source: Chaabene et al. (2018). Tests for the Assessment of Sport-Specific Performance in Olympic Combat Sports: A Systematic Review With Practical Recommendations. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.00386)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Yo-Yo intermittent recovery test showed a test-retest coefficient of variation of 4.9%, peak heart rate similar to an exhaustive incremental treadmill test (187 ± 2 vs 189 ± 2 bpm) with higher peak blood lactate, an eightfold increase in muscle lactate and reductions in muscle creatine phosphate (51%) and glycogen (23%), and elite soccer players improved Yo-Yo performance by 25 ± 6% and VO2max by 7% during a precompetition period.
Effect/estimate: Test-retest CV 4.9%; peak HR 187 ± 2 bpm; Yo-Yo improved 25 ± 6% vs VO2max 7%
Population: Male athletes (soccer) | level: Elite and recreational | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Validation study with muscle biopsies | n: n=17 plus 37 elite soccer players
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer (soccer)
LIMITATIONS: Soccer players, not boxers; male only; the running-based movement pattern differs from boxing footwork; boxing-specific normative data does not exist for this test.
PPBF implication: Feasible, equipment-light PPBF field test for intermittent capacity (cones, tape, audio track). Note explicitly: NO boxing normative data — PPBF must build its own local reference distribution.
Source: Krustrup et al. (2003). The yo-yo intermittent recovery test: physiological response, reliability, and validity. Med Sci Sports Exerc. (doi:10.1249/01.MSS.0000058441.94520.32)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test and its sport-specific variants have demonstrated reliability, usefulness and validity across multiple populations, including intraclass correlation coefficients above 0.94 and coefficients of variation of 1.6% for maximal speed in young elite ice hockey players, with validity established against the running version used as a cardiovascular fitness reference marker.
Effect/estimate: ICC >0.94; CV 1.6% for maximal speed
Population: Team and individual sport athletes | level: Sub-elite to elite | sex: Male and female (validated separately) | age: Youth to adult
Design: Reliability and validity studies | n: Multiple cohorts
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Not validated in boxing; requires ~40 m of space and an audio track; no boxing normative data.
PPBF implication: Alternative intermittent-capacity test with change-of-direction demand closer to boxing footwork than a straight-line test. Same caveat: PPBF must build local norms.
Source: Buchheit et al. (2011). Reliability, usefulness, and validity of the 30-15 Intermittent Ice Test in young elite ice hockey players. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181d686b7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Studies of the countermovement jump and isometric mid-thigh pull report high relative reliability (ICC 0.97 and above in an elite sample) but that most IMTP parameters showed marginal ability to detect chronic change (smallest worthwhile change less than the standard error of measurement) except peak vertical force parameters, which showed good usefulness (SWC greater than SEM).
Effect/estimate: ICC 0.97+; most IMTP parameters SWC<SEM; peak force SWC>SEM
Population: Elite and young professional athletes | level: Elite / professional | sex: Male and female (sex-based analysis in one study) | age: Youth to adult
Design: Reliability and usefulness studies | n: n=45 elite; n=20 young soccer players
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Requires a force plate; most derived parameters are NOT sensitive enough to detect real change even when reliable; not boxing-validated.
PPBF implication: Key distinction PPBF must implement: RELIABLE is not the same as SENSITIVE TO CHANGE. Only report metrics whose smallest worthwhile change exceeds their measurement error. Most force-plate derivatives fail this test.
Source: Pojskić et al. (2025). Are counter movement jump and isometric mid-thigh pull tests reliable, valid, and sensitive measurement instruments when performed after maximal cardiopulmonary exercise testing? A sex-based analysis in elite athletes. Front Physiol. (doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1663590)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review with meta-analysis of 24 appraised studies investigating whether Functional Movement Screen composite scores predict subsequent injury, and a separate systematic review and meta-analysis reporting good reliability and validity alongside pooled odds ratios for a score of 14 or below, together indicate that the FMS composite score has poor predictive value for musculoskeletal injury.
Effect/estimate: Composite score predictive value poor despite acceptable reliability
Population: Athletes and military populations | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic reviews with meta-analysis | n: 24 studies (one review); 9 predictive-value studies (other)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport / military transfer
LIMITATIONS: Predominantly male; heterogeneous injury definitions; screening tests generally perform poorly as individual-level predictors regardless of reliability.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT use FMS or similar composite movement screens as an injury-risk gate. Movement screening may inform coaching and exercise selection; it must not generate a risk score that restricts participation.
Source: Moran et al. (2017). Do Functional Movement Screen (FMS) composite scores predict subsequent injury? A systematic review with meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096938)

Effect/estimate: Reliability established; predictive validity examined across asymmetry, reach and composite
Population: Athletes across sports | level: Mixed | sex: Male and female | age: Adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 57 studies (9 reliability, 36 discriminant)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Predictive validity for injury is weak in the broader literature (see also A5-141 for the general problem with screening tests); heterogeneous populations; no boxing data.
PPBF implication: Same rule as FMS: PPBF may use balance/reach testing descriptively, never as an injury-prediction gate. This is a hard constraint on the injury-risk engine.

Effect/estimate: Acceptable reliability as an upper-body power proxy
Population: Older adults and physically active adults | level: Recreational | sex: Male and female | age: Adult to older adult
Design: Validity and reliability studies | n: Multiple small cohorts
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer; NOT validated in boxers
LIMITATIONS: Validated primarily in older adults and general physically active adults, NOT in boxers or combat athletes; throw distance depends on technique and release angle; no boxing normative data.
PPBF implication: Pragmatic, near-zero-cost PPBF upper-body power test (one medicine ball, a tape measure, a wall). Flag clearly: validated outside boxing, so PPBF must establish its own reliability and reference range before trending it.
Source: Strand et al. (2022). Validity and Reliability of the Seated Medicine Ball Throw as a Measure of Upper Body Power in Older Women. J Strength Cond Res. (doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004333)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Reviews of heart rate variability monitoring in athletes describe its application to training adaptation and prescription, while a separate review of heart rate monitoring notes both applications and limitations of heart-rate-derived indices for monitoring training status.
Effect/estimate: Application frameworks; substantial day-to-day variability noted
Population: Endurance and other athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Reviews | n: Multiple studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Other-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: HRV shows large within-individual day-to-day variation requiring rolling averages and long baselines; measurement conditions (posture, time of day, breathing) strongly affect values; no boxing-specific HRV guidance located.
PPBF implication: HRV is NOT recommended as a PPBF priority: it requires consistent daily measurement conditions that a community gym cannot enforce, and adds cost without clear benefit over sRPE plus a wellness questionnaire. Record as a future option.
Source: Lundstrom et al. (2022). Practices and Applications of Heart Rate Variability Monitoring in Endurance Athletes. Int J Sports Med. (doi:10.1055/a-1864-9726)

At the World Boxing Championships bouts for both men and women comprise three rounds of three minutes with a one-minute break.
Effect/estimate: 3x3 min with 1 min rest; age categories U15/U17/U19/Elite/Masters
Population: Amateur boxers under World Boxing | level: International amateur | sex: Male and female | age: 15 to 40+
Design: Governing-body rulebook | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific — jurisdictional rule

PPBF implication: PPBF conditioning must be built around the actual format an athlete competes under. Store sanctioning body, age category and round format as athlete-record fields — do not hardcode 3x3.

Population: Amateur boxers under USA Boxing | level: Domestic amateur, all divisions | sex: Male and female | age: 8 to 40
Design: Governing-body rulebook | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific — jurisdictional rule

Effect/estimate: Sparring requires documented medical clearance; minimum age 10; concussion protocol mandatory after head-blow stoppage
Population: Registered boxers in England | level: Recreational and competitive amateur | sex: Male and female | age: 10 to 40
Design: Governing-body rulebook | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific — jurisdictional rule (England, NOT the USA)

State regulation (e.g. Virginia Administrative Code 18VAC120-40-342) codifies equivalent minimums.
Effect/estimate: TKO from head blows: min 30 days; KO: min 60 days; mandatory 7-day post-event rest; physician decision final
Population: Professional boxers under North American commissions | level: Professional | sex: Male and female | age: Adult
Design: Regulatory guideline and state administrative code | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific — jurisdictional regulation
LIMITATIONS: These are REGULATORY MINIMUMS for professional boxing under North American commissions, not physiologically derived recovery periods, and they vary by jurisdiction. Amateur governing bodies set their own separate suspensions. A minimum suspension expiring is NOT a medical clearance.
PPBF implication: DEFINES THE SHADOW BOUNDARY PRECISELY: SHADOW may store suspension_start, suspension_minimum_days and suspension_source, and may display 'administrative minimum elapsed: yes/no'. It must NEVER render that as cleared, eligible, or safe to spar. The physician's decision is final and is the only clearance.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A joint American Academy of Pediatrics and Canadian Paediatric Society policy statement notes that although boxing provides benefits including exercise, self-discipline and self-confidence, the sport encourages and rewards deliberate blows to the head and face, that participants are at risk of head, face and neck injuries including chronic and even fatal neurologic injuries with concussion among the most common injuries, and that these organisations oppose boxing as a sport for children and adolescents and recommend that physicians vigorously oppose youth boxing and encourage alternative sports in which intentional head blows are not central.
Effect/estimate: Opposition to youth boxing participation
Population: Children and adolescents | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Under 19 y
Design: Policy statement (professional medical bodies) | n: Expert panel
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: A policy position reflecting a risk-benefit judgement by paediatric bodies, not a quantified risk estimate; published 2011 and predates the current concussion consensus and much head-impact-sensor evidence; it opposes competitive boxing involving intentional head blows, and does not address non-contact boxing-based training programmes.
PPBF implication: PPBF MUST engage with this position honestly in guardian-facing material rather than omit it. It is the strongest argument for PPBF's NON-CONTACT youth lane (Module 044) and for keeping head contact out of the youth pathway. Do not present youth boxing as endorsed by paediatric bodies — it is not.
Source:  et al. (2011). Policy statement—Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics. (doi:10.1542/peds.2011-1165)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite GB amateur boxers under 5-year medical surveillance, the hand was the most frequently injured body location overall, in training and in competition, for both new and recurrent injuries.
Effect/estimate: Competition total injury rate reported as 828 per 1000 h; hand injury rate in competition 302 per 1000 h; hand significantly higher than other locations
Population: GB amateur boxing squad | level: Elite amateur | sex: Mixed (squad, predominantly male) | age: Senior (approx. 18-34)
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance | n: 66 boxers passing through squad, 2005-2009
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Single national squad; medically diagnosed injuries only; denominators for elite squad hours may not generalise to club/youth settings; rates per 1000 h in competition are not comparable to per-session gym metrics
PPBF implication: Hand/wrist protection is the highest-yield equipment-and-technique target in a boxing programme; justifies making wrapping a governed SOP rather than a style preference. Hand-injury events should be a first-class entity in pilot.coach_observations / progression_gaps.
Source: Loosemore M et al. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study. Br J Sports Med 2015 (PMID 26192194; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Carpometacarpal joint instability in elite boxers is severe enough to require surgical fusion in a referral series, most commonly of the index and middle CMC joints and more often in the trailing (rear) hand.
Effect/estimate: 82% (31/38) returned to the same level of boxing at a median of 8 months post-surgery (range 3-27 months); trailing hand affected in 87.5%
Population: Elite boxers referred for surgery | level: Elite (amateur and professional) | sex: 37/38 male | age: Mean age 24.1 y
Design: Retrospective single-surgeon cohort | n: 38 boxers, 40 hands, 101 CMC joints fused
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Surgical referral series = selection bias toward severe cases; single surgeon; no control group; does not establish that any wrapping method prevents CMC injury
PPBF implication: Rear-hand dominance of CMC injury is a concrete asymmetry SHADOW can surface (rear-hand power volume vs. lead) for coach review. Long return-to-boxing timelines justify conservative early flagging of persistent dorsal hand pain to medical.
Source: Ng CY et al. Hand Carpometacarpal Joint Instability in Elite Boxers: Injury Characteristics, Surgical Technique, and Outcomes. J Hand Surg Am 2022 (PMID 36307285; DOI 10.1016/j.jhsa.2022.07.021)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a consecutive series of 100 boxing hand injuries, 39% involved the thumb region (attributed mainly to forced thumb abduction) and 35% involved the bases of metacarpals 2-5 including the wrist joint (attributed to forced wrist flexion).
Effect/estimate: 39% thumb region; 35% metacarpal bases/wrist; 26% phalanges and remaining metacarpals
Population: Boxers presenting with hand injury | level: Not stratified in abstract | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Not stated in abstract
Design: Consecutive case series | n: 100 consecutive hand injuries
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: 1987 case series; no denominator, no exposure data, mechanisms inferred clinically rather than measured; equipment and rules have changed since
PPBF implication: Supplies the mechanical rationale for the two non-negotiable wrap checkpoints: the thumb must be tied back to the hand (anti-abduction) and the wrist must be secured against forced flexion. Mechanism is clinical inference, not a measured causal test.
Source: Noble C. Hand injuries in boxing. Am J Sports Med 1987 (PMID 3661815; DOI 10.1177/036354658701500408)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Boxer's knuckle is disruption of the MCP extensor hood/sagittal band with extensor tendon subluxation; direct surgical repair in professional athletes has been reported to restore full range of motion and allow return to professional sport.
Effect/estimate: All athletes regained full range of motion and returned to professional sport
Population: Professional athletes (including boxers) | level: Professional | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective case series | n: 8 professional athletes, 11 MCP extensor mechanism repairs
Boxing-specific: Partly (mixed professional athletes) | transfer status: Direct/near-direct evidence
LIMITATIONS: Small surgical series without controls; outcome definition is surgeon-reported; says nothing about prevention or about whether wrapping alters incidence
PPBF implication: Defines the structure that knuckle padding is nominally protecting. PPBF coaches should treat persistent dorsal MCP pain/swelling with a sense of extensor-hood subluxation as a medical referral trigger, not a 'tape it and continue' item.
Source: Hame SL, Melone CP Jr. Boxer's knuckle in the professional athlete. Am J Sports Med 2000 (PMID 11101112; DOI 10.1177/03635465000280061701)

text_content:
[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] Boxer's knuckle and traumatic carpal boss are described in the surgical literature as the two most disabling hand injuries specific to boxing, with distinct anatomy and predictable pathology.
Effect/estimate: No pooled effect estimate; descriptive surgical review
Population: Boxers referred to hand surgery | level: Professional and elite | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Narrative clinical review | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review by treating surgeons; no incidence denominator; conclusions about 'most disabling' are clinical judgement, not measured
PPBF implication: Supports a two-item dorsal-hand symptom screen (dorsal MCP vs. dorsal carpal/CMC) in PPBF athlete journals, routed to medical rather than interpreted by SHADOW.
Source: Melone CP Jr et al. Disabling hand injuries in boxing: boxer's knuckle and traumatic carpal boss. Clin Sports Med 2009 (PMID 19819405; DOI 10.1016/j.csm.2009.06.004)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] Non-union of scaphoid fractures in boxers is documented in the orthopaedic literature as a recognised therapeutic problem.
Effect/estimate: No abstract available; no effect estimate retrievable
Population: Boxers with scaphoid fracture | level: Not stated | sex: Not stated | age: Not stated
Design: Case series (abstract not available in PubMed record) | n: Not retrievable from PubMed record
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: PubMed record carries no abstract; claim is limited to the existence and title of the source. Incidence of scaphoid injury in boxing is NOT established by this record. Do not quote any rate.
PPBF implication: Scaphoid/anatomical-snuffbox pain after a punch injury is a red-flag referral, not a wrap-adjustment problem. SHADOW must route snuffbox tenderness to medical with no interpretation.
Source: Nigst H, Tonkin M. Ununited fractures of the scaphoid in boxers. A therapeutic dilemma. Am J Sports Med 1980 (PMID 7435763; DOI 10.1177/036354658000800611)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a 10-year emergency-department series of punch injuries, the fifth metacarpal was the most commonly fractured bone and the extensor digitorum communis the most commonly injured tendon.
Effect/estimate: 64% had osseous pathology; 59% punched a solid object; 30.5% required operating-room surgery
Population: ED patients after punch injury (mostly punching a solid object) | level: Not sport-specific; general population | sex: 968 male / 84 female | age: Mean age 24.6 +/- 7.2 y
Design: Retrospective ED cohort | n: 1052 patients
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-POPULATION TRANSFER - unprotected punch trauma, not gloved/wrapped boxing
LIMITATIONS: This is unprotected punching (often altercation-related), NOT gloved-and-wrapped boxing. Rates and patterns must not be presented as boxing incidence. Alcohol and intent confound the sample.
PPBF implication: Useful contrast case for coach education: what the hand does when struck without protection. Must be labelled non-boxing in any SHADOW-surfaced explanation so it is not read as a boxing risk figure.
Source: Analysis of Punch Injuries: Clinical Characteristics, Management and Outcomes. Acta Chir Orthop Traumatol Cech 2024 (PMID 39342643; DOI 10.55095/ACHOT2024/029)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a US nationally representative emergency-department sample of boxing-related injuries (1990-2008), the hand was the most commonly injured body region and punching-bag work accounted for a substantial share of presentations.
Effect/estimate: Hand 33.0% and head/neck 22.5% of injured regions; fracture most common diagnosis 27.5%; punching-bag-related 36.8%; injury rate 12.7 per 1000 participants in 2003
Population: US emergency department presentations coded as boxing injury | level: Mixed, recreational-weighted | sex: 90.9% male | age: All ages; 12-17 and 18-24 subgroups reported
Design: Retrospective analysis of national probability sample (NEISS) | n: Estimated 165,602 injuries over 19 years (95% CI 134,891-196,313)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (US, recreational-weighted)
LIMITATIONS: ED-presenting injuries only; the boxing code includes unsupervised recreational bag work; participation denominator is an estimate; data end in 2008
PPBF implication: Bag work is not a low-risk station. PPBF should apply the same wrap/glove standard and coach supervision at heavy-bag stations as in sparring, and log bag-station hand complaints.
Source: Potter MR, Snyder AJ, Smith GA. Boxing injuries presenting to U.S. emergency departments, 1990-2008. Am J Prev Med 2011 (PMID 21406281; DOI 10.1016/j.amepre.2010.12.018)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of amateur boxing found competition injury incidence far exceeds training incidence, with the upper limb the most commonly injured region in the training setting.
Effect/estimate: Competition IIR 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 min (95% CI 4.2-10.9); training IIR 1.3 per 1000 h (95% CI 0.2-7.0). Head/neck median 72% of competition injuries; upper limb median 49% of training injuries. Authors summarise this as approximately 1 injury per 2.5 h of competition and per 772 h of training.
Population: Amateur boxers in prospective cohort studies | level: Amateur | sex: Mixed; most included cohorts male-dominant | age: Predominantly adult amateur
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts | n: 17 eligible studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Wide confidence intervals and high heterogeneity; injury definitions vary between included studies; few female-specific or youth-specific cohorts; no causal test of any preventive measure
PPBF implication: Anchors the training/competition split in PPBF's risk model: competition-day equipment governance (wrap inspection, glove issue) is a distinct high-risk control point from routine gym sessions. Exposure denominators should be recorded in pilot.sessions so PPBF can compute its own rates.
Source: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport 2022 (PMID 36195527; DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology reported significantly higher injury incidence rates in professional than in amateur or female boxing groups, and lower amateur rates in 2010-2019 studies than in earlier ones.
Effect/estimate: Pooled overall injury IR 223.9 per 1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4); professional subgroup 399.8 vs amateur/female lower; amateur IR per 1000 boxers 76.6 (2010-2019) vs 250.6 (earlier), p<.000
Population: Organised boxing worldwide | level: Professional, amateur and female subgroups | sex: Mixed; female analysed as a separate subgroup | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis (level of evidence 3) | n: 14 studies included from 9584 screened; 11/14 rated moderate quality
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Single-arm pooling of heterogeneous designs; 'female' treated as a subgroup rather than stratified within level, confounding sex with competitive context; secular decline may reflect surveillance and rule changes rather than true risk reduction; correlation, not causation
PPBF implication: Professional-level risk figures must never be shown against a youth or novice PPBF athlete. SHADOW's evidence layer needs a competitive-level tag on every risk statement it surfaces.
Source: Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. Orthop J Sports Med 2023 (PMID 37025124; DOI 10.1177/23259671221127669)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In Nevada professional boxing over 2001-2003, facial laceration was the most common injury and hand injury the second most common.
Effect/estimate: Overall injury incidence 17.1 per 100 boxer-matches (3.4 per 100 boxer-rounds); facial laceration 51%, hand injury 17%, eye injury 14%, nose 5%
Population: Nevada professional boxers | level: Professional | sex: Male and female (female incidence documented) | age: Adult
Design: Pair-matched case-control analysis of commission data | n: 524 matches
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (professional)
LIMITATIONS: Single state commission, 2001-2003; professional rules (8-10 oz gloves, no headguard, longer bouts) differ substantially from amateur and youth; not transferable to PPBF youth population
PPBF implication: Explains why professional corners carry cut kits and why cut management is a defined, licensed role. PPBF must define that role and its holder before any competition lane opens.
Source: Zazryn TR et al. / Injury risk in professional boxing. South Med J 2005 (PMID 16295814; DOI 10.1097/01.smj.0000182498.19288.e2)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Injury surveillance at an elite women's national boxing championship in India recorded injury rates using bout and hour denominators, demonstrating that female-specific boxing surveillance is feasible but sparse.
Effect/estimate: Injury rate 43.98 per 1000 athlete bouts (95% CI 33.71-54.07) and 293.21 per 1000 athlete hours
Population: Elite Indian female boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Tournament injury surveillance | n: 235 female boxers at one championship
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (female)
LIMITATIONS: Single tournament, single country; short observation window; competition only, no training exposure; rates not directly comparable to multi-year squad surveillance
PPBF implication: Female-specific boxing injury evidence is thin; PPBF should not assume male-derived equipment or wrap standards transfer without checking, and should record sex on every injury observation.
Source: Injury surveillance during elite women's national boxing championship in India. Med J Armed Forces India 2021 (PMID 37193531; DOI 10.1016/j.mjafi.2021.03.016)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed-methods implementation study in Australian amateur boxing found injury surveillance implementable at events but identified specific barriers and facilitators in the amateur boxing community.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative themes including value of data; maintenance domain not evaluated
Population: Australian amateur boxing community (athletes, coaches, promoters, referees, medical staff, officials) | level: Amateur | sex: Mixed | age: Not stratified in abstract
Design: Mixed methods: semi-structured interviews plus RE-AIM-framed implementation trial | n: Interviews plus implementation across 5 amateur boxing events
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Implementation and acceptability study, not an injury-rate study; maintenance/sustainability not assessed; Australian governance context
PPBF implication: Directly supports PPBF building event-level injury capture into the platform, and warns that sustaining it (the maintenance domain) is the unproven part - design for low-friction capture at ringside.
Source: Is it feasible to implement an injury surveillance system for amateur boxing events in Australia? A mixed methods study. J Sci Med Sport 2025 (PMID 41421883; DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2025.12.007)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] There is no randomised controlled trial establishing that any specific hand-wrapping material or method reduces hand or wrist injury incidence in boxing. The practice rests on mechanical reasoning, governing-body mandate and coaching tradition.
Effect/estimate: TBD - no effect estimate exists. PubMed searches for hand wrapping trials in boxing returned no controlled prevention trial.
Population: Boxers of all levels | level: All | sex: All | age: All
Design: Absence of trial evidence identified across PubMed searches on boxing hand wrap/bandage/wrist protection | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Not applicable - gap statement
LIMITATIONS: Absence of evidence in the searched databases is not proof of absence; grey literature and non-indexed governing-body technical reports were not exhaustively searched. Wrapping is nonetheless mandatory under every rulebook examined, so an unwrapped control arm would be neither legal nor ethical in competition.
PPBF implication: PPBF must present the wrap SOP as a mandated safety procedure with mechanical rationale and rule compliance - NOT as an evidence-based injury-prevention intervention. SHADOW must never claim wrapping prevents injury.
Source: INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE - no qualifying trial identified (INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A clinical review of hand and wrist injuries in boxing and martial arts asserts there is clear evidence that hand protection reduces the risk of hand injury and that technique/target training is an important component of prevention.
Effect/estimate: No effect size given; assertion is narrative and not supported in the abstract by a pooled estimate
Population: Boxers and martial artists | level: Mixed | sex: Not stratified | age: Not stratified
Design: Narrative clinical review (Hand Clinics) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Partly (boxing and martial arts combined) | transfer status: Mixed combat-sport evidence
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative review assertion, not a trial result. It is listed as CONTESTED because it conflicts with A6-015: the underlying controlled evidence for that claim was not located. Treat the strength of the wording in the source with caution.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a double-blind crossover trial of 12 elite boxers, a silicone-based hand wrapping produced slightly higher measured total punch force and lower off-axis force wastage than a gauze-based wrapping.
Effect/estimate: Silicone 436 +/- 33 N vs gauze 372 +/- 12 N total force (p<0.001); force wastage 2.0% (silicone) vs 3.8% (gauze) (p<0.001); silicone lengthened fist-target contact time
Population: Elite boxers | level: Elite | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Double-blind crossover trial with material testing | n: 12 elite boxers; 5 maximal punches per condition
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Very small sample; force delivery to a target is NOT an injury outcome - the study does not show reduced hand injury; higher delivered force could plausibly raise opponent head-impact loading, which was not assessed; silicone wraps are not legal competition hand protection under the rulebooks examined
PPBF implication: Warns against equipment marketed on force-transfer grounds. PPBF gear policy should evaluate hand protection on rule compliance and comfort/fit, not on punch-force claims - and should note that increasing delivered force is not an athlete-welfare goal in a youth programme.
Source: Enhanced boxing punch impact with silicone cushioning. Front Sports Act Living 2024 (PMID 39176237; DOI 10.3389/fspor.2024.1358224)

Only a clear transparent water bottle. Under no circumstance may seconds administer supplemental oxygen. Escalating caution/warning/removal penalties for prohibited activity.

Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Rule 26, Coaches/Seconds) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - US amateur jurisdiction only

PPBF implication: Corner scope is rule-bounded and jurisdiction-specific. SHADOW must never suggest a cut or swelling intervention; the app's role is to display the applicable permitted-agent list for the sanctioning body of that event and name the qualified human who owns the decision.
Source: USA Boxing National Rulebook, Rule 26 Coaches/Seconds (revision marked 12/31/2021) (Not applicable (rulebook))

Effect/estimate: Criteria in stated order: number of quality blows on target area (most important), domination by technical and tactical superiority, competitiveness. Allocation: 10-9 close round, 10-8 clear winner, 10-7 total dominance. Five judges at national competitions; three or five otherwise.
Population: USA Boxing competitions | level: Amateur | sex: All | age: All
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Rule 14, Scoring System) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - US amateur jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: Revision marked 12/31/2021. Criteria are qualitative; the rulebook does not define a quantitative threshold for 'quality blow', so any PPBF scoring model is an interpretation and not the official standard.
PPBF implication: PPBF scoring-literacy training and any film-tagging schema should mirror these three criteria in this order. Any SHADOW round-score estimate must be labelled a training aid, never a prediction of an official verdict.
Source: USA Boxing National Rulebook, Rule 14 Scoring System (10-Point-Must) (revision marked 12/31/2021) (Not applicable (rulebook))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] England Boxing permits up to three coaches at the corner during the round interval with defined positions, restricts nutrition to water from a clear plastic bottle, and restricts cut treatment to an officially authorised individual with the required accreditation.
Effect/estimate: Three coaches may attend during the interval: one may enter the ring, one on the apron, one on the floor. Boxer may stand or sit but must face the centre of the ring throughout. Only water from a clear plastic drinking bottle. Cuts may only be treated by an officially authorised individual with the required accreditation. Seconds seating area 1 m from the corner within a 1.5 m x 2.5 m designated area.
Population: Coaches/seconds at England Boxing competitions | level: Amateur | sex: Not applicable | age: Not applicable
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Annex C1, Round Interval; Section 5.6 Seconds) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - England/UK jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: 2026 edition as retrieved. Corner headcount and permitted substances differ from USA Boxing and World Boxing - do not present as universal.
PPBF implication: Gives the concrete corner choreography PPBF's 60-second sequence must respect: who is where, what may be given, and who may touch a cut. The accreditation requirement means PPBF must name a qualified cut-authorised person before any competition lane opens.
Source: England Boxing Technical & Competition Rules 2026, Annex C1 Round Interval Procedures and Section 5.6 Seconds (Not applicable (rulebook))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] England Boxing prohibits sparring for any boxer under 10 years old, requires an annual medical and Fit to Box declaration before sparring, and requires all sparring to be supervised by an active fully licensed Level 2 coach.
Effect/estimate: No sparring under age 10 for safeguarding and safety reasons; annual medical, Fit to Box declaration and no active medical suspension required; supervision by an active fully licensed Level 2 coach required; a child under 10 may join a club and participate in classes but may not box competitively, take part in a skills bout, or spar; minors matched within a 12-month age gap and (outside championships) within 2 kg
Population: England Boxing registered boxers | level: Amateur and recreational | sex: All | age: 10 and above; under 10 prohibited from sparring
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Section 5.7, Sparring; Section 2.3 Minors) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - England/UK jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: 2026 edition as retrieved. USA Boxing's Prep division permits competition from age 8 - a direct jurisdictional conflict on the minimum-age question that PPBF must resolve as a policy decision, not a technical one.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] World Boxing mandates Velcro bandages for U17 and U19 competition, permits either Velcro bandages or professional handwraps for Elite competition as specified in event rules, and gives exact material specifications for both.
Effect/estimate: Velcro bandages: two rolls 3.5-4.5 m long, 5.7 cm wide, stretchy cotton with Velcro closure. Professional handwraps: 2 rolls 5 cm x 15 m gauze (one per hand), 2 rolls 5 cm x 10 m gauze for a knuckle pad, 2 rolls 2.5 cm x 13 m zinc oxide tape, 1 roll 1.25 cm x 13 m zinc oxide tape for between the fingers. Prohibited: any substance or foreign material; covering the knuckles with zinc oxide tape; stacking gauze and tape; placing zinc oxide tape directly on the skin.
Population: World Boxing competitors | level: U17, U19 and Elite international amateur | sex: Male and female | age: U17 through Elite
Design: Primary international-federation rulebook (Rule 13.2) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - international federation
LIMITATIONS: World Boxing Competition Rules in force November 2024 as retrieved; event-specific rules may vary and must be read alongside the Event Invitation. Age-graded: youth categories are NOT permitted the gauze-and-tape format.
PPBF implication: This is the single most useful youth-safety anchor in the whole track: an international federation restricts under-19 athletes to the simpler Velcro format. PPBF should mirror that - gauze-and-tape is not a youth training procedure. The 'no tape directly on skin' and 'no stacking' rules are checklist items.
Source: World Boxing Competition Rules (in force November 2024), Rule 13.2 Professional handwraps and Velcro bandages (Not applicable (rulebook))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] World Boxing permits up to three seconds per corner with only one entering the ring during rest periods, and restricts in-bout cut care to adrenaline 1/1000 and non-petroleum skin-protective jelly.
Effect/estimate: Up to three seconds may accompany a boxer; only two may mount the apron and only one may enter the ring during rest periods; in the case of a cut, seconds may administer only adrenaline 1/1000 and non-petroleum skin-protective jelly during the bout; seconds may carry ice bags, Enswell, 4x4 gauze padding and swabs; one bag max 30 x 20 x 20 cm; supplemental oxygen and inhalers prohibited
Population: Seconds at World Boxing competitions | level: International amateur | sex: Not applicable | age: Not applicable
Design: Primary international-federation rulebook (Rule 3, The Seconds) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - international federation
LIMITATIONS: World Boxing's permitted-agent list is materially narrower than USA Boxing's Rule 26 list. Presenting either as 'the' corner standard would be wrong; the applicable list is set by the sanctioning body of the specific event.
PPBF implication: Registry-level conflict for synthesis: permitted corner agents differ by sanctioning body. PPBF's corner card must be generated per-event from the governing body's own list, with a human sign-off, and must default to the most restrictive option when the sanctioning body is unknown.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a laboratory punch-machine study, an AIBA-approved headguard substantially reduced peak linear and angular headform accelerations compared with a bare headform.
Effect/estimate: Peak contact forces 1.9-5.9 kN. At 8.3 m/s fist-glove impacts, mean peak resultant headform acceleration approx. 130 g bare vs approx. 85 g forehead impacts. At 6.85 m/s bare, mean peak angular accelerations 5200-5600 rad/s2, almost halved by the headguard.
Population: Instrumented Hybrid III head and neck system (laboratory) | level: Not applicable (lab) | sex: Not applicable | age: Not applicable
Design: Laboratory linear-impactor study | n: Impacts at selected speeds 4.1-8.3 m/s; single approved headguard model
Boxing-specific: Yes (boxing headguard, boxing-style impactor) | transfer status: LAB EVIDENCE - not in-competition injury outcomes
LIMITATIONS: Headform is not a human head; a single approved model tested; reduced headform acceleration is a surrogate, not a concussion-incidence outcome; does not address behavioural compensation, visibility, or the number of head impacts a boxer receives while wearing one
PPBF implication: Half of the headguard controversy: mechanically, headguards attenuate impact to a headform. PPBF should present this as lab evidence and pair it with A6-035/A6-036 rather than citing it alone.
Source: Boxing headguard performance in punch machine tests. Br J Sports Med 2015 (PMID 26175022; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2015-095094)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A cross-sectional observational study of AIBA competitions reported that stoppages due to head blows decreased significantly without head guards, alongside a notable increase in cuts.
Effect/estimate: Stoppages due to head blows significantly decreased without head guards; notable increase in cuts. Authors conclude removing head guards may reduce the already small risk of acute brain injury in amateur boxing.
Population: Boxers in World Series Boxing and AIBA world championships | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional observational, prospectively recorded by ringside physicians | n: WSB vs other AIBA competitions; 2009, 2011 (with) and 2013 (without) world championships
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (elite senior male only)
LIMITATIONS: Observational, not randomised. Stoppage rate is a referee/physician decision, not a measure of brain injury. WSB differs from championship boxing in more than headguard use (bout length, experience, professional context), so the comparison is confounded. Correlation, not causation. Elite senior male only - no youth, no female data.
PPBF implication: The other half of the controversy. PPBF must not extrapolate an elite senior male observational finding to youth or female boxers, where headguards remain mandatory under both England Boxing and USA Boxing.
Source: Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments - A Cross-Sectional Observational Study. Clin J Sport Med 2017 (PMID 27116592; DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000322)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of protective headgear in Olympic boxing concluded headguards protect well against lacerations and skull fractures, that less is known about protection against concussion and other traumatic brain injuries, and that AIBA's removal decision should be viewed with caution.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative synthesis: protective against lacerations and skull fractures; uncertain against concussion/TBI. Most analysed studies used indirect evidence (self-report or observation) with relatively small non-representative samples; almost no randomised controlled trials, longitudinal designs, or recreational-boxing samples.
Population: Boxers with headguards as a study factor | level: Predominantly elite/Olympic; recreational samples largely absent | sex: Predominantly male | age: Predominantly adult
Design: Systematic literature review with methodological quality assessment | n: 39 articles included; five databases plus grey literature, publications from 1980 onward
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Review of a weak underlying literature; the conclusion is essentially that the evidence base cannot settle the question. Does not support either a pro- or anti-headguard position as established fact.
PPBF implication: This is the correct framing for PPBF coach education: headguards demonstrably reduce cuts and skull fracture; their effect on concussion is unresolved; the elite removal decision is contested. SHADOW must present all three positions together and never resolve the debate for a coach.
Source: Concussions, cuts and cracked bones: A systematic literature review on protective headgear and head injury prevention in Olympic boxing. Eur J Sport Sci 2021 (PMID 33607924; DOI 10.1080/17461391.2021.1872711)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Comparison of elite amateur bouts before and after the 2013 rules change found reduced punch volume and increased ring and defensive movement post-change, with an increase in technical knockouts and skin splits, and concluded that any increased concussive risk is equivocal.
Effect/estimate: Reductions post-2013 in total punches thrown, rear-hand punches, rear-hand hooks, punches landed, uppercuts and body punches (all p<0.05); increases in ring movement and defensive movement (both p<0.004); rounds with standing counts fell from 9% to 3%; bouts not lasting full duration rose from 1.7% to 4.2%
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur (Olympic and World Championship) | sex: Male | age: Mean age 24.3 +/- 3.2 y
Design: Retrospective video notational analysis | n: 29 Olympic (pre-2013) and 50 World Championship (post-2013) bouts; 99 male boxers
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (elite senior male)
LIMITATIONS: Video analysis of different competitions in different years; the 2013 change bundled headguard removal with other rule and scoring changes, so effects cannot be attributed to headguards alone. Elite male only.
PPBF implication: Demonstrates that equipment and rule changes reshape technical behaviour, not just injury rates. Any PPBF skill model trained on pre-2013 or professional footage carries a rule-era bias that must be recorded as metadata on film-tagging records.
Source: Comparison of amateur boxing before and after the 2013 rules change and the impact on boxers' safety. Br J Sports Med 2017 (PMID 28954796; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2017-097667)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of 59 years of Olympic-style boxing verdicts found rule changes were followed by measurable shifts in the rates of health-relevant verdict types, including changes after the introduction of the standing count, mandatory head guard and computerised scoring.
Effect/estimate: RSCI rate increased 0.72% to 2.42% (p<0.03) after the standing-count rule; with mandatory head guard, lower RSCI (0.60%, p<0.001) but higher RSCH (1.31% to 4.92%, p<0.001) and RSC (9.71% to 13.05%, p<0.03); KO rate fell 6.44% to 2.09% (p<0.001) with computerised scoring
Population: Olympic boxing tournament bouts 1952-2011 | level: Elite amateur | sex: Predominantly male over the period | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective analysis of tournament records | n: 29,357 bouts
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Ecological time-series from web-sourced records; many co-occurring changes across six decades; verdict categories are officiating decisions, not clinical diagnoses; strictly correlational
PPBF implication: Important nuance for the headguard debate: this record associates mandatory head guards with LOWER injury stoppages but HIGHER head-blow stoppages - a direction opposite to the simplest reading of A6-035. Flag to synthesis as an internal conflict in the headguard literature.
Source: Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health. Br J Sports Med 2013 (PMID 23314931; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2012-091771)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] An umbrella review of systematic reviews examined whether mouthguards prevent dentofacial injuries in athletes; a dental-traumatology overview separately states mouthguards are proven devices that reduce the probability of and damage to orofacial tissues.
Effect/estimate: No single pooled effect extracted from the abstract; the dental-traumatology overview also notes existing mouthguard standards appear arbitrarily selected rather than derived from clinical evidence
Population: Athletes across contact and collision sports | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mixed
Design: Umbrella review of systematic reviews (AMSTAR 2 appraised); plus narrative standards overview | n: Umbrella review across MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane and DOSS
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER - evidence base is dominated by rugby, hockey, field sports; boxing-specific mouthguard trials were not located
LIMITATIONS: Umbrella reviews inherit the weaknesses of their component reviews; certainty of underlying evidence is frequently rated low. The orofacial-protection claim is much better supported than any concussion claim (see A6-040). No boxing-specific dental-injury trial identified.
PPBF implication: Mouthguards are justified to athletes and guardians on dental and orofacial grounds. That is the claim PPBF and SHADOW should make - it is defensible.
Source: Impact of mouthguards on the prevention of dentofacial injuries and sports performance among athletes: An umbrella review. J Indian Soc Pedod Prev Dent 2025; and Sports mouthguard overview: Materials, fabrication techniques, existing standards, and future research needs. Dent Traumatol 2022 (PMID 40586455; DOI 10.4103/jisppd.jisppd_55_25; PMID 36436198; DOI 10.1111/edt.12809)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] Evidence that mouthguards prevent concussion is inconsistent and much weaker than the orofacial-protection evidence: individual case-control studies report lower odds of concussion with mouthguard use, but the mechanism and the strength of evidence remain disputed.
Effect/estimate: Ice hockey: any mouthguard use adjusted OR for concussion 0.36 (95% CI 0.17-0.73); off-the-shelf adjusted OR 0.31 (95% CI 0.14-0.65); dental custom-fit a non-significant 49% lower odds. College study: OR 0.101 (p=0.041) but very small numbers in the matched comparison (7/28 vs 1/28, p=0.051).
Population: Youth ice hockey players; college athletes in collision/contact sports | level: Youth and collegiate | sex: Mixed | age: Youth and young adult
Design: Nested case-control within prospective cohorts; separate propensity-score-matched case-control | n: 315 concussion cases and 270 controls (ice hockey); 115 analysed participants (college case-control)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER - ice hockey and collegiate collision sports; NO boxing-specific mouthguard concussion evidence located
LIMITATIONS: Observational designs cannot establish causation; mouthguard users may differ systematically from non-users (equipment-conscious behaviour, coaching, level of play). The college study is very small and partly non-significant. The counterintuitive finding that off-the-shelf outperformed custom-fit argues for residual confounding. Boxing exposure (repeated deliberate head blows) is not represented at all.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT tell athletes or parents that a mouthguard protects the brain. Mandate mouthguards for dental/orofacial protection and rule compliance; state plainly that concussion protection is unproven. This is a direct anti-overclaim guardrail for SHADOW's chat layer.
Source: Chisholm DA et al. Mouthguard use in youth ice hockey and the risk of concussion: nested case-control study of 315 cases. Int J Environ Res Public Health 2020 (PMID 31937578; DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2019-101011; PMID 32580527; DOI 10.3390/ijerph17124493)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The systematic review of prevention strategies informing the Amsterdam 2022 consensus process evaluated protective equipment among other interventions, and the resulting consensus statement is the reference standard for concussion management in sport.
Effect/estimate: Consensus process yielded CRT6, SCAT6, Child SCAT6 and SCOAT6 tools
Population: Athletes across sports | level: All | sex: All | age: All, with child-specific tools
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42019152982) informing an international consensus statement | n: Eight databases searched October 2019, updated March 2022
Boxing-specific: No - cross-sport consensus | transfer status: CROSS-SPORT CONSENSUS - boxing is not the primary evidence base
LIMITATIONS: Consensus statements aggregate heterogeneous sport contexts; boxing (deliberate repeated head impact) is not well represented. Consensus is expert judgement layered on systematic review, not a trial result.
PPBF implication: PPBF's concussion pathway should point to CRT6 and the SCAT6 family as the recognition and assessment instruments used by qualified humans. SHADOW must never administer, score, or interpret them, and never clear an athlete.
Source: Patricios JS et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport - Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med 2023; and Prevention strategies and modifiable risk factors for sport-related concussions and head impacts: a systematic review and meta-analysis. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Meta-analytic evidence indicates mouthguard use lowers VO2max and maximal minute ventilation overall, but custom-made mouthguards showed no significant effect on these parameters.
Effect/estimate: Significant reductions in VO2max (95% CI -2.638 to -1.728) and VEmax (95% CI -4.103 to -1.354) favouring no mouthguard; subgroup analysis showed no significant effect for custom-made mouthguards
Population: Athletes in randomised clinical trials of mouthguard wear during exercise testing | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male in component studies | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs | n: 14 studies included
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT/LAB TRANSFER - exercise testing, not boxing rounds
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory exercise testing with facemask apparatus that itself interacts with mouthguard fit; statistical significance does not establish practical significance - a separate crossover study found the differences negligible in practical terms. No boxing-specific data.
PPBF implication: Gives a defensible, non-marketing reason to prefer a well-fitted (ideally custom or professionally fitted) mouthguard: fit quality, not brand claims. Useful when an athlete complains of breathing difficulty - route persistent complaints to a dentist, not to a coach workaround.
Source: Mouthguard Use and Cardiopulmonary Capacity - A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med Int Open 2017; supporting: Effects of boil-and-bite and custom-fit mouthguards on cardiorespiratory responses to aerobic exercise. J Sports Med Phys Fitness 2019 (PMID 30539104; DOI 10.1055/s-0043-117599; PMID 31565911; DOI 10.23736/S0022-4707.19.09714-7)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A randomised crossover study in young active adults found self-adapted mouthguards with breathing channels significantly increased airway resistance and reduced ventilation at maximum load.
Effect/estimate: Airway resistance 0.53 +/- 0.16 vs 0.35 +/- 0.10 kPa*L (p<0.01); ventilation at max load 118.4 +/- 28.17 vs 128.2 +/- 32.16 L/min (p<0.01); higher submaximal blood lactate with the mouthguard (p<0.01)
Population: Healthy active young adults | level: Recreational/active | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: 25.12 +/- 2.19 y
Design: Randomised crossover incremental exertion test | n: 17 participants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-POPULATION TRANSFER - cycle/incremental testing in non-boxers
LIMITATIONS: Small sample; non-boxing exercise mode; 'young athletes' in the title refers to young active adults rather than child athletes; effect on boxing round performance not tested
PPBF implication: Supports treating poor mouthguard fit as a fixable performance and comfort problem, and supports professional fitting where affordable. Do not use this to justify removing or thinning a mouthguard - it is mandatory equipment.
Source: Decreased exercise capacity in young athletes using self-adapted mouthguards. Eur J Appl Physiol 2021 (PMID 33713202; DOI 10.1007/s00421-021-04659-8)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Mouthguards become microbially contaminated in use and can be measurably decontaminated by specific agents; separate work in young footballers documented surface deterioration and poor handling of mouthguards.
Effect/estimate: Hydrogen peroxide reduced Enterococcus faecalis load by 84.19%; 0.5% sodium hypochlorite reduced Candida albicans load by 92.95%; authors conclude hydrogen peroxide, 0.5% NaOCl and a commercial oral care foam gave optimum disinfection
Population: EVA mouthguards contaminated in vitro; and mouthguards used by young footballers | level: Not applicable / youth sport | sex: Not applicable | age: Youth in the field study
Design: In vitro decontamination study with SEM; plus field study of mouthguard condition and handling | n: In vitro treatment arms A-H; field study of young football players' mouthguards
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: LAB / OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER - in vitro and youth football
LIMITATIONS: In vitro study on a limited organism panel; agents tested are not automatically appropriate for youth home use, and hypochlorite handling by minors raises its own safety issue. Field deterioration data are from football, not boxing.
PPBF implication: Justifies a written mouthguard care and replacement standard in PPBF gear policy. The specific cleaning agent for youth home use should be set by PPBF's medical/dental adviser, not selected from an in vitro paper - the exact protocol is TBD.
Source: Microbial Contamination and Disinfection of Sport Mouthguard: In Vitro Study. Curr Microbiol 2019; and Surface deterioration and poor handling of sports mouthguards for young football players. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Contact breast injury is common in female contact sport and is substantially under-reported to coaching and medical staff; the evidence base for breast protective equipment in contact, combat and pseudo-contact sport is still developing.
Effect/estimate: In U18 international female rugby: contact breast injury incidence 39%, exercise-induced breast pain 43%; 77% of those with contact breast injury had multiple incidents in the previous year; 64% did not report the injury and none were reported to coaching or medical personnel; 27% reported breast pain inhibited performance
Population: Female athletes in contact sports; under-18 international female rugby players | level: Elite and international age-grade | sex: Female | age: Adult and under-18
Design: Systematic review; plus cross-sectional survey | n: Systematic review of contact breast injuries; survey n=110 U18 international players (17.0 +/- 0.7 y)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-SPORT TRANSFER - rugby and mixed contact sports; boxing-specific breast injury data were not located
LIMITATIONS: Rugby contact mechanics differ from boxing (tackle vs punch). Self-report survey. Boxing-specific incidence is unknown. The BJSM piece on evidence-based breast protective equipment had no abstract in the PubMed record, so only its existence and framing are cited.
PPBF implication: Under-reporting is the actionable finding. PPBF should build a low-friction, private reporting route for breast injury and pain (not a public floor conversation), with a female staff contact named. Note that both England Boxing and World Boxing make breast protectors discretionary, not mandatory - so equipment alone will not close this gap.
Source: Bibby A, Kenny I, Cahalan R. Contact Breast Injuries Among Female Athletes: A Systematic Review. Sports Med 2024; 'Don't tell the coach': contact breast injury and breast pain in under-18 international female rugby players. text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Groin protection is mandatory for male boxers and breast protection is discretionary for female boxers under England Boxing, World Boxing and USA Boxing, with specific construction constraints on breast protectors.
Effect/estimate: England Boxing: groin protection mandatory for male boxers; not mandatory for female boxers to wear either breast or groin protector; a breast protector must protect soft tissue up to where breast protrusion merges with the chest wall, must not shield any other target area, and must have no metal part except back fastenings. World Boxing: men must wear a groin protector; women may; breast protector must follow natural breast contours, add no protection to surrounding areas, and not cover any target area including the sternum. USA Boxing: cup protector must be worn by male boxers; women may wear a groin protector if they choose; breast protector optional for women.
Population: Amateur competitors | level: Amateur, international and national | sex: Male and female, differentiated | age: All categories
Design: Primary rulebooks (England Boxing 8.4; World Boxing 13.8; USA Boxing Rule 40.2/40.3) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - three jurisdictions, concordant on this point
LIMITATIONS: Editions as retrieved (England Boxing 2026; World Boxing Nov 2024; USA Boxing revision marked 12/31/2021). The rules constrain protector design so tightly that protective capacity is limited by design - which is relevant to the under-reporting finding in A6-045.
PPBF implication: Equipment matrix must record mandatory-vs-discretionary per sex per jurisdiction. Because breast protection is discretionary everywhere checked, PPBF cannot rely on a rule to solve the injury-reporting problem - the reporting route is the control.
Source: England Boxing Technical & Competition Rules 2026 s8.4; World Boxing Competition Rules Nov 2024 r13.8; USA Boxing National Rulebook Rule 40.2-40.3 (Not applicable (rulebooks))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Systematic review evidence shows combat sport athletes routinely undertake rapid weight loss in the days before competition followed by rapid weight regain.
Effect/estimate: Review quantified magnitude of rapid weight loss and regain across boxing, judo, MMA, taekwondo and wrestling; specific magnitudes vary by sport and are reported per-sport in the source
Population: Combat sport athletes across five sports including boxing | level: Mixed, largely adult competitive | sex: 156 female, 4276 male | age: Predominantly adult
Design: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017055279) | n: 16 full-text studies; 4432 participants
Boxing-specific: Partly - boxing is one of five sports included | transfer status: COMBAT-SPORT EVIDENCE (includes boxing)
LIMITATIONS: Heavily male sample (96%); pooled across sports with different weigh-in-to-competition intervals; self-report methods in many component studies
PPBF implication: PPBF must have an explicit no-weight-cutting position for youth, and SHADOW must refuse to generate any weight-reduction plan. Route all weight-category questions to a qualified human (registered dietitian / physician) with guardian involvement for minors.
Source: The Magnitude of Rapid Weight Loss and Rapid Weight Gain in Combat Sport Athletes Preparing for Competition: A Systematic Review. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab 2019 (PMID 30299200; DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of California State Athletic Commission data found almost all male professional boxers gained body mass between the official weigh-in and competition.
Effect/estimate: 389 of 399 (97.5%) gained weight between official weigh-in and competition; total absolute body mass gained 4.4 +/- 2.2 kg
Population: Male professional boxers licensed in California | level: Professional | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective analysis of official commission weight data 2015-2018 | n: 399 athletes
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (professional male)
LIMITATIONS: Professional boxing with day-before weigh-ins; does NOT describe amateur or youth boxing, where same-day weigh-in structurally limits this practice (see A6-024). Observational commission data; no health outcomes measured.
PPBF implication: Shows the weigh-in schedule is the lever, not athlete willpower. PPBF should note this when explaining to athletes and guardians why amateur same-day weigh-ins exist. Never present the professional pattern as a model.
Source: Rapid weight gain following weight cutting in male professional boxers. Phys Sportsmed 2021 (PMID 34310264; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2021.1960780)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Meta-analytic and review evidence indicates rapid weight loss impairs exercise performance measures and is associated with markers of acute kidney stress, with recovery time between weigh-in and competition modifying the effect.
Effect/estimate: Meta-analysis compared maximal strength, maximal power, anaerobic capacity and repeated high-intensity effort pre-RWL, immediately post-RWL, and 3-36 h after recovery. Renal review: creatinine, blood urea nitrogen and urine specific gravity significantly increased after RWL in the majority of included studies.
Population: Combat sport athletes | level: Mixed competitive | sex: Mixed, male-dominant | age: Predominantly adult
Design: Meta-analysis of pre/post rapid weight loss performance; plus systematic reviews of renal markers and judo outcomes | n: Meta-analysis across combat sports; renal review of studies with approx. 5% weight loss within a week
Boxing-specific: Partly - combat sports including boxing | transfer status: COMBAT-SPORT EVIDENCE
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous protocols and recovery windows; renal markers are surrogate measures of dehydration and acute stress, not diagnoses of kidney injury; most participants adult male
PPBF implication: Gives PPBF a health-and-performance argument against cutting that does not require moralising. Any individual weight guidance is a medical/dietetic decision - SHADOW must refuse and route.
Source: Effects of Weight Cutting on Exercise Performance in Combat Athletes: A Meta-Analysis. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2022; Effects of Rapid Weight Loss on Kidney Function in Combat Sport Athletes. Medicina 2021; Effects of Rapid Weight Loss on Judo Athletes: A Systematic Review. text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite youth Olympic-style boxers across 12 European countries, rapid weight loss was not associated with competitive success, while boxing experience was.
Effect/estimate: Boxing experience related to competitive outcome (OR 1.33, 95% CI 1.06-1.66; Nagelkerke R2 = .11). Only 25% of youth boxers were in the rapid weight loss group; more than 45% self-reported combining different weight-cutting methods simultaneously.
Population: Elite youth Olympic-style boxers, 12 European countries | level: Elite youth amateur | sex: All male | age: 17.1 +/- 0.9 y
Design: Questionnaire study with dichotomous competitive-outcome follow-up | n: 83 male youth boxers
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (elite youth male)
LIMITATIONS: Self-report questionnaire; single continental championship; all male; small sample; absence of association is not proof of no effect. Does not measure health harms.
PPBF implication: The strongest single message for a youth programme: in elite youth boxers, cutting weight did not predict winning - experience did. PPBF can use this in athlete and guardian education. It remains coach and medical territory; SHADOW presents the evidence, never a plan.
Source: Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe. Int J Sports Physiol Perform 2018 (PMID 29182408; DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0733)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Dermatophyte and staphylococcal skin infections are documented in combat-sport and shared-equipment settings, transmitted primarily by person-to-person and surface contact, and MRSA can survive on sports surfaces for extended periods.
Effect/estimate: In the junior cohort, 11/319 (3.5%) harboured dermatophytic fungi, all male. Experimental study: CA-MRSA USA-300 survival on artificial turf was biphasic, with viable organisms persisting up to 20-50 days depending on nutrient conditions.
Population: Wrestlers, judo athletes, junior combat-sport participants, general athletes; plus experimental surfaces | level: Mixed, largely amateur and junior | sex: Mixed | age: Junior (16.4 +/- 1.3 y) and adult
Design: Narrative review; cross-sectional epidemiology; experimental survival study | n: 319 junior sports participants (143 combat, 176 non-combat); experimental turf study
Boxing-specific: No - wrestling/judo dominate the evidence | transfer status: OTHER-COMBAT-SPORT AND LAB TRANSFER - grappling sports have far more skin-to-skin contact than boxing; direct transfer to boxing is not established
LIMITATIONS: Boxing involves gloved contact and shared equipment rather than sustained skin-to-skin grappling, so grappling-derived incidence should not be applied to boxing. The turf survival study is experimental, not a transmission study in a gym.
PPBF implication: Supports mandatory single-athlete wraps, washing and full drying between sessions, and a no-shared-mouthguard rule. It does not support alarmist messaging - the boxing-specific transmission risk from wraps is not quantified and is a PPBF surveillance TBD.
Source: Adams BB. Tinea gladiatorum: wrestling's emerging foe. Sports Med 2000; Epidemiology of dermatophytosis in junior combat and non-combat sports participants. Mycoses 2012; Community-associated methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus survival on artificial turf substrates.
