[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Shared gym equipment surfaces carry diverse cultivable bacteria dominated by skin-associated taxa, with device-specific contamination patterns and temporal dynamics across a training day.
Effect/estimate: 248 bacterial isolates representing 61 species across 32 families, predominantly skin-associated taxa; device-specific composite contamination indices developed
Population: Public fitness facility equipment surfaces | level: Not applicable | sex: Not applicable | age: Not applicable
Design: Repeated-measures observational surface sampling with MALDI-TOF MS identification | n: 180 surface samples from 12 gym devices, sampled three times daily over five weekdays
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-SETTING TRANSFER - fitness facility, not a boxing gym; bags, pads and gloves were not the sampled devices
LIMITATIONS: Presence of cultivable bacteria on surfaces is not evidence of infection transmission or of clinical harm. No boxing equipment sampled. No intervention tested.
PPBF implication: Supports a scheduled cleaning routine for shared gloves, pads and bags. The concrete cleaning standard PPBF should cite is USA Boxing's own 10% bleach or comparable wipes requirement (A6-020/A6-021), which is rule-backed rather than inferred.
Source: Microbial Contamination of Gym Equipment: Diversity Patterns, Temporal Dynamics, Staphylococcus Hotspots, and Device-Level Risk Indices. Pathogens 2026 (PMID 42515034; DOI 10.3390/pathogens15070707)

Population: Boxing coaches holding pads/mitts | level: All | sex: All | age: Adult coaches
Design: Absence of evidence across targeted PubMed searches | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes (the gap is boxing-specific) | transfer status: Not applicable - gap statement

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Systematic review and meta-analysis of upper-limb strikes in combat sports found straight and reverse punches produce the largest mean impact forces and are performed at high velocities.
Effect/estimate: Highest recorded mean force for a straight punch 3427 N; straight and reverse punches had larger mean impact forces than a kung fu punch (p<0.001); strike velocities over 10 m/s reported for these punches
Population: Combat sport athletes and self-defence practitioners | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male in component studies | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 28 studies describing 9 kinds of strikes
Boxing-specific: Partly - boxing among several combat sports | transfer status: COMBAT-SPORT EVIDENCE - measurement conditions vary widely between component studies
LIMITATIONS: Measurement instruments, target compliance and protocols differ substantially across the 28 studies, so pooled force values are not directly comparable to a hand-held pad. Force to an instrumented target is not the load transmitted to a coach's joint.
PPBF implication: Gives an order-of-magnitude sense of what a pad holder absorbs and justifies pad-holding technique training and coach rotation as prudent practice - explicitly labelled as inference, since no pad-holder injury data exist.
Source: Force and velocity of impact during upper limb strikes in combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Biomech 2020 (PMID 32677587; DOI 10.1080/14763141.2020.1778075)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A reliable amateur boxing performance-analysis template has been developed; intra-observer reliability was high but inter-observer agreement was substantially lower and varied with analyst experience.
Effect/estimate: Intra-observer: non-significant differences between observations (p>0.05), 80-100% agreement. Inter-observer: proportion of agreement ranged 33-100%, with no systematic bias between observations (p>0.05)
Population: Competitive amateur boxing footage | level: Amateur | sex: Not stated in abstract | age: Not stated in abstract
Design: Notational analysis reliability study | n: Two analysts (an amateur boxer and an experienced analyst) coding competitive bouts
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Two analysts only; the 33% lower bound on inter-observer agreement is a serious limitation for any multi-coach tagging system; reliability of a template does not establish validity of the indicators as performance predictors
PPBF implication: Critical constraint for PPBF film tagging: multi-coach tagging will disagree. The data model must store tagger identity and allow disagreement rather than collapsing to a single 'truth', and PPBF must run its own inter-rater reliability check before any tag drives a recommendation.
Source: The development of a reliable amateur boxing performance analysis template. J Sports Sci 2012 (PMID 23121380; DOI 10.1080/02640414.2012.738922)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Canadian Paediatric Society jointly oppose boxing as a sport for children and adolescents because the sport encourages and rewards deliberate blows to the head and face.
Effect/estimate: Position: both organisations oppose boxing for children and adolescents and recommend physicians oppose youth boxing and encourage alternative sports without intentional head blows. The statements also acknowledge benefits including exercise, self-discipline and self-confidence.
Population: Children and adolescents under 19 in North America | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Under 19
Design: Joint policy statement of two paediatric professional bodies | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Professional-body position, not primary data
LIMITATIONS: A position statement is expert consensus, not an experiment; it is dated 2011/2012 and predates the 2013 rule changes and subsequent surveillance. It is a real, current-standing position that PPBF's governance must engage with rather than ignore.
PPBF implication: MUST be surfaced honestly in PPBF's youth governance documentation and guardian communication. It is the strongest external challenge to a youth boxing programme and the case for non-contact and skills lanes (modules 043/044) should be made against it explicitly, by named humans, not by SHADOW.
Source: American Academy of Pediatrics, Canadian Paediatric Society. Policy statement - Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics 2011; and joint statement in Paediatr Child Health 2012 (PMID 21873697; DOI 10.1542/peds.2011-1165; PMID 23277756; DOI 10.1093/pch/17.1.39)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A US national emergency-department analysis found facial injury in a minority of paediatric boxing and martial arts presentations, with fractures a substantial share of those facial injuries.
Effect/estimate: 264/4978 (5.3%) experienced facial injury; over 20% (n=60) of reported facial injuries were fractures
Population: US paediatric emergency-department patients after boxing or martial arts trauma | level: Mixed, recreational-weighted | sex: Not stratified in abstract | age: Under 18
Design: Cross-sectional analysis of the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System, 2010-2019 | n: 4978 paediatric patients; 264 with facial injury
Boxing-specific: Partly - boxing and martial arts combined | transfer status: Direct-adjacent evidence (paediatric, US, combined disciplines)
LIMITATIONS: Boxing and martial arts are pooled and cannot be separated; ED presentations only; no exposure denominator, so no rate can be derived; 'martial arts' spans very different contact profiles
PPBF implication: Supports mandatory headgear and mouthguard in PPBF youth training regardless of the elite headguard debate, and supports an explicit facial-injury escalation path to medical.
Source: Children in Boxing and Martial Arts Should Be Better Guarded From Facial Injuries. Craniomaxillofac Trauma Reconstr 2021 (PMID 35633771; DOI 10.1177/19433875211016666)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguards have been used to characterise head impact exposure during boxing and MMA sparring and competition in both men and women.
Effect/estimate: Peak linear and peak angular acceleration calculated for video-verified true-positive impacts; comparisons across sport, activity type and sex
Population: Boxing and MMA athletes | level: Trained combat athletes | sex: 23 athletes, of whom 4 women | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification (level of evidence 3) | n: 23 athletes
Boxing-specific: Partly - boxing and MMA | transfer status: Direct-adjacent evidence
LIMITATIONS: Small sample, especially for women (n=4); instrumented mouthguards require video verification because of false positives; head kinematics are a surrogate for brain loading, not an injury outcome
PPBF implication: If PPBF ever considers instrumented mouthguards, this sets expectations: video verification is required, sample sizes are small, and the output is exposure data for humans to interpret - not a readiness or clearance signal. SHADOW must never convert impact counts into a clearance decision.
Source: Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts. Orthop J Sports Med 2021 (PMID 34901294; DOI 10.1177/23259671211059815)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Boxing carries documented ocular injury risk, with periocular laceration the most common eye injury and a minority of injuries involving retinal or glaucomatous pathology.
Effect/estimate: Eye trauma represented 47.63% of boxing injuries vs 25.59% of MMA injuries; periocular laceration most common in both; 2-3% retinal in both sports; 3.27% glaucomatous in boxing; orbital fracture 3.14% of boxing eye injuries vs 17.62% in MMA
Population: Boxers and MMA contestants in Nevada Athletic Commission records; and Italian Boxing Federation clinical archive | level: Professional and elite amateur | sex: Predominantly male | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective cohort of commission injury records; plus long-term clinical archive review | n: 1539 boxing injuries from 4313 contests (2000-2020); 956 boxers with complete ophthalmological history across 10,697 examinations (1982-1998)
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence (professional-weighted)
LIMITATIONS: Commission records capture reported injuries at professional events; the Italian archive is historical and predates current rules; percentages are shares of injuries, not incidence rates; no amateur youth data
PPBF implication: Supports a mandatory ophthalmic component in the annual medical and a hard escalation rule for any visual symptom. Vision complaints are a physician decision - SHADOW routes and never assesses.
Source: Eye Trauma in Mixed Martial Arts and Boxing. Ophthalmic Plast Reconstr Surg 2023; and Ocular complications of boxing. Br J Sports Med 2005 (PMID 37656909; DOI 10.1097/IOP.0000000000002510; PMID 15665199; DOI 10.1136/bjsm.2003.006643)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Professional bare-knuckle fighting has been the subject of a dedicated injury-epidemiology study across state-sanctioned events, providing a contrast case for gloved boxing.
Effect/estimate: Incidence rates by injury type and location calculated; the study's purpose was to distinguish bare-knuckle patterns from traditional padded-glove boxing
Population: Professional bare-knuckle fighters at state-sanctioned US events | level: Professional | sex: Not stratified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Sequential observational data collection 2018-2020 | n: 141 bouts (282 fighter-exposures)
Boxing-specific: Adjacent - bare-knuckle, not gloved boxing | transfer status: ADJACENT-DISCIPLINE CONTRAST - must not be used as a boxing risk figure
LIMITATIONS: Short observation window; small number of bouts; professional adults only; entirely inapplicable to a youth or amateur programme
PPBF implication: Useful only as coach-education contrast for why gloves and wraps exist. PPBF must never cite bare-knuckle figures in any athlete- or guardian-facing material.
Source: Epidemiology of professional bare-knuckle fighting injuries. Phys Sportsmed 2021 (PMID 34380362; DOI 10.1080/00913847.2021.1955604)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An international consensus statement defines standards for monitoring athlete training loads, and evidence indicates subjective self-report measures can be more sensitive than some objective measures to changes in athlete wellbeing.
Effect/estimate: Consensus recommendations on internal and external load constructs and monitoring practice

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Michigan administrative rule sets weight-class-dependent gauze and tape limits for professional boxing hand wraps, prohibits any substance other than cloth-based tape on the wraps, and requires wraps to be adjusted in the dressing room under supervision of a department representative.
Effect/estimate: Standard classes: soft gauze not more than 10 yards long and 2 inches wide per hand, held by not more than 6 feet of cloth-based tape per hand. Light heavyweight, cruiserweight and heavyweight: gauze not more than 12 yards, tape not more than 8 feet per hand. MMA: gauze not more than 13 yards x 2 inches with not more than 10 feet of 1-inch tape, tape may cross the back of the hand twice and may cover the knuckles when clenched. Bandages must be evenly distributed. Water or any other substance other than cloth-based tape prohibited.
Population: Professional boxing contestants in Michigan | level: Professional | sex: All | age: Adult
Design: Primary state regulation (Mich. Admin. Code R. 339.207) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - Michigan jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: Retrieved via the Legal Information Institute mirror of the Michigan Administrative Code (notes: 2005 AACS; 2009 AACS; 2019 MR 20, effective 10/16/2019). State regulations are updated periodically - re-verify against the official state source before operational use. Note the MMA knuckle-coverage allowance is the opposite of the boxing rule - do not conflate.
PPBF implication: Demonstrates that professional wrap limits vary by state AND by weight class. Any PPBF professional-lane content must be generated per-jurisdiction from the governing regulation, never from a generic template.
Source: Mich. Admin. Code R. 339.207 - Hand, foot, and ankle wrap specifications for all contestants (Not applicable (regulation))

Effect/estimate: Soft gauze cloth not more than 20 yards in length and 2 inches in width; held by white adhesive tape not more than 8 feet long and 1.5 inches wide; evenly distributed across the hand; tape must not cover any part of the knuckles when the hand is clenched; liquid or substance on gauze or tape strictly prohibited; wrapping must occur in the dressing room area; completed wrap approved by commission representative or inspector signing with permanent marker; no adjustments after signing; the opponent's manager or chief cornerman may witness the wrapping.
Population: Professional boxers in Indiana | level: Professional | sex: All | age: Adult
Design: Primary state regulation (68 IAC 24-4-5) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - Indiana jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: Retrieved via the Legal Information Institute mirror (filed Aug 28 2012; readopted 9/19/2018 and 10/1/2024). Re-verify against the official Indiana source before operational use. Note Indiana's 20-yard gauze allowance differs sharply from Michigan's 10-12 yards - a real numeric conflict between US states.
PPBF implication: Supplies the two procedural controls PPBF should adopt even in training: wrap in a designated area under supervision, and a signature/sign-off that freezes the wrap. The opponent-witness provision is the anti-tampering rationale behind the whole professional procedure.
Source: 68 IAC 24-4-5 - Hand wraps (Indiana Gaming Commission) (Not applicable (regulation))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] WBC Amateur regulations restrict bandage type and length, prohibit tapes/rubber/adhesives beyond a single small fastening piece, require a supervisor seal or signature before gloving, and specify disqualification of the boxer and suspension of the trainer if the seal is missing or removed.

Population: WBC Amateur competitors and trainers | level: Amateur (WBC Amateur sanctioning) | sex: All | age: Adult categories; children's categories stated as in process
Design: Primary sanctioning-body regulation (WBC Amateur Rule 3, The Bandages) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - WBC Amateur sanctioning only
LIMITATIONS: 2024 edition as retrieved; the regulation itself states children's category glove specifications are still in process. This sanctioning body's rules differ substantially from USA Boxing, England Boxing and World Boxing - it is one of several parallel systems, not a universal standard.

Source: World Boxing Council Amateur Competition Rules 2024, Rule 3 The Bandages and Rule 2 Gloves and Headgears (Not applicable (regulation))

Population: Boxing Canada registered competitors | level: Amateur (Canadian domestic) | sex: Male and female | age: Youth, Elite, Masters
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Boxing Canada Articles and Rules) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - Canadian jurisdiction only

Source: Boxing Canada Articles and Rules (December 2023 edition), sections 6 Gloves, 6.4 Hand wraps, 7 Headguards (Not applicable (rulebook))

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] USA Boxing prescribes mandatory minimum medical restriction periods after a knockout or severe head blow, classified by the ringside doctor, with escalating periods for repeated loss of consciousness and a prohibition on training or sparring during the restriction.
Effect/estimate: No loss of consciousness: minimum 30 days. LOC under one minute: minimum 90 days. LOC over one minute: minimum 180 days. Second LOC within 90 days of resuming: the highest applicable restriction doubled. Three LOCs within 365 days: minimum 540 days from the third. A boxer under medical restriction must not train or spar. Protective measures apply if a knockout or concussion occurs in training or anywhere else, and the coach is responsible for reporting all incidents to USA Boxing. Return requires written clearance from a qualified medical doctor.
Population: USA Boxing registered boxers | level: Amateur | sex: All | age: All divisions
Design: Primary governing-body rulebook (Rule 5, protective restrictive measures) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - US amateur jurisdiction only
LIMITATIONS: Revision marked 12/31/2021 - re-verify. These are administrative minimum restrictions set by the governing body; they are not a clinical return-to-play protocol and do not replace the Amsterdam 2022 consensus pathway applied by a clinician.
PPBF implication: Maps to pilot.shadow_medical_administrative_status. SHADOW may TRACK an administrative restriction date entered by an authorised human and warn when an assignment would violate it; SHADOW must never set, shorten, or clear a restriction, and never issue clearance. The medical decision owner is the ringside physician / treating clinician.
Source: USA Boxing National Rulebook, Rule 5 protective restrictive measures (revision marked 12/31/2021) (Not applicable (rulebook))

Design: Primary rulebooks (USA Boxing 36.7-36.8; England Boxing 8.2.8; World Boxing 13.1.4) | n: Not applicable

Do NOT publish an invented hours figure.
Source: USA Boxing National Rulebook Rule 36.7-36.8; England Boxing Technical & Competition Rules 2026 s8.2.8; World Boxing Competition Rules Nov 2024 r13.1.4 (Not applicable (rulebooks))

USA Boxing: a longer named list including Avetine, Vaseline, Collodion, Thrombin Solution, Micro Fibrilar Collagen, Gelfoam, Surgicel and Adrenaline 1/1000, with ice bags, No-Swell and swabs permissible.
Population: Boxers with cuts during competition | level: Amateur (three jurisdictions compared) | sex: All | age: All
Design: Cross-jurisdiction primary rule comparison | n: Three governing bodies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - genuinely divergent between bodies
LIMITATIONS: Editions as retrieved. This is a real conflict, not an ambiguity: an agent permitted at a USA Boxing event may not be permitted at a World Boxing event. The applicable list is always that of the sanctioning body for that specific event.
PPBF implication: SHADOW must be hard-blocked from any cut or swelling instruction. The app's only permitted behaviour is to display the sanctioning body's own permitted list for that event and name the accredited human who owns the action. Where the sanctioning body is unknown, display nothing and escalate.
Source: England Boxing Technical & Competition Rules 2026 Annex C1 2.4.1; World Boxing Competition Rules Nov 2024 r3.1.6-3.1.8; USA Boxing National Rulebook Rule 26.2 (Not applicable (rulebooks))

Population: Registered amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: All | age: All
Design: Primary rulebooks (USA Boxing passbook provisions; England Boxing Digital BCR1 / The Locker) | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Primary rule - two jurisdictions, concordant on the principle

Effect/estimate: Wrist extensor orthoses differ across styles in their effects on dexterity and grip strength; no boxing-relevant effect estimate exists
Population: Clinical wrist/forearm orthosis populations | level: Not applicable | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Clinical orthosis studies | n: Varies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: CLINICAL-POPULATION TRANSFER - explicitly weak; do not use to justify any wrap method
LIMITATIONS: Clinical orthoses are rigid or semi-rigid devices for pathological wrists; boxing hand wraps are soft circumferential textile. The mechanical situations are not comparable and the transfer is flagged as unsupported.
PPBF implication: Recorded specifically to close off a tempting but invalid inference: clinical wrist-brace evidence does NOT support any claim about boxing wraps. SHADOW must not cite orthosis literature as wrap evidence.
Source: Wrist extensor orthoses: dexterity and grip strength across four styles. Am J Occup Ther 1991 (PMID 2000923)

Design: Narrative/topical review | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: No - cross-sport | transfer status: CROSS-SPORT - boxing is a high-exposure case but not the primary evidence base

Source: Understanding the Consequences of Repetitive Subconcussive Head Impacts in Sport. Front Hum Neurosci 2019 (PMID 31551732)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A one-year prospective cohort of Victorian amateur and professional boxers recorded an overall injury rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing, with most injuries to the head region and acute training injuries less common and less severe than bout injuries.
Effect/estimate: Overall injury rate 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing; 71% of injuries to the head region (95% CI -3.7 to 89.4 as reported); concussion the most common single injury at 33%
Population: Registered amateur and professional boxers, Victoria, Australia | level: 33 amateur and 14 active professional | sex: Not stratified in abstract | age: Adult
Design: Prospective cohort with one-year follow-up (2004-2005) | n: 47 boxers; 21 injuries
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Small volunteer cohort; wide and implausibly bounded confidence interval as reported in the abstract; single Australian state; 2004-2005 data predating the 2013 rule changes
PPBF implication: Provides a per-1000-hour training-inclusive denominator PPBF can structure its own exposure capture around. Note the authors' framing that boxing injury rates were comparable to or lower than other contact sports - a claim PPBF should present with its confidence caveats intact.
Source: Zazryn TR, Finch CF, McCrory P. A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing. Br J Sports Med 2006 (PMID 16807306; DOI 10.1136/bjsm.2006.025924)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective cohort of Victorian professional boxing recorded 214 injuries over 8.5 years, an injury rate of 23.6 per 100 professional fights, with the majority lacerations to the head and face.

Population: Professional boxers registered with the Professional Boxing and Combat Sports Board of Victoria | level: Professional | sex: Male and female (gender examined as a variable) | age: 18 to 43 years

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A prospective five-month survey of Irish amateur boxing found hand, wrist and facial injuries related to direct impact occurred more frequently in competition than training, while injuries to other body parts were predominantly chronic and training-associated.
Effect/estimate: Competition incidence 0.92 injuries per man-hour of play (0.7 injuries per boxer per year); training incidence 0.69 injuries per boxer per year; cerebral injuries reported only in competition, mostly mild concussion
Population: Competitors at Dublin amateur tournaments and members of six Dublin amateur boxing clubs | level: Amateur | sex: Not stratified in abstract | age: Over 16 years
Design: Prospective five-month injury survey (Nov 1992 - Mar 1993) | n: Tournament competitors plus club members over 16
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: Direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: 1992-93 data, predating multiple rule and equipment changes; single city; short observation window; injury definitions differ from modern surveillance standards
PPBF implication: Historical corroboration that hand and wrist impact injury concentrates in competition while training injuries skew chronic - supports separating acute-impact and overuse complaint types in PPBF's observation taxonomy.
Source: Porter M, O'Brien M. Incidence and severity of injuries resulting from amateur boxing in Ireland. Clin J Sport Med 1996 (PMID 8673583; DOI 10.1097/00042752-199604000-00006)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of hand injuries in combat sports concluded that conclusive comparative studies on the incidence and severity of combat-sport-related hand injuries could not be found in the literature.
Effect/estimate: Authors report that conclusive comparative studies on incidence and severity of hand injuries directly related to combat sport action could not be found
Population: Combat sport athletes | level: Mixed | sex: Predominantly male in the underlying literature | age: Predominantly 20-29
Design: Systematic review of PubMed/MEDLINE and Cochrane to January 2015 with secondary reference search | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: Partly - combat sports broadly | transfer status: COMBAT-SPORT EVIDENCE - a gap finding
LIMITATIONS: Search current to January 2015; German-language publication; the finding is an absence of comparative evidence, which does not mean absence of risk
PPBF implication: Independent corroboration of the central gap in this track: even the comparative incidence of combat-sport hand injury is not established, let alone the preventive effect of wrapping. Strengthens the case for PPBF's own surveillance (validation plan V1).
Source: [Hand injuries from combat sports]. Unfallchirurg 2015 (PMID 26013389; DOI 10.1007/s00113-015-0014-y)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of mpox in contact sports argued that sports with significant skin-to-skin contact - explicitly including wrestling and other combat sports - are settings where infectious skin diseases spread rapidly, and set out preventive considerations.
Effect/estimate: No incidence estimate for combat sport; the review notes mpox had not reached the athletic community at the time of writing
Population: Athletes in contact sports | level: All | sex: All | age: All
Design: Narrative review / expert commentary | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: OTHER-COMBAT-SPORT TRANSFER - grappling sports have far more skin-to-skin contact than gloved boxing
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review with a forward-looking argument rather than measured transmission data; boxing's gloved contact profile differs materially from wrestling; must not be presented as a boxing risk estimate
PPBF implication: Supports having a written skin-lesion exclusion and reporting policy owned by PPBF's medical adviser, and a no-shared-equipment rule. SHADOW must never assess a skin lesion - it routes to a clinician.
Source: Mpox and Monkeypox Virus: Special Considerations for Athletes in Contact Sports. Sports Med 2023 (PMID 36848020; DOI 10.1007/s40279-023-01812-5)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC's current consensus position on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport is the 2023 statement, which supersedes the 2018 RED-S update; it introduces updated Health and Performance Conceptual Models, a new Physiological Model, and the REDs Clinical Assessment Tool Version 2 (CAT2) for severity/risk-stratified detection.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative framework; no single numeric threshold endorsed as diagnostic
Population: Athletes (female and male) across sports | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: Not age-restricted
Design: Consensus statement (expert panel, >170 studies reviewed since 2018) | n: NA (consensus)
Boxing-specific: No — general athlete population | transfer status: Direct transfer of a general-athlete consensus to boxing; boxing is a weight-category sport and is in the higher-risk group
LIMITATIONS: Consensus statements reflect expert interpretation, not pooled effect estimates; CAT2 requires trained clinician administration
PPBF implication: SHADOW must reference the 2023 IOC REDs consensus as the governing framework for any energy-availability content; CAT2 administration is a clinician function, not an app function.
Source: Mountjoy M, et al. 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023. (PMID 37752011 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106994)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Low energy availability is common in athlete populations: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis found 2737 of 6118 athletes (44.7%) across 46 studies were classified as having LEA (44.2% of female, 49.4% of male athletes).
Effect/estimate: 44.7% pooled LEA prevalence (44.2% female, 49.4% male)
Population: Athletes across sports; endurance, aesthetic and weight-class sports over-represented | level: Mixed (mostly competitive) | sex: Both | age: Mixed adult and adolescent
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023469253); 59 studies included | n: 6118 athletes across 46 prevalence studies
Boxing-specific: No — pooled across sports including weight-class sports | transfer status: Prevalence estimates rest heavily on screening questionnaires rather than measured energy availability; not boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous LEA definitions and screening instruments across studies; prevalence is not incidence; screening tools have limited positive predictive value
PPBF implication: PPBF should assume a non-trivial baseline LEA risk in any weight-category cohort and build screening-to-referral routing rather than in-app energy prescriptions.
Source: Ackerman KE, et al. Low Energy Availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med. 2024. (PMID 39485653 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02130-0)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Low energy availability risk is measurable in female combat-sport athletes during the pre-competition period and is associated with altered physiological function in that window.
Effect/estimate: Effect sizes not extractable from abstract; direction reported as adverse in the LEA group
Population: Chinese female combat athletes (judo, freestyle wrestling, sanda) | level: National/elite | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional screening (LEAF-Q, EDE-Q) with a small prospective subgroup | n: 84 screened; 11 judo athletes in the prospective subgroup
Boxing-specific: No — combat sport but not boxing | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Very small prospective subgroup (n=11); single-country sample; questionnaire-based LEA classification; not generalisable to youth or to US community programmes
PPBF implication: Supports a pre-competition LEA screening trigger for female PPBF boxers, routed to a dietitian — not an in-app score.
Source: Zhang Y, et al. The impact of low energy availability risk on pre-competition physiological function in Chinese female combat athletes. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2025. (PMID 40254934 / DOI 10.1080/15502783.2025.2490170)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The existence of REDs as a discrete syndrome is contested in the literature; at least one 2024 peer-reviewed critique explicitly questions whether the syndrome, as defined, exists.
Effect/estimate: No pooled estimate; the disagreement is definitional and causal-inferential, not a dispute about the harm of severe energy deficiency
Population: Athlete populations | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: All
Design: Narrative critique / commentary | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A — methodological debate
LIMITATIONS: A critique is not evidence of absence of harm; the underlying harms of severe energy deficiency are separately well-documented
PPBF implication: SHADOW should present REDs as the dominant consensus framework while flagging the live scientific debate; it must not present REDs risk output as diagnostic.
Source: Areta JL, et al. Does Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Syndrome Exist? Sports Med. 2024. (PMID 39287777 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02108-y)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Carbohydrate intake should be judged by whether carbohydrate availability is adequate for the specific session; during sustained high-intensity events lasting about one hour, small carbohydrate amounts (including mouth rinsing alone) can enhance performance via central nervous system effects, while 30-60 g/h is an appropriate target for longer events and up to 90 g/h may benefit events over 2.5 h.
Effect/estimate: 30-60 g/h for longer events; up to 90 g/h for >2.5 h; mouth-rinse effect for ~1 h events
Population: Trained athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both (predominantly male study base) | age: Adult
Design: Authoritative narrative review underpinning IOC/IAAF guidance | n: NA (review)
Boxing-specific: No — endurance-sport derived | transfer status: Endurance-sport transfer; a 3x3 min amateur bout or a 3x2 min youth bout is far shorter than the durations these intake rates were derived for
LIMITATIONS: The 30-90 g/h intake targets do not apply to a boxing bout; only the ~1 h/mouth-rinse and daily-availability principles plausibly transfer
PPBF implication: PPBF fueling structures should target carbohydrate availability across the training day, not in-bout carbohydrate feeding.
Source: Burke LM, Hawley JA, Wong SHS, Jeukendrup AE. Carbohydrates for training and competition. J Sports Sci. 2011. (PMID 21660838 / DOI 10.1080/02640414.2011.585473)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Endogenous glycogen stores are maximised by a high-carbohydrate diet of 8-12 g carbohydrate/kg/day, and are depleted most by high-volume exercise.
Effect/estimate: 8-12 g/kg/day for maximal glycogen storage
Population: Healthy exercising adults, particularly highly trained individuals | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both (male-dominated study base) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN, systematic literature appraisal) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General-sport transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: 8-12 g/kg/day is an upper-bound glycogen-loading figure derived largely from endurance contexts; it is not a routine intake for a boxer and is not appropriate as a default target
PPBF implication: SHADOW may surface the range with its endurance-context caveat; it must never compute a per-athlete gram target.
Source: Kerksick CM, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: nutrient timing. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017. (PMID 28919842 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-017-0189-4)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Deliberate periodised carbohydrate restriction ('train low') has not been shown to produce a consistent performance advantage over high carbohydrate availability in endurance-trained athletes.
Effect/estimate: No consistent performance benefit reported
Population: Endurance-trained athletes | level: Trained | sex: Both (male-dominated) | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No — endurance athletes | transfer status: Endurance transfer; no boxing-specific train-low evidence identified
LIMITATIONS: Endurance-only population; short intervention durations; heterogeneous 'train low' protocols; the 2023 IOC REDs consensus separately flags low carbohydrate availability as a REDs contributor
PPBF implication: PPBF should not adopt train-low protocols; combined with REDs risk in a weight-category sport the risk/benefit is unfavourable.
Source: Gejl KD, Nybo L. Performance effects of periodized carbohydrate restriction in endurance trained athletes - a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021. (PMID 34001184 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-021-00435-3)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Carbohydrate mouth rinsing improves cycling time-trial performance in a pooled analysis, and a separate meta-analysis examined its effect on muscle strength and muscular endurance.
Effect/estimate: Positive pooled effect for cycling time trial; strength/endurance effects examined separately with smaller and less consistent effects
Population: Healthy exercising adults | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Both (male-dominated) | age: Adult
Design: Systematic reviews with meta-analysis (two separate) | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No — cycling and general resistance-exercise populations | transfer status: Non-boxing transfer; no boxing-specific mouth-rinse trial identified
LIMITATIONS: Effect is small and context-dependent; benefit is largest in a fasted or glycogen-depleted state; no combat-sport replication located
PPBF implication: A plausible, low-risk, zero-cost tool for a boxer who cannot tolerate food close to a bout; label as untested in boxing.
Source: Brietzke C, et al. Effects of Carbohydrate Mouth Rinse on Cycling Time Trial Performance. Sports Med. 2019; and Ataide-Silva T, et al. Crit Rev Food Sci Nutr. 2022. (PMID 30488186 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-018-1029-7; PMID 35373671 / DOI 10.1080/10408398.2022.2057417)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A daily protein intake of 1.4-2.0 g/kg body weight/day is sufficient for most exercising individuals to build and maintain muscle mass; higher intakes of 2.3-3.1 g/kg/day may be needed to maximise retention of lean body mass in resistance-trained individuals during hypocaloric periods.
Effect/estimate: 1.4-2.0 g/kg/d general; 2.3-3.1 g/kg/d during energy restriction in resistance-trained individuals
Population: Healthy exercising individuals; resistance-trained individuals for the hypocaloric range | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Both (male-dominated evidence base) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General-sport transfer; the hypocaloric range is directly relevant to a boxer in a longitudinal weight descent
LIMITATIONS: Ranges derive largely from adult male resistance-training studies; upper range is not validated in youth or in adolescents still growing; intakes are population ranges, not individual prescriptions
PPBF implication: SHADOW may display the population range with caveats; a per-athlete gram target during weight descent is a dietitian decision.
Source: Jager R, et al. International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017. (PMID 28642676 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-017-0177-8)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a randomised trial of young men in a ~40% energy deficit combined with intense exercise, a higher protein intake (2.4 g/kg/d) produced greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss than a lower intake (1.2 g/kg/d) over four weeks.
Effect/estimate: Higher-protein group showed greater lean mass gain and greater fat mass loss over 4 weeks
Population: Young healthy men | level: Recreationally active | sex: Male only | age: Young adult
Design: Single-blind randomised parallel-group trial | n: n=40 (20 per group)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Non-boxing, male-only transfer; the energy deficit was severe and supervised
LIMITATIONS: Male-only; four weeks; a ~40% deficit under full dietary control is not replicable in a community gym; no female or adolescent replication in this trial
PPBF implication: Supports 'protein first' as the framing principle for any supervised weight descent; the specific 2.4 g/kg figure must not be auto-applied.
Source: Longland TM, et al. Higher compared with lower dietary protein during an energy deficit combined with intense exercise promotes greater lean mass gain and fat mass loss. Am J Clin Nutr. 2016. (PMID 26817506 / DOI 10.3945/ajcn.115.119339)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Per-meal muscle protein synthesis shows a saturable dose relationship; approximately 20 g of high-quality protein maximally stimulated myofibrillar protein synthesis after leg resistance exercise in young men, while after whole-body resistance exercise 40 g produced a greater response than 20 g.
Effect/estimate: Saturation near 20 g after single-limb work; greater response at 40 g after whole-body work
Population: Healthy young resistance-trained men | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Male only | age: Young adult
Design: Two acute dose-response crossover trials plus a narrative review of distribution | n: n=6 (Moore 2009); resistance-trained males (Macnaughton 2016)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Non-boxing, male-only, acute-mechanistic transfer
LIMITATIONS: Very small samples; acute muscle protein synthesis is a surrogate, not a performance or hypertrophy outcome; dose scales with the lean mass activated; not validated in youth or female athletes
PPBF implication: Justifies a 'protein at each main meal' STRUCTURE in PPBF education rather than a gram-per-meal prescription.
Source: Moore DR, et al. Am J Clin Nutr. 2009; Macnaughton LS, et al. Physiol Rep. 2016; Murphy CH, et al. Nutrients 2020 (distribution review). (PMID 19056590 / DOI 10.3945/ajcn.2008.26401; PMID 27511985 / DOI 10.14814/phy2.12893; PMID 32429355 / DOI 10.3390/nu12051441)

text_content:
[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] Whether spreading protein evenly across meals improves muscle-related outcomes is not settled; a 2020 review found the observational and randomised evidence supporting the distribution concept is inconsistent.
Effect/estimate: No consistent benefit demonstrated for even distribution over total daily intake
Population: Adults, mixed training status | level: Mixed | sex: Both | age: Adult to older adult
Design: Narrative/systematic review of observational and RCT evidence | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer
LIMITATIONS: Total daily protein intake appears to dominate; distribution effects, if present, are small; boxing-specific data absent
PPBF implication: PPBF should teach total daily protein adequacy first; even distribution is a reasonable habit, not an evidence-mandated rule.
Source: Murphy CH, et al. Protein Distribution and Muscle-Related Outcomes: Does the Evidence Support the Concept? Nutrients. 2020. (PMID 32429355 / DOI 10.3390/nu12051441)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The case for high-fat/low-carbohydrate diets improving sports performance has been re-examined in the peer-reviewed literature and remains unresolved rather than settled in either direction.
Effect/estimate: No pooled estimate; the review frames the question as open
Population: Trained athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both (male-dominated) | age: Adult
Design: Narrative review / opinion in a peer-reviewed journal | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Endurance-dominated evidence base
LIMITATIONS: High-fat approaches reduce the capacity for high-intensity work in several reported contexts; no boxing-specific trial identified; the debate is largely endurance-framed
PPBF implication: PPBF should not endorse a low-carbohydrate/high-fat approach for boxers; fat intake guidance should come from the ACSM/AND/DC joint position stand.
Source: Burke LM. Re-Examining High-Fat Diets for Sports Performance: Did We Call the 'Nail in the Coffin' Too Soon? Sports Med. 2015. (PMID 26553488 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-015-0393-9)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The goal of prehydrating is to begin activity euhydrated with normal plasma electrolytes; drinking during exercise should prevent excessive dehydration (defined in the position stand as greater than 2% body-weight loss from water deficit) and excessive electrolyte change. Sweat rate and sweat electrolyte content vary considerably between individuals, so fluid replacement should be individualised.
Effect/estimate: >2% body-weight water deficit is the stated threshold for 'excessive' dehydration
Population: Individuals performing physical activity | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adult (position stand scope)
Design: Position stand (ACSM) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General exercise-science transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: 2007 position stand; the 2% figure is a threshold below which performance decrement is generally avoided, not a validated individual trigger; individual variability is explicitly large
PPBF implication: Supports a session pre/post body-weight change log in PPBF as an observation, not as an automated hydration verdict.
Source: Sawka MN, et al. American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2007. (PMID 17277604 / DOI 10.1249/mss.0b013e31802ca597)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Overhydration is a distinct and potentially fatal risk: exercise-associated hyponatraemia is addressed by a dedicated international consensus development conference, whose 3rd statement was published in 2015.
Effect/estimate: No single numeric threshold appropriate for app use; diagnosis is biochemical (serum sodium)
Population: Exercising individuals; endurance and military populations most reported | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: International consensus development conference statement | n: NA (consensus)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer; relevant to boxers who 'water load' before a weigh-in
LIMITATIONS: Most documented cases arise in prolonged endurance events; the boxing-specific risk from deliberate water loading before weigh-in is plausible but not quantified in the literature located
PPBF implication: PPBF must state that 'drink more' is not universally safe advice and that water loading protocols are outside the app's scope entirely.
Source: Hew-Butler T, et al. Statement of the 3rd International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Br J Sports Med. 2015. (PMID 26227507 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2015-095004)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Dehydration assessment requires distinguishing loss of hypo-osmotic body water (intracellular dehydration) from iso-osmotic loss (extracellular dehydration); single-measure field methods have meaningful diagnostic and biological variation.
Effect/estimate: No single field method is presented as sufficient alone; method error is the review's central theme
Population: Humans; athlete and laboratory populations | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Comprehensive review of assessment methods | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General physiology transfer
LIMITATIONS: Field hydration measures (urine specific gravity, urine colour, body-mass change) each carry error; combining measures is recommended over relying on one
PPBF implication: SHADOW must not convert a single hydration measure into a clearance or readiness verdict; it may log the measure with its uncertainty.
Source: Cheuvront SN, Kenefick RW. Dehydration: physiology, assessment, and performance effects. Compr Physiol. 2014. (PMID 24692140 / DOI 10.1002/cphy.c130017)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sweating rate and sweat sodium concentration vary substantially within and between individuals, and unstandardised sweat-testing methods produce inconsistent or inaccurate results.
Effect/estimate: Large intra- and inter-individual variability; no defensible population default value
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Methodological review | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer
LIMITATIONS: Because variability is large and method-dependent, any single sweat sodium figure applied to an athlete is unreliable
PPBF implication: PPBF must not publish a default electrolyte replacement number; TBD pending in-gym sweat-rate measurement if ever undertaken.
Source: Baker LB. Sweating Rate and Sweat Sodium Concentration in Athletes: A Review of Methodology and Intra/Interindividual Variability. Sports Med. 2017. (PMID 28332116 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-017-0691-5)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Iron deficiency is common in athlete populations, with reported deficiency in approximately 15-35% of female athlete cohorts and approximately 5-11% of male athlete cohorts; exercise-induced elevation of hepcidin is a proposed contributing mechanism.
Effect/estimate: ~15-35% of female athlete cohorts; ~5-11% of male athlete cohorts
Population: Athletes, especially female and endurance athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both, with female predominance | age: Adult
Design: Narrative review | n: NA (review of cohorts)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer; no boxing-specific prevalence located
LIMITATIONS: Cohort prevalence ranges depend heavily on the ferritin cut-off used, which is not standardised; endurance-weighted evidence base; correlation between exercise and hepcidin does not establish causation of clinical deficiency
PPBF implication: Iron status is a blood test ordered and interpreted by a physician; SHADOW may raise a referral flag, never a supplement recommendation.
Source: Sim M, et al. Iron considerations for the athlete: a narrative review. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019. (PMID 31055680 / DOI 10.1007/s00421-019-04157-y)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The interpretation of iron status in athletic females has been argued to require a shift from the older paradigm, indicating the ferritin thresholds and screening approach are not settled.
Effect/estimate: No single agreed ferritin threshold; the paper's argument is that the conventional paradigm is inadequate
Population: Athletic females | level: Trained to elite | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Peer-reviewed perspective/review | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female-athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Threshold disagreement means any app-side numeric iron rule would encode a contested value
PPBF implication: PPBF must not hard-code a ferritin cut-off; the value is TBD and owned by the athlete's physician.
Source: Sim M, Dawson B, Landers G, Trinder D, Peeling P (author set per record). Iron status in athletic females, a shift in perspective on an old paradigm. J Sports Sci. 2021. (PMID 33583330 / DOI 10.1080/02640414.2021.1885782)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Iron deficiency and iron deficiency anaemia are documented in adolescent athletes of both sexes, including in sports that are not calorie-restricting.
Effect/estimate: Prevalence stratified by ferritin thresholds (mild <=30, moderate <=20, severe <=10 ug/L)
Population: Adolescent basketball and football players in Israel | level: Youth club/competitive | sex: Both | age: 11-18 years
Design: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of clinical records | n: 476 (350 male, 126 female)
Boxing-specific: No — ball sports | transfer status: Other-sport transfer to youth boxing
LIMITATIONS: Two sports-medicine centres in one country; retrospective clinical records; ball-sport population, not weight-category athletes
PPBF implication: Supports including iron in PPBF's youth medical-referral prompts, not in any app-side calculation.
Source: Constantini N, et al. Iron Deficiency and Anemia in Male and Female Adolescent Athletes Who Engage in Ball Games. J Clin Med. 2023. (PMID 36769618 / DOI 10.3390/jcm12030970)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in athletes, oral vitamin D supplementation raised serum 25(OH)D concentrations; the effect on physical performance was the separate question the review was designed to test.
Effect/estimate: Consistent increase in serum 25(OH)D; performance effects reported as far less consistent
Population: Athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs | n: 13 RCTs (2005-2016)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Small number of trials; heterogeneous doses, baseline status, latitude and season; raising a biomarker is not the same as improving performance
PPBF implication: Vitamin D testing and dosing is a physician decision; SHADOW may not suggest a dose.
Source: Farrokhyar F, et al. Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation on Serum 25-Hydroxyvitamin D Concentrations and Physical Performance in Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Med. 2017. (PMID 28577257 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-017-0749-4)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Vitamin D insufficiency prevalence in elite athletes has been estimated in a systematic review and meta-analysis that also examined differences between sexes and between adults and adolescents.
Effect/estimate: Prevalence estimate with sex and age-group subgroup comparisons
Population: Elite athletes | level: Elite | sex: Both | age: Adults and adolescents
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Prevalence depends on the insufficiency cut-off used and on latitude and season, both explicitly identified as moderators
PPBF implication: Punxsutawney's latitude and an indoor training environment are plausible risk modifiers; this is a physician-screening prompt, not an app rule.
Source: Wilson-Barnes SL, et al. Prevalence and novel risk factors for vitamin D insufficiency in elite athletes: systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Nutr. 2022. (PMID 35882673 / DOI 10.1007/s00394-022-02967-z)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC supplements consensus notes that calcium intakes of 1500 mg/day and 1500-2000 IU vitamin D are recommended to optimise bone health specifically in athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction, and that skin exposure to sunlight normally accounts for about 90% of vitamin D supply.
Effect/estimate: Calcium 1500 mg/day; vitamin D 1500-2000 IU/day in that specific clinical subgroup
Population: Athletes with low energy availability or menstrual dysfunction | level: Elite/high-performance | sex: Both, with female emphasis for the menstrual-dysfunction subgroup | age: Adult
Design: Consensus statement | n: NA (consensus)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General high-performance athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: These figures apply to a defined clinical subgroup under medical management, not to a general gym population, and must not be generalised
PPBF implication: These are clinician-managed values; SHADOW may cite them in coach education, never issue them to an athlete.
Source: Maughan RJ, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018. (PMID 29540367 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC consensus identifies a small set of supplements with good evidence of direct performance benefit: caffeine, creatine (as creatine monohydrate), nitrate, sodium bicarbonate, and possibly beta-alanine; a complete nutritional assessment should precede any supplement decision.
Effect/estimate: Five named agents with 'good evidence'; all other categories are framed as unsupported or risk-bearing
Population: High-performance athletes | level: Elite/high-performance | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Consensus statement | n: NA (consensus)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: High-performance athlete transfer; explicitly not addressed to youth or community athletes
LIMITATIONS: The consensus is written for high-performance adult athletes; it does not endorse supplement use in youth, and the assessment-first requirement is frequently ignored in practice
PPBF implication: PPBF's default position is food-first and no supplements for minors; the five-agent list is coach-education content only.
Source: Maughan RJ, et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. Br J Sports Med. 2018 (also IJSNEM 2018). (PMID 29540367 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2018-099027; parallel publication PMID 29589768 / DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0020)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Caffeine improves exercise performance at doses of 3-6 mg/kg body mass; very high doses (about 9 mg/kg) are associated with a high incidence of side effects without additional benefit, and the most common timing is 60 minutes pre-exercise.
Effect/estimate: 3-6 mg/kg effective; minimum effective dose possibly as low as 2 mg/kg; >=9 mg/kg no added benefit and more side effects
Population: Healthy exercising adults | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Both, though the underlying study base is predominantly young men | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) plus umbrella review of 21 meta-analyses | n: 21 meta-analyses across 11 reviews (umbrella)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General exercise transfer; sodium-bicarbonate and combat-specific work exists separately but caffeine trials in boxing were not located
LIMITATIONS: Umbrella review graded most evidence as moderate with some low to very low quality; most included studies were in young men; caffeine is not on the WADA Prohibited List but is on the Monitoring Program; it affects sleep and anxiety
PPBF implication: PPBF position: no caffeine supplementation guidance for minors; adult content is education only, with sleep and anxiety caveats.
Source: Guest NS, et al. ISSN position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021; Grgic J, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2020 (umbrella review). (PMID 33388079 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-020-00383-4; PMID 30926628 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2018-100278)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Creatine monohydrate increases intramuscular creatine and improves high-intensity exercise performance; a commonly cited protocol is a loading phase of 20 g/day for 5 days followed by 3-5 g/day maintenance, or approximately 0.1 g/kg body mass/day.
Effect/estimate: Loading 20 g/day x 5 days; maintenance 3-5 g/day or ~0.1 g/kg/day
Population: Healthy exercising adults | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Both (male-dominated base) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) plus a follow-up ISSN review of common questions | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General exercise transfer; no boxing-specific creatine trial located
LIMITATIONS: Creatine causes intracellular water retention and an increase in body mass, which is a direct conflict for a weight-category athlete near a weigh-in; the ISSN position addresses safety in adults, not in a community youth programme
PPBF implication: The mass-gain effect makes creatine a weight-making conflict; PPBF should route any adult interest to a dietitian and prohibit recommendation to minors.
Source: Kreider RB, et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2017; Antonio J, et al. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021. (PMID 28615996 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-017-0173-z; PMID 33557850 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-021-00412-w)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] Whether the physiological benefits and safety profile of creatine established in adults extend to children and adolescents is not established; the literature on paediatric creatine use is described as limited relative to the adult evidence base.
Effect/estimate: No adequate paediatric efficacy or long-term safety dataset identified
Population: Children and adolescents | level: Youth | sex: Both | age: Paediatric/adolescent
Design: Narrative reviews (two) | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: N/A — the gap is the finding
LIMITATIONS: Absence of demonstrated harm is not demonstration of safety; the paediatric literature is dominated by clinical rather than athletic applications
PPBF implication: PPBF position: SHADOW must never recommend creatine to a minor; any parent/athlete question routes to a physician and dietitian.
Source: Jagim AR, Kerksick CM. Creatine Supplementation in Children and Adolescents. Nutrients. 2021; and Creatine supplementation in the pediatric and adolescent athlete - a literature review. J Orthop. 2023. (PMID 33670822 / DOI 10.3390/nu13020664; PMID 37008451 / DOI 10.1016/j.jor.2023.03.010)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sodium bicarbonate at doses from 0.2 to 0.5 g/kg improves muscular endurance performance and performance in combat sports including boxing, judo, karate, taekwondo and wrestling; ergogenic effects are most established for high-intensity tasks lasting between 30 seconds and 12 minutes, and 0.2 g/kg appears to be the minimum effective single dose.
Effect/estimate: 0.2-0.5 g/kg; minimum effective single dose 0.2 g/kg; effects established for 30 s to 12 min tasks
Population: Exercising adults including combat-sport athletes | level: Trained to elite | sex: Both (the position stand states effects in men and women) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) plus a combat-sport-specific systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 8 studies in the combat-sport meta-analysis (PEDro 8-9)
Boxing-specific: Partially — boxing is named in the ISSN position stand; the combat meta-analysis is judo-weighted | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence exists but the pooled combat analysis is small and judo-dominated; direct boxing trials are sparse
LIMITATIONS: Gastrointestinal distress at ergogenic doses is explicitly flagged by the IOC consensus and can impair rather than improve performance; the combat-sport meta-analysis is based on only eight studies with surrogate outcomes (blood lactate, RPE, Wingate power, Special Judo Fitness Test)
PPBF implication: Not appropriate for PPBF youth or novice lanes; the GI-distress risk near a bout is a real harm pathway.
Source: Grgic J, et al. ISSN position stand: sodium bicarbonate and exercise performance. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2021; de Oliveira LF, et al. Curr Nutr Rep. 2022. (PMID 34503527 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-021-00458-w; PMID 35394616 / DOI 10.1007/s13668-022-00396-2)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Four weeks of beta-alanine supplementation at 4-6 g daily significantly increases muscle carnosine and has been shown to improve exercise performance, with more pronounced effects in open end-point tasks lasting 1 to 4 minutes; the only reported side effect is paraesthesia, attenuable with divided lower doses of about 1.6 g or a sustained-release formula.
Effect/estimate: 4-6 g/day for at least 2-4 weeks; effects strongest for 1-4 min tasks; divided 1.6 g doses reduce paraesthesia
Population: Healthy exercising adults | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Both (male-dominated base) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No — the 1-4 min task window overlaps a boxing round but no boxing-specific trial was located | transfer status: General exercise transfer with a plausible task-duration match to boxing rounds
LIMITATIONS: 2015 position stand; the IOC consensus lists beta-alanine only as 'possibly' evidence-supported; strength and long-duration endurance effects are explicitly stated as needing more research
PPBF implication: Task-duration match makes beta-alanine a plausible boxing hypothesis; it remains untested in boxing and out of scope for PPBF youth lanes.
Source: Trexler ET, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: Beta-Alanine. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2015. (PMID 26175657 / DOI 10.1186/s12970-015-0090-y)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a meta-analysis of 123 studies and 1705 participants, inorganic nitrate ingestion produced a small but statistically significant improvement in exercise performance (SMD 0.101; 95% CI 0.051 to 0.151; I-squared 0%), with nitrate salt supplements not as effective as beetroot juice.
Effect/estimate: SMD 0.101 (95% CI 0.051-0.151), P<0.001, I-squared 0%
Population: Healthy adults | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis and meta-regression | n: 123 studies, 1705 participants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer; no boxing-specific nitrate trial located
LIMITATIONS: The pooled effect is small; oral antibacterial mouthwash use abolishes the nitrate-nitrite conversion pathway; most trials are in endurance contexts
PPBF implication: A food-first route (leafy greens, beetroot) is low-cost and food-access-compatible; the expected effect is small and unproven in boxing.
Source: Gao C, et al. Factors that Moderate the Effect of Nitrate Ingestion on Exercise Performance in Adults: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analyses and Meta-Regressions. Adv Nutr. 2022. (PMID 35580578 / DOI 10.1093/advances/nmac054)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Undeclared doping substances are highly prevalent in commercial sports nutrition supplements: of 66 high-risk products purchased from Dutch web shops, 25 (38%) contained undeclared doping substances including the stimulants oxilofrine, BMPEA and NBDMPEA.
Effect/estimate: 38% (25/66) contained undeclared doping substances
Population: Commercially available sports nutrition supplements | level: N/A (product testing) | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Laboratory analysis by an ISO 17025 accredited screen (LGC) | n: 66 products from 21 brands across 17 web shops
Boxing-specific: No — product-level, not athlete-level | transfer status: N/A — applies to any athlete purchasing supplements
LIMITATIONS: Deliberately targeted high-risk product categories, so 38% is not the market-wide contamination rate; single-country web-shop sample; contamination prevalence varies enormously by product category
PPBF implication: PPBF should treat any non-certified supplement as a live anti-doping and health risk and say so plainly to athletes and parents.
Source: Duiven E, et al. Undeclared Doping Substances are Highly Prevalent in Commercial Sports Nutrition Supplements. J Sports Sci Med. 2021. (PMID 34211326 / DOI 10.52082/jssm.2021.328)

Effect/estimate: No numeric threshold; the principle is categorical
Population: All athletes subject to the WADA Code | level: All levels subject to testing | sex: Both | age: All
Design: Regulatory instrument / agency guidance | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Applies to any PPBF athlete competing under a WADA Code signatory
LIMITATIONS: Jurisdictional scope matters: not every PPBF athlete is subject to the Code at every level of competition, and professional boxing commissions operate their own testing regimes
PPBF implication: PPBF athlete and parent education must state strict liability explicitly before any supplement conversation.
Source: World Anti-Doping Agency. Strict Liability in Anti-Doping (Questions & Answers). (URL (no DOI/PMID))

Effect/estimate: Risk reduction, not elimination; no numeric residual-risk figure is given
Population: Athletes subject to US anti-doping jurisdiction | level: All levels subject to testing | sex: Both | age: All

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 2025 systematic review of doping in combat sports reported that anabolic agents, diuretics, hormone modulators and NSAIDs are commonly detected, particularly among athletes in heavier weight categories and those engaging in rapid weight loss.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative pattern only; the review included only six studies
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: Competitive to elite | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: 6 of 21 identified articles met inclusion criteria
Boxing-specific: Partially — combat sports including boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence directly relevant to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Only six included studies; the association between rapid weight loss and diuretic detection is correlational and does not establish that weight cutting causes doping; detection rates reflect testing programmes, not true prevalence
PPBF implication: The diuretic-plus-weight-cut pattern is a specific PPBF education point: the fastest weight-making shortcuts are also anti-doping violations.
Source: Doping in combat sports: a systematic review. Phys Sportsmed. 2025. (PMID 39754586 / DOI 10.1080/00913847.2025.2449812)

Effect/estimate: Same-day (daily) weigh-in; zero tolerance for overweight
Population: Amateur boxers under USA Boxing sanction | level: Amateur, all age divisions | sex: Both | age: All USA Boxing divisions
Design: Governing-body rulebook | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct

PPBF implication: The same-day weigh-in is the single most important protective feature of the amateur lane PPBF operates in; PPBF must never help an athlete plan around it.
Source: USA Boxing National Rule Book (editions revised 1 January 2024 and 1 January 2025). (URL (no DOI/PMID))

Population: Boxers under World Boxing sanction | level: International amateur | sex: Both | age: All

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Professional boxing typically uses a day-before weigh-in, and this differs by jurisdiction: the British Boxing Board of Control requires weigh-in not less than 24 and not more than 36 hours before a tournament, while Pennsylvania regulation requires professional weigh-in no more than 24 hours (30 hours under extenuating circumstances) before the contracted contest time and allows an overweight boxer no more than 3 pounds of loss in a 3-hour reweigh window.
Effect/estimate: BBBofC: 24-36 h before tournament. Pennsylvania: <=24 h (30 h extenuating); 3 lb maximum loss in the 3-hour reweigh
Population: Professional boxers | level: Professional | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Primary regulatory instruments (national board and state code) | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct
LIMITATIONS: Jurisdiction-specific; these values must not be presented as universal. Florida's amateur provision (weigh-in within 28 hours) and New York's commission-determined timing differ again
PPBF implication: PPBF operates in Pennsylvania; the PA professional rule is the locally relevant one and should be named in coach education alongside the USA Boxing amateur rule.
Source: British Boxing Board of Control, The Rules of Boxing (3.2.2); 58 Pa. Code s.21.4 Conduct of contests; Fla. Admin. Code Ann. R. 61K1-4.016. (URL (no DOI/PMID))

Population: Professional boxers in WBC-sanctioned title bouts | level: Professional championship | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Sanctioning-body programme | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct

PPBF implication: The 30/14/7-day check STRUCTURE is a transferable governance idea for PPBF; the specific percentages are WBC's, not evidence-derived, and must not be adopted as PPBF numbers without validation.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Rapid weight loss is highly prevalent in child and adolescent combat athletes, reported at 25% to 94% depending on sport, age and competition level, with a magnitude ranging from about 1% to 6.3 (SD 3.7) percent of body mass; the review's authors conclude RWL needs stringent regulation and ideally should be banned in this population.
Effect/estimate: Prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3 +/- 3.7% body mass
Population: Children and adolescent combat athletes | level: Youth competitive to elite youth | sex: Both | age: Children and adolescents
Design: Systematic review | n: Not extracted (multiple studies across combat sports)
Boxing-specific: Partially — combat sports including boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport youth evidence, directly applicable to PPBF's youth lane
LIMITATIONS: Wide prevalence range reflects heterogeneous self-report instruments; self-reported RWL is subject to recall and social-desirability bias; the recommendation to ban is the authors' conclusion, not a governing-body rule
PPBF implication: This is the primary published support for PPBF adopting a categorical prohibition on youth weight cutting.
Source: Berkovich BE, et al. Patterns of weight cycling in youth Olympic combat sports: a systematic review. J Eat Disord. 2022. (PMID 35614520 / DOI 10.1186/s40337-022-00595-w)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a systematic review of 16 studies (4432 participants: 156 female, 4276 male) across boxing, judo, MMA, taekwondo and wrestling, the largest changes in body mass occurred in mixed martial arts cohorts, with rapid weight loss of 7.4 (SD 1.1) kg (about 10%) and rapid weight gain of 7.4 (SD 2.8) kg (11.7 +/- 4.7%); recovery duration permitted ranged from 3 to 32 hours.
Effect/estimate: MMA extremes: RWL 7.4 +/- 1.1 kg (~10%); RWG 7.4 +/- 2.8 kg (11.7 +/- 4.7%); recovery window 3-32 h
Population: Combat-sport athletes preparing for competition | level: Competitive to elite | sex: Both, heavily male (4276 of 4432) | age: Adult (predominantly)
Design: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42017055279) | n: 4432 participants across 16 studies
Boxing-specific: Partially — boxing is one of five sports included | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence directly relevant; the MMA extremes are not boxing values
LIMITATIONS: Only 3 of 16 studies reported RWL directly (14 reported RWG); female representation is 3.5% of the sample; the review explicitly flags a lack of data; the extremes are MMA-specific and must not be presented as boxing figures
PPBF implication: Magnitude scales with the recovery window the ruleset permits; the same-day amateur weigh-in structurally limits the incentive.
Source: Barley OR, Chapman DW, Abbiss CR. The Magnitude of Rapid Weight Loss and Rapid Weight Gain in Combat Sport Athletes Preparing for Competition: A Systematic Review. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019. (PMID 30299200 / DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2018-0165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In official California State Athletic Commission data on 399 male professional boxers (2015-2018), 389 (97.5%) gained weight between official weigh-in and competition, with a mean gain of 4.4 (SD 2.2) kg, corresponding to 7.2 (SD 3.5) percent of body mass; 82 athletes (20.6%) gained 10% or more, and international-promotion competitors gained more than regional competitors (8.0 +/- 3.0% vs 6.6 +/- 3.7%).
Effect/estimate: 97.5% gained weight; mean 4.4 +/- 2.2 kg (7.2 +/- 3.5%); 20.6% gained >=10%; international 8.0 +/- 3.0% vs regional 6.6 +/- 3.7% (p<0.001)
Population: Male professional boxers licensed in California | level: Professional | sex: Male only | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective analysis of official commission weight records | n: 399 athletes
Boxing-specific: Yes — professional boxing | transfer status: N/A — direct boxing evidence, but professional (day-before weigh-in) not amateur
LIMITATIONS: Single-state commission records; male only; measures weight regain, which is an indirect indicator of the preceding weight cut, not a direct measure of it
PPBF implication: This is the strongest boxing-specific quantification available and should anchor PPBF's professional-lane risk education.
Source: Rapid weight gain following weight cutting in male professional boxers. Phys Sportsmed. 2021 (California State Athletic Commission data 2015-2018). (PMID 34310264 / DOI 10.1080/00913847.2021.1960780)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 17 male elite amateur boxers, a body-mass loss of 5.6 (SD 1.7) percent achieved by fluid and food restriction plus induced sweat loss produced measurable decreases in total body water (6.0 +/- 0.9%), extracellular water (12.4 +/- 7.6%), total haemoglobin mass (5.3 +/- 3.8%) and blood volume (7.6%).
Effect/estimate: 5.6 +/- 1.7% body-mass loss; total body water -6.0 +/- 0.9%; extracellular water -12.4 +/- 7.6%; total haemoglobin mass -5.3 +/- 3.8%; blood volume -7.6%
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male only | age: Mean age 19.2 (SD 2.9) years
Design: Case-control study | n: 17 (10 weight-loss group, 7 control)
Boxing-specific: Yes — amateur boxing | transfer status: N/A — direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Very small sample (n=17), male only, young adult; CO-rebreathing and bioimpedance estimates carry their own error; a reduction in total haemoglobin mass has implications for oxygen carriage that this study did not link to bout outcome
PPBF implication: Demonstrates that a boxer's weight cut is a measurable haematological and fluid-compartment event, not merely a scale number.
Source: Reljic D, et al. Rapid weight loss and the body fluid balance and hemoglobin mass of elite amateur boxers. J Athl Train. 2013. (PMID 23672332 / DOI 10.4085/1062-6050-48.1.05)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of weight cutting in combat athletes found exercise performance was unchanged between pre-rapid-weight-loss and post-rapid-weight-gain (g = 0.22; 95% CI -0.18 to 0.62), but small reductions immediately post-RWL in maximal strength (g = -0.29; 95% CI -0.54 to -0.03) and repeated high-intensity-effort performance (g = -0.37; 95% CI -0.59 to -0.16).
Effect/estimate: Pre-RWL vs post-RWG g=0.22 (95% CI -0.18 to 0.62, non-significant); post-RWL maximal strength g=-0.29; repeated high-intensity effort g=-0.37
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: Competitive to elite | sex: Both, male-dominated | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: Not extracted; recovery windows 3-36 h
Boxing-specific: Partially — combat sports including boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence; laboratory performance tests, not bout performance
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory tests are surrogates for competitive boxing performance; the recovery window varied from 3 to 36 hours, so the null pre-to-post-RWG result cannot be applied to a same-day amateur weigh-in with a short recovery window; absence of a detected decrement is not evidence of safety
PPBF implication: Critical for PPBF messaging: 'performance largely recovers' is a professional-lane, long-recovery-window finding and must not be extended to same-day amateur weigh-ins or to health outcomes.
Source: Effects of Weight Cutting on Exercise Performance in Combat Athletes: A Meta-Analysis. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022. (PMID 35523423 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2021-0104)
