text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Two boxing studies found rapid weight loss and post-weigh-in weight regain were not associated with competitive success: in 100 elite Australian boxers (30 women, 70 men) regain did not differ between winners and losers, and in 83 elite European youth male boxers boxing experience rather than RWL predicted medal winning.
Effect/estimate: Australia: pre-bout mass above weigh-in by 2.12 +/- 1.62% (men) and 1.49 +/- 1.65% (women); no difference between winners and losers. Europe: boxing experience OR 1.33 (95% CI 1.06-1.66) for competitive success; only 25% were in the RWL group
Population: Elite amateur boxers (Australian national championships; European youth championships) | level: Elite amateur and elite youth | sex: Both (Australian sample); male only (European youth sample) | age: Adult (Australia); mean 17.1 (SD 0.9) years (Europe)
Design: Two observational field studies | n: 100 and 83 boxers
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: Observational; absence of an association in these samples does not prove weight cutting confers no advantage in other contexts; the European study was male-only and single-championship; competitive success is a coarse binary outcome
PPBF implication: This is the strongest counter-argument PPBF coaches can give athletes: in boxing specifically, the cut has not been shown to buy wins.
Source: Reale R, et al. Weight Regain: No Link to Success in a Real-Life Multiday Boxing Tournament. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2016; Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018. (PMID 27834565 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0311; PMID 29182408 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0733)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In the same European youth boxing study, more than 45% of the 83 boxers self-reported using several weight-cutting methods simultaneously that are known to be serious health hazards, and 33% reported muscle weakness as a consequence of rapid weight loss.
Effect/estimate: >45% used multiple hazardous methods simultaneously; 33% reported muscle weakness
Population: Elite youth male boxers from 12 European countries | level: Elite youth | sex: Male only | age: Mean 17.1 (SD 0.9) years
Design: Cross-sectional questionnaire | n: 83
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; male only; elite youth sample not representative of a community club; symptom reporting is subjective
PPBF implication: Combined-method cutting in minors is documented in boxing; PPBF's prohibition and its escalation triggers must name the specific methods.
Source: Rapid Weight Loss Is Not Associated With Competitive Success in Elite Youth Olympic-Style Boxers in Europe. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018. (PMID 29182408 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0733)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Three previously healthy collegiate wrestlers died during November-December 1997 while engaged in intentional rapid weight loss; all three restricted food and fluid and maximised sweat losses by exercising vigorously in hot environments while wearing vapour-impermeable suits under warm-up suits, producing dehydration and hyperthermia.
Effect/estimate: 3 deaths in a 33-day period; the fatal method combination is explicitly described
Population: Collegiate wrestlers (USA) | level: Collegiate | sex: Male | age: Young adult
Design: Public-health outbreak investigation (case series) | n: 3 deaths
Boxing-specific: No — wrestling | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer; the method combination is identical to that reported in boxing
LIMITATIONS: Case series, not a rate; the underlying incidence of death from rapid weight loss is not established; wrestling's rules and weigh-in structure differ from boxing's
PPBF implication: These deaths are the historical basis for the NCAA weight-management programme and are the core of PPBF's prohibited-practices list.
Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hyperthermia and dehydration-related deaths associated with intentional rapid weight loss in three collegiate wrestlers - North Carolina, Wisconsin, and Michigan, November-December 1997. MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep. 1998 (also reported in JAMA). (PMID 9480411 (MMWR); PMID 9515985 (JAMA reprint))

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 12 male wrestlers, high-intensity sport-specific training combined with rapid weight loss produced significant increases in kidney function markers compared with identical training without rapid weight loss: blood urea nitrogen (p=0.002), uric acid (p<0.001) and serum creatinine (p=0.006).
Effect/estimate: BUN p=0.002; uric acid p<0.001; serum creatinine p=0.006; Cystatin-C slightly elevated after both phases
Population: Male wrestlers | level: Competitive | sex: Male only | age: Adult
Design: Within-subject two-phase experimental study | n: 12
Boxing-specific: No — wrestling | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Very small sample (n=12); male only; biochemical markers are surrogates and their elevation does not equal clinical acute kidney injury; short-term study with no follow-up
PPBF implication: Renal strain is a documented harm pathway; any PPBF athlete presenting with symptoms after a cut is a physician referral, not a coach judgement.
Source: Rapid weight loss can increase the risk of acute kidney injury in wrestlers. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2023. (PMID 37397266 / DOI 10.1136/bmjsem-2023-001617)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Rapid weight loss in elite judo athletes affected balance and reaction time as well as strength; a separate study found 5% rapid weight loss over 48 hours significantly worsened urine specific gravity and affected judo-specific performance measures.
Effect/estimate: Balance and reaction time decrements post weigh-in; USG significantly higher after 5% loss
Population: Elite judo athletes | level: Elite | sex: Both (38 athletes, mixed) and male only (n=18 study) | age: Mean 20.6 (SD 2.6) years; adult
Design: Two controlled field studies | n: 38 and 18
Boxing-specific: No — judo | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer to boxing
LIMITATIONS: Judo is not boxing; small samples; the boxing-specific consequence for a sport where head-impact avoidance depends on reaction time and balance is inferred, not measured
PPBF implication: Degraded balance and reaction time in a sport where the athlete is being punched in the head is the single most important PPBF safety argument; label it as judo-transfer, not boxing-proven.
Source: Effects of Rapid Weight Loss on Balance and Reaction Time in Elite Judo Athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018; Effect of Rapid Weight Loss on Hydration Status and Performance in Elite Judo Athletes. Biology. 2022. (PMID 29809054 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2018-0089; PMID 35453700 / DOI 10.3390/biology11040500)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] The evidence on whether rapid weight loss impairs physical performance is not uniform: one study reported that rapid weight loss of up to five percent of body mass in less than seven days did not affect physical performance, and an updated systematic review found no clear consistent negative effect across performance parameters.
Effect/estimate: No significant performance decrement detected at <=5% loss over <7 days in the cited work
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: Competitive to elite | sex: Both, male-dominated | age: Adult
Design: Primary study plus updated systematic review | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: Partially — combat sports | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence
LIMITATIONS: These null findings concern PHYSICAL PERFORMANCE measured in a laboratory, not health, not cognition, not head-impact tolerance, and not youth; a null result in an underpowered study is weak evidence of no effect; performance neutrality is not a safety endorsement
PPBF implication: SHADOW must present both sides: performance-neutrality findings exist and are frequently used to justify cutting; they do not address health, youth, or same-day weigh-in contexts.
Source: Rapid Weight Loss of Up to Five Percent of the Body Mass in Less Than 7 Days Does Not Affect Physical Performance. Front Physiol. 2022; Effects of Different Rapid Weight Loss Strategies and Percentages on Performance-Related Parameters in Combat Sports: An Updated Systematic Review. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2023. (PMID 35492609 / DOI 10.3389/fphys.2022.830229; PMID 36982067 / DOI 10.3390/ijerph20065158)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The NCAA wrestling weight management programme requires a urine specific gravity of 1.020 or lower before body-composition assessment, sets a minimum competitive weight based on 5% body fat for men (with a separate women's packet using a 12% floor), and limits descent to a maximum of 1.5% of body weight per week.
Effect/estimate: USG <=1.020; 5% body fat floor (men) / 12% (women); maximum 1.5% body weight loss per week
Population: NCAA collegiate wrestlers | level: Collegiate | sex: Both (separate men's and women's programmes) | age: Young adult
Design: Governing-body regulatory programme | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No — wrestling | transfer status: Other-combat-sport regulatory transfer; boxing has no equivalent programme
LIMITATIONS: The NCAA's own packet states the 1.020 threshold is partly evidence-based and partly arbitrary; state high-school federations use 1.025 instead, showing the threshold is not settled; body-fat floors are derived from prediction equations with their own error
PPBF implication: This is the best-developed regulatory model PPBF could adapt; its numbers are wrestling's and would require PPBF validation before adoption.
Source: NCAA Wrestling Weight Management Program Packets (men's and women's, 2023-24 through 2025-26 editions). (URL (no DOI/PMID))

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The National Athletic Trainers' Association published a position statement on safe weight loss and maintenance practices in sport and exercise, providing recommendations for athletic trainers and guidance for athletes, coaches and parents, and identifying fluid restriction and pathogenic weight-control behaviours as unsafe practices.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative recommendations; no single numeric rate endorsed in the abstract
Population: Athletes and active clients | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: All
Design: Professional-body position statement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: 2011 statement; addressed primarily to athletic trainers, a role PPBF may not staff; recommendations require a qualified professional to apply
PPBF implication: PPBF should name which qualified human holds this role locally; if no athletic trainer is on staff, the referral goes to the athlete's physician.

Effect/estimate: Qualitative; the documents describe unhealthy practices and recommend they be discouraged
Population: Children and adolescents in sport | level: Youth | sex: Both | age: Children and adolescents

Boxing-specific: No — general youth sport, explicitly including weight-class sports | transfer status: Direct paediatric authority applicable to PPBF's youth lane
LIMITATIONS: Guidance is addressed to paediatricians, not to coaches or software; the 2005 policy statement is superseded in practice by the 2017 clinical report
PPBF implication: Together with the youth weight-cycling systematic review, this is the professional-body basis for PPBF's categorical youth prohibition.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 2025 ISSN position stand on combat sports states that post-weigh-in oral rehydration solutions of 1 to 1.5 litres per hour with sodium in the 50-90 mmol range should take precedence, followed by fast-acting carbohydrate at up to 60 g/h, and that protocols should aim to regain at least 10% of body mass; the same statement acknowledges that the long-term effects of frequent weight cuts on health and performance are unknown.
Effect/estimate: ORS 1-1.5 L/h with 50-90 mmol sodium; carbohydrate <=60 g/h; post-weigh-in carbohydrate 8-12 g/kg after significant depletion or 4-7 g/kg after modest restriction; target regain >=10% body mass
Population: Combat-sport athletes, primarily MMA and day-before-weigh-in sports | level: Competitive to professional | sex: Both (evidence base male-dominated) | age: Adult
Design: Position stand (ISSN) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: Partially — combat sports; MMA-weighted | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence; the recovery protocols assume a day-before weigh-in with hours of recovery, which does not exist in same-day amateur boxing
LIMITATIONS: This position stand also describes acute water-loss methods (sauna, hot water immersion, mummy wraps, water loading, sodium restriction) that PPBF prohibits; PPBF's disagreement is a governance choice about a youth-serving community programme, not a claim that the position stand is wrong for supervised professional MMA. The stand itself states the long-term health effects are unknown, and its recovery protocols are irrelevant to a same-day weigh-in
PPBF implication: MAJOR CONFLICT FOR SYNTHESIS: a current ISSN position stand describes weight-cut methods PPBF prohibits. PPBF must state explicitly that it declines to implement those sections for a youth-serving community programme and why.
Source: Jagim AR, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutrition and weight cut strategies for mixed martial arts and other combat sports. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2025. (PMID 40059405 / DOI 10.1080/15502783.2025.2467909)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Female Athlete Triad comprises low energy availability with or without disordered eating, menstrual dysfunction, and low bone mineral density; the 2014 Coalition consensus provides screening, diagnosis, treatment and return-to-play guidance for physicians and healthcare providers. A parallel Male Athlete Triad consensus was published in 2021.
Effect/estimate: Three-component construct; clinical guidance rather than numeric thresholds for app use
Population: Physically active girls and women; and male athletes for the parallel statement | level: All levels | sex: Female (Triad); Male (Male Triad) | age: Adolescent and adult
Design: Consensus statements | n: NA (consensus)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female/male athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Return-to-play decisions under these statements are explicitly clinical; the Triad framework and the newer REDs framework overlap and are not fully reconciled in the literature
PPBF implication: Return-to-play under a Triad diagnosis is a physician decision; SHADOW may hold the administrative status flag only.
Source: De Souza MJ, et al. 2014 Female Athlete Triad Coalition Consensus Statement on Treatment and Return to Play. Br J Sports Med. 2014; Nattiv A, et al. The Male Athlete Triad - Part II. Clin J Sport Med. 2021. (PMID 24463911 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2013-093218; PMID 34091538 / DOI 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000948)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The ISSN position stand on the female athlete states that female athletes have unique hormone profiles influencing physiology and nutritional needs across the lifespan and recommends that athletes of reproductive age track hormonal status against training and recovery to determine individual patterns.
Effect/estimate: Recommends individual tracking rather than a population prescription
Population: Female athletes across the lifespan | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Female | age: Reproductive age through post-menopausal
Design: Position stand (ISSN) | n: NA (position stand)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General female-athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: The female-athlete evidence base is substantially smaller than the male base across most nutrition topics; menstrual-cycle-phase nutrition recommendations remain largely hypothesis-level
PPBF implication: Menstrual-cycle data is special-category health data; PPBF must treat any tracking as opt-in, privacy-tiered, and never coach-visible by default.
Source: Sims ST, et al. International society of sports nutrition position stand: nutritional concerns of the female athlete. J Int Soc Sports Nutr. 2023. (PMID 37221858 / DOI 10.1080/15502783.2023.2204066)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Amenorrhoea in adolescent female athletes should not be considered normal; low energy availability is a common cause, and because adolescence is a critical period for bone accrual, delayed menarche and secondary amenorrhoea are of particular concern in young athletes.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative clinical position; no app-usable numeric threshold
Population: Adolescent female athletes | level: All levels | sex: Female | age: Adolescent
Design: Peer-reviewed review in a paediatric journal | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General adolescent female athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Review, not a trial; causal attribution of amenorrhoea to LEA in an individual requires clinical exclusion of other causes
PPBF implication: Amenorrhoea reported by a PPBF adolescent athlete is a physician referral with no coach-side interpretation.
Source: Amenorrhoea in adolescent female athletes. Lancet Child Adolesc Health. 2018. (PMID 30119761 / DOI 10.1016/S2352-4642(18)30145-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Adolescent, female and masters athletes have distinct nutritional requirements arising from age- and sex-related physiological changes in addition to training demands, with education focused on long-term health and on at-risk dietary patterns including sustained restricted eating and low calcium, vitamin D or iron intakes.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative; identifies at-risk patterns rather than numeric targets
Population: Adolescent, female and masters athletes | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adolescent through masters
Design: Review in a sports nutrition journal | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General special-population transfer
LIMITATIONS: Narrative review; each of the three populations is under-researched relative to adult male athletes

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Contrary to earlier thinking, youth do not have less effective thermoregulatory ability, insufficient cardiovascular capacity, or lower exertion tolerance than adults when exercising in the heat provided adequate hydration is maintained; the primary determinants of reduced performance and exertional heat-illness risk in youth are poor hydration status, undue exertion, and insufficient recovery between repeated bouts.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative; identifies hydration status, exertion and recovery as the primary determinants
Population: Exercising children and adolescents | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Children and adolescents
Design: Professional-body policy statement (AAP) | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General youth transfer
LIMITATIONS: 2011 statement; concerns environmental heat exposure generally rather than deliberate heat exposure for weight making
PPBF implication: Directly contradicts any use of sauna, hot rooms or impermeable suits with minors at PPBF; deliberate hydration compromise removes the very protection this statement depends on.
Source: American Academy of Pediatrics Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness and Council on School Health. Policy statement - Climatic heat stress and exercising children and adolescents. Pediatrics. 2011. (PMID 21824876 / DOI 10.1542/peds.2011-1664)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC REDs body-composition subgroup found that higher body fat was negatively associated with endurance performance and that muscle-mass gain benefited performance across sports, but that body composition did not contribute to talent identification and no unique cut-off signifying a performance advantage was identified; body composition is one of many variables and its influence should not be overstated.
Effect/estimate: No unique body-composition cut-off identified as conferring a performance advantage
Population: Athletes across sports | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Mixed
Design: Critical review of 29 longitudinal, prospective or intervention studies plus an international practitioner survey | n: 29 studies plus survey respondents
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Association is not causation; the review explicitly cautions against overstating body composition's role; the survey component reflects current practice rather than evidence
PPBF implication: PPBF must not display a body-fat target or a leanness ranking to any athlete; no cut-off exists to justify one.
Source: Ackerman KE, et al. Best practice recommendations for body composition considerations in sport to reduce health and performance risks: a critical review, original survey and expert opinion by a subgroup of the IOC consensus on REDs. Br J Sports Med. 2023. (PMID 37752006 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106812)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Interpreting body-composition change requires the least significant change concept; same-day consecutive DXA scans capture technical error only, while consecutive-day scans additionally capture short-term biological variation, which is the relevant error term for longitudinal monitoring.
Effect/estimate: Least significant change differs between same-day and consecutive-day protocols; the consecutive-day estimate is larger
Population: Resistance-trained athletes | level: Trained | sex: Not extracted | age: Adult
Design: Methodological study | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General measurement transfer
LIMITATIONS: DXA-specific; site- and machine-specific; PPBF is unlikely to have DXA access, so the practical error term for whatever method PPBF uses is unmeasured
PPBF implication: Any PPBF body-composition trend line must carry a measurement-error band; PPBF's own least significant change is TBD and must be measured before trends are displayed.
Source: Same-Day Vs Consecutive-Day Precision Error of Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry for Interpreting Body Composition Change in Resistance-Trained Athletes. J Clin Densitom. 2018. (PMID 30454952 / DOI 10.1016/j.jocd.2018.10.005)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Bioelectrical impedance vector analysis has been systematically reviewed for use in sport and exercise, covering body composition, hydration status and related characteristics; hydration status is itself a determinant of impedance-based estimates.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative synthesis; no single validated accuracy figure applicable across devices
Population: Athletes and exercising populations | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General measurement transfer
LIMITATIONS: Impedance measures are confounded by hydration status, which is precisely the variable that is disturbed in a weight-cutting athlete; consumer body-fat scales are the least accurate implementation
PPBF implication: A consumer impedance scale in a boxing gym will read an athlete's dehydration as fat loss; PPBF should not use one for body-composition decisions.
Source: Castizo-Olier J, et al. Bioelectrical impedance vector analysis (BIVA) in sport and exercise: Systematic review and future perspectives. PLoS One. 2018. (PMID 29879146 / DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0197957)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Exercise-induced gastrointestinal syndrome and exercise-associated gastrointestinal symptoms are common in endurance athletes; a systematic review examined whether repeated exposure of the gut to nutrients before and during exercise ('gut training') improves gastrointestinal integrity, function and symptoms.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative synthesis; gut-training protocols vary widely
Population: Endurance athletes | level: Trained | sex: Both, male-dominated | age: Adult
Design: Systematic literature review across five databases | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No — endurance athletes | transfer status: Endurance transfer; no boxing-specific gut-training evidence located
LIMITATIONS: Endurance-derived; the practical relevance to a 3x3 min bout is limited, but the principle of rehearsing competition-day feeding in training does transfer
PPBF implication: PPBF's practical rule is 'nothing new on competition day', rehearsed in training - the transferable principle without the endurance intake volumes.
Source: The Effect of Gut-Training and Feeding-Challenge on Markers of Gastrointestinal Status in Response to Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Literature Review. Sports Med. 2023. (PMID 37061651 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-023-01841-0)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] A systematic review of randomised trials examined the effect of probiotic supplementation on gastrointestinal symptoms in athletes.
Effect/estimate: No clear consistent benefit extractable; strains, doses and outcome measures are heterogeneous
Population: Athletes | level: Recreational to elite | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer
LIMITATIONS: Probiotic strain specificity means results do not generalise across products; no boxing evidence; commercial products are a cost burden with unproven benefit
PPBF implication: PPBF should not recommend probiotics; the cost is real and the benefit is unestablished.
Source: Effects of Probiotics Supplementation on Gastrointestinal Symptoms in Athletes: A Systematic Review of Randomised Controlled Trials. Nutrients. 2022. (PMID 35807826 / DOI 10.3390/nu14132645)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Co-ingestion of protein with carbohydrate after exercise has been examined for its effect on muscle glycogen restoration and functional capacity; a separate systematic review assessed whether carbohydrate with protein increases the rate of muscle glycogen resynthesis compared with carbohydrate alone.
Effect/estimate: Benefit of adding protein is most apparent when carbohydrate intake is sub-optimal; at adequate carbohydrate intakes the additional glycogen effect diminishes
Population: Exercising adults | level: Recreational to trained | sex: Both, male-dominated | age: Adult
Design: Review plus systematic review | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General exercise transfer
LIMITATIONS: Glycogen resynthesis rate is a surrogate for recovery; the practical relevance depends on how soon the next session occurs, which in a community programme is usually the next day
PPBF implication: With 24 hours between PPBF sessions, aggressive post-session refuelling is rarely necessary; a normal mixed meal is sufficient and cheaper.
Source: Restoration of Muscle Glycogen and Functional Capacity: Role of Post-Exercise Carbohydrate and Protein Co-Ingestion. Nutrients. 2018; The Effect of Consuming Carbohydrate With and Without Protein on the Rate of Muscle Glycogen Re-synthesis. Sports Med Open. 2021. (PMID 29473893 / DOI 10.3390/nu10020253; PMID 33507402 / DOI 10.1186/s40798-020-00297-0)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Food insecurity is documented among collegiate athletes at rates the reviewed literature describes as exceeding those of the general student population, driven by financial demands, time commitments and the energy demands of sport.
Effect/estimate: Elevated prevalence relative to non-athlete students; specific pooled rate not extracted
Population: US collegiate athletes | level: Collegiate | sex: Both | age: Young adult
Design: Scoping review of 18 peer-reviewed and grey-literature articles | n: 18 articles
Boxing-specific: No — collegiate athletes | transfer status: Transfer to a community youth boxing programme is an inference, not a measured finding
LIMITATIONS: Collegiate population, not a community youth gym; scoping review including grey literature; self-reported food security instruments; no PPBF-specific data exists
PPBF implication: Establishes that food insecurity in athletes is a real, published phenomenon; the PPBF-local rate is TBD and would require a validated screening instrument administered with safeguarding review.
Source: Prevalence of and Contributors to Food Insecurity among College Athletes: A Scoping Review. Nutrients. 2024. (PMID 38732593 / DOI 10.3390/nu16091346)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Elite male and female boxers show a propensity for low body fat; supporting the metabolic demands of a boxing match and recovering between rounds requires a high level of cardiorespiratory fitness, and international boxers show high peak and mean anaerobic power output.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative physiological profile; no nutrition prescription derived
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Both, with more data in males | age: Adult
Design: Critical review | n: NA
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct
LIMITATIONS: Review notes that somatotype studies in boxing are limited; low body fat in elite boxers is an observed correlate of elite status, not evidence that reducing body fat causes improved performance
PPBF implication: Important framing for PPBF coaches: elite boxers being lean is an association, not a target to impose on a developing athlete.
Source: Chaabene H, et al. Amateur boxing: physical and physiological attributes. Sports Med. 2015. (PMID 25358529 / DOI 10.1007/s40279-014-0274-7)

Effect/estimate: Characterises acute responses; specific values not extracted
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur to elite amateur | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: Yes — boxing-specific | transfer status: N/A — direct

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The joint position statement of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, Dietitians of Canada and the American College of Sports Medicine states explicitly that athletes should be referred to a registered dietitian/nutritionist for a personalised nutrition plan, and identifies the Certified Specialist in Sports Dietetics as the credentialed sports nutrition expert in the US and Canada.
Effect/estimate: No numeric value; the referral boundary is the finding
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: All
Design: Joint professional-body position statement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer
LIMITATIONS: Availability of a registered dietitian, and specifically a CSSD, may be limited in a rural community setting; the statement does not solve access, only names the correct role

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IAAF (World Athletics) 2019 consensus on Nutrition for Athletics provides periodised guidance covering pre-event, within-event and between-event eating, and identifies athletes at risk of relative energy deficiency in sport arising from a mismatch between energy intake and exercise energy expenditure.
Effect/estimate: Event-specific periodised guidance rather than a single target
Population: Track and field athletes across event types | level: Elite | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: International federation consensus statement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No — athletics | transfer status: Other-sport transfer; the multi-round, multi-day tournament structure of amateur boxing is closest to athletics' heats-and-finals structure
LIMITATIONS: Athletics events differ substantially from boxing in duration and energy system contribution; the between-event eating structure is the most transferable element
PPBF implication: The heats-and-finals between-event eating structure is the right model for a multi-bout amateur boxing tournament day.
Source: Burke LM, et al. International Association of Athletics Federations Consensus Statement 2019: Nutrition for Athletics. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019. (PMID 30952204 / DOI 10.1123/ijsnem.2019-0065)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a standardised survey of 260 high-calibre Australian competitors across wrestling, boxing, judo and taekwondo using a validated rapid weight loss score, weight-loss practices varied between sports, with variation attributed to competition level and culture.
Effect/estimate: Sport-level variation in RWLS; specific per-sport scores not extracted
Population: Australian Olympic combat sport athletes | level: High-calibre competitive | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional survey using a validated instrument (RWLS) | n: 260
Boxing-specific: Partially — boxing is one of four sports surveyed | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence including boxing
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; single country; culture and competition level are confounded; the RWLS is a relative severity index, not a health risk score
PPBF implication: Gym culture is a modifiable determinant of weight-cutting behaviour; this is the lever PPBF actually controls.
Source: Reale R, Slater G, Burke LM. Weight Management Practices of Australian Olympic Combat Sport Athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2018. (PMID 28872383 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0553)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] The relationship between weigh-in timing and weight-cutting magnitude is structural: reviews of Olympic combat sports note that official weigh-ins occur anywhere from 3 to 24 hours before competition and that the time available for recovery after weigh-in determines the magnitude and methods of acute body-mass manipulation.
Effect/estimate: Weigh-in-to-competition interval of 3-24 h across Olympic combat sports; magnitude scales with recovery time available
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Competitive to elite | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Two authoritative reviews with a decision-tree framework | n: NA (reviews)
Boxing-specific: Partially — Olympic combat sports including boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport evidence directly applicable
LIMITATIONS: The causal claim that shortening the recovery window reduces cutting is well-reasoned and consistent with the regain data, but a controlled test of rule change against cutting behaviour was not located
PPBF implication: Explains why the USA Boxing same-day weigh-in is protective and why PPBF should never advocate for a rule change toward day-before weigh-ins at any level it can influence.
Source: Reale R, Slater G, Burke LM. Acute-Weight-Loss Strategies for Combat Sports and Applications to Olympic Success. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2017; Reale R, Slater G, Burke LM. Individualised dietary strategies for Olympic combat sports. Eur J Sport Sci. 2017. (PMID 27347784 / DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2016-0211; PMID 28316263 / DOI 10.1080/17461391.2017.1297489)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Rapid body mass loss in combat athletes affected erythropoiesis and haemolysis without impairing aerobic performance in one study, indicating that haematological disturbance can occur without a detectable performance signal.
Effect/estimate: Erythropoiesis and haemolysis markers affected; aerobic performance not impaired
Population: Combat athletes | level: Competitive | sex: Not extracted | age: Adult
Design: Primary study | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No — combat athletes, sport not boxing-specific in the record | transfer status: Combat-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Single study; biomarker changes without a performance decrement are difficult to interpret clinically; no long-term follow-up
PPBF implication: Reinforces that 'performance was fine' does not mean 'nothing happened physiologically' - a key PPBF coach-education point.
Source: Rapid body mass loss affects erythropoiesis and hemolysis but does not impair aerobic performance in combat athletes. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2015. (PMID 25916419 / DOI 10.1111/sms.12485)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The effects of rapid weight loss have been examined separately in male and female wrestlers, indicating that sex-disaggregated analysis of weight-cutting effects is now being undertaken.
Effect/estimate: Effect estimates not extracted
Population: Male and female wrestlers | level: Competitive | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Primary study | n: Not extracted
Boxing-specific: No — wrestling | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Wrestling, not boxing; female combat-sport samples remain small across this literature (156 of 4432 participants in the main systematic review were female)
PPBF implication: The sex-disaggregated weight-cutting evidence base is thin; PPBF should not assume male-derived findings apply to female boxers.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Disordered eating risk and mental health concerns have been documented in combat-sport athletes competing under weight categories, with performance pressures and weight categories identified as contributing stressors.
Effect/estimate: Association between psychological health indicators and disordered eating patterns; effect sizes not extracted
Population: Lebanese national black-belt taekwondo players | level: National | sex: Both | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional study | n: 110
Boxing-specific: No — taekwondo | transfer status: Other-combat-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Single-country cross-sectional design; cross-sectional association cannot establish that weight categories cause disordered eating; taekwondo, not boxing
PPBF implication: Disordered eating screening in a weight-category youth programme is a safeguarding and clinical matter; SHADOW may only route, never assess.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Low energy availability is defined by energy availability relative to fat-free mass rather than by energy balance, and this distinction matters because an athlete can be in energy balance while in low energy availability.
Effect/estimate: Conceptual definition; PPBF should not adopt a numeric threshold, since measuring energy availability requires measured intake, measured exercise energy expenditure and measured fat-free mass
Population: Endurance-trained men (this review); athletes generally | level: Trained | sex: Male (this review) | age: Adult
Design: Mini-review | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General transfer; the definitional point is universal
LIMITATIONS: Measuring energy availability accurately in a community setting is impractical: all three inputs carry substantial error, which is why screening questionnaires are used instead and why they are imperfect
PPBF implication: SHADOW must NOT compute an energy availability value; the inputs are not obtainable to acceptable accuracy at PPBF and a false-precision number would be actively harmful.
Source: Hungry runners - low energy availability in male endurance athletes and its impact on performance and testosterone: mini-review. Eur J Transl Myol. 2023. (PMID 37052052 / DOI 10.4081/ejtm.2023.11104)

Effect/estimate: Prevalence and risk synthesis; within-day energy balance introduced as an additional construct
Population: Athletes | level: All levels | sex: Both | age: Mixed
Design: Updated narrative review | n: NA
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: General athlete transfer

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A boxing performance-analysis template achieved high intra-observer agreement (80-100%) but markedly weaker inter-observer agreement (33-100% across indicators); agreement reached 100% only when a plus-or-minus-one tolerance was applied.
Effect/estimate: Intra 80-100% agreement; inter 33-100%; 100% within +/-1
Population: Competitive amateur boxing footage | level: Amateur | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Instrument development with intra- and inter-observer reliability testing | n: Two analysts of differing experience
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Small number of analysts; agreement metrics are proportion-of-agreement and sign tests rather than chance-corrected kappa; sample of bouts not stated in the abstract
PPBF implication: PPBF must report counts with an explicit tolerance band and must never treat a single coder's counts as exact. This is the empirical basis for the A8V-M04 double-coding requirement.
Source: Thomson E, Lamb K, Nicholas C (2013). The development of a reliable amateur boxing performance analysis template. J Sports Sci. (PMID 23121380 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2012.738922)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite amateur bouts under the Ten Point Must System, winners punched more accurately than losers (33% vs 23% landed; 17% vs 27% air punches), while total punches thrown, defence and interaction time were similar.
Effect/estimate: %Hit 33 vs 23; %Air 17 vs 27; %Hit plus movement index classified 85% of outcomes
Population: Elite amateur boxers in a national championship | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Observational notational analysis of competition | n: 26 elite male competitors
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Single championship; male only; the 85% classification describes what judges rewarded, not a causal performance model; correlation is not causation
PPBF implication: Accuracy, not volume, is the coachable indicator. PPBF must never display punch volume as a performance figure without its accuracy denominator.
Source: Human behaviours associated with dominance in elite amateur boxing bouts (2017). PLoS ONE. (PMID 29287064 / doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0188675)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Elite male amateur boxing at Olympic semifinal and final level involved an activity rate of about 1.4 actions per second, comprising roughly 20 punches, 2.5 defensive movements and 47 vertical hip movements per minute over three rounds of about 200 seconds.
Effect/estimate: ~1.4 actions/s; ~20 punches/min; ~2.5 defensive movements/min; ~47 vertical hip movements/min; rounds ~200 s
Population: Olympic-level male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult (mean 25.1 y)
Design: Video-based activity profiling of competition | n: 29 bouts, 39 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Olympic elite males only; the authors themselves note technical discrimination between winners and losers is difficult and outcome may hinge on which punch judges score; pre-2013 rule set
PPBF implication: This is an external reference point for what elite performance looks like. It is NOT a PPBF target and must never be presented to a youth or novice athlete as one.
Source: Davis P et al. (2014). The activity profile of elite male amateur boxing. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. (PMID 24912199 / doi:10.1123/ijspp.2013-0474)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Comparing elite amateur bouts before and after the 2013 rule change, total punches thrown, rear-hand punches, rear hooks, punches landed, uppercuts and body punches all decreased, while ring movement and defensive movements increased; foot movement rose by a reported 20%.
Effect/estimate: 20% increase in foot movement; standing counts fell from 9% to 3% of rounds; bouts not lasting full duration rose from 1.7% to 4.2%
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult (mean 24.3 y)
Design: Video comparison of 29 Olympic (pre-2013) and 50 World Championship (post-2013) bouts | n: 99 male boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Two different competitions rather than a controlled comparison; male elite only; other factors changed alongside the rules
PPBF implication: Rule-set version must be stored with every bout (crosswalk A8-X120). Historical boxing norms are not portable across rule eras.
Source: Davis P et al. (2018). Comparison of amateur boxing before and after the 2013 rules change and the impact on boxers' safety. Br J Sports Med. (PMID 28954796 / doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097667)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 2023 IBA Women's World Championship finals, winners performed fewer offensive actions than losers but achieved a higher offensive effectiveness ratio across all rounds; pivoting and shifting back followed by counterattack were associated with winning, while parrying and single counterpunches were associated with losing.
Effect/estimate: Winners 635 vs losers 688 offensive actions; OER winners 0.39/0.38/0.39 vs losers 0.26/0.28/0.29 by round
Population: Elite female amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Notational analysis using a customised offensive-defensive interaction cycle framework, coded in Kinovea | n: 12 final bouts; 1323 offensive and 1456 defensive actions
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Twelve bouts at one championship; elite female only; winner-loser association is not causal and the finding may reflect what judges rewarded
PPBF implication: Supplies the OER and DER definitions used in crosswalk items A8-X014 and A8-X015, and directly justifies the counter-after-defence label A8V-D13.
Source: Notational Analysis of the Final Matches of the 2023 IBA Women's World Boxing Championships (2025). J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. (PMID 40981049 / doi:10.3390/jfmk10030350)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 2023 IBA Women's World Championship finals, fighting, punching, clinching, no-fighting and arbitral-interruption phases differed significantly across rounds, and the fighting-to-non-fighting time ratio varied by weight category, with heavyweight categories relying more on clinching.
Effect/estimate: Significant round differences for punching, clinching, no-fighting and arbitral interruption (all p<0.01)
Population: Elite female amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Female | age: Adult
Design: Video time-motion analysis of 3x3-minute finals | n: 12 final bouts across 12 weight categories
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: One bout per weight category, so category comparisons rest on n=1; elite female only
PPBF implication: There is no single correct fighting-to-non-fighting ratio. PPBF must not set a target for this metric; it is a description of style, not quality.
Source: Time-Motion Analysis of the 2023 Women's World Boxing Championships Finals (2025). Sports (Basel). (PMID 40559699 / doi:10.3390/sports13060187)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Phases of lead and rear straight and hook punches were defined using ground reaction force, EMG, high-speed video and striking dynamometry, producing a shared phase structure for describing punching research.
Effect/estimate: Phase definitions for four punch types; no accuracy statistic applicable
Population: Experienced competitive boxers | level: Competitive (level not further specified) | sex: Male (mean mass 95.66 kg) | age: Adult (mean 25.6 y)
Design: Mixed-method laboratory study | n: 10 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Ten participants, laboratory maximal-effort punches, high-speed video; whether phases are resolvable at consumer phone frame rates is untested
PPBF implication: Supplies the punch-phase vocabulary (A8V-B10 to B12). Frame-rate adequacy for PPBF footage is TBD (crosswalk A8-X003).
Source: Lenetsky S et al. (2020). Defining the Phases of Boxing Punches: A Mixed-Method Approach. J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 30789570 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002895)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A multimodal system fusing wearable sensor and video data with query-by-committee active learning reported 91.41% accuracy for rear-hand punch classification while reducing labelling effort to about one-sixth of the usual requirement.
Effect/estimate: 91.41% accuracy at 15% of typical labelling effort
Population: Boxers (details not stated in abstract) | level: Not stated | sex: Not stated | age: Not stated
Design: Machine-learning methods study | n: Not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: The paper itself states video-based classification is less accurate than sensor-based due to motion blur; sample and setting not described in the abstract; accuracy is for a research setup, not gym footage from a single phone
PPBF implication: Automated punch classification is a research capability, not a deployable PPBF feature. Listed as DO_NOT_BUILD_YET (crosswalk A8-X121).
Source: An active machine learning framework for automatic boxing punch recognition and classification using upper limb kinematics (2025). PLoS ONE. (PMID 40338954 / doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0322490)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A multimodal deep-learning framework combining 3D-ResNet video features with a BERT-encoded psychological profile reported 91.2% accuracy and 90.9% F1 on boxing action recognition, outperforming video-only and psychology-only baselines.
Effect/estimate: 91.2% accuracy; 90.9% F1
Population: Research video datasets (HMDB51-Boxing subset and a constructed PsyBox-20 dataset) | level: Not applicable | sex: Not stated | age: Not stated
Design: Deep-learning methods study | n: Dataset-level, not athlete-level
Boxing-specific: Partially - uses boxing action datasets | transfer status: N/A
LIMITATIONS: Benchmark datasets, not ecological gym footage; the psychological signal came from standardised self-report scales linked to clips, not inferred from images; no external validation
PPBF implication: Important negative point for PPBF: this paper does NOT show that mental state can be read from video. It shows that self-reported state, supplied separately, improved a classifier. Emotion inference from video remains prohibited (A8V-P08).
Source: Integrating psychological profiling with deep learning for enhanced boxing action recognition (2026). Sci Rep. (PMID 41513933 / doi:10.1038/s41598-025-34771-0)

[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] A transformer approach processing raw video without pose estimation reported 90% accuracy on fencing actions and 83.25% on boxing actions.
Effect/estimate: 83.25% accuracy on boxing actions
Population: Research video of fencing and boxing | level: Not stated | sex: Not stated | age: Not stated
Design: Computer-science methods paper (arXiv preprint) | n: Not stated
Boxing-specific: Partially | transfer status: N/A

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of markerless motion capture during jumping tasks pooled sagittal-plane RMSE of 5.3 degrees at the hip (95% CI 2.9-7.6), 4.4 at the knee (2.9-5.9) and 4.9 at the ankle (3.9-5.9), with a pooled jump-height bias of -2.9 cm (95% CI -8.1 to 2.3) and heterogeneity from low to substantial.
Effect/estimate: Hip RMSE 5.3 deg; knee 4.4 deg; ankle 4.9 deg; jump height bias -2.9 cm
Population: Mixed - laboratory and field jumping tasks | level: Mixed | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, six databases) | n: 20 studies
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM NON-BOXING TASKS - jumping is a planar, unoccluded, single-person task; boxing is none of those
LIMITATIONS: Performance varies widely between systems and contexts; wide prediction intervals; the authors advise system-specific evidence
PPBF implication: Even under favourable conditions, markerless angle error is several degrees. PPBF should not present pose-derived joint angles as measurements (crosswalk A8-X122).
Source: Are we there yet? Systematic review and meta-analysis of validity and reliability of automated markerless motion capture during jumping tasks (2025). J Sports Sci. (PMID 41293872 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2025.2589689)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Testing OpenPose against manual analysis on two-camera 200 Hz footage from a World Championship long jump, coefficients of multiple determination for joint-angle waveforms varied widely and agreement for discrete data was generally poor, with an average ICC across variables of 0.17.
Effect/estimate: Average ICC across variables 0.17; knee-angle CMD ~0.73, hip ~0.37-0.39, ankle ~0.16-0.25
Population: Elite long jumpers in competition | level: Elite | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Concurrent-validity comparison of markerless versus manual digitisation | n: One take-off recording per athlete, men's Long Jump final
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM NON-BOXING SPORT - athletics, single unoccluded athlete, two synchronised 200 Hz cameras
LIMITATIONS: Single event; one movement; a favourable capture setup that still produced poor discrete agreement
PPBF implication: This is the most directly relevant warning available: pose estimation degraded badly in a real competition with better cameras than PPBF will have. Strong support for the do-not-build-yet position on pose-derived measures.
Source: Feasibility of OpenPose markerless motion analysis in a real athletics competition (2024). Front Sports Act Living. (PMID 38250008 / doi:10.3389/fspor.2023.1298003)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A comparative assessment of 16 monocular 2D and 3D human pose estimation frameworks against synchronised gold-standard motion capture found MeTRAbs best overall, with AlphaPose, rtmlib and YOLOv7 the top 2D performers, evaluated by weighted mean absolute error and weighted ICC on joint angles.
Effect/estimate: Framework ranking by weighted MAE and weighted ICC
Population: Nine individuals performing eight exercises, two camera views | level: Not applicable | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Benchmark comparison of 16 frameworks against marker-based reference; review of 118 papers | n: 9 participants, 8 exercises
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM NON-BOXING EXERCISE TASKS
LIMITATIONS: Exercise videos with a monocular RGB camera, not contact-sport footage; nine participants; no occlusion by a second person
PPBF implication: If PPBF ever pilots pose estimation, framework choice matters and must be recorded per clip. Does not change the do-not-build-yet position for boxing.
Source: A Comparative Assessment of Accuracy in Video-Based Monocular Human Pose Estimation Frameworks (2026). IEEE Trans Pattern Anal Mach Intell. (PMID 41805522 / doi:10.1109/TPAMI.2026.3672463)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Across 115 boxing sparring rounds with 5168 video-identified head-contact events, an instrumented mouthguard, skin patch and headgear patch showed sensitivities of 35%, 86% and 78% and specificities of 90%, 76% and 75% respectively, though positive predictive values for head impacts exceeded 96%.
Effect/estimate: Sensitivity 35% / 86% / 78%; specificity 90% / 76% / 75%; PPV >96%
Population: Competitive boxers in sparring | level: Competitive amateur | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Prospective validation against three-camera video reference | n: 7 boxers, 115 sparring rounds, 5168 video-identified events
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Seven boxers; three cameras used to establish the video reference, which a single gym camera will not match; sensors were also more likely to trigger on impacts near the sensor
PPBF implication: Video, coded by humans with adequate camera coverage, is currently the better-verified way to count head contacts in boxing. It also means a single-camera PPBF setup will undercount. Head-contact counts are exposure records only.
Source: Capturing Head Impacts in Boxing: A Video-Based Comparison of Three Wearable Sensors (2023). Ann Biomed Eng. (PMID 37728812 / doi:10.1007/s10439-023-03369-w)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Assessing 442 boxing sparring events per sensor, high-quality kinematic traces were obtained in 53% of events for the mouthguard, 20% for the skin patch and 26% for the headgear patch; high-quality recordings were less frequent for impacts near the sensor, and even among carefully selected simultaneous high-quality recordings there was little to no association between the sensors' measurements.
Effect/estimate: High-quality traces in 53% / 20% / 26%; Spearman rho >= 0.043 between sensors
Population: Competitive boxers in sparring | level: Competitive amateur | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Prospective signal-quality assessment with pre-defined objective criteria | n: 442 events per sensor
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Small participant pool; quality criteria are the authors' own; findings concern kinematic magnitude, not event counting
PPBF implication: Wearable head-impact magnitudes must not be used for any PPBF individual decision. Counts from different devices are not interchangeable and must never be pooled (crosswalk A8-X049).
Source: Quality Issues in Kinematic Traces from Three Head Impact Sensors in Boxing (2024). Ann Biomed Eng. (PMID 39625630 / doi:10.1007/s10439-024-03647-1)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Monitoring seven competitive boxers with instrumented mouthguards across sparring sessions, group symptom scores did not differ pre- to post-sparring (median change in total symptom severity -1, p=0.85), symptom scores were lower at 48 hours than pre-session, and no strong association was found between session-specific exposure and symptom change; four of sixteen sessions from three participants showed a symptom-severity change greater than 5.
Effect/estimate: Median change in TSSS -1 (p=0.85, r=0.07); 48h vs pre p=0.02, r=0.55; 4/16 sessions with change >5
Population: Competitive boxers | level: Competitive amateur | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Exploratory observational cohort with SCAT5 symptom scale | n: 7 boxers, 16 sessions
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Seven participants, exploratory and qualitative analysis, no control condition; the authors state the acute dose-response relationship remains elusive
PPBF implication: There is no defensible sparring-volume or impact-dose threshold PPBF could implement. Sparring volume guidance is TBD and owned by the head coach with medical input, not by SHADOW.
Source: Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring (2026). J Sci Med Sport. (PMID 41672855 / doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2026.01.018)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of amateur boxing found pooled competition injury incidence of 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 minutes (4.2-10.9), and training incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (0.2-7.0); the head and neck were the most commonly injured region in competition (median 72%) and the upper limb in training (median 49%).
Effect/estimate: Competition IIR 54.7/1000 AE and 6.8/1000 min; training IIR 1.3/1000 h; head and neck median 72% of competition injuries
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: Mixed / mostly male | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Wide confidence intervals, especially for training incidence; heterogeneous injury definitions; predominantly male samples
PPBF implication: Justifies both the safety-event branch of the ontology (A8V-J) and the injury-surveillance gap at crosswalk A8-X050. Head and hand are the priority regions.
Source: Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis (2022). J Sci Med Sport. (PMID 36195527 / doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In five years of prospective surveillance of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad, hand injuries were the most frequent location overall and in both training and competition; competition total injury rate was 828 per 1000 hours with a hand injury rate of 302 per 1000 hours, and concussion incidence was comparatively low.
Effect/estimate: Competition total 828 per 1000 h; hand 302 per 1000 h
Population: Elite amateur boxers (GB squad) | level: Elite amateur | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance, 2005-2009 | n: 66 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Single national squad; per-1000-hour competition rates are high because competition exposure hours are small; medically diagnosed injuries only, so under-reporting of minor complaints is likely
PPBF implication: Supports the wrap-check field (crosswalk A8-X052) and the hand-distress observation label (A8V-J07) as high-prior, low-cost items.
Source: Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study (2015). Br J Sports Med. (PMID 26192194 / doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis of expert versus non-expert perceptual anticipation in combat sports found large effects for response accuracy (1.51; 95% CI 1.15-1.87) and reaction time (-0.91; 95% CI -1.08 to -0.73), with expertise effects more pronounced when the stimulus was closer to the real-world setting.
Effect/estimate: Accuracy SMD 1.51 (1.15-1.87); reaction time SMD -0.91 (-1.08 to -0.73)
Population: Combat-sport athletes across disciplines | level: Mixed expert and non-expert | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis, seven databases, random-effects | n: 27 studies, 233 datasets
Boxing-specific: Partially - combat sports broadly, not boxing alone | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT - includes non-boxing disciplines
LIMITATIONS: Expert-novice designs are cross-sectional and cannot establish that training causes the difference; publication bias in expertise research is a known concern
PPBF implication: Supports representative-stimulus design for any PPBF perceptual work, and supports coding decision-related labels as coach judgement rather than measurement. Does NOT license selection use.
Source: A comparison of perceptual anticipation in combat sports between experts and non-experts: systematic review and meta-analysis (2022). Front Psychol. (PMID 36389534 / doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2022.961960)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A methodological quality checklist for observational-methodology studies was developed and validated with 54 judges, yielding 16 items across 11 criteria with adequate intercoder reliability coefficients.
Effect/estimate: 16 items, 11 criteria; adequate reliability coefficients
Population: Observational-methodology researchers | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: Adult
Design: Instrument development with expert judging (Osterlind indexes) and Cohen's kappa intercoder testing | n: 54 judges
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM RESEARCH METHODOLOGY - discipline-agnostic
LIMITATIONS: Validated on soccer observational studies; not a sport-performance finding
PPBF implication: Provides the quality framework the PPBF ontology should be assessed against before any label class is promoted from UNTESTED (crosswalk A8-X117).
Source: Chacon-Moscoso S et al. (2019). Methodological quality checklist for studies based on observational methodology (MQCOM). Psicothema. (PMID 31634092 / doi:10.7334/psicothema2019.116)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed observational instrument for Olympic taekwondo, combining field formats and category systems across six criteria and 25 categories, achieved optimal generalizability coefficients when applied to 2374 actions from 10 Olympic bouts.
Effect/estimate: Optimal G coefficients; lag-sequential and polar-coordinate pattern findings
Population: Olympic taekwondo competitors | level: Elite | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Instrument design, validation and generalizability analysis | n: 10 bouts, 12 competitors, 2374 actions
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM ANOTHER STRIKING COMBAT SPORT - taekwondo is a kicking sport with electronic scoring
LIMITATIONS: Single Olympic tournament; taekwondo scoring differs fundamentally from boxing; generalizability coefficients reported as 'optimal' without values in the abstract
PPBF implication: Demonstrates the design-validate-test sequence PPBF should follow, and shows that six criteria with about 25 categories is a workable instrument size - a useful ceiling check on the A8 starter set.
Source: Design, validation, and testing of an observational tool for technical and tactical analysis in the taekwondo competition at the 2016 Olympic games (2020). Physiol Behav. (PMID 32535137 / doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2020.112980)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The JUTACTIC judo observation instrument, with 8 fixed and 13 variable criteria, was validated by an 11-expert panel with intra- and inter-observer reliability established via Fleiss kappa and Krippendorff alpha, and generalizability analysis indicated roughly seven matches are needed to characterise a competitor's behaviour.
Effect/estimate: About seven matches needed for accurate individual behavioural analysis
Population: Olympic judo champions | level: Elite | sex: Mixed | age: Adult
Design: Instrument development with expert content validity and generalizability analysis | n: Rio 2016 Olympic champions' matches; 11 experts
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM ANOTHER COMBAT SPORT - judo is a grappling sport
LIMITATIONS: Grappling sport; small match sample; the seven-match figure is judo-specific and must not be transferred to boxing
PPBF implication: The finding that multiple bouts are needed before an individual profile stabilises is the important transferable lesson. How many boxing rounds PPBF needs is TBD.
Source: Observation system for the technical-tactical analysis of judo by the Rio 2016 Olympic champions (JUTACTIC) (2024). PLoS ONE. (PMID 38768169 / doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0303689)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Coach Feedback Analysis System, with six categories and eighteen feedback types, was developed and validated across 600 minutes of footage from four team sports and multiple competitive levels and age groups, achieving above-acceptable inter- and intra-observer agreement and expert-panel face validity.
Effect/estimate: Above-acceptable inter- and intra-observer agreement (values not given in abstract)
Population: Coaches in hurling, football, Australian Rules football and women's rugby union | level: Amateur, academy and professional | sex: Male teams unless specified; one women's team | age: u14, u16 and adult
Design: Instrument development and reliability study | n: 600 minutes of footage across four sports
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM TEAM SPORTS - no boxing or combat-sport validation
LIMITATIONS: Team sports only; specific agreement values not stated in the abstract; coaching contexts differ substantially from a boxing gym floor
PPBF implication: Offers a ready structure for the coach-feedback capture at crosswalk A8-X020, but it must be treated as untested in boxing and used for coach development only, never for evaluation.
Source: Development, validation and reliability of the Coach Feedback Analysis System (2025). J Sports Sci. (PMID 40968546 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2025.2561346)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A handball observational instrument combining automatic and manual variables achieved expert agreement of Cohen's kappa 0.889 and, for two observers analysing a Champions League match, intra-observer reliability of alpha 0.984 / ICC 0.970 / kappa 0.917 for automatic variables and alpha 0.959 / ICC 0.923 / kappa 0.858 for manual variables.
Effect/estimate: Expert kappa 0.889; automatic intra alpha 0.984, ICC 0.970, kappa 0.917; manual intra alpha 0.959, ICC 0.923, kappa 0.858
Population: Elite handball | level: Elite | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Instrument design and validation with expert panel and two observers | n: 10 experts; one Champions League match; two observers
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM A TEAM INVASION SPORT - open court, unoccluded players, ball-based events
LIMITATIONS: One match, two observers with 1.5-2 years experience; handball has a tracked ball and far less mutual occlusion than boxing; automatic variables were higher-agreement than manual ones, which reflects the easier detection problem
PPBF implication: Shows the target reliability an AI-assisted observational tool can reach in a favourable sport. Boxing should expect lower, which is why the A8 ontology sets differentiated targets by label class.
Source: Development and Validation of an Observational Game Analysis Tool with Artificial Intelligence for Handball: Handball.ai (2023). Sensors. (PMID 37571498 / doi:10.3390/s23156714)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Kinovea 2D motion-analysis software was assessed against AutoCAD reference measurements at four camera perspectives (90, 75, 60 and 45 degrees) with three observers making two attempts each, examining both validity and intra- and inter-rater reliability by perspective.
Effect/estimate: Validity and reliability assessed across four camera perspectives (specific values not in abstract)
Population: Wire-frame lower-limb model in pendular motion | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Concurrent-validity and reliability study against a geometric gold standard | n: One structure, three observers, two attempts, four perspectives
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM A LABORATORY PHANTOM - not a moving human, not a contact sport
LIMITATIONS: A rigid wire structure, not a boxer; the point of the study is precisely that perspective matters
PPBF implication: Directly justifies the camera-view field at crosswalk A8-X002 and the A8V-A10 label. Kinovea is the tool the published women's boxing notational analyses used, so it is a realistic PPBF choice.
Source: Puig-Divi A et al. (2019). Validity and reliability of the Kinovea program in obtaining angles and distances using coordinates in 4 perspectives. PLoS ONE. (PMID 31166989 / doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0216448)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] For gait joint angles at initial contact in 50 healthy subjects, Kinovea showed intra-rater ICC above 0.85 and inter-rater ICC above 0.90 at hip, knee and ankle, with Bland-Altman disagreement of about plus or minus 5 degrees intra-rater, plus or minus 2.5 degrees inter-rater, and about 2.5 to 5 degrees versus Vicon.
Effect/estimate: Intra ICC >0.85; inter ICC >0.90; agreement approximately +/-2.5 to +/-5 degrees
Population: Healthy adults | level: N/A | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Reliability and agreement study versus a 3D motion system | n: 50 subjects, two observers, two sessions
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM CLINICAL GAIT ANALYSIS - planar, slow, unoccluded, single person
LIMITATIONS: Gait is the easiest possible case; boxing involves rapid rotation, occlusion and two bodies
PPBF implication: Sets a realistic upper bound: even in ideal conditions, 2D video angle agreement is a few degrees. PPBF should present angles as approximate discussion aids, never as assessments.
Source: Reliability of Kinovea Software and Agreement with a Three-Dimensional Motion System for Gait Analysis in Healthy Subjects (2020). Sensors. (PMID 32498380 / doi:10.3390/s20113154)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Pad-based and bag-based boxing-specific protocols of identical structure produced different physiological responses in elite amateur boxers, with higher blood lactate (2.7 vs 2.3 mmol/L), average heart rate (160 vs 150 b/min) and average oxygen consumption (38.00 vs 34.40 ml/kg/min) for pads compared with bag.
Effect/estimate: BLa 2.7 vs 2.3 mmol/L; HRave 160 vs 150 b/min; VO2ave 38.00 vs 34.40 ml/kg/min
Population: Elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult (mean 22 y)
Design: Within-subject comparison of two 3x3-minute protocols | n: 14 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Fourteen elite male amateurs; single session per modality; findings may not hold for novice or youth athletes
PPBF implication: Makes the training-modality field (crosswalk A8-X047) mandatory rather than optional. Pooling pad and bag load misrepresents both.
Source: Finlay MJ et al. (2020). Physical Response to Pad- and Bag-Based Boxing-Specific Training Modalities. J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 30358696 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002928)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of RPE and session-RPE in combat-sport activities reported significant correlations between RPE, blood lactate and heart rate, with a stronger RPE-lactate correlation for official striking matches (r=0.81) than grappling matches (r=0.53), and session-RPE correlating moderately to largely with heart-rate-based training-load methods.
Effect/estimate: RPE-lactate r=0.81 striking vs r=0.53 grappling; session-RPE vs Edwards TL r=0.58-0.95; vs Banister TRIMP r=0.52-0.86
Population: Combat-sport athletes across disciplines | level: Mixed | sex: Mostly male | age: Mixed, including youth
Design: Narrative short review | n: Not stated - review of multiple studies
Boxing-specific: Partially - striking combat sports include boxing | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Short narrative review rather than a systematic one; correlation with physiological markers does not make RPE a substitute for them; scale version varies across the underlying studies
PPBF implication: Supports RPE as a feasible PPBF load measure but requires the scale version to be recorded (crosswalk A8-X045). No PPBF load threshold is derivable from this.
Source: Slimani M et al. (2017). Rating of Perceived Exertion for Quantification of Training and Combat Loads During Combat Sport-Specific Activities: A Short Review. J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 28933715 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002047)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In seven national-level boxers, rear-straight reaction time lengthened significantly across a 3x3-minute sparring load during the precompetition period (to 390 ms) compared with the competition period (to 310 ms), and both rear and lead straight punch forces were greater at all measurement points during precompetition than competition.
Effect/estimate: Rear straight RT 390 ms (precompetition) vs 310 ms (competition) after round 3
Population: National-level male boxers | level: National amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult (mean 20.3 y)
Design: Repeated-measures within-athlete comparison across two training periods | n: 7 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Seven athletes; two training periods differ in many ways beyond sparring load; no control condition
PPBF implication: Justifies the fatigue-context field (A8V-K06 and crosswalk A8-X110): a technical label without its within-session position is not interpretable.
Source: Effects of Sparring Load on Reaction Speed and Punch Force During the Precompetition and Competition Periods in Boxing (2017). J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 28538306 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001885)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A framework fusing inertial measurement units in the gloves with uniplanar videography and OpenPose in six elite male boxers under a punch fatigue protocol found the dominant side fatigued more than the non-dominant, and tracking simulations showed shoulder abduction and elevation moments increased across the protocol.
Effect/estimate: Dominant side fatigued more than non-dominant; increased shoulder abduction and elevation moments
Population: Elite male boxers | level: Elite | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Methods development with statistical parametric mapping and optimal-control tracking simulation | n: 6 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Six athletes; the authors note the approach would need to move to ecologically valid contexts with multiple IMUs and cameras; OpenPose labelled only left-side upper-limb landmarks in the sagittal plane
PPBF implication: Laterality asymmetry is real but the evidence base is six athletes in a laboratory protocol. Crosswalk A8-X103 is marked low priority and must not produce an injury-risk output.
Source: Fusing Accelerometry with Videography to Monitor the Effect of Fatigue on Punching Performance in Elite Boxers (2020). Sensors. (PMID 33050436 / doi:10.3390/s20205749)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 studies covering nine strike types found straight and reverse punches produced larger mean impact forces than a kung fu punch, a palm strike had lower velocity than reverse, straight or junzuki punches, and the highest recorded mean force was 3427 N for a straight punch.
Effect/estimate: Highest mean force 3427 N (straight punch); high-speed strikes over 10 m/s
Population: Combat-sport athletes across disciplines | level: Mixed | sex: Mostly male | age: Adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Scopus, Web of Science) | n: 28 studies, 9 strike types
Boxing-specific: Partially - boxing included among several striking disciplines | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous instrumentation across studies makes pooled force values only loosely comparable; predominantly male adult samples
PPBF implication: Provides an external reference range for punch force but confirms that values from different instruments are not interchangeable (crosswalk A8-X030).
Source: Force and velocity of impact during upper limb strikes in combat sports: a systematic review and meta-analysis (2020). Sports Biomech. (PMID 32677587 / doi:10.1080/14763141.2020.1778075)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of sport-specific performance tests in Olympic combat sports found the majority of studies (74%) had samples under 30, nearly a third insufficiently described participants, 72% did not adequately report inclusion or exclusion criteria, 62% incompletely described or omitted familiarisation, and 60% reported no details on testing-condition stability.
Effect/estimate: 74% n<30; 72% inadequate inclusion criteria; 62% inadequate familiarisation; 60% no testing-condition detail
Population: Amateur boxing, fencing, judo, karate, taekwondo and wrestling athletes | level: Mixed, largely elite | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review of validation studies | n: 39 studies
Boxing-specific: Partially - amateur boxing included | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Assesses reporting quality rather than test performance; findings are about the literature, not about any specific test
PPBF implication: The combat-sport testing literature is methodologically weak. PPBF should treat published combat-sport test norms with caution and prioritise its own reliability work (crosswalk A8-X088).
Source: Chaabene H et al. (2018). Tests for the Assessment of Sport-Specific Performance in Olympic Combat Sports: A Systematic Review With Practical Recommendations. Front Physiol. (PMID 29692739 / doi:10.3389/fphys.2018.00386)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Learners given self-control over combined split-screen video feedback and expert modelling during golf-chip practice showed significantly higher form and accuracy scores on a transfer test, higher perceived competence, and recalled more critical task features than a yoked group.
Effect/estimate: Significantly higher form and accuracy on transfer; higher perceived competence
Population: Adult learners of a golf chip shot | level: Novice | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Randomised self-control versus yoked motor-learning experiment with retention and transfer tests | n: Not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM A SELF-PACED CLOSED SKILL - golf chipping has no opponent, no time pressure and no contact
LIMITATIONS: Small laboratory task; whether learner-controlled review helps in an open, opposed skill like boxing is untested
PPBF implication: Supports building athlete-controlled review (crosswalk A8-X024) but the transfer to boxing is an explicit hypothesis, not an established finding.
Source: Self-control over combined video feedback and modeling facilitates motor learning (2016). Hum Mov Sci. (PMID 26874750 / doi:10.1016/j.humov.2016.01.014)
