text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Eight expert female volleyball attackers from a national team, split into experimental and control groups, completed eight reflective sessions of clip viewing, self-analysis and joint player-coach analysis; the experimental group showed significant improvement in tactical knowledge measured by verbal-protocol problem representation.
Effect/estimate: Significant increase in verbalized conditions and conceptual sophistication in the experimental group
Population: Expert female volleyball attackers, Spanish National Team | level: Elite | sex: Female | age: Adult (mean 26 y)
Design: Controlled intervention with verbal-protocol assessment | n: 8 players (4 experimental, 4 control)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM A TEAM SPORT - volleyball, no physical contact, different decision structure
LIMITATIONS: Four participants per group; expert adult athletes; verbal-protocol outcome rather than on-court performance
PPBF implication: The three-phase structure (view, self-analyse, joint analysis) is a concrete, low-cost protocol PPBF could pilot. Very small sample, non-boxing, so it is a hypothesis for PPBF.
Source: An Intervention Based on Video Feedback and Questioning to Improve Tactical Knowledge in Expert Female Volleyball Players (2016). Percept Mot Skills. (PMID 27287052 / doi:10.1177/0031512516650628)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Across 193 young athletes and six coaches, information was completely retained in 31.6% of feedback episodes with a mean per-episode retention of 63%; athletes' practice level, attention during feedback, and the number of different ideas transmitted by the coach were predictive of retention.
Effect/estimate: Complete retention in 31.6% of episodes; mean per-episode retention 63%
Population: Young athletes | level: Youth / developmental | sex: 79 boys, 114 girls | age: 9-13 years
Design: Observational study with content analysis of recorded feedback and athlete interviews | n: 193 athletes, 6 coaches
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM MIXED YOUTH SPORT - not boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional and correlational; retention measured by recall interview, not by performance change; sport composition not stated in the abstract
PPBF implication: Directly relevant to PPBF's youth population: most of what a coach says is not retained. Supports the athlete recall check at crosswalk A8-X025 and argues for fewer, clearer film-study points per session.
Source: Variables affecting athletes' retention of coaches' feedback (2013). Percept Mot Skills. (PMID 24611244 / doi:10.2466/22.10.PMS.117x16z7)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport produced a consensus statement on sport-related concussion, with a companion paediatric-specific recommendation set derived from the Amsterdam 2023 process.
Effect/estimate: Not applicable - guidance document
Population: Athletes across sports, including paediatric populations | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: Paediatric and adult
Design: International expert consensus statement | n: Consensus process, not a single sample
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: APPLIES ACROSS SPORTS INCLUDING BOXING
LIMITATIONS: Consensus statements sit below systematic reviews in the evidence hierarchy and reflect expert judgement where trial evidence is limited
PPBF implication: The governing authority for concussion recognition, management and return to play is a qualified clinician. Every A8V-J label and prohibited-label row routes to that human. SHADOW may never make or gate these decisions.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The American Academy of Pediatrics and the Canadian Paediatric Society oppose boxing as a sport for children and adolescents because it encourages and rewards deliberate blows to the head and face, placing participants at risk of head, face and neck injuries including chronic and fatal neurologic injury.
Effect/estimate: Not applicable - position statement
Population: Children and adolescents in North America | level: Youth | sex: Boys and girls | age: Under 19 years
Design: Professional body policy statement | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: A position statement, not a study; represents these bodies' judgement, and other bodies and jurisdictions permit and regulate youth boxing rather than opposing it
PPBF implication: PPBF must hold this position explicitly in its governance record rather than omit it. It raises, not lowers, the bar for youth head-contact exposure decisions, all of which belong to qualified humans.
Source: American Academy of Pediatrics / Canadian Paediatric Society (2011). Policy statement - Boxing participation by children and adolescents. Pediatrics. (PMID 21873697 / doi:10.1542/peds.2011-1165)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] USA Boxing technical rules specify a Ten Point Must System in which five judges are seated and three are randomly selected per bout for scoring, with 10 points to the round winner and 9 or fewer down to 6 for the loser; USA Boxing competition rules state that once a decision is determined it is final with no further review, and that personal video recordings are not accepted for USA Boxing competitions.
Effect/estimate: 10-point must; 5 judges with 3 randomly selected
Population: USA Boxing sanctioned competition | level: Amateur | sex: Mixed | age: All sanctioned age divisions
Design: Governing-body rulebook | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - USA Boxing only; IBA, World Boxing, England Boxing, Boxing Canada and professional commissions differ
LIMITATIONS: Rule books change annually; the 2026 USA Boxing Rule Book is in effect for the calendar year; the excerpted PDFs retrieved are not necessarily the current edition and PPBF must check against the current rule book
PPBF implication: Any PPBF film-study output is coaching material only. SHADOW must never present a video-derived score as a scoring judgement, and must never be used to dispute an official result.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] England Boxing safeguarding policy requires written parental consent before filming children, with films stored securely and handed to the child or parent or destroyed once their use ends; the British Amateur Boxing Association policy similarly requires a photography consent form while explicitly permitting video as a legitimate coaching aid provided participants and parents are aware and storage is careful.
Effect/estimate: Not applicable - policy requirement
Population: Children and young people in boxing in England / Great Britain | level: All levels | sex: Mixed | age: Under 18
Design: Governing-body safeguarding policy | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - England and Great Britain; US clubs are governed by USA Boxing policy, state law and federal privacy rules
LIMITATIONS: Policy rather than empirical evidence; PPBF operates in the United States, so England Boxing policy is a reference standard, not a binding rule
PPBF implication: Video consent must be a distinct waiver type from video publication consent (crosswalk A8-X066), and partner consent must be resolved before any sparring clip is coded (A8-X094). The permission of video as a coaching aid supports the whole film-study lane.

Effect/estimate: Not applicable - methodology
Population: Categorical observer agreement methodology | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Methodological paper | n: Not applicable
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: DISCIPLINE-AGNOSTIC METHODOLOGY
LIMITATIONS: The widely quoted verbal descriptors for kappa ranges are conventions proposed by the authors, not empirically derived thresholds, and kappa is sensitive to label prevalence

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mobile application for measuring strike response time in combat sports showed no significant difference from simultaneous high-speed camera measurement (p=0.56), a very strong correlation (r=0.993), a trivial effect size and a typical error of measurement of 1.4%.
Effect/estimate: r=0.993; TEM 1.4%; g<0.25; p=0.56
Population: Combat-sport athletes | level: Not stated | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional validation against high-speed camera and a programmed computer simulator | n: 2 athletes, 59 strikes
Boxing-specific: Partially - combat sports | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Two athletes; validation of the timing mechanism rather than of a performance construct; no evidence that the measure predicts anything in boxing

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysing 990 rounds ending in concussion and 627 ending in submission resignation, head trauma was the leading cause of concussion (about 90%), with concussion combats showing higher frequencies of distance head-strike actions than submission combats.
Effect/estimate: Head trauma about 90% of concussion causes; distance head strikes 13 (6,25) vs 9 (4,18)
Population: Professional MMA athletes | level: Professional | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Retrospective analysis of officially diagnosed severe injuries with technical-tactical coding | n: 990 concussion rounds, 627 submission rounds
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM MIXED MARTIAL ARTS

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 78 Para Taekwondo matches at the 2020 Tokyo Paralympics, winners had significantly higher kick-to-score ratios than non-winners (male 38.3% vs 19.4%; female 32.7% vs 11.0%) with fewer attack attempts, and logistic regression showed kick-to-score ratio significantly predicted match outcome for both sexes.
Effect/estimate: Kick-to-score male 38.3+/-17.37% vs 19.4+/-11.95%; female 32.7+/-18.17% vs 11.0+/-7.72%; OR 1.10 male, 1.19 female
Population: Para Taekwondo athletes | level: Elite Paralympic | sex: Male and female analysed separately | age: Adult
Design: Notational analysis with frame-by-frame coding and logistic regression | n: 78 matches (36 men's, 42 women's)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM PARA TAEKWONDO - kicking sport with electronic scoring and adaptive classification
LIMITATIONS: Different sport, scoring system and classification structure; association with outcome is not causal
PPBF implication: Converges with the elite amateur boxing accuracy finding: efficiency separates winners more consistently than volume across several combat sports. This convergence strengthens the case for accuracy-first coaching indicators, but each sport's own evidence remains primary.
Source: Comparisons of tactical and technical performance factors between winners and non-winners in Para Taekwondo (2024). J Sports Sci. (PMID 39508424 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2024.2416812)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed-methods study of implementing amateur boxing injury surveillance in Australia generated three themes: value of data, trust built through rapport with the boxing community, and barriers to implementation including fear, resistance to change, and process requirements; the implementation trial covered five events and 210 registered participants.
Effect/estimate: Three themes; RE-AIM indicators evaluated except maintenance
Population: Australian amateur boxing community (athletes, coaches, promoters, referees, medical professionals, officials) | level: Amateur | sex: Mixed | age: Not stated
Design: Mixed methods: reflexive thematic analysis plus a RE-AIM-framed implementation trial | n: 5 events, 210 registered participants
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - Australia
LIMITATIONS: Single-country context; maintenance domain not evaluated, so long-term sustainability is unknown
PPBF implication: PPBF should expect fear and resistance when introducing systematic video coding and safety-event logging, and should invest in trust and in showing coaches the value of their own data before mandating burden.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of male amateur boxing competition reported activity-to-rest ratios higher in elite (18:1) than novice (9:1) boxers, with significant round-wise differences in novices (round 1 16:1, round 2 8:1, round 3 6:1), and noted triple-punch combinations among the technical features distinguishing bouts.
Effect/estimate: Activity-to-rest 18:1 elite vs 9:1 novice; novice by round 16:1, 8:1, 6:1
Population: Male amateur boxers | level: Elite and novice | sex: Male | age: Any age category per the review scope
Design: Narrative brief review | n: Not stated - review of multiple studies
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Narrative rather than systematic review; male only; ratios depend on how activity and rest were operationalised in each underlying study
PPBF implication: Confirms that elite reference values must never be applied to novice or youth PPBF athletes: the same metric means something different at each level. Competitive level is a mandatory context field on every derived indicator.
Source: Slimani M et al. (2017). Performance Aspects and Physiological Responses in Male Amateur Boxing Competitions: A Brief Review. J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 28081033 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001643)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] T-pattern analysis of 15 professional championship fights ending in the first or second round found a higher percentage of individual T-patterns and greater decisional complexity in winners than losers, though chi-square testing did not support the group difference.
Effect/estimate: Higher percentage of individual T-patterns in winners; chi-square not significant
Population: Professional boxing champions | level: Professional elite | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Observational methodology with T-pattern (Theme) analysis; mixed registration agreed by two former professional boxers | n: 15 fights
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Fifteen fights, all ending early, which is an unrepresentative sample of professional bouts; the headline difference was not statistically supported; coders were former boxers rather than trained analysts
PPBF implication: Sequential-pattern analysis is a plausible future direction for PPBF exchange-level data but the boxing evidence for it is currently weak. Listed as a research direction, not a build item.
Source: Professional boxing analysis with T-Patterns (2021). Physiol Behav. (PMID 33493543 / doi:10.1016/j.physbeh.2021.113329)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Evaluating two instrumented mouthguards against a reference sensor on three unembalmed cadaver heads impacted with hook (4 m/s) and uppercut (3 m/s) punches, one mouthguard underpredicted most kinematic measures with validation regression slopes between 0.72 and 1.04 while the other overpredicted all of them.
Effect/estimate: Regression slopes 0.72-1.04 (underprediction) for one device; overprediction for the other
Population: Post-mortem human subjects | level: Not applicable | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory validation against a rigidly mounted reference sensor | n: 3 cadaver heads, two mouthguard models
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-relevant impact conditions
LIMITATIONS: Three cadaver heads; laboratory impacts at fixed velocities; post-mortem tissue response differs from living tissue
PPBF implication: Reinforces that head-impact magnitude from wearables is device-dependent and directionally biased. PPBF must not use these values for individual welfare decisions (crosswalk A8-X049).
Source: Accuracy of Instrumented Mouthguards During Direct Jaw Impacts Seen in Boxing (2024). Ann Biomed Eng. (PMID 39028399 / doi:10.1007/s10439-024-03586-x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Using a custom-fit instrumented mouthguard with synchronised video verification of true-positive impacts across boxing and MMA training and competition, peak linear and angular accelerations were compared by sport, activity type and sex.
Effect/estimate: Comparisons by sport, activity type and sex reported; specific values not in the abstract
Population: Boxing and MMA athletes | level: Not fully stated | sex: 23 athletes including 4 women | age: Adult
Design: Cross-sectional study, level of evidence 3, with video verification of sensor events | n: 23 athletes
Boxing-specific: Partially - boxing and MMA | transfer status: MIXED COMBAT SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Four female participants, so sex comparisons are severely underpowered; cross-sectional; custom-fit device may not represent boil-and-bite performance
PPBF implication: Female-specific head-impact evidence in combat sport is very thin. PPBF must not assume male-derived exposure patterns apply to its female athletes, and this is a named evidence gap.
Source: Characterizing Head Impact Exposure in Men and Women During Boxing and Mixed Martial Arts (2021). Orthop J Sports Med. (PMID 34901294 / doi:10.1177/23259671211059815)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 27 intercollegiate male boxers sparring two two-minute rounds with instrumented headgear, an average of 27.63 (SD 17.87) impacts above a 9.6 g threshold were recorded per boxer with average peak linear acceleration of 23.48 g (SD 15.20); small declines in delayed memory and an improvement in response time were observed pre- to post-sparring, and number of impacts plus concussion history predicted degraded memory performance.
Effect/estimate: 27.63 +/- 17.87 impacts above 9.6 g; PLA 23.48 +/- 15.20 g; PRA 1761.40 +/- 1064.34 rad/s^2
Population: Intercollegiate male boxers | level: Collegiate amateur | sex: Male | age: Young adult
Design: Pre-post neurocognitive testing with instrumented headgear | n: 27 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: No control group; two computerised test batteries with known practice effects; instrumented headgear has the sensor-quality limitations documented elsewhere in this registry; associations are not causal
PPBF implication: Illustrative of the exposure literature but not a basis for any PPBF threshold. Neurocognitive interpretation belongs to qualified clinicians, never to SHADOW.
Source: Quantifying head impacts and neurocognitive performance in collegiate boxers (2021). J Sports Sci. (PMID 34930100 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2021.2001175)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a Simon-like task judging glove colour in attack postures, beginner boxers' responses resembled a defence-related pattern, expert boxers' resembled counterattacks, and non-athletes were unaffected by the unattended punch-direction information.
Effect/estimate: Group-dependent compatibility effects
Population: Expert boxers, beginner boxers and non-athletes | level: Expert and beginner | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Laboratory cognitive experiment | n: Not stated in abstract
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific stimuli, laboratory task
LIMITATIONS: Laboratory key-press task, not in-ring behaviour; cross-sectional expertise comparison cannot establish that training causes the difference
PPBF implication: Supports treating decision-related ontology labels (A8V-H) as coach interpretation of behaviour whose underlying processes are expertise-dependent and not directly observable on film.
Source: What boxing-related stimuli reveal about response behaviour (2015). J Sports Sci. (PMID 25385452 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2014.977939)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 12-session implicit perceptual-motor training programme with highly skilled junior female karate fighters improved video-based decision-making accuracy in the implicit group relative to matched motor-training placebo and control groups, and shifted visual search toward fewer locations for longer durations.
Effect/estimate: Significant decision-accuracy improvement in the implicit group only
Population: Highly skilled junior female karate fighters | level: Highly skilled junior | sex: Female | age: Adolescent (mean 15.7 y)
Design: Controlled three-group intervention with video-based and on-mat decision tests and eye tracking | n: 18 participants (6 per group)
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM KARATE - a different striking sport with different scoring and contact rules
LIMITATIONS: Six participants per group; significant improvement only emerged by the final session; on-mat versus video test results differed
PPBF implication: Encouraging for a future PPBF perceptual-training lane but the sample is very small and non-boxing. Classified as a hypothesis for PPBF, not a basis for building.
Source: Effect of Implicit Perceptual-Motor Training on Decision-Making Skills and Underpinning Gaze Behavior in Combat Athletes (2016). Percept Mot Skills. (PMID 27371637 / doi:10.1177/0031512516656816)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Eleven elite French boxers in an adaptive first-person virtual-reality boxing task showed outcome performance resilient to gaze-contingent blur regardless of its location in the visual field, though peripheral blur changed gaze behaviour, with less time on the opponent's left hand and plexus and more on the head and other areas.
Effect/estimate: No outcome performance effect of blur; significant gaze-allocation differences under peripheral blur
Population: Elite boxers | level: Elite | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Within-subject virtual-reality experiment with eye tracking | n: 11 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: VIRTUAL REALITY, not live sparring
LIMITATIONS: Eleven athletes; virtual environment despite preserved perception-action coupling; outcome measure is task-specific
PPBF implication: Cautions against inferring what a boxer is attending to from where their head is pointing on film. Reinforces that gaze and attention labels are outside the A8 ontology's observable scope.
Source: Virtual reality boxing: impact of gaze-contingent blur on elite boxers performance and gaze behavior (2024). Front Sports Act Living. (PMID 39777017 / doi:10.3389/fspor.2024.1430719)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In 76 participants (32 martial arts athletes with over five years' experience and 36 non-athletes) predicting kick targets from temporally occluded clips with varying head occlusion, there was no significant effect of expertise on accuracy, head occlusion did not significantly influence performance, and both groups performed well above chance.
Effect/estimate: No significant expertise effect; no significant head-occlusion effect; both groups above chance
Population: Martial arts athletes and non-athletes | level: Experienced and novice | sex: Not stated | age: Adult
Design: Video occlusion experiment with spatial and temporal occlusion | n: 76 participants
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM MARTIAL ARTS KICKING - not boxing punching
LIMITATIONS: A negative finding that contrasts with the combat-sport anticipation meta-analysis; single kicking task; may reflect task ease given both groups performed above chance
PPBF implication: A genuine conflict in the literature: this study found no expertise advantage where the meta-analysis found a large one. PPBF should not encode any specific 'tell' or cue-location claim as verified. Flagged for the synthesis agent.
Source: The role of the opponent's head in perception of kick target location in martial arts (2024). Front Sports Act Living. (PMID 39687496 / doi:10.3389/fspor.2024.1468209)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A case study of an elite academy soccer head coach found his video-based coaching was used strategically to fulfil objectives he understood to be expected of him within the club environment, rather than being a neutral pedagogical act.
Effect/estimate: Three thematic categories describing micropolitical use of performance analysis
Population: One elite academy soccer head coach | level: Professional academy | sex: Male | age: Adult coach, junior squad
Design: Qualitative case study: 6 semi-structured interviews and 10 field observations | n: 1 coach
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM ELITE ACADEMY SOCCER
LIMITATIONS: Single-case qualitative study; findings are interpretive and not generalisable in a statistical sense
PPBF implication: A useful caution: video-analysis systems get used for organisational purposes, not only coaching ones. PPBF should design so that film-study data cannot easily become a performance-management tool for coaches or a ranking tool for athletes.
Source: A coach's political use of video-based feedback: a case study in elite-level academy soccer (2015). J Sports Sci. (PMID 25939483 / doi:10.1080/02640414.2015.1039464)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover with ten male boxers ingesting 6 mg/kg caffeine before simulated matches, heart rate and RPE differed significantly between rounds but not between caffeine and placebo conditions.
Effect/estimate: HR between rounds F=131.3, p=.001; RPE F=40.6, p=.001; no condition effect for HR (F=0.46, p=.51)
Population: Male boxers | level: Not fully stated | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover | n: 10 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Ten participants; simulated rather than official matches; the abstract reports the physiological analysis, and the notational outcomes are not fully extractable from it
PPBF implication: Included to show that notational outcomes have been used as endpoints in controlled boxing trials, which is the design PPBF would need for any intervention claim. No nutrition guidance is drawn from this and none may be.
Source: Caffeine ingestion changes time-motion and technical-tactical aspects in simulated boxing matches (2018). Eur J Sport Sci. (PMID 29738282 / doi:10.1080/17461391.2018.1465599)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Nine male senior elite amateur boxers completing a 3x3-minute boxing-specific exercise protocol showed blood lactate rising significantly each round (2.4, 3.3, 4.3 mmol/L) with significantly lower average and peak heart rates in round 1 than rounds 2 and 3.
Effect/estimate: BLa round 1 2.4 +/- 1.3, round 2 3.3 +/- 1.7, round 3 4.3 +/- 2.6 mmol/L
Population: Senior elite male amateur boxers | level: Elite amateur | sex: Male | age: Adult
Design: Within-subject physiological profiling of a boxing-specific protocol | n: 9 boxers
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: N/A - boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Nine elite adult males; a simulation protocol rather than live sparring or competition
PPBF implication: Round is the correct unit of analysis for load as well as for technique, which aligns the physical-preparation lane with the ontology's round-level structure (A8V-B02).
Source: Finlay MJ et al. (2018). Quantifying the Physical Response to a Contemporary Amateur Boxing Simulation. J Strength Cond Res. (PMID 29570596 / doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001926)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis comparing markerless and marker-based 3D motion capture in gait analysis found good to excellent accuracy for spatiotemporal parameters, moderate to excellent agreement at hip and knee but poor concurrent validity and reliability at the ankle, with pooled ICCs of 0.81 to 0.98 for walking speed, step time and step length.
Effect/estimate: Pooled ICC 0.81-0.98 for walking speed, step time and step length; poor ankle validity
Population: Adults undergoing gait analysis | level: N/A | sex: Mixed | age: Mostly adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PRISMA, COSMIN risk of bias) | n: 22 studies from 2047 screened
Boxing-specific: NO | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM CLINICAL GAIT - the most favourable possible case for markerless capture
LIMITATIONS: Gait is planar, slow, unoccluded and single-person; distal joints performed worst, and distal segments are exactly what matters in punching
PPBF implication: Markerless capture works acceptably for gross spatiotemporal variables in easy conditions and poorly for distal joints. PPBF should not expect usable hand or wrist kinematics from gym video.
Source: Accuracy, Validity, and Reliability of Markerless vs Marker-Based 3D Motion Capture in Gait Analysis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (2024). Sensors. (PMID 38894476 / doi:10.3390/s24113686)

text_content:

Effect/estimate: Mean errors 3.0 / 4.1 / 4.0 degrees; hip running CMC 0.65 with 15-degree systematic offset

Source: Chacon-Moscoso S et al. (2019). Methodological quality checklist for studies based on observational methodology (MQCOM). Psicothema. (PMID 31634092 / doi:10.7334/psicothema2019.116)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Out-of-school-time (OST) program quality for low-income adolescents depends on identifiable staffing practices (leadership, professional development, community connection) and on recruitment that removes transport and cost barriers and uses familiar community spaces; seven engagement levers were synthesised (agency, relevance, competence, belonging, exposure, safety/wellness).
Effect/estimate: Qualitative synthesis; no pooled effect size reported
Population: US out-of-school-time programs serving low-income adolescents | level: recreational/community | sex: mixed | age: 11-18
Design: PRISMA systematic review | n: 118 studies / 100 discrete programs
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from youth-development/OST programming to boxing gym operations — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: US-only; heterogeneous designs; 'promising practice' not causal; no boxing programs identified
PPBF implication: Anchors the staffing/onboarding and access columns of operating_model_comparison; supports treating transport and cost as first-class operational variables, not athlete attributes.
Source: Levine et al., Journal of Adolescence, 2025 (PMID 40275615; doi:10.1002/jad.12506)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Youth engagement in OST programs was associated with program content and perceived staff quality (caring, competent); a monetary incentive trended NEGATIVELY with engagement.
Effect/estimate: Program content and staff quality strongly associated with engagement; incentive-engagement association negative (trend). Correlational — not causal.
Population: Primarily low-income US middle/high-school youth across 30 OST programs | level: recreational/community | sex: mixed (51% female) | age: approx 11-18
Design: Cross-sectional multilevel modelling | n: n=435 youth, 30 programs
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from OST youth programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional; self-report; correlation is not causation; no boxing setting
PPBF implication: Coach quality is an operational variable SHADOW can track (observations, retention) — argues against paying/incentivising attendance as a retention lever without testing.
Source: Greene et al., Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 2012 (PMID 22971849; doi:10.1007/s10964-012-9814-3)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Differing intensities of training and technical assistance (business-as-usual vs performance feedback vs coaching) to OST frontline staff were associated with different levels of staff- and program-level implementation.
Effect/estimate: Directional association only; no effect size
Population: Federally funded OST programs in low-resource US communities | level: recreational/community | sex: mixed | age: school-age
Design: Observational multi-site case study | n: 3 programs
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from OST staff development — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: 3 sites; no control; small-n case study; cannot separate TA dose from site differences
PPBF implication: Coach/volunteer onboarding burden should be modelled as a tiered variable (orientation vs feedback vs coaching), not a binary 'trained' flag.
Source: Farrell et al., American Journal of Community Psychology, 2019 (PMID 30968415; doi:10.1002/ajcp.12330)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Benefits of after-school program attendance are conditional: better outcomes when staff-child relationships are positive and non-conflictual, when a variety of age-appropriate activities are offered from which children can choose, and when children attend REGULARLY.
Effect/estimate: Mixed findings across full-time after-school programs; heterogeneity attributed to population, activity type and staff training
Population: US children and adolescents in after-school settings | level: recreational/community | sex: mixed | age: 5-18
Design: Narrative review of the out-of-school literature | n: not applicable (review)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from after-school programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Narrative (not systematic) review; pre-2005 literature base; heterogeneity acknowledged by the authors themselves
PPBF implication: Justifies making attendance REGULARITY (not headcount) the primary operational KPI and making athlete choice a design requirement of station-rotation and open-gym models.
Source: Vandell et al., Advances in Child Development and Behavior, 2005 (PMID 16101114; doi:10.1016/s0065-2407(05)80004-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A comparative analysis of 11 youth-worker competency frameworks in the OST field identified 12 shared core competency areas; the age of youth served and the development of mid-level managers were identified as factors under-addressed by existing frameworks.
Effect/estimate: 12 common competency areas identified
Population: OST youth-work workforce (US) | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: staff (adults)
Design: Descriptive comparative document analysis | n: 11 frameworks
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from youth-work workforce standards — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Document analysis; frameworks are consensus artefacts, not validated instruments; no outcome linkage
PPBF implication: Supports a PPBF role competency matrix separating head coach / assistant coach / floor volunteer / mid-level program lead — and flags mid-level lead as the role that fails first when a gym scales.
Source: Vance, Child & Youth Care Forum, 2010 (PMID 21170418; doi:10.1007/s10566-010-9116-4)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In an 8-month after-school physical activity programme there was a significant negative linear trend between attendance level and change in percent body fat and fat mass, and a significant positive linear trend between attendance and cardiovascular fitness.
Effect/estimate: Significant linear trends for %BF, fat mass and CVF; BMI and waist circumference not influenced by attendance
Population: US 3rd-grade children, 9 elementary schools | level: recreational | sex: mixed | age: mean 8.7 y
Design: Prospective intervention with attendance-graded analysis | n: n=278
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Attendance is self-selected — dose-response here is associational, not randomised; outcome is body composition/fitness, not boxing skill
PPBF implication: Supports SHADOW storing attendance as a graded dose variable per athlete per block rather than a binary present/absent, and reporting dose alongside any outcome claim.
Source: Yin et al., International Journal of Obesity, 2005 (PMID 16385751; doi:10.1038/sj.ijo.0803061)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a 3-year after-school PA programme, year-by-year dose-response analysis showed the clearest beneficial effects on percent body fat and cardiorespiratory fitness for youth attending at least 60% of sessions.
Effect/estimate: Treatment x time interactions: %BF p=0.009; CRF p=0.0003. Clearest benefit at >=60% session attendance. Gains rebounded to control levels over summers.
Population: US 3rd-grade children, 18 elementary schools | level: recreational | sex: mixed | age: approx 8-9 y at baseline
Design: Cluster-randomised trial with dose analysis | n: n=574
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: 60% is a post-hoc threshold in an obesity-prevention programme; NOT a validated boxing training threshold; summer rebound shows benefit is not durable without continued dose
PPBF implication: The only defensible attendance threshold in the literature we located comes from a non-boxing obesity trial. PPBF must derive its own thresholds; use 60% only as a starting hypothesis to test, never as an implemented gate.
Source: Yin et al., Childhood Obesity, 2012 (PMID 22799482; doi:10.1089/chi.2011.0085)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Process evaluation of a 90-minute, 3x/week after-school PA club reported MEAN ATTENDANCE OF 41%, with year-3 attendance higher than earlier years.
Effect/estimate: Mean attendance 41%
Population: US 5th-8th grade girls, majority minority and/or low SES, 24 schools | level: recreational | sex: female | age: approx 10-14
Design: Process evaluation nested in a group-randomised controlled trial | n: N=1519 girls; 56-67 girls per school
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from after-school PA programming — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Single programme, single-sex, school-hosted; attendance depends heavily on host-site logistics
PPBF implication: Daily attendance should be planned as a FRACTION of enrolment, not equal to it. Facility, coach and equipment sizing must be driven by observed attendance rate, which SHADOW already has the raw data to compute.
Source: Robbins et al., BMC Public Health, 2016 (PMID 27473613; doi:10.1186/s12889-016-3329-x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A before-school PA programme in a low-resource urban district reached 82% of capacity (188 of 230 slots); median session attendance among study participants was 90% (IQR 56-97%); mean 33% of session time was accelerometer-measured MVPA (mean 16.3 minutes).
Effect/estimate: 82% capacity fill; median 90% attendance (IQR 56-97%); 33% (SD 16%) of session in MVPA
Population: US elementary/middle school students, racially and socioeconomically diverse urban district | level: recreational | sex: mixed (48% male) | age: mean 9.3 y
Design: Mixed-methods RE-AIM implementation evaluation | n: 3 schools; 188 enrolled; 128 with consent
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from school-based PA programme delivery — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Small number of schools; consented subsample; wide IQR shows attendance is highly variable between individuals
PPBF implication: Shows capacity fill and attendance rate are separate metrics that must both be tracked; the wide IQR is the operational case for per-athlete attendance trajectories rather than program-level averages.
Source: Whooten et al., Preventing Chronic Disease, 2020 (PMID 33006544; doi:10.5888/pcd17.190445)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Meta-analysis of secondary-school physical education found students spent a pooled mean of 40.5% (95% CI 34.8-46.2) of lesson time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity; middle-school 48.6% (41.3-55.9).
Effect/estimate: Pooled 40.5% of lesson in MVPA (95% CI 34.8-46.2)
Population: Secondary school students, 7 countries | level: school PE (non-competitive) | sex: mixed | age: approx 11-18
Design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42014009649) | n: 28 articles / 25 studies; 15 studies in meta-analysis
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from school PE to gym floor time-on-task — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: PE is not boxing training; measurement heterogeneity (accelerometry, HR, pedometer, observation); MVPA is not a skill-acquisition measure
PPBF implication: Scheduled session length overstates effective training dose by roughly a factor of two in comparable group settings. Session-block planning in the app should distinguish scheduled minutes from estimated engaged minutes.
Source: Hollis et al., International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity, 2017 (PMID 28438171; doi:10.1186/s12966-017-0504-0)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Systematic observation of Year 7 PE lessons found mean 56.9% (SD 18.7) of class time in MVPA but only just over 6% of class time in SKILL INSTRUCTION, with game play occupying about 44% of lesson context.
Effect/estimate: 56.9% MVPA; ~6% skill instruction; ~44% game play; teachers promoted PA ~31% of class time
Population: Year 7 students, 6 secondary schools, New South Wales, Australia | level: school PE | sex: mixed | age: approx 12-13
Design: Systematic direct observation (SOFIT-type), cross-sectional | n: 81 lessons, 6 schools
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from school PE observation to coached group sessions — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: One Australian state; PE curriculum context; the low skill-instruction figure may not generalise to a technique-led boxing session
PPBF implication: Group models can be active without being instructional. PPBF should measure coached-contact minutes per athlete separately from session attendance — this is the metric that distinguishes open gym from a class.
Source: Dudley et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2011 (PMID 22173034; doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2011.10.005)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In secondary schools serving low-income communities, 39% of PE lesson time was spent in MVPA and less than 10% in vigorous activity; urban lessons had significantly more MVPA than rural (P=0.04); more experienced teachers delivered significantly more vigorous activity (P=0.02).
Effect/estimate: 39% of lesson in MVPA; rural < urban (P=0.04); instructor experience associated with vigorous activity (P=0.04/0.02)
Population: Grade 7 students, 10 disadvantaged secondary schools, Australia | level: school PE | sex: mixed | age: approx 12-13
Design: Cross-sectional systematic observation (SOFIT) | n: 100 lessons, 10 schools
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from school PE — LABELLED TRANSFER; rural finding is directly relevant to PPBF's setting
LIMITATIONS: Observational; instructor experience is confounded with school and cohort; small number of rural schools
PPBF implication: Coach experience is an operational input with measurable session-quality consequences — supports capturing coach tenure/certification level on every session record so SHADOW can adjust expectations rather than penalising a novice coach's cohort.
Source: Sutherland et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2014 (PMID 25559053; doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2014.12.003)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Capacity in community sport clubs is theorised and evidenced as multidimensional — human resources, finance, infrastructure/process, planning/development, and external relationships — rather than a single 'size' or 'budget' variable.
Effect/estimate: Framework; no single effect size
Population: Community/nonprofit sport clubs (Canada and comparable high-income contexts) | level: community/amateur | sex: mixed | age: all
Design: Conceptual/empirical framework development in the nonprofit and sport-management literature | n: see source
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from community sport management to boxing gym operations — LABELLED TRANSFER (closest available discipline)
LIMITATIONS: Predominantly Canadian/European club structures (member-owned, volunteer-governed) which differ from a US 501c3 boxing gym; framework, not a predictive model
PPBF implication: Operating-model selection should be scored on five capacity dimensions, not enrolment alone. This is the structural basis for the capacity columns in operating_model_comparison.csv.
Source: Doherty, Misener & Cuskelly, Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, 2013 (doi:10.1177/0899764013509892)

Effect/estimate: Qualitative; no effect size
Population: Nonprofit community sport organisation | level: community | sex: mixed | age: all
Design: Qualitative case study | n: single organisation
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from nonprofit community sport — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: n=1 organisation; qualitative; not a boxing gym

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In nonprofit sport clubs, organisational resource levels help explain the organisational problems clubs report (including volunteer and financial problems).
Effect/estimate: Resource-problem associations reported; associational, not causal
Population: German nonprofit sport clubs | level: community/amateur | sex: mixed | age: all
Design: Quantitative survey analysis of a national club panel | n: see source
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from European club sport — LABELLED TRANSFER; European clubs are member-subscription bodies, materially different from a US free-access nonprofit
LIMITATIONS: National context specific; cross-sectional; self-reported problems
PPBF implication: Supports building an early-warning signal set keyed to resource strain (volunteer hours, unfilled coach slots, cash runway) rather than to enrolment counts.
Source: Wicker & Breuer, VOLUNTAS, 2012 (doi:10.1007/s11266-012-9272-2)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Voluntary sport organisations exhibit a 'core and peripheral' volunteer structure — a small core carries disproportionate role load and commitment while a larger periphery contributes episodically.
Effect/estimate: Structural pattern; no pooled estimate
Population: Voluntary sport organisations | level: community/amateur | sex: mixed | age: adults
Design: Empirical study of volunteer roles and commitment | n: see source
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from voluntary sport organisations — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Non-US context; cross-sectional; 'core' is defined differently across studies
PPBF implication: Counting 'number of volunteers' overstates capacity. PPBF should track CORE volunteer count (screened, rostered, recurring) separately from episodic helpers, because only the core can be scheduled against supervision ratios.
Source: Sport in Society, 2013 — 'Volunteer roles, involvement and commitment in voluntary sport organizations: evidence of core and peripheral volunteers' (doi:10.1080/17430437.2013.828902)

text_content:
[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] In community-based clubs, volunteer coaches' retention and development are shaped by club-level support structures and club culture and norms, including whether the club addresses behaviour that undermines the coaching role.
Effect/estimate: Themes: retention and recruitment, support structures, club culture and norms. No quantitative estimate.
Population: Volunteer women coaches, 3 Gaelic football clubs, Ireland | level: non-elite community | sex: female | age: adults
Design: Qualitative interview study with creative non-fiction synthesis | n: n=11 coaches
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from Gaelic football club volunteering — LABELLED TRANSFER; single sport, single country, female coaches only
LIMITATIONS: n=11; one sport; one country; findings are interpretive not generalisable estimates
PPBF implication: Volunteer attrition should be treated as a CLUB-CULTURE signal SHADOW can surface to the board, not an individual failing — supports a coach-retention field on the coach record with reason codes.
Source: Hogan et al., Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 2022 (PMID 35434613; doi:10.3389/fspor.2022.809092)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An RCT found that tailored support from trained older PEER VOLUNTEERS produced significantly more moderate-to-vigorous physical activity at 18-month follow-up than a typical community offering, despite similar gains at 16 weeks.
Effect/estimate: Groups equivalent at 16 weeks; peer-supported group significantly higher MVPA at 18 months (intent-to-treat)
Population: Sedentary older adults, US community setting | level: recreational | sex: mixed | age: older adults
Design: Randomised controlled trial | n: 7 peer volunteers, 81 sedentary adults; retention 85% at 16 weeks, 61% at 18 months
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from older-adult community PA to volunteer-delivered gym models — LABELLED TRANSFER; population is older adults, NOT youth
LIMITATIONS: Small n; self-report MVPA logs with accelerometry only in a subsample; 61% follow-up at 18 months; older-adult sample
PPBF implication: Trained peer/volunteer delivery is a defensible capacity multiplier for ADULT and masters lanes; do NOT extrapolate this to unsupervised volunteer delivery for minors, which is governed by safeguarding rules, not efficacy evidence.
Source: Buman et al., Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2011 (PMID 21918240)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A school-based peer-led high-intensity interval training programme BUILT ON BOXING AND WHOLE-BODY EXERCISES was feasible to deliver by older pupils; recruitment was 72% for peer-recipients, 74% for controls and 42% for peer-leaders.
Effect/estimate: Recruitment 72%/74%/42%; feasibility outcomes only, not efficacy
Population: Year 7 pupils (peer-recipients) and Year 12-13 pupils (peer-leaders), one school, North East England | level: recreational/school | sex: mixed | age: 12.1 (SD 0.3) recipients; 17.3 (SD 0.4) leaders
Design: Non-randomised controlled feasibility trial | n: 21 recipients, 23 controls, 5 peer-leaders
Boxing-specific: partially — boxing-based exercise content, not boxing skill training or sparring | transfer status: PARTIAL boxing relevance (boxing-derived movement content in a school setting); NOT evidence about boxing gyms
LIMITATIONS: One school; n=5 peer-leaders; feasibility design; peer-leader recruitment was the weak point (42%)
PPBF implication: Recruiting the LEADERS is harder than recruiting the participants. A PPBF senior-athlete-as-assistant lane must plan for leader supply as the binding constraint — and leaders who are minors cannot substitute for adult supervision.
Source: Weston et al., BMC Public Health, 2026 (PMID 41735920; doi:10.1186/s12889-026-26543-w)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a French boxing (savate) instructional setting, a STRUCTURED trained-peer-tutoring programme produced higher coaching-skill scores in tutors than untrained peer tutoring; effects on offensive/defensive outcomes differed by sex.
Effect/estimate: Trained peer tutoring > untrained on coaching skills; interaction effects by sex on offensive/defensive outcomes; untrained tutors reported higher self-efficacy
Population: College-age novice French boxing participants, France | level: novice | sex: male and female | age: college age (adults)
Design: 2x2 factorial experimental design (sex x training type) | n: n=32; six 2-hour lessons
Boxing-specific: YES — French boxing (savate), a striking combat sport; not Olympic-style boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport specific but SAVATE, novice adults, small n — do not treat as amateur-boxing evidence
LIMITATIONS: n=32; single task; short duration; savate not Olympic boxing; adults not youth
PPBF implication: If PPBF uses senior athletes as tutors, TRAIN them explicitly — untrained tutors reported higher self-efficacy without higher skill, i.e. confidence is not a competence signal SHADOW should trust.
Source: Legrain et al., Journal of Sports Sciences, 2003 (PMID 12848388; doi:10.1080/0264041031000101872)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of rural US youth found barriers and facilitators to structured out-of-school physical activity at environmental/program level (programs and facilities, transportation and accessibility, resources and infrastructure, safety, cost/fees), social level (family, peers) and individual level (interest, skill, time).
Effect/estimate: Qualitative ecological synthesis; no pooled estimate
Population: Rural-dwelling US youth | level: recreational/community | sex: mixed | age: 6-17
Design: Systematic review (Medline, PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL; 2000-2024) | n: 3,070 screened; 39 articles included
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from rural youth PA participation — LABELLED TRANSFER; rural US context matches PPBF's setting closely
LIMITATIONS: Studies excluded participants with additional needs; heterogeneous designs; barriers are self-reported
PPBF implication: The single most contextually relevant source for PPBF. Transportation, cost/fees and facility availability must be first-class fields in the scenario matrix and in athlete intake, not afterthoughts.
Source: Johnson et al., BMC Public Health, 2026 (PMID 41620730; doi:10.1186/s12889-026-26205-x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Youth from low-affluence families reported fewer days/week of physical activity, fewer sports sampled, and lower rates of ever playing sports; the four disproportionately reported barriers were fear of injury, not feeling welcome on teams, expense, and transportation.
Effect/estimate: Middle-schoolers from high-affluence families ~3x higher odds of meeting PA recommendations; high-affluence high-schoolers ~3x higher odds of ever participating in sports
Population: Students in grades 5-12, King County, Washington, USA | level: recreational and organised sport | sex: mixed (50% girls) | age: approx 10-18
Design: Cross-sectional survey | n: n=1038 (58% non-White; 32% non-English home language)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from US youth sport participation — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional, single US county, self-report; correlation not causation
PPBF implication: 'Don't feel welcome' sits alongside cost and transport as a modifiable barrier — supports a belonging/welcome measure in the intake and early-attrition signal set, not just a fee waiver.
Source: Tandon et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2021 (PMID 34209544; doi:10.3390/ijerph18136946)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a state-wide sports voucher programme, parents in the most disadvantaged quartile were about twice as likely never to have heard of the programme (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.31-3.16) and more than twice as likely to register but not redeem the voucher (OR 2.68, 95% CI 1.27-5.63) compared with the least disadvantaged quartile.
Effect/estimate: OR 2.04 (1.31-3.16) never heard; OR 1.94 (1.26-3.00) heard but not registered; OR 2.68 (1.27-5.63) registered but not redeemed
Population: Parents/carers of children, New South Wales, Australia | level: organised community sport | sex: mixed | age: children (program-eligible ages)
Design: Cross-sectional analysis linking a population health survey with programme registration data | n: Population health survey + full registration database
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from Australian sport-voucher policy — LABELLED TRANSFER; jurisdictionally specific
LIMITATIONS: Australian policy design; cross-sectional; awareness is self-reported
PPBF implication: A free-access nonprofit model does not automatically achieve equitable reach. PPBF must measure AWARENESS and CONVERSION separately from enrolment, and treat 'registered but never attended' as a distinct, actionable state.
Source: Owen et al., Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 2020 (PMID 32061526; doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2020.01.015)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Across five Australian jurisdictions the median sports voucher value was AU$150 against a national median annual child sport expenditure of AU$447 (IQR 194.2-936); vouchers covered 27% of reported expenditure nationally, rising to over 60% in the most disadvantaged populations.
Effect/estimate: Median voucher AU$150; median annual expenditure AU$447 (IQR 194.2-936); 27% of expenditure covered nationally, >60% in most disadvantaged
Population: Australian children 0-14 years | level: organised community sport | sex: mixed | age: 0-14
Design: Policy/expenditure analysis using national participation survey data | n: AusPlay national survey + five jurisdictional schemes
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from Australian policy — LABELLED TRANSFER; AUD figures are NOT transferable to US pricing
LIMITATIONS: Currency, cost base and policy design are Australian; expenditure self-reported
PPBF implication: Do NOT import these dollar figures. The transferable finding is structural: participation cost is more than the fee, so a free-membership model still leaves equipment, travel and incidental costs as barriers PPBF must budget for.
Source: Reece et al., BMC Public Health, 2020 (PMID 31910846; doi:10.1186/s12889-019-8049-6)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Parental decisions about children's organised sport were strongly influenced by time; financial cost influenced lower-income families and families of girls; and for rural families the availability of a wider variety of local sporting activities influenced participation decisions.
Effect/estimate: Time P<0.00; cost for lower income p=0.01 and for girls p=0.04; variety for rural families p=0.05
Population: Parents of children aged 5-17, New South Wales, Australia | level: organised sport | sex: parents of both sexes of child | age: 5-17
Design: Computer-assisted telephone interview survey | n: n=402 parents; 63% of children participated in organised sport
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from Australian parent survey — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Telephone sampling; 2010 data; Australian; parent report not child behaviour
PPBF implication: Schedule design (time-of-day, day-of-week, session length) is an equity lever, not just a logistics choice — supports modelling session blocks against guardian work patterns in the scenario matrix.
Source: Hardy et al., Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health, 2010 (PMID 20105247; doi:10.1111/j.1440-1754.2009.01661.x)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Qualitative work in a predominantly rural, Hispanic county identified participation factors across public-policy, community (access to programming, gender expectations, economic challenges, weather), organisational (resources, high cost to families), and interpersonal (quality coaches, scheduling, peer) levels.
Effect/estimate: Thematic; no quantitative estimate
Population: Rural, predominantly Hispanic girls, parents and coaches/staff, Southern California border region, USA | level: community sport | sex: female | age: youth
Design: Qualitative semi-structured interview study | n: 15 girls, 18 parents, 4 coaches/staff
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from rural Hispanic girls' sport participation — LABELLED TRANSFER; one county, one demographic
LIMITATIONS: Small qualitative sample; single county; findings are context-bound
PPBF implication: Girls' participation in a combat sport in a rural setting will have model-specific barriers (gender expectations, coach quality). Supports a female-lane review question in the coach-review workflow, not a generic retention alert.
Source: Johnson et al., BMC Public Health, 2025 (PMID 41469629; doi:10.1186/s12889-025-25686-6)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A survey of North Carolina public school principals found 88.9% of responding schools shared their facilities; formal written agreements were more common for gyms and outdoor athletic fields; schools with more low-income or Black students were LESS likely to share; the most frequent reason for not sharing was that no outside group had ever asked.
Effect/estimate: 88.9% share; equity gradient in sharing; 'never asked' the leading non-sharing reason
Population: North Carolina public schools, USA | level: not applicable (facility access) | sex: not applicable | age: not applicable
Design: Cross-sectional statewide survey | n: 1182 responses of 2359 invited (50.1% response)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from US school shared-use policy — LABELLED TRANSFER; state-specific but US-relevant
LIMITATIONS: One state; 50% response rate (non-response bias likely toward sharing schools); self-report by principals
PPBF implication: For the school/community-partnership operating model, the practical first action is simply to ASK, with a written agreement drafted for indoor space. Supports a partnership-agreement artefact type in the document store.
Source: Kanters et al., Preventive Medicine, 2014 (PMID 25451325; doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2014.10.003)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Direct observation (SOPARC) in schools with shared or open use found most facilities EMPTY during non-school hours; formal programming was positively associated with both facility use and physical activity levels.
Effect/estimate: Formal programming positively associated with use and PA; most facilities otherwise unused
Population: 20 schools across North Carolina, USA | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: community users
Design: Observational study using SOPARC and structured activity surveys with hierarchical linear models | n: 20 schools
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from shared-use policy research — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: One state; observation windows may miss episodic use; no boxing-specific facilities
PPBF implication: A satellite or school-partnership site without a scheduled, staffed session will sit empty. Model 'partnership site' as requiring a named coach and a fixed block, not merely a key and an agreement.
Source: Carlton et al., Preventive Medicine, 2016 (PMID 27568234; doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2016.08.037)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In four low-income New Jersey cities, shared use of school physical activity facilities declined significantly from 2010-11 to 2019-20 for both indoor (66.2% to 46.3%) and outdoor (46.1% to 31.6%) facilities (P=.002 for both); more facilities per school was associated with higher odds of shared use.
Effect/estimate: Indoor 66.2%→46.3%; outdoor 46.1%→31.6%; P=.002 both
Population: K-12 public schools in 4 low-income New Jersey cities, USA | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: not applicable
Design: Longitudinal repeated cross-sectional surveys with multivariable logistic regression | n: 94-124 schools/year; N=1096 surveys
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from US shared-use trends — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Four cities in one state; survey of school personnel; drivers of decline not established
PPBF implication: Do not plan a school-partnership model on the assumption that access persists. Treat partnership access as an annually re-negotiated dependency with an explicit renewal date field.
Source: Raval et al., Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2025 (PMID 40550499; doi:10.1123/jpah.2024-0810)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] School administrators reported a lower prevalence of FORMAL shared-use agreements (38.5%) than informal ones (65.6%); top perceived barriers were costs and liability concerns; perceived benefits included improved relationships with taxpayers and community organisations.
Effect/estimate: 38.5% formal, 65.6% informal, 9.3% neither
Population: Ohio school administrators (mostly superintendents), USA | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: not applicable
Design: Cross-sectional email survey via a state professional listserv | n: n=96
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from US shared-use policy — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Convenience listserv sample n=96; single state; self-selection likely
PPBF implication: Liability and cost are the negotiation levers. PPBF should carry a standard insurance certificate and cost-share offer into any partnership conversation — an operational artefact, not a research finding.
Source: Chace & Vilvens, Journal of Physical Activity and Health, 2014 (PMID 25153851; doi:10.1123/jpah.2014-0214)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC youth athlete development review presents safeguarding principles from the International Safeguarding Children in Sport Founders Group with eight underlying pillars intended to underpin adoption and implementation of safeguarding strategies by sport organisations.
Effect/estimate: Framework of 8 safeguarding pillars; no effect size
Population: Child athletes in organised sport, international | level: all levels | sex: mixed | age: under 18
Design: Narrative review and framework, IOC-affiliated | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no (all-sport) | transfer status: Applies to organised sport generally including boxing — NOT a transfer, this is in-scope guidance
LIMITATIONS: Framework, not an evaluated intervention; adoption evidence limited; not jurisdiction-specific
PPBF implication: Provides the top-level safeguarding architecture for age_and_safeguarding_operations.md; PPBF safeguarding policy should be mapped against these pillars and audited annually by a named human role.
Source: Mountjoy et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2015 (PMID 26084527; doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094619)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The IOC has published a consensus statement on interpersonal violence and safeguarding in sport (2024), superseding and extending the 2016 harassment and abuse consensus statement.
Effect/estimate: Consensus recommendations; no effect size
Population: Athletes across sport, international | level: all levels | sex: mixed | age: all
Design: Expert consensus statement | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no (all-sport) | transfer status: In-scope consensus guidance for organised sport including boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, not trial evidence; implementation in small community clubs is not evaluated in the statement
PPBF implication: Cite as the current international consensus anchor; the 2016 statement (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096121) should be treated as superseded for policy drafting.
Source: IOC consensus statement: interpersonal violence and safeguarding in sport, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2024 (doi:10.1136/bjsports-2024-108766)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A general-population retrospective survey of adults who played organised sport before age 18 in the Netherlands and Belgium found 38% reported psychological violence, 11% physical violence and 14% sexual violence in sport; ethnic minority, LGB, disabled athletes and international-level competitors reported significantly more.
Effect/estimate: 38% psychological, 11% physical, 14% sexual violence
Population: Adults in NL/BE prescreened for organised sport participation before age 18 | level: all levels including recreational | sex: balanced gender ratio | age: retrospective recall of under-18 experience
Design: Large-scale retrospective online prevalence survey | n: over 4,000 respondents
Boxing-specific: no (all-sport) | transfer status: Cross-sport prevalence; NOT boxing-specific — do not present as a boxing rate
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective self-report; recall and non-response bias; NL/BE only; rates not sport-disaggregated in this report
PPBF implication: Establishes that safeguarding risk is a baseline condition of organised youth sport, not an exceptional event — supports mandatory safeguarding controls in EVERY operating model, including recreational open gym.
Source: Vertommen et al., Child Abuse & Neglect, 2015 (PMID 26516053; doi:10.1016/j.chiabu.2015.10.006)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In the same prevalence dataset, perpetrators of interpersonal violence in sport were predominantly MALE PEER ATHLETES frequently operating in groups; physical violence by coaches tended to be less severe than by other perpetrators, whereas sexual violence committed by a coach was significantly more severe.
Effect/estimate: Perpetrator profile analysis; severity differences by perpetrator role
Population: Victim-respondents from the NL/BE retrospective survey | level: all levels | sex: mixed victims; predominantly male perpetrators | age: under-18 experience
Design: Secondary analysis of retrospective victim survey | n: n=4043
Boxing-specific: no (all-sport) | transfer status: Cross-sport; peer-perpetration finding is highly relevant to a shared-floor gym
LIMITATIONS: Victim-reported perpetrator characteristics; retrospective; NL/BE
PPBF implication: Supervision design must cover PEER-TO-PEER risk (locker rooms, warm-up areas, unstructured waiting time), not only adult-child interaction. Directly shapes the changing/bathroom and open-gym policies.
Source: Vertommen et al., Child Abuse & Neglect, 2016 (PMID 27923185; doi:10.1016/j.chiabu.2016.11.029)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Severe childhood sexual, physical and psychological interpersonal violence in sport was associated with more adult psychological distress and reduced quality of life; polyvictimisation showed the strongest correlation with poorer wellbeing.
Effect/estimate: Significant associations; polyvictimisation strongest. Associational, not causal.
Population: General population sample of former youth sport participants, NL/BE | level: all levels | sex: mixed | age: adults reporting childhood experience
Design: Cross-sectional regression analysis (BSI-18, WHOQOL-Bref) controlling for demographics, recent life events, relatives' problems | n: N=4043
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional; retrospective; cannot establish causation; NL/BE
PPBF implication: Raises the stakes of safeguarding controls above compliance framing; supports never letting SHADOW auto-close a safeguarding concern and always routing to the named Welfare/Safeguarding Officer.
Source: Vertommen et al., Child Abuse & Neglect, 2017 (PMID 29253798; doi:10.1016/j.chiabu.2017.12.013)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review found higher reported rates of sport-related neglect, psychological and sexual abuse among girls and higher reported physical abuse among boys; boys reported more peer-perpetrated violence and disclosed more often to coaches, girls reported more coach-perpetrated violence and disclosed more often to parents.
Effect/estimate: Directional gender differences in prevalence, perpetrator and disclosure recipient; inconsistent measurement across studies noted
Population: Children/adults who participated in organised sport before age 18 | level: organised sport, all levels | sex: compared by gender | age: under 18 (retrospective and current)
Design: Systematic review (PsycInfo, MedLine, Scopus to May 2024) | n: 509 unique articles screened; 22 included
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous measurement tools; underreporting concerns across genders; not sport-disaggregated
PPBF implication: Disclosure routes differ by gender — PPBF must offer MULTIPLE named disclosure recipients (coach, welfare officer, guardian channel) rather than a single reporting path.
Source: Shiau et al., Trauma, Violence & Abuse, 2025 (PMID 41014171; doi:10.1177/15248380251372157)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review commissioned for the Australian Royal Commission synthesised over 400 sources on institutional child sexual abuse across six youth-serving organisation settings (including sport) and set out organisational risk patterns and prevention/policy recommendations.
Effect/estimate: Risk and prevention synthesis; no effect size
Population: Youth-serving organisations in the US, UK and Australia | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: children and adolescents
Design: Comprehensive literature review informing a national Royal Commission | n: over 400 primarily research articles
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from youth-serving-organisation prevention research — LABELLED TRANSFER; sport is one of the six settings covered
LIMITATIONS: Narrative synthesis; heterogeneous evidence quality; recommendations are consensus-derived
PPBF implication: Supports building PPBF's safeguarding controls at the ORGANISATIONAL level (environment design, monitoring, response) rather than relying on screening alone.
Source: Kaufman et al., Journal of Interpersonal Violence, 2019 (PMID 31488027; doi:10.1177/0886260519869239)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of Australian Royal Commission data applied a capable-guardianship model to outside-school-hours care, schools and SPORTING institutions, identifying barriers that underpin adults' failure to intervene when children are at risk.
Effect/estimate: Identified guardianship dimensions and barriers; no quantitative estimate
Population: Youth-serving institutional settings including sport, Australia | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: children
Design: Qualitative secondary analysis of Royal Commission evidence using Reynald's guardianship model | n: three institutional settings
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from institutional child-protection research — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Australian inquiry data; qualitative; retrospective institutional records
PPBF implication: Having a second adult present is necessary but not sufficient — that adult must be willing and able to intervene. Supports explicit intervention-expectation training and a low-friction near-miss log (shadow_near_misses already exists in the schema).
Source: Lockitch et al., Journal of Child Sexual Abuse, 2022 (PMID 36225125; doi:10.1080/10538712.2022.2133042)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The CDC's guidance for youth-serving organisations sets out six key components of child sexual abuse prevention: screening and selecting employees and volunteers; guidelines on interactions between individuals; monitoring behaviour; ensuring safe environments; responding to inappropriate behaviour, breaches and allegations; and training.
Effect/estimate: Six-component framework; the document itself notes not all strategies apply to all organisations
Population: US youth-serving organisations | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: children and youth
Design: Federal public-health guidance document | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Applies to US youth-serving organisations including boxing gyms — in-scope guidance, not a transfer
LIMITATIONS: 2007 publication (CDC has stated an update was in development); guidance not an evaluated intervention; jurisdictional legal review is explicitly required by the document
PPBF implication: Use the six components as the section spine of PPBF's safeguarding operations doc and as the compliance_rules categories in the existing pilot.compliance_rules table.
Source: Saul & Audage, Preventing Child Sexual Abuse Within Youth-Serving Organizations: Getting Started on Policies and Procedures, CDC, 2007 (No DOI/PMID — CDC Stacks record)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Under the U.S. Center for SafeSport Minor Athlete Abuse Prevention Policies (MAAPP), all one-on-one in-program contact between an Adult Participant and a Minor Athlete must be observable and interruptible except in emergency circumstances; individual training sessions must be observable and interruptible even with written parent/guardian consent; and adults may not transport a minor athlete one-on-one during in-program travel.
Effect/estimate: Policy requirement; no effect estimate. Effectiveness of MAAPP as implemented has not been established by trial evidence.
Population: U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Movement — NGBs, Local Affiliated Organizations and their Adult Participants | level: all levels within the Movement | sex: not applicable | age: minor athletes (under 18)
Design: Mandatory policy instrument (not a study) | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: Applies to USA Boxing as an NGB and to its Local Affiliated Organizations | transfer status: Directly in scope for a US boxing club affiliated to USA Boxing; NOT automatically binding on non-affiliated gyms

Screening frequency and cost-share arrangements are stated on the USA Boxing membership pages; SafeSport training cadence is stated in the rulebook as every other year while the membership page requires certification for passbook issue — organisations should verify current cadence directly with USA Boxing.

Design: Governing-body rulebook and membership policy | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: YES — boxing-specific governing-body requirement | transfer status: Directly boxing-specific and US-specific; does NOT describe England Boxing, Boxing Canada or professional commissions

PPBF implication: Volunteer/coach screening is an annual recurring cost and an annual expiry event. PPBF needs an expiry-tracking field per coach and per volunteer with a blocking gate on floor assignment; the pilot.volunteers and pilot.staff tables currently carry no credential-expiry column (PARTIAL).
Source: USA Boxing membership and coach pages; USA Boxing National Rule Book (No DOI — governing-body document)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Pennsylvania's Child Protective Services Law (as amended by Act 153 of 2014 and Act 15 of 2015) requires adults with direct contact with children — including unpaid volunteers — to obtain the Pennsylvania State Police criminal history check, the Pennsylvania Child Abuse History Clearance, and an FBI fingerprint-based criminal history check; certifications must be renewed at a minimum of every 60 months. Volunteers who have been continuous PA residents for the past ten years and are not disqualified may submit an affidavit in lieu of the FBI check.
Effect/estimate: Three clearances; 60-month renewal; FBI affidavit exemption for 10-year continuous PA residents in unpaid roles
Population: Employees and volunteers with direct contact with children in Pennsylvania, USA | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: adults (and per some sources, individuals 14+ in qualifying roles)
Design: State statute and implementing agency guidance | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no — applies to any PA youth-serving organisation including a boxing gym | transfer status: PENNSYLVANIA-SPECIFIC statutory requirement — directly binding on PPBF; not applicable in other states
LIMITATIONS: Secondary sources (university HR pages, PA DHS Keep Kids Safe page) were used; the operative text is the CPSL itself. Applicability to specific PPBF roles requires legal review — this is not legal advice.
PPBF implication: This is the binding screening baseline for PPBF volunteers. Every operating model that puts an unscreened adult on the floor with minors is non-viable in PA. Clearance status and expiry must be a hard gate on volunteer scheduling; the pilot.volunteers table has no clearance fields today (ABSENT).
Source: Pennsylvania Child Protective Services Law (Act 153 of 2014, as amended by Act 15 of 2015); PA Department of Human Services, Child Abuse Clearances (No DOI — statute/agency page)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Pennsylvania licensed child care center regulations set maximum group sizes and staff:child ratios of 1:12 with maximum group size 24 for young school-age and 1:15 with maximum group size 30 for older school-age, requiring 2 staff for the maximum group; separately, at least two facility persons must be present whenever two or more children are in care.
Effect/estimate: Young school-age 1:12, max group 24; older school-age 1:15, max group 30
Population: Licensed child care centers in Pennsylvania (NOT sport programs) | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: school-age
Design: State regulation (55 Pa. Code Chapter 3270) | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER — these are CHILD CARE licensing ratios, NOT sport-coaching ratios. A boxing gym is generally not a licensed child care facility. Use only as an external reference anchor, never as a claimed requirement.
LIMITATIONS: Whether PPBF's programme falls under child care licensure is a legal question requiring counsel. Ratios designed for custodial care do not account for combat-sport hazard exposure, which may warrant tighter ratios during contact activity.
PPBF implication: The ONLY numeric supervision ratio we could verify for PA school-age settings comes from child care licensure, not sport. PPBF supervision ratios must therefore be labelled PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER and validated; they should be at least as tight as these anchors during any contact activity.
Source: 55 Pa. Code § 3270.51 (Similar age level); 55 Pa. Code § 3270.54 (minimum number of facility persons) (No DOI — state code)
