[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) has been applied in over 2,800 publications; the authors encourage pragmatic use of key dimensions rather than comprehensive application of all elements.

Population: Public health and health behaviour change programmes, clinical/community/corporate settings | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: all

LIMITATIONS: Framework, not an intervention; the review itself notes inconsistent and partial application in practice
PPBF implication: RE-AIM is the recommended evaluation spine for the PPBF pilot plan: Reach (who enrols vs who is eligible), Adoption (which sites/coaches run it), Implementation (fidelity, dose), Maintenance (retention, model persistence).
Source: Glasgow et al., Frontiers in Public Health, 2019 (PMID 30984733; doi:10.3389/fpubh.2019.00064)

Population: Children aged 5-11 in controlled PA interventions | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: 5-11
Design: Systematic review using the RE-AIM framework | n: 78 studies
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from PA intervention literature — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Reporting quality is not the same as programme quality; 12-year search window
PPBF implication: Explains WHY operational parameters (start-up cost, staffing, sustainability) are missing from the literature: researchers routinely do not report them. PPBF must generate these numbers internally — they will not be found in papers.
Source: McGoey et al., Preventive Medicine, 2015 (PMID 26582207; doi:10.1016/j.ypmed.2015.11.004)

Population: Community-based physical activity programme, real-world setting | level: community | sex: mixed | age: children and adolescents

Population: Public health, NGO, government and community-based organisations | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: adults (workforce)
Design: Systematic review | n: 14 papers
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from public health capacity building — LABELLED TRANSFER

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A literature review of strategies to build community capacity for physical activity promotion among adults 50+ identified five strategy groups (coalitions/networks, professional training, layperson training, strengthening target-population competence/awareness, financial resource allocation); feasibility and acceptability were demonstrated but intervention effects on PA behaviour were inconsistent, and the one study systematically comparing approaches found no benefit of intensified capacity building.
Effect/estimate: Inconsistent PA effects; no benefit found from intensified capacity building in the single comparative study
Population: Community programmes for adults aged 50+ | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: 50+
Design: Literature review (PsycInfo, Web of Science, plus grey literature project databases) | n: 14 studies (16 articles)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from older-adult community PA capacity building — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Review, not meta-analysis; older-adult focus; grey literature inclusion complicates quality appraisal
PPBF implication: Guards against over-investing in capacity-building activity as an end in itself. PPBF should tie any capacity investment to a measured floor-level outcome (sessions delivered, coached minutes, retention).
Source: Ubert et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 2017 (PMID 28902146; doi:10.3390/ijerph14091058)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise referral schemes found pooled uptake of 66% (95% CI 57-75) in observational studies and 81% (68-94) in RCTs, and pooled adherence of 49% (40-59) observational and 43% (32-54) in RCTs; women were more likely to begin but less likely to adhere than men, and older people were more likely both to begin and to adhere.
Effect/estimate: Uptake 66% (57-75) obs / 81% (68-94) RCT; adherence 49% (40-59) obs / 43% (32-54) RCT
Population: Adults referred to community exercise schemes (predominantly UK) | level: recreational | sex: both, with sex differences reported | age: adults
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 20 studies (6 RCTs, 14 observational)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from adult exercise referral schemes — LABELLED TRANSFER; ADULT population, healthcare-referred, mostly UK. Do NOT apply these percentages to youth boxing enrolment.
LIMITATIONS: Substantial heterogeneity; no standardised definitions of uptake/adherence; adult clinical-referral pathway differs fundamentally from a community gym walk-in
PPBF implication: Roughly half of enrolled adults not adhering is the norm in comparable community schemes. PPBF planning should size facilities and coaching against expected adherence, and should treat non-adherence as a design problem rather than an athlete deficiency.
Source: Pavey et al., Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health, 2012 (PMID 22493474; doi:10.1136/jech-2011-200354)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Qualitative longitudinal study of mHealth app users identified two dimensions explaining continued use — assessment of the app and its capabilities, and persistence toward the health goal — and produced a framework of four post-initial-use decisions: abandon, limit use, switch app, continue use.
Effect/estimate: Framework; no quantitative estimate
Population: Adult mHealth app users | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: adults
Design: Qualitative longitudinal study (interviews and diaries) | n: 17 participants; 34 interviews; 193 diaries over two weeks
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from consumer mHealth to a coach-support app — LABELLED TRANSFER; note the PPBF app's primary users are COACHES and guardians, not self-directed consumers
LIMITATIONS: n=17; two-week window; consumer wellness apps not coach-support tools
PPBF implication: For the hybrid in-person + digital operating model, digital-component abandonment should be an expected default state with a designed fallback (paper/coach-entered), not a failure condition.
Source: Vaghefi & Tulu, JMIR mHealth and uHealth, 2019 (PMID 31469081; doi:10.2196/12983)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of an eHealth lifestyle platform classified dropouts with 89% precision using a random forest with 11 predictor variables; the most significant predictors were the intervention provider, two weeks of inactivity, and the number of coach advices received.
Effect/estimate: 89% precision for dropout classification on the holdout set; top predictors: provider, 2 weeks inactivity, number of coach advices
Population: Patients using an eHealth lifestyle platform for chronic lifestyle disease | level: not applicable | sex: mixed | age: adults
Design: Retrospective predictive modelling (logistic regression, decision trees, random forest) with 80/20 train-holdout split | n: n=2684 patients (2147 train/CV, 537 holdout)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from clinical eHealth to community sport attendance modelling — LABELLED TRANSFER; population and outcome differ substantially
LIMITATIONS: Single platform; precision reported without full confusion-matrix context here; provider being the top predictor suggests site effects dominate individual traits
PPBF implication: Supports an inactivity-window attrition signal in SHADOW. The finding that PROVIDER was the strongest predictor is the operationally important one: attrition is primarily a site/coach property, so any athlete-level risk score must be adjusted for site or it will mislabel athletes.
Source: Pedersen et al., Journal of Medical Internet Research, 2019 (PMID 31486409; doi:10.2196/13617)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A scoping review of inclusive out-of-school-time physical activity programmes for children and youth with physical disabilities found programmes varied in age groups, GROUP SIZES and durations, were mostly recreational, and were most commonly led by rehabilitation staff; best-practice recommendations centre on an abilities-based approach with common group goals, cooperative activities, mastery-oriented individualised instruction and developmentally appropriate challenge.
Effect/estimate: Positive effects on social skills/relationships, physical skill development, psychological wellbeing; group size varied, no optimum identified
Population: Children and youth with physical disabilities in OST physical activity programmes | level: predominantly recreational | sex: both genders | age: children and youth
Design: Scoping review with quality appraisal (only studies rated >=60% informed recommendations) | n: 17 studies (9 qualitative, 5 quantitative, 3 mixed)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from inclusive OST PA programming to adaptive boxing — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Small heterogeneous evidence base; rehabilitation-staff-led programmes may not generalise to coach-led gyms; no group-size optimum derivable
PPBF implication: The inclusive/adaptive operating model needs individualised instruction within a common group goal — this is a station-rotation or small-group structure, not a large single-block class. Staffing implications follow directly.
Source: Arbour-Nicitopoulos et al., Adapted Physical Activity Quarterly, 2018 (PMID 29338295; doi:10.1123/apaq.2017-0012)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Lack of disability awareness among fitness professionals is a well-established barrier to exercise participation for people with disabilities; a 90-minute video training plus resource manual significantly improved group fitness instructors' confidence to adapt classes, though pre-existing disability attitudes were already high and did not change significantly.
Effect/estimate: Significant improvement in confidence to adapt classes; no significant change in attitudes
Population: Community-based group fitness instructors at one US recreation center | level: not applicable | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adults (instructors)
Design: Pre/post/2-month follow-up pilot with semi-structured interviews | n: n=10 instructors
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from community fitness instruction — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: n=10; single site; self-report outcomes; no participant-level outcomes measured
PPBF implication: A short, structured adaptation training is a low-cost prerequisite for the inclusive/adaptive model — it is a capability gate to record on the coach record, distinct from safeguarding certification.
Source: Adamson et al., Adapted Physical Activity Quarterly, 2023 (PMID 36720236; doi:10.1123/apaq.2022-0012)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Community-based boxing programmes for people with Parkinson's disease have been implemented and evaluated in small studies reporting improvements in balance, functional gait and quality of life; a 2019 review concluded implementation had ACCELERATED BEYOND CURRENT EVIDENCE, with only two eligible studies totalling 37 participants at that time.
Effect/estimate: Balance confidence, mobility and quality of life reported to improve with programmes of 24-36 sessions over 12 weeks; risk of bias low in the two trials but reporting against CERT incomplete
Population: Adults with Parkinson's disease in community boxing programmes | level: non-competitive, non-contact | sex: mixed | age: predominantly older adults
Design: Systematic literature review plus website quality appraisal (QUEST) | n: 2 studies, 37 participants; 9 websites appraised
Boxing-specific: YES — non-contact boxing, clinical population | transfer status: Boxing-specific but a CLINICAL adult population; does NOT transfer to youth amateur boxing
LIMITATIONS: Only 2 studies at review; small n; incomplete intervention reporting; medications not always documented
PPBF implication: Non-contact adaptive boxing is a viable, revenue- and grant-relevant programme lane with genuine (if thin) evidence. It is also a cautionary example of a boxing programme scaling ahead of its evidence — exactly the failure SHADOW's evidence ledger exists to prevent.
Source: Morris et al., Frontiers in Neurology, 2019 (PMID 31866923; doi:10.3389/fneur.2019.01222)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A community boxing programme for people with Parkinson's disease started classes with 10 participants and, at 18-month follow-up, consisted of four boxing sessions per week led by three instructors with 40 participants; 81% of patients and 80% of instructors were very satisfied at the workshop stage.
Effect/estimate: 10 participants at launch → 40 participants, 4 sessions/week, 3 instructors at 18 months
Population: People with Parkinson's disease and boxing instructors, community setting | level: non-competitive | sex: 62% men among patients | age: adults
Design: Implementation/acceptability evaluation with 18-month follow-up questionnaire | n: 26 patients and 10 instructors at workshop; 40 participants at 18 months; 17 questionnaire respondents at follow-up
Boxing-specific: YES — boxing programme, clinical adult population | transfer status: Boxing-specific operational data, but a CLINICAL ADULT lane — do not present as a youth-gym growth curve
LIMITATIONS: Single programme; 17/40 responded at follow-up; no comparison programme; success case (publication bias toward programmes that survived)
PPBF implication: The only real published boxing-programme scaling datapoint we located: roughly 13 participants per instructor across 4 weekly sessions in a non-contact adult lane. Use as a REFERENCE POINT for the adaptive lane only, explicitly not as a youth ratio.
Source: Domingos et al., Journal of Parkinson's Disease, 2019 (PMID 31282426; doi:10.3233/JPD-191616)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A survey of a franchised non-contact boxing programme for Parkinson's disease drew 2,054 enrolled respondents (1,709 eligible: 1,333 current, 166 previous, 210 never-participants); current participants reported better median quality-of-life and exercise self-efficacy scores than previous and never-participants, and the sample was 97% Caucasian.
Effect/estimate: Median PDQ-39 25 (current) vs 36 and 32 (previous/never), p<0.01; SEE 54 vs 43 and 48, p<0.01. Cross-sectional — self-selection cannot be excluded.
Population: Adults with Parkinson's disease aware of the programme, predominantly US | level: non-competitive, non-contact | sex: 59% male among current participants | age: median age 69
Design: Cross-sectional survey (PDQ-39, Self-Efficacy for Exercise scale) | n: 1,709 analysed
Boxing-specific: YES — franchised non-contact boxing model | transfer status: Boxing-specific, ADULT CLINICAL, franchise model — relevant to the multi-organisation/franchise operating model analysis, not to youth operations
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional; healthy/adherent-user bias (current participants may differ at baseline); 97% Caucasian sample is a stark equity signal; self-report
PPBF implication: Demonstrates that a franchised boxing model can reach national scale AND that such a model can reach a demographically narrow population. Equity monitoring must be built into any PPBF multi-site expansion from day one.
Source: Larson et al., Disability and Rehabilitation, 2021 (PMID 34498995; doi:10.1080/09638288.2021.1963854)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective study of a community-based boxing programme for Parkinson's disease described 90-minute sessions comprising warm-up, boxing drills, strength and endurance exercises and cool-down, including multiple 30-60 second high-intensity intervals; participants averaged 2.8 (SD 0.8) sessions per week over 6.1 (SD 0.8) months.
Effect/estimate: 90-minute sessions; 2.8 (SD 0.8) sessions/week; 6.1 (SD 0.8) months; significant FAB improvement above published MDC
Population: Individuals with Parkinson's disease, Hoehn and Yahr stage 1-3 | level: non-competitive | sex: not stated in abstract | age: adults
Design: Retrospective cross-sectional analysis of de-identified programme data | n: n=12
Boxing-specific: YES — boxing session structure | transfer status: Boxing-specific but ADULT CLINICAL; the SESSION ARCHITECTURE is more transferable than the dose
LIMITATIONS: n=12; retrospective; no control; single programme
PPBF implication: Gives a published, citable session-block template (warm-up / drills / conditioning / cool-down with interval work) for the adaptive lane; PPBF youth session blocks must be derived separately and validated.
Source: Moore et al., International Journal of Exercise Science, 2021 (PMID 35096235; doi:10.70252/BNAX9498)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 10-week manualised non-contact boxing group programme (90-minute sessions twice weekly) for adults with major depressive disorder or generalised anxiety disorder reported 89% retention, 84% attendance and 98% satisfaction in a feasibility trial (ISRCTN23023309).
Effect/estimate: Retention 89%, attendance 84%, satisfaction 98%; symptom reductions reported but uncontrolled and n=8
Population: Adult psychiatric outpatients with MDD or GAD, Toronto, Canada | level: non-competitive, non-contact | sex: 5 female, 3 male | age: adults
Design: Single-arm pre-post feasibility trial | n: n=8 analysed (9 recruited)
Boxing-specific: YES — non-contact boxing programme | transfer status: Boxing-specific, ADULT CLINICAL, tiny sample — feasibility signal only
LIMITATIONS: n=8; single arm; no control; symptom changes cannot be attributed to the intervention
PPBF implication: Supports a manualised non-contact adult lane as an operationally distinct model (fixed cohort, closed 10-week block, referral intake). Symptom outcomes must NOT be claimed by PPBF; any mental-health framing is a clinician's call.
Source: Bozdarov et al., PLOS ONE, 2025 (PMID 39913542; doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0318364)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of head trauma in boxing found boxers had a significantly elevated concussion risk compared with other combat sports (risk ratio 0.253 vs 0.065, P<0.001), and reported cavum septum pellucidum in 147 of 631 boxers (23.30%) and brain atrophy in 125 of 411 (30.41%).
Effect/estimate: Concussion RR 0.253 (boxing) vs 0.065 (other combat sports), P<0.001; CSP 23.30%; atrophy 30.41%
Population: Amateur and professional boxers | level: amateur and professional | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract | age: not disaggregated
Design: PRISMA systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 35 of 84 articles included; 631 and 411 boxers in the respective pooled analyses
Boxing-specific: YES — directly boxing-specific | transfer status: Boxing-specific; note the pooled samples mix amateur and professional and are heavily weighted toward historical professional cohorts
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous historical studies; professional and amateur pooled; imaging findings from older cohorts under different rules; does not establish risk for non-contact or recreational boxing
PPBF implication: Establishes why contact intensity must be an explicit operating-model dimension with human-owned clearance. SHADOW must never gate, clear or predict contact readiness; that decision belongs to a qualified physician and the coaching staff.
Source: Donnelly et al., Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine, 2023 (PMID 37862081; doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000001195)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Association of Ringside Physicians position statement holds that headguards are effective in reducing facial lacerations and auricular injury but should NOT be relied upon to reduce the risk of concussion or other traumatic brain injury, and that changes in athlete behaviour toward more risk-taking when wearing headguards may offset any biomechanical risk reduction.
Effect/estimate: Laceration reduction supported; concussion prevention not supported; human studies lacking
Population: Combat sport athletes including boxers | level: amateur and professional | sex: policies recommended to be standardised for men and women in the absence of gender-difference data | age: all ages of participation
Design: Position statement | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: YES | transfer status: Boxing/combat-sport specific
LIMITATIONS: Position statement, not a trial; the statement itself calls for further research
PPBF implication: Equipment provision (headguards) is an operational cost and a laceration-control measure, NOT a concussion control. Any PPBF messaging or app copy implying headguard = brain protection would be a safety misstatement.
Source: deWeber et al., The Physician and Sportsmedicine, 2023 (PMID 37559553; doi:10.1080/00913847.2023.2242415)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of youth Olympic combat sports found rapid weight loss highly prevalent (25-94% depending on sport, age and competition level), commonly achieved by increasing exercise, restricting fluid and food, training in impermeable suits and sauna use, with magnitude ranging from about 1% to 6.3% (SD 3.7) of body mass; the authors concluded RWL needs stringent regulation and ideally should be banned in this population.
Effect/estimate: Prevalence 25-94%; magnitude ~1% to 6.3% (SD 3.7) body mass
Population: Children and adolescent combat sport athletes (Olympic combat sports) | level: competitive, official competition context | sex: mixed | age: youth/adolescent
Design: Systematic review | n: see source (studies conducted in official competition context only)
Boxing-specific: partially — Olympic combat sports including boxing | transfer status: Combat-sport specific and youth-specific — highly relevant to a competitive youth boxing lane
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous sports and definitions; self-report; competition-context studies only
PPBF implication: A competition-heavy youth operating model carries a documented weight-cutting hazard. PPBF must have a written no-youth-weight-cutting policy owned by a named human role; SHADOW must never generate, recommend, or optimise a weight-management target for a minor.
Source: Lakicevic et al., Journal of Eating Disorders, 2022 (PMID 35614520; doi:10.1186/s40337-022-00595-w)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In elite youth Olympic-style boxers from 12 European countries, rapid weight loss was NOT associated with competitive success; boxing experience was the significant predictor of medalling (odds ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.06-1.66, Nagelkerke R=.11); only 25% were in the RWL group, over 45% self-reported combining multiple weight-cutting methods known to be health hazards, and 33% experienced muscle weakness as a consequence.
Effect/estimate: Experience OR 1.33 (1.06-1.66); RWL not associated with success; 45% combined hazardous methods; 33% muscle weakness
Population: Elite youth Olympic-style boxers, 12 European countries | level: elite youth amateur | sex: all male | age: mean 17.1 (SD 0.9) years
Design: Questionnaire study with prospective competition-outcome follow-up | n: N=83
Boxing-specific: YES — Olympic-style boxing | transfer status: Boxing-specific, elite youth, MALE ONLY, European — do not generalise to female or novice boxers
LIMITATIONS: N=83; male only; self-report; single championship outcome; low model R
PPBF implication: Gives PPBF a boxing-specific, evidence-backed talking point for coaches and guardians: cutting weight did not predict winning in this cohort, experience did. Supports an experience-and-development framing in the competitive lane.
Source: Zubac et al., International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 2018 (PMID 29182408; doi:10.1123/ijspp.2016-0733)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An IOC Medical Commission ad hoc working group review and position statement concluded there are no generally accepted optimum values for body weight or percentage fat mass across sports and no gold-standard body-composition method for athletes, and called for sport- and gender-specific prevention programmes, criteria for 'does not start' decisions in athletes with eating disorders, and modification of regulations in some sports.
Effect/estimate: Explicit statement that no optimum body-composition values exist
Population: Athletes in weight-sensitive sports | level: elite and sub-elite | sex: both, with explicit call for gender-specific programmes | age: not restricted
Design: Review and position statement | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no — weight-sensitive sports generally, which includes boxing | transfer status: Applies to boxing as a weight-category sport
LIMITATIONS: Position statement; 2013 publication; does not resolve the referral-threshold question it raises
PPBF implication: Direct authority for refusing to publish any body-composition target in the app. If a coach or guardian asks SHADOW for a weight target, the correct behaviour is to decline and route to a qualified clinician.
Source: Sundgot-Borgen et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2013 (PMID 24115480; doi:10.1136/bjsports-2013-092966)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Position-stand and review evidence on youth resistance training holds that appropriately designed and QUALIFIED-SUPERVISED resistance training is safe and effective for young athletes and contributes to injury prevention.
Effect/estimate: Safety and efficacy conditional on qualified supervision and appropriate programme design
Population: Children and adolescents / young athletes | level: youth sport, all levels | sex: mixed | age: youth
Design: Position statement (NSCA) and narrative review | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from youth strength and conditioning to the boxing gym floor — LABELLED TRANSFER; widely accepted across youth sport
LIMITATIONS: Position statements reflect expert consensus over a heterogeneous literature; 'qualified supervision' is not operationally quantified as a ratio

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The AOSSM early sport specialisation consensus concluded there is no evidence that young children benefit from early sport specialisation in the majority of sports, that specialised youth are subject to overuse injury and burnout, and that early multisport participation does not deter long-term competitive success.
Effect/estimate: Consensus position; no effect size
Population: Youth athletes | level: youth sport | sex: mixed | age: children and adolescents
Design: Consensus statement (think tank / roundtable) | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from youth sport consensus — LABELLED TRANSFER; consistent with the AMSSM research-agenda statement
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, not systematic review; the parallel AMSSM summit statement explicitly notes methodological limitations in the underlying specialisation literature

Effect/estimate: Framework; no effect size
Population: US sports-based youth development programmes | level: community/recreational | sex: mixed | age: youth
Design: Conceptual/definitional paper within a youth-development framework | n: not applicable
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from sports-based youth development — LABELLED TRANSFER

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed-methods systematic review of sports schools found student-athletes receive considerable academic and athletic support and more intensified training and competition with high-level partners, but REGULARLY MISS SCHOOL, and that heterogeneous evaluation methods make cross-study comparison and consensus on impacts difficult.
Effect/estimate: Both positive and negative immediate, short- and long-term impacts identified; no pooled estimate
Population: Sports school student-athletes, international | level: intensified/competitive youth | sex: mixed | age: school-age adolescents
Design: Mixed-methods systematic review (PRISMA; 8 databases to Feb 2021; MMAT quality appraisal) | n: 46 articles
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from intensified youth sport structures — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Heterogeneous outcomes and designs; sports-school context is more intensive than a community gym's competition camp
PPBF implication: The competition-camp operating model should carry an explicit academic/school-conflict monitoring requirement and a documented off-ramp back to the recreational lane.
Source: Thompson et al., Sports Medicine, 2022 (PMID 35260992; doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01664-5)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Process evaluation of a physical-activity-based positive youth development programme across 29 sites found variability in implementation and identified five categories of influencing factors: contextual/environmental (parental involvement, relationships with school personnel), organisational (implementation support, staff responsiveness), programme-specific (curriculum design), coach factors (existing relationships with participants, responsiveness), and youth factors (behavioural and discipline issues).
Effect/estimate: Implementation scores varied across sites; five factor categories identified
Population: Girls participating in a physical-activity-based PYD programme, US | level: recreational | sex: female | age: youth
Design: Mixed-method multi-site process evaluation (focus groups, site visits, implementation checklists) | n: 29 sites
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from multi-site PYD programme delivery — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: Single programme; self-report implementation checklists; female-only
PPBF implication: Site-to-site variability is the norm in multi-site delivery. A PPBF multi-org model needs a fidelity checklist per site and must expect — and record — adaptation rather than assume uniformity.
Source: Iachini et al., Evaluation and Program Planning, 2014 (PMID 24858574; doi:10.1016/j.evalprogplan.2014.05.001)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a K-5 school-based physical activity programme, odds of programme delivery among trained respondents were 2.64 times (95% CI 1.22-5.47) the odds among untrained respondents; more frequent implementation (>=3 times/week) was associated with partner support (OR 2.43, 95% CI 1.27-4.73), and 72.4% of implementers provided activities only 1-2 times/week.
Effect/estimate: Training OR 2.64 (1.22-5.47); partner support and >=3x/week OR 2.43 (1.27-4.73); 72.4% delivered 1-2x/week
Population: K-5 teachers implementing a school PA programme with Cooperative Extension/SNAP-Ed partner support, US | level: not applicable | sex: not applicable | age: K-5 students served
Design: Cross-sectional survey with logistic regression | n: n=355 teachers
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER from school PA programme implementation — LABELLED TRANSFER; teacher implementers, not coaches
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional self-report; non-response bias; association not causation
PPBF implication: For the school/community-partnership model, an external partner organisation providing ongoing support (not just an initial training) is associated with higher delivery frequency — a concrete argument for a named PPBF liaison role per partner site.
Source: Packebush et al., Journal of School Health, 2025 (PMID 39800562; doi:10.1111/josh.13531)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Interviews with high school athletic trainers across 26 US states and DC identified implementation barriers to state concussion laws including athletes underreporting symptoms, lack of communication, resistance from parents and coaches, sport culture, cost of and access to medical care, and lack of understanding of concussion; a separate content analysis found 68% (n=34) of states require concussion education for coaches with significant variability in requirements and enforcement.
Effect/estimate: 68% of states require coach concussion education; barriers thematically identified
Population: US high schools and state youth sport governing bodies | level: high school interscholastic sport | sex: mixed | age: adolescents
Design: Qualitative interview study (n=64 athletic trainers) and qualitative content analysis of state statutes and governing-body handbooks | n: 64 interviews; 50 states + DC policy review
Boxing-specific: no — interscholastic sport, but the mechanism generalises | transfer status: TRANSFER from US concussion-law implementation to combat-sport safety policy — LABELLED TRANSFER
LIMITATIONS: High schools with athletic trainers on staff (better resourced than a community gym); interviews from 2014-2016 academic years for the barrier study
PPBF implication: Written safety policy does not equal delivered safety practice. SHADOW's role is to make the gap visible (education expiry, removal-from-play logging, escalation records) while the decisions stay with qualified humans — and state requirements must be verified locally, never assumed.
Source: Coxe et al., Journal of Adolescent Health, 2019; Davies & Bird, Journal of Athletic Training, 2018; Asgari et al., PM&R, 2024 (PMID 31757625; doi:10.1016/j.jadohealth.2019.08.016. Related: PMID 30284457; doi:10.4085/1062-6050-529-17; PMID 39444245; doi:10.1002/pmrj.13274)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of amateur boxing reported a pooled TRAINING injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0) versus a competition rate of 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), with training injuries predominantly upper-limb (median 49%) and sprains/strains (median 60%), while competition injuries were predominantly head and neck (median 72%).
Effect/estimate: Training IIR 1.3/1000 h (95% CI 0.2-7.0); competition 6.8/1000 min (95% CI 4.2-10.9)
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur | sex: mixed | age: not disaggregated in the pooled estimate
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (17 studies, random-effects) | n: 17 eligible cohort studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Very wide CI on the training estimate indicates substantial heterogeneity and imprecision. Pooled across studies with differing injury definitions and exposure capture. Does NOT decompose training exposure by activity type, so it cannot by itself justify any specific per-activity ratio.
PPBF implication: Supports tiering by activity: training risk is concentrated in upper-limb overuse (a technique-monitoring problem) while head/neck risk concentrates where contact occurs. This is the evidential basis for treating bag work and sparring as different supervision tiers — but the ratio VALUES remain PPBF assumptions.
Source: Alevras et al. (2022). Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. (PMID 36195527 / DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A separate systematic review and meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology reported pooled injury incidence of 223.9 per 1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4) and 13.0 per 1000 minutes of competition, with professional boxing rates significantly higher than amateur and female subgroups.
Effect/estimate: 223.9/1000 boxers (95% CI 157.5-290.4); professional IR 399.8 vs lower amateur/female
Population: Boxers across organized boxing | level: Professional and amateur, disaggregated | sex: male and female subgroups reported | age: adult predominantly
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis (14 studies; 11/14 rated moderate quality) | n: 14 studies
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Most included studies of moderate quality only. Estimates are competition-weighted; they do not describe gym training risk by activity. Professional-amateur difference is descriptive, not causal.
PPBF implication: Confirms competitive level materially changes risk, so PPBF ratios must be banded by level as well as age. Does NOT supply a supervision ratio.
Source: Mao et al. (2023). Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. Orthop J Sports Med. (PMID 37025124 / DOI 10.1177/23259671221127669)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Analysis of 7712 athlete exposures across three consecutive Olympic Games found a competition injury incidence in boxing of 9.2 per 1000 minutes (95% CI 7.6-10.9), significantly higher than wrestling, though a lower proportion of boxing injuries caused more than seven days' absence (21.0%) than wrestling, judo or taekwondo.
Effect/estimate: Boxing 9.2/1000 min (95% CI 7.6-10.9); 21.0% of boxing injuries >7 days absence
Population: Olympic combat sport athletes | level: Elite | sex: male and female; no difference in injury risk by sex reported | age: adult elite
Design: Prospective cohort using IOC injury surveillance across three Games | n: 7712 athlete exposures
Boxing-specific: Yes (boxing as one of four compared sports) | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but ELITE COMPETITION ONLY
LIMITATIONS: Elite competition only. Cannot be transferred to youth or novice gym training, and says nothing about supervision.
PPBF implication: Reinforces that competition/sparring is the high-consequence tier. EXPLICIT TRANSFER FLAG: elite competition data must not be used to set youth training ratios.
Source: Lystad et al. (2020). Injury incidence, severity and profile in Olympic combat sports: a comparative analysis of 7712 athlete exposures from three consecutive Olympic Games. Br J Sports Med. (PMID 33219113 / DOI 10.1136/bjsports-2020-102958)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A one-year prospective cohort of 33 amateur and 14 professional boxers in Victoria, Australia recorded 21 injuries and an overall rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing, with 71% to the head region and concussion the most common single injury; the authors noted that considerable training time drives high total exposure.
Effect/estimate: 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing; 71% head region (95% CI reported as -3.7 to 89.4)
Population: Amateur and professional boxers, Victoria Australia | level: Amateur and professional | sex: predominantly male; both sexes registered | age: adult
Design: Prospective cohort, 1-year follow-up | n: 47 boxers; 21 injuries
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Small sample (47) and few events (21); the reported confidence interval on the head-region proportion spans an implausible range, indicating severe imprecision. Volunteer sample. 2004-2005 data. Confidence rated low on precision grounds despite the prospective design.
PPBF implication: Supports the general point that cumulative TRAINING exposure, not just bouts, carries the risk load — which is precisely why gym-floor supervision design matters. Too imprecise to parameterise anything.
Source: Zazryn et al. (2006). A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing. Br J Sports Med. (PMID 16807306 / DOI 10.1136/bjsm.2006.025924)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A mixed-methods implementation study of an injury surveillance system at five amateur boxing events in Australia identified facilitators and barriers across athletes, coaches, promoters, referees, medical professionals and governing-body officials, with 'value of data' emerging as a primary theme.

Population: Australian amateur boxing community | level: Amateur | sex: mixed | age: not specified
Design: Mixed methods: reflexive thematic analysis plus RE-AIM-framed implementation trial | n: 5 events; interview sample not extracted
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC, Australian context
LIMITATIONS: Implementation feasibility, not injury rates. Maintenance (long-term sustainability) was explicitly not evaluated — the domain most relevant to PPBF's ongoing logging ambitions.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguards were used to measure head impact exposure in 22 male cadets during a compulsory introductory boxing course at the U.S. Military Academy, establishing baseline head-impact frequency and severity for beginner-level instruction.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective analysis of Australian news media reports identified 163 boxing-related fatalities between 1832 and 2020, of which 74.8% were professional and 24.5% amateur, with traumatic brain injury the most common cause (74.2%).
Effect/estimate: 74.8% professional; TBI 74.2% of causes
Population: Australian boxing, historical | level: Professional and amateur | sex: not disaggregated | age: not disaggregated
Design: Retrospective media-report analysis | n: 163 fatalities over 188 years
Boxing-specific: Yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC, Australian, historical
LIMITATIONS: Media reports are an incomplete and biased ascertainment source with no denominator, so NO rate can be computed. Historical span crosses enormous changes in rules and medical supervision. Descriptive only.
PPBF implication: Justifies treating open sparring as the highest supervision tier and requiring an immediate-stop capability. Must NOT be used to state any probability of harm at PPBF.
Source: Alevras et al. (2021). Boxing-related fatalities in Australia: A retrospective analysis of news media reports. J Sci Med Sport. (PMID 34602333 / DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2021.08.002)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In an accelerometer study of 281 elementary students across 12 weeks, a statistically significant interaction between lesson context and class size was found, with the largest difference in percentage of wear time in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity between fitness lessons in small classes and motor-skill lessons in large classes (beta = 14.8%, 95% CI 5.7-23.9).
Effect/estimate: beta = 14.8% MVPA wear time (95% CI 5.7-23.9) for the extreme contrast
Population: Elementary school students, private school, Utah USA | level: Non-athlete / school PE | sex: 137 male, 144 female | age: grades 1-5
Design: Observational, accelerometry, multi-level mixed effects model | n: 281 students
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: NON-BOXING, school PE, elementary age — TRANSFER IS INDIRECT
LIMITATIONS: Observational: class size was not randomised, so this is ASSOCIATION, NOT CAUSATION — smaller classes may co-occur with other differences. Single private school. The effect is an interaction of size WITH lesson content, so size alone is not the actionable lever.
PPBF implication: Best available quantitative support for the intuition that group size affects active engagement, but it is school-PE and correlational. It supports MEASURING active time per athlete at PPBF (a computed output of capacity_model.py); it does not license a capacity number.
Source: Kirkham-King et al. (2017). Elementary physical education: A focus on fitness activities and smaller class sizes are associated with higher levels of physical activity. Prev Med Rep. (PMID 29034147 / DOI 10.1016/j.pmedr.2017.09.007)

Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: NON-BOXING, US high school setting — organisational analogue for a small community club

Correlation only — presence of a trainer is not shown to CAUSE preparedness.
Source: Hedberg et al. (2024). Emergency Action Planning in United States High Schools. Sports Health. (PMID 39370662 / DOI 10.1177/19417381241277833)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a six-week, eleven-session study of physical education students learning sprint hurdles, an increasing contextual interference practice schedule and a blocked schedule did not differ on retention tests, but the increasing-CI group performed better on a delayed transfer test 40 days after acquisition.
Effect/estimate: No retention difference; increasing-CI superior on delayed TRANSFER
Population: Physical education students | level: Novice | sex: not disaggregated in abstract | age: student (tertiary PE)
Design: Controlled trial, two practice schedules, retention at 10 and 40 days plus transfer test | n: 46 (n=23 per group)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: NON-BOXING (athletics/hurdles), novice learners — MECHANISM TRANSFER ONLY
LIMITATIONS: Small groups. Different motor task from boxing. ACUTE PERFORMANCE vs RETENTION vs TRANSFER are explicitly dissociated here — the benefit appeared only on delayed transfer, which is exactly the outcome a gym is least likely to measure.
PPBF implication: Station rotation IS a contextual-interference manipulation. This supports varying station content across a rotation rather than blocking it, but PPBF must not claim a within-session performance benefit — the evidence is for delayed transfer, and it comes from a non-boxing task.
Source: Makaruk et al. (2024). The learning of sprint hurdles: A comparative study on increasing contextual interference and blocked practice schedules. PLoS One. (PMID 38198493 / DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0289916)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a sample of US youth club basketball organisations, written-and-practised EAPs, coach CPR requirements and AED access were all uncommon, and most clubs had no affiliated athletic trainer or medical director.
Effect/estimate: 6% had a written EAP practised annually; 35% required coach CPR training; AED available at practices 45%, games 35%; >50% had no athletic trainer or medical director
Population: Amateur Athletic Union club coaches/administrators (US) | level: youth club | sex: mixed | age: youth
Design: Cross-sectional survey | n: 53 of 449 invited (12% response)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Other-sport youth club transfer; strongly analogous organisational form
LIMITATIONS: 12% response rate and n=53 — very low precision; treat percentages as directional only, not as PPBF targets
PPBF implication: Baseline expectation for an unmanaged club is poor. PPBF should treat CPR/AED coverage and an on-site AED as explicit, auditable roster attributes rather than assumed.
Source: Mason S, et al. Emergency Preparedness for Sudden Cardiac Arrest in Amateur Athletic Union Basketball Teams. Clin J Sport Med. 2022. (PMID 35995597; doi 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001062)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Placing an AED in a community club does not by itself produce a prepared club: knowledge of the EAP and of AED location is frequently absent among club members even after a funded AED/CPR programme.
Effect/estimate: Australia: 56% had no previous AED training; 41% did not have or did not know if they had an EAP. Ireland: 7% knew where the club EAP was or how to access it
Population: Community sports club/facility members (Victoria, Australia; Irish GAA clubs) | level: community club | sex: mixed | age: adult members
Design: Two cross-sectional surveys | n: 191 respondents (Australia); 267 respondents (Ireland)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Community club transfer — directly analogous setting
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; two different national contexts; volunteer response bias
PPBF implication: The gym-open checklist must include a physical AED-location and pad/battery-expiry check, and orientation must include walking new staff to the AED. Knowledge is the failure mode, not hardware.
Source: Fortington LV, et al. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2019. | O'Connor S, et al. Phys Sportsmed. 2020. (PMID 31275605; doi 10.1136/bmjsem-2019-000536 | PMID 31829067; doi 10.1080/00913847.2019.1704666)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In sports-related sudden cardiac arrest, bystander presence, bystander CPR and bystander AED use are each associated with substantially higher survival.
Effect/estimate: Bystander presence OR 2.55 (95% CI 1.48-4.37); bystander CPR OR 3.84 (2.36-6.25); bystander AED OR 5.25 (3.58-7.70)
Population: Sports-related sudden cardiac arrest patients | level: mixed (recreational to competitive) | sex: predominantly male in included cohorts | age: mixed adult and youth
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 non-randomised studies (GRADE: moderate certainty) | n: Bystander presence 9 studies/988 patients; bystander CPR 23 studies/2523; bystander AED 19 studies/1227
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Transfer from mixed sport to boxing; the physiological mechanism is sport-independent
LIMITATIONS: All non-randomised; confounding by arrest witnessing and location likely inflates effects; heterogeneity moderate for CPR (I2=54%)
PPBF implication: Justifies a hard PPBF staffing rule: no session runs without at least one current CPR/AED-trained adult on the floor. This is a governance rule, not a SHADOW decision.
Source: Michelland L, et al. Association between basic life support and survival in sports-related sudden cardiac arrest: a meta-analysis. Eur Heart J. 2023. (PMID 36285872; doi 10.1093/eurheartj/ehac586)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Even where bystander CPR is common in exercise-related cardiac arrest, bystander AED use lags well behind it, and survival to discharge is far from universal.
Effect/estimate: Bystander CPR median 71% (IQR 59-87%); bystander AED use median 31% (IQR 19-42%); survival to hospital discharge median 32% (IQR 24-49%)
Population: Exercise-related out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (during exercise or within 1 hour of cessation) | level: mixed | sex: predominantly male (median 92%) | age: median age 51 (IQR 39-56)
Design: Systematic review of 29 observational studies | n: median study sample 91
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Mixed-sport transfer; median age 51 means this is not a youth-athlete estimate
LIMITATIONS: Median-of-medians summary, not a pooled estimate; heterogeneous case definitions; population older than PPBF youth cohort
PPBF implication: AED USE — not AED ownership — is the weak link. Drill scenarios must require someone to physically fetch and open the AED, not narrate it.
Source: Grubic N, et al. Bystander interventions and survival after exercise-related sudden cardiac arrest: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2022. (PMID 34853034; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2021-104623)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sudden cardiac arrest in sport is commonly mis-recognised because collapse is followed by continued respiratory movements or gasping, and by seizure-like or abnormal eye findings; early AED use had the strongest association with survival in a video-based case series.
Effect/estimate: Gasping/continued respiratory movement in 31/31 visible-chest cases; fellow athletes initiated CPR in 0/42 competitive young athlete cases; survival with early AED use 19/22 (86%)
Population: Video-recorded sports-related sudden cardiac arrest events worldwide | level: mixed, including elite | sex: 47/48 male (98%) | age: athletes (not stratified)
Design: Retrospective video case-series analysis | n: 48 recorded events
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Mixed-sport transfer; recognition cues are physiological and sport-independent
LIMITATIONS: Selection bias (only videoed and publicised events); denominators unknown; not a survival estimate for the general case
PPBF implication: Recognition cue card in the SOP must state explicitly that gasping is NOT breathing and that seizure-like activity after collapse should be treated as cardiac arrest until proven otherwise. Escalation is EMS + AED, never a SHADOW judgement.
Source: Ungaro C, et al. Sports-related sudden cardiac arrest: a video analysis of presenting features, management and outcomes. Br J Sports Med. 2026. (PMID 41135968; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2025-110275)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Survival from cardiac arrest depends on a linked system — recognition, activation of EMS, early high-quality CPR, early defibrillation, and post-arrest care — not on any single element.
Effect/estimate: Systems-of-care framework; no single pooled effect
Population: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, general | level: NA | sex: mixed | age: all ages
Design: Guideline (systematic evidence review) | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: General resuscitation science applied to a sport facility
LIMITATIONS: Guideline, US-centric (AHA); jurisdictional resuscitation councils differ in detail (ERC, ILCOR)
PPBF implication: PPBF EAP should be written as a chain, with a named owner per link and a time target per link, so a drill can be scored link-by-link.
Source: Berg KM, et al. Part 7: Systems of Care: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care. Circulation. 2020. (PMID 33081524; doi 10.1161/CIR.0000000000000899)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The leading causes of sudden death in organised sport extend beyond cardiac arrest to head and neck injury, exertional heat stroke, exertional sickling, asthma, and environmental hazards; an EAP should cover all of them.
Effect/estimate: Condition list and management recommendations (qualitative)
Population: Organised sport participants | level: all | sex: mixed | age: not restricted
Design: Position statement | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: General athletic transfer; heat and sickling are less boxing-typical but not absent (weight-making, hot gyms)
LIMITATIONS: Position statement; US context; some conditions (lightning) irrelevant to an indoor boxing gym
PPBF implication: The PPBF incident matrix must be multi-hazard, not cardiac-only. Drives the event_category taxonomy in incident_near_miss_and_escalation_matrix.csv.
Source: Casa DJ, et al. NATA Position Statement: Preventing Sudden Death in Sports. J Athl Train. 2012. (PMID 22488236; doi 10.4085/1062-6050-47.1.96)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Exertional heat illness is preventable and recognisable, and exertional heat stroke remains a leading cause of sudden death in sport; recognition and immediate cooling protocols belong in the venue EAP.
Effect/estimate: Recommendation set (qualitative)
Population: Athletes in warm/hot training environments | level: all | sex: mixed | age: not restricted
Design: Position statement | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Transfer from outdoor/field sport; boxing-relevant via unventilated gyms, sweat suits and weight-making practices
LIMITATIONS: No boxing-gym-specific thresholds; wet-bulb globe temperature policies are written for outdoor sport
PPBF implication: Add heat/humidity to the daily facility check and an explicit prohibition on plastic/rubber sweat suits in the SOP. Environmental thresholds for an indoor boxing gym are TBD.
Source: Casa DJ, et al. NATA Position Statement: Exertional Heat Illnesses. J Athl Train. 2015. (PMID 26381473; doi 10.4085/1062-6050-50.9.07)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Any athlete with suspected sport-related concussion must be immediately removed from play and not return the same day; the Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6) is the non-clinician recognition instrument, and diagnosis and clearance are healthcare-professional decisions.
Effect/estimate: Consensus recommendation; CRT6/SCAT6/SCOAT6 tool set
Population: Sport participants, all sports | level: all, including community sport | sex: mixed | age: child, adolescent, adult (separate child tools)
Design: International consensus statement informed by 10 commissioned systematic reviews | n: NA (consensus process over 3.5 years)
Boxing-specific: no (combat sport included in scope of sport-related concussion generally) | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus applied to boxing; boxing differs in that head contact is intentional and repetitive
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, not trial evidence; the CISG process has attracted criticism regarding industry involvement and long-term-risk framing; boxing-specific data are thin
PPBF implication: SOP-12 concussion escalation. SHADOW may present the CRT6 red-flag checklist, timestamp removal, and notify the guardian and the designated medical contact. SHADOW must never diagnose, never clear, and never compute a return-to-play date.
Source: Patricios JS, et al. Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport - Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med. 2023. (PMID 37316210; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2023-106898)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] CRT6 is the published recognition tool designed for use by non-medically-trained individuals to identify a suspected concussion and trigger removal.
Effect/estimate: Tool (red flags, observable signs, symptom and memory prompts)
Population: Non-clinician sideline responders | level: all | sex: mixed | age: all
Design: Consensus-derived clinical tool | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport tool used in a boxing gym context
LIMITATIONS: A recognition tool, not a diagnostic tool; sensitivity/specificity in community boxing settings not established
PPBF implication: Attach CRT6 as a printed ringside card and as a read-only in-app checklist. SHADOW renders it; a coach completes it; a clinician interprets it.
Source: Echemendia RJ, et al. The Concussion Recognition Tool 6 (CRT6). Br J Sports Med. 2023. (PMID 37316201; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2023-107021)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Adolescent athletes who continued to play after a concussion took markedly longer to recover than those removed immediately.
Effect/estimate: Recovery 44.4 (SD 36.0) days for those who played on vs 22.0 (SD 18.7) days for those removed (p=.003); 8.80x more likely to have protracted (>=21 d) recovery
Population: Adolescent athletes with diagnosed sport-related concussion | level: high school | sex: mixed | age: ~13-18 (mean ~15.5 y)
Design: Prospective repeated-measures cohort | n: 69 (35 removed, 34 continued)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Other-sport adolescent transfer to youth boxing
LIMITATIONS: Small sample; not randomised — athletes who play on may have had different injury severity or reporting behaviour; single-centre
PPBF implication: Gives PPBF a concrete reason to write 'when in doubt, sit them out' into the SOP as a non-negotiable coach action. Confounded by indication — state as association, not proof.
Source: Elbin RJ, et al. Removal From Play After Concussion and Recovery Time. Pediatrics. 2016. (PMID 27573089; doi 10.1542/peds.2016-0910)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a large multi-site collegiate cohort, immediate removal from activity after sport-related concussion was associated with less time lost and shorter symptom duration than delayed removal.
Effect/estimate: 63.6% were delayed-removal; immediate removal associated with less time missed and shorter symptom duration after adjustment (R2 change .022-.046, p<=.001)
Population: US collegiate and service academy athletes | level: collegiate/elite amateur | sex: mixed | age: ~18-23
Design: Prospective multi-site cohort (NCAA/DoD CARE Consortium) | n: 506 diagnosed concussions, 18 sports, 25 institutions
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Other-sport collegiate transfer
LIMITATIONS: Observational; removal timing is not randomised; effect sizes modest in variance-explained terms
PPBF implication: Supports logging removal TIMESTAMP as a first-class field: time of suspected event, time of removal, delta. SHADOW may compute and display the delta for after-action review only.
Source: Asken BM, et al. Immediate Removal From Activity After Sport-Related Concussion Is Associated With Shorter Clinical Recovery. Am J Sports Med. 2018. (PMID 29558195; doi 10.1177/0363546518757984)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Pooled across studies, athletes who delayed reporting or continued playing recovered several days later than those who reported or were removed immediately.
Effect/estimate: SMD 0.36 days (95% CI 0.066-0.662), p=0.017; immediate reporters recovered 5.4 days (95% CI -10.14 to -0.75) sooner
Population: Athletes with concussion | level: mixed (high school to collegiate) | sex: mixed | age: adolescent to young adult
Design: Systematic review with meta-analysis | n: 12 studies
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport transfer
LIMITATIONS: Small number of studies; heterogeneous definitions of 'delayed'; the raw-score CI is wide and crosses close to zero
PPBF implication: Reporting culture is the intervention target. PPBF should measure self-report latency as a programme KPI and never penalise an athlete for reporting.
Source: Barnhart M, et al. The Influence of Timing of Reporting and Clinic Presentation on Concussion Recovery Outcomes. Sports Med. 2021. (PMID 33761129; doi 10.1007/s40279-021-01444-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] For children (5-12) and adolescents (13-18), strict rest is not recommended; early return to light physical activity and reduced screen time support recovery, and subacute assessment requires a multimodal tool.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative recommendations; SCAT diagnostic discrimination best within first 72 hours
Population: Children 5-12 and adolescents 13-18 | level: all | sex: mixed | age: 5-18
Design: Consensus recommendations derived from systematic reviews | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport paediatric consensus applied to youth boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus; limited paediatric trial evidence; nothing boxing-specific
PPBF implication: PPBF must not encode a rest-until-symptom-free rule. Any graduated return content in the app is educational only and is executed under a clinician's written plan.
Source: Davis GA, et al. Pediatric Sport-Related Concussion: Recommendations From the Amsterdam Consensus Statement 2023. Pediatrics. 2024. (PMID 38044802; doi 10.1542/peds.2023-063489)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Boxing carries an elevated concussion risk relative to other combat sports, and studies of boxers report high proportions with cavum septum pellucidum, brain atrophy and cognitive abnormality; headguard benefit is contested.
Effect/estimate: Concussion risk ratio 0.253 in boxing vs 0.065 in other combat sports (p<0.001); cavum septum pellucidum 147/631 (23.30%); brain atrophy 125/411 (30.41%)
Population: Amateur and professional boxers | level: amateur and professional | sex: not disaggregated in the pooled figures | age: adult
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 35 included articles; 631 boxers for cavum analysis, 411 for atrophy
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific — no transfer assumption required
LIMITATIONS: Heavily weighted to older professional-boxer cohorts and to eras with different medical oversight; selection bias in imaging cohorts; the neurodegenerative proportions are NOT applicable to a youth non-contact PPBF programme
PPBF implication: Justifies conservative sparring-authorisation SOP and cumulative head-contact logging. Do NOT present these prevalence figures to parents as PPBF risk — they describe professional-era cohorts.
Source: Donnelly K, et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Investigating Head Trauma in Boxing. Clin J Sport Med. 2023. (PMID 37862081; doi 10.1097/JSM.0000000000001195)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguards can quantify head impact exposure in boxing sparring; in beginner boxing courses most measured impacts were of low magnitude, with a right-skewed distribution and rare higher-magnitude events.
Effect/estimate: Cadets: mean peak linear acceleration 16.5 (SD 7.1) g, max 70.8 g; 640/809 (79.1%) between 10 and 20 g; mean peak angular acceleration 1.52 (SD 0.96) krad/s2
Population: US Military Academy cadets in a compulsory introductory boxing course; separately, amateur boxers and MMA athletes | level: novice/introductory and amateur | sex: male (n=22) in the cadet study; 23 athletes of whom 4 women in the boxing/MMA study | age: 19.9 (SD 1.1) years in cadet study
Design: Instrumented mouthguard observational studies with video verification | n: 205 player-bouts / 809 verified impacts (cadets); 896 verified impacts (boxing/MMA)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific but novice adult male military population — not youth, not female-representative
LIMITATIONS: Very small samples; sensor artefact possible despite video verification; no dose-response to clinical outcome established; no safe threshold exists
PPBF implication: Head-impact instrumentation is a plausible future PPBF research instrument, NOT a clearance device. No g-force threshold may be used to gate participation — none is validated.
Source: Fetchko K, et al. Mil Med. 2023. | Jansen AE, et al. Orthop J Sports Med. 2021. (PMID 37948285; doi 10.1093/milmed/usad249 | PMID 34901294; doi 10.1177/23259671211059815)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Amateur boxing injury rates are far higher in competition than in training, and the injured region differs: head and neck dominate in competition, upper limb in training.
Effect/estimate: Competition 54.7 injuries/1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8/1000 min (4.2-10.9); training 1.3/1000 h (0.2-7.0). Competition head/neck median 72% (range 46-100%); training upper limb median 49% (40-53%)
Population: Amateur boxers | level: amateur | sex: mixed (not fully disaggregated) | age: mostly adult amateur
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific
LIMITATIONS: Very wide confidence intervals, especially for training; inconsistent injury definitions and exposure denominators across studies
PPBF implication: Training-phase SOP should weight hand/wrist protection and technique; competition-day SOP should weight head/neck response. Distinct checklists, not one generic one.
Source: Alevras AJ, et al. Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2022. (PMID 36195527; doi 10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In an elite amateur squad tracked prospectively, the hand was the most injured location overall and in both training and competition, and more injuries occurred in training than competition.
Effect/estimate: Total competition injury rate 828/1000 h; competition hand injury rate 302/1000 h; concussion incidence comparatively low
Population: Great Britain amateur boxing squad | level: elite amateur | sex: mixed squad (not disaggregated) | age: adult
Design: 5-year prospective injury surveillance | n: 66 boxers, 2005-2009
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: Boxing-specific but ELITE — do not apply these rates to novices or youth
LIMITATIONS: Single national squad; medically-diagnosed injury definition inflates rates relative to time-loss definitions; elite training volumes
PPBF implication: Hand-wrap technique check and glove-condition check earn a place on the DAILY session checklist, not the monthly one. Supports an equipment-retirement criterion for compressed glove padding.
Source: Loosemore M, et al. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study. Br J Sports Med. 2015. (PMID 26192194; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Dentofacial injury is common across combat sports, supporting a mandatory mouthguard rule for any contact activity.
Effect/estimate: Pooled dental injury prevalence 25.2% (12.3-40.8%); dentofacial 30.3% (18.1-44.1%); I2 = 100%
Population: Combat sports practitioners across 14 disciplines including boxing | level: mixed | sex: mixed | age: mixed
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis | n: 27 studies included
Boxing-specific: partly (boxing among 14 sports studied) | transfer status: Combat-sport pooled estimate, not boxing-isolated
LIMITATIONS: I2 = 100% — extreme heterogeneity means the pooled figure should not be read as a single population risk; retrospective self-report common in included studies
PPBF implication: Mouthguard = mandatory equipment gate for any contact drill. Encode as a hard pre-contact checklist item; SHADOW may block a contact-session draft from being ISSUED until the item is ticked by a coach, but a coach makes the contact decision.
Source: Polmann H, et al. Prevalence of dentofacial injuries among combat sports practitioners: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Dent Traumatol. 2019 (epub); 2020 issue. (PMID 31420968; doi 10.1111/edt.12508)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Prospective injury and illness data across Olympic combat sports are too heterogeneous in severity classification and exposure measurement to allow direct cross-sport comparison, which limits prevention-programme design.
Effect/estimate: Boxing: head/face 45.8%, wrist 12.0%, lower back 7.8% of injuries (level 1/2b evidence)
Population: Elite Olympic combat sport athletes (boxing, judo, taekwondo, wrestling) | level: elite | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Systematic review of prospective studies (>12 weeks) | n: 9 studies, most at moderate risk of bias
Boxing-specific: partly | transfer status: Boxing rows are boxing-specific; the methodological conclusion is cross-sport
LIMITATIONS: Moderate risk of bias in 6/9 studies; elite-only; no consensus injury definition
PPBF implication: PPBF should adopt ONE explicit injury definition and ONE exposure denominator (athlete-exposures and athlete-hours) from day one, so its own data are poolable. This is a data-model decision, not a coaching one.
Source: Bromley SJ, et al. A systematic review of prospective epidemiological research into injury and illness in Olympic combat sport. Br J Sports Med. 2018. (PMID 28954799; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2016-097313)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Skin and soft-tissue infection is the dominant infectious-outbreak category in close-contact sport, with MRSA and tinea the leading pathogens.
Effect/estimate: MRSA 7/21 (33%), tinea 6/21 (29%); skin and soft tissue was the site in 15/21 (71%); 12/21 (57%) involved high school or collegiate competitors
Population: Competitive athletes, 2005-2010 outbreak literature | level: high school and collegiate mainly | sex: mixed | age: adolescent to adult
Design: Literature review of reported outbreaks | n: 21 outbreaks/clusters identified
Boxing-specific: no — predominantly wrestling, judo, American football | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM GRAPPLING/COLLISION SPORT. Boxing has far less sustained skin-to-skin contact than wrestling; the shared-equipment and shared-surface routes transfer better than the skin-to-skin route
LIMITATIONS: Publication bias toward investigated outbreaks; denominators absent; predates current MRSA epidemiology
PPBF implication: Hygiene SOP is justified, but PPBF must state the transfer caveat in writing so nobody claims wrestling incidence rates apply to boxing.
Source: Collins CJ, O'Connell B. Infectious disease outbreaks in competitive sports, 2005-2010. J Athl Train. 2012. (PMID 23068588; doi 10.4085/1062-6050-47.5.02)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In NCAA men's wrestling surveillance, skin infections were identified overwhelmingly during practice rather than competition, most caused time loss of 24 hours or more, and infections clustered heavily in a minority of team-seasons.
Effect/estimate: Overall rate 14.23/10,000 AEs (95% CI 11.59-16.86); 22.3% recurrent; 65.2% of infections attributable to 5 team-seasons; 89.3% identified during practice; 74.1% caused >=24 h time loss; viral rate 1.72x bacterial
Population: NCAA men's wrestling student-athletes | level: collegiate | sex: male | age: ~18-23
Design: Descriptive epidemiology from injury surveillance | n: 112 skin infections in 87 athletes across 78,720 athlete-exposures; 35 team-seasons
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING-DERIVED. Male-only. Applies to PPBF chiefly as evidence that clustering is environmental/organisational, not random
LIMITATIONS: Male wrestling only; athletic-trainer-reported so undercounts unpresented cases; no boxing equivalent identified
PPBF implication: Clustering in a minority of team-seasons is the actionable finding: outbreaks are a facility/practice-culture signal. PPBF should track infections per athlete-exposure and flag clustering for a human hygiene review.
Source: Herzog MM, et al. Epidemiology of Skin Infections in Men's Wrestling: NCAA Surveillance Data 2009-10 to 2013-14. J Athl Train. 2017. (PMID 28362160; doi 10.4085/1062-6050-52.2.16)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Tinea gladiatorum, predominantly caused by Trichophyton tonsurans, spreads primarily by direct skin-to-skin contact in contact-sport athletes, with reported prevalence varying enormously across settings.
Effect/estimate: Reported prevalence ranged from 2.4% to 100% across studies
Population: Wrestlers and other contact-sport athletes | level: school through elite | sex: predominantly male in reported series | age: adolescent to adult
Design: Systematic review of incidence studies plus narrative review | n: multiple studies pooled narratively
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING-DERIVED; boxing exposure is lower but non-zero (clinch, shared gloves, shared bags, shared mats)
LIMITATIONS: The 2.4-100% range is a statement of heterogeneity, not a usable risk estimate; case definitions and diagnostic methods vary widely
PPBF implication: Skin-check protocol in the checklists document. Recognition is a coach/staff task; DIAGNOSIS and exclusion-from-participation are health decisions for a qualified clinician.
Source: Zalewski A, et al. Tinea Gladiatorum: Epidemiology, Clinical Aspects, and Management. J Clin Med. 2022. | Adams BB. Tinea corporis gladiatorum. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2002. (PMID 35887830; doi 10.3390/jcm11144066 | PMID 12140477; doi 10.1067/mjd.2002.120603)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] Evidence on environmental (mat) reservoirs for dermatophytes is mixed: one Iranian study cultured T. tonsurans from a third of surveyed mats, while another found no positive mat cultures and concluded person-to-person spread predominated.
Effect/estimate: 2011: 19.2% of wrestlers infected; 8/24 mats (33.3%) heavily contaminated with T. tonsurans. 2020: 6.5% (278/4240) confirmed; no positive dermatophyte culture obtained from mats
Population: Wrestlers and combat athletes in Iran | level: club/competitive | sex: male-dominant | age: 10-19 most frequent group in one study
Design: Two cross-sectional clinico-epidemiological studies with environmental sampling | n: 270 wrestlers / 240 mat touch preparations (2011); 4240 athletes screened, 631 suspected (2020)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Wrestling/combat-sport transfer; mat contamination is directly relevant to a boxing gym floor
LIMITATIONS: Two studies, same region, conflicting environmental results; culture sensitivity from surfaces is poor and a negative culture does not prove absence; neither study tested a cleaning intervention
PPBF implication: Mat cleaning is justified on precaution and on general disinfection principles, but PPBF must NOT claim mat cleaning prevents a specified fraction of infections. Frequency is a PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER, not an evidence-derived number.
Source: Aghamirian MR, Ghiasian SA. Mycoses. 2011. | Kermani F, et al. Mycoses. 2020. (PMID 19917034; doi 10.1111/j.1439-0507.2009.01809.x | PMID 32096252; doi 10.1111/myc.13069)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Prophylactic oral valacyclovir substantially reduced herpes gladiatorum outbreaks at a 28-day high-school wrestling camp over a 10-year observational period.
Effect/estimate: 84.7% decrease in probability of an outbreak among prophylaxis users; 36 outbreaks total
Population: High-school wrestlers at a summer camp, Minnesota | level: high school | sex: not stated (wrestling camp, presumed predominantly male) | age: 13-18
Design: Observational cohort over 10 seasons (comparison group = non-users) | n: 2793 athletes completing camp; 1995 (71%) used antiviral
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING-DERIVED and setting-specific (residential camp, extreme skin-to-skin exposure). Transfer to boxing is weak
LIMITATIONS: Not randomised — users self-selected; unmeasured confounding; camp setting not comparable to a community gym; a MEDICATION decision, entirely outside PPBF and SHADOW authority
PPBF implication: Recorded for completeness of the evidence base ONLY. PPBF and SHADOW must never recommend, suggest, or route toward prophylactic medication. Any antiviral question goes to the athlete's clinician.
Source: Anderson BJ, McGuire DP, et al. Prophylactic Valacyclovir to Prevent Outbreaks of Primary Herpes Gladiatorum at a 28-Day Wrestling Camp: A 10-Year Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2016. (PMID 26540599; doi 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000255)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Weekly oral fluconazole reduced tinea gladiatorum incidence versus placebo in a randomised trial in wrestlers, and a long observational programme reported a large drop in incidence.
Effect/estimate: RCT: infection in 6% (fluconazole) vs 22% (placebo) vs 18% (not enrolled), p<0.05. Longitudinal: incidence fell from 67.4% to 3.5% over 10 years
Population: Wrestlers (high school and competitive) | level: high school | sex: predominantly male | age: adolescent
Design: Double-blind placebo-controlled trial (2000); prospective 10-year longitudinal study (2009) | n: RCT: not stated in abstract; longitudinal: 373 participants
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING-DERIVED. Not transferable to boxing as a practice recommendation
LIMITATIONS: The 67.4%-to-3.5% figure is uncontrolled before-after over a decade with concurrent hygiene changes — not attributable to the drug alone; systemic antifungal prophylaxis in minors raises safety and stewardship questions
PPBF implication: Evidence-base completeness only. OUT OF SCOPE for PPBF and prohibited for SHADOW: no medication recommendations, especially for minors.
Source: Kohl TD, et al. Pediatr Infect Dis J. 2000. | Brickman K, et al. Clin J Sport Med. 2009. (PMID 10959739; doi 10.1097/00006454-200008000-00009 | PMID 19741315; doi 10.1097/JSM.0b013e3181b2f397)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A survey of Pennsylvania high-school wrestling programmes found schools using more preventive practices reported MORE ringworm infections, and coaches were frequently involved in making the diagnosis.
Effect/estimate: 84.7% of responding schools had >=1 diagnosed case; 33% of affected teams had a wrestler miss a match; more preventive practices associated with MORE infections (p<0.05); 60% of coaches involved in diagnosis
Population: Pennsylvania high school wrestling programmes | level: high school | sex: male | age: adolescent
Design: Retrospective mail survey | n: 42.4% response rate
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Wrestling-derived; the surveillance-bias lesson is general
LIMITATIONS: Almost certainly reverse causation and detection bias — programmes with outbreaks adopt more practices and look harder. Do NOT read as evidence that prevention causes infection
PPBF implication: Two lessons: (1) infection counts rise when you start looking, so PPBF must not interpret an early rise in recorded skin findings as a hygiene failure; (2) COACHES DIAGNOSING is a documented and undesirable practice — PPBF SOP explicitly forbids it.
Source: Kohl TD, et al. Tinea gladiatorum: Pennsylvania's experience. Clin J Sport Med. 2002. (PMID 12011724; doi 10.1097/00042752-200205000-00004)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Community-associated MRSA skin and soft-tissue infection occurs in contact-sport teams, is transmitted person-to-person and via shared equipment, and carries meaningful morbidity.
Effect/estimate: 33/491 (6.7%) diagnosed with MRSA; abscess 70%, cellulitis 16%; 90% underwent surgical drainage; 27% received IV antibiotics; extremity infections 30 vs truncal 7; occurred predominantly in the first third of the season (p<0.001)
Population: Collegiate American football players; athletic populations generally | level: collegiate | sex: male | age: ~18-23
Design: Multi-programme retrospective analysis plus narrative reviews | n: 491 collegiate football players (33 infected)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: COLLISION-SPORT TRANSFER. Abrasion + shared equipment routes are plausible in boxing; the turf-abrasion route is not
LIMITATIONS: Single-sport, male, three programmes; the widely-cited 'up to 70% hospitalised' figure derives from selected outbreak reports, not a representative denominator
PPBF implication: Justifies: no sharing of personal protective equipment, cover-all-wounds rule, immediate reporting of any draining lesion, and prompt referral. Referral, not treatment.
Source: Bowers AL, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2008. | Rihn JA, et al. Am J Sports Med. 2005. | Redziniak DE, et al. Int J Sports Med. 2009. (PMID 18614960; doi 10.1249/MSS.0b013e31816f1534 | PMID 16314668 | PMID 19468969)
