text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] NFHS and NCAA guidance specify minimum treatment durations before return to contact for common infectious skin lesions (e.g. 72 hours of topical antifungal for tinea corporis; 120 hours of oral antiviral for recurrent herpes gladiatorum; 72 hours after incision and drainage for MRSA abscess with no further drainage), while acknowledging the underlying evidence is limited.
Effect/estimate: Tinea corporis: >=72 h topical antifungal. Tinea capitis: 14 days oral. Primary HSV: 10-14 days oral antiviral. Recurrent HSV: >=120 h oral antiviral. MRSA abscess: I&D plus >=72 h treatment with no further drainage. Scabies/head lice: 24 h after topical treatment. Conjunctivitis: 24 h treatment and no discharge
Population: US high school and collegiate contact-sport athletes, wrestling-centred | level: high school and collegiate | sex: mixed (rules written around wrestling) | age: adolescent to young adult
Design: Governing-body position statement and medical release form; underlying evidence base explicitly acknowledged as incomplete by the issuing body | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no — written for wrestling | transfer status: WRESTLING RULEBOOK TRANSFER. Boxing bodies do not publish an equivalent skin-lesion table; applying these to boxing is a conservative organisational choice, not a boxing rule
LIMITATIONS: NFHS itself states no definitive data allow prediction of when a lesion stops shedding transmissible organisms. Peer-reviewed commentary notes HSV DNA can be detected by PCR after 5 days of antiviral therapy, with unknown relation to infectivity. These are administrative return thresholds, not biological clearance
PPBF implication: PPBF may ADOPT these thresholds as its house exclusion standard by governance decision, and SHADOW may display the adopted table and compute an earliest-eligible-return DATE for coach reference. SHADOW must never decide that a lesion is or is not infectious, and return requires written clinician clearance.
Source: NFHS Sports Medicine Advisory Committee. Sports-Related Skin Infections Position Statement and Guidelines (2022 revision) and NFHS Medical Release Form for Participation with Skin Lesion(s). | Pujalte GGA, et al. More Than Skin Deep: Dermatologic Conditions in Athletes. Sports Health. 2022. (PMID 35034516; doi 10.1177/19417381211065026 (commentary); NFHS statement has no DOI)

text_content:
[COACHING/FILM-STUDY INTERPRETATION] Daily pre-practice and pre-competition skin checks are the recommended prevention practice in wrestling; the recognition step is performed by staff, the diagnosis and clearance by a health-care professional.
Effect/estimate: Practice recommendation; no controlled effect estimate located
Population: High school wrestlers | level: high school | sex: mixed | age: adolescent
Design: Governing-body educational guidance | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING PRACTICE STANDARD. In boxing the exposure is lower, so daily whole-body checks may be disproportionate; a visible-skin check is the proportionate analogue
LIMITATIONS: No trial evidence that skin-check frequency reduces infection incidence; the practice is also a privacy and safeguarding-sensitive activity with minors
PPBF implication: PPBF adopts a VISIBLE-SKIN check (face, neck, hands, forearms) at check-in, performed in an open area, never a private body inspection of a minor. Safeguarding constraint overrides hygiene convenience.
Source: National Federation of State High School Associations. Prevention Key to Reducing Skin Infections in High School Wrestling (NFHS article). (INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — no DOI/PMID; governing-body web article)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Hepatitis B transmission has been documented within contact-sport clubs, and hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for contact and collision sport athletes and for adolescent athletes.
Effect/estimate: 9/70 (13%) with occult HBV infection by PCR; 8/70 (11%) with HBV DNA detectable in sweat; correlation between blood and sweat HBV DNA r=0.52, p<0.01. Japan: identical full-length HBV sequences (subgenotype C2) in 3 club members, consistent with horizontal transmission
Population: Contact-sport athletes; Olympic wrestlers (Turkey); a wrestling club (Japan) | level: elite and club | sex: male in the cited studies | age: adolescent and adult
Design: Narrative review with recommendations; cross-sectional serology study; molecular case-series | n: 70 Olympic wrestlers (serology); 3 linked cases (Japan)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: WRESTLING-DERIVED; boxing involves bleeding facial injury, so the blood-exposure route is directly relevant
LIMITATIONS: Small samples; the sweat-transmission pathway is inferred, not demonstrated experimentally; single-country serology may not generalise; vaccination policy is a public-health decision, not a gym decision
PPBF implication: Universal precautions and a stop-for-blood rule belong in the SOP: any bleeding stops the drill, wound is covered before return, blood-contaminated surfaces and clothing are handled with gloves and disinfected. PPBF does not advise on vaccination — it signposts to the athlete's clinician or public health.
Source: Kordi R, Wallace WA. Br J Sports Med. 2004. | Bereket-Yucel S. Br J Sports Med. 2007. | Takata Y, et al. Am J Case Rep. 2020. (PMID 15562159; doi 10.1136/bjsm.2004.011643 | PMID 17331974; doi 10.1136/bjsm.2006.032847 | PMID 32863382; doi 10.12659/AJCR.925044)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Hand-contact surfaces of exercise equipment were frequently contaminated with rhinovirus, and in a one-week trial, twice-daily disinfection did not reduce the prevalence of viral isolation.
Effect/estimate: Viruses (generally rhinovirus) on 63/100 (63%) surfaces; weight equipment 73% vs aerobic 51% (p=0.026); viral positivity 48% before cleaning vs 86% after (no reduction); no pathogenic bacteria cultured
Population: Two fitness centres in a US military community | level: NA (general fitness users) | sex: mixed | age: adult
Design: Observational culture study plus before-after disinfection intervention | n: 100 hand-contact surfaces
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: General fitness facility; boxing gyms share the fomite structure (bags, gloves, ropes, handles)
LIMITATIONS: Single week, two facilities, 2006 methods; culture positivity is not the same as transmissible dose; disinfection protocol, product and contact time were not characterised, so this is NOT evidence that correct disinfection fails
PPBF implication: Critical caveat for the cleaning schedule: a wipe-down that ignores label contact time is theatre. The SOP must specify product, dilution and dwell time, and must not promise an infection-rate reduction.
Source: Goldhammer KA, et al. Prospective study of bacterial and viral contamination of exercise equipment. Clin J Sport Med. 2006. (PMID 16377973; doi 10.1097/01.jsm.0000181436.41268.1f)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Cultivable surface contamination on gym equipment is dominated by skin-associated taxa and varies strongly by time of day, with midday sampling markedly more likely to be contaminated than morning.
Effect/estimate: Skin-associated taxa 72.2% of isolates; adjusted OR for contamination at noon vs morning 7.19 (p<0.001); overall diversity stable across devices (Shannon p=0.44)
Population: A single public fitness facility | level: NA | sex: NA | age: NA
Design: Repeated-measures observational surface sampling with MALDI-TOF identification and mixed-effects modelling | n: 180 surface samples from 12 devices, 3 times daily over 5 weekdays; 248 isolates, 61 species
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: General fitness facility transfer
LIMITATIONS: Single facility, one week, culture-based; contamination is not infection; no clinical outcome measured
PPBF implication: Supports a MID-DAY / between-session reset clean rather than open-and-close only. Exact frequency remains a PROPOSED PPBF PARAMETER pending PPBF's own occupancy data.
Source: Martens M, et al. Microbial Contamination of Gym Equipment: Diversity Patterns, Temporal Dynamics, Staphylococcus Hotspots, and Device-Level Risk Indices. Pathogens. 2026. (PMID 42515034; doi 10.3390/pathogens15070707)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An EPA-registered disinfectant only achieves its labelled kill claim if the surface stays visibly wet for the full labelled contact time; applying and immediately wiping does not disinfect to the stated standard.
Effect/estimate: Contact time is product-specific and label-specified; the surface must be visibly wet for its full duration, reapplying if it dries
Population: Any hard-surface disinfection setting | level: NA | sex: NA | age: NA
Design: Regulatory guidance | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Direct — regulatory requirement, not a sport finding
LIMITATIONS: US EPA framework; other jurisdictions use different registration schemes (e.g. Health Canada DIN, EU BPR). Contact times differ per product and per target organism, so no single number can be written into an SOP
PPBF implication: The cleaning schedule must record PRODUCT + EPA REG. NO. + LABEL CONTACT TIME per surface class, and the checklist must ask 'kept wet for the full label time?' rather than 'wiped?'. SHADOW may store and display the label parameters; it must never invent a contact time.
Source: US Environmental Protection Agency. Selected EPA-Registered Disinfectants — how to use them properly (contact time guidance). | US CDC. Environmental Cleaning & Disinfection: What is Contact Time? (INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — regulatory guidance, no DOI/PMID)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Non-accidental violence in sport spans psychological, physical, sexual harassment and abuse, and neglect; child, disabled, elite and LGBT athletes are at highest risk, psychological abuse underlies the other forms, and organisational silence is a recognised aggravating factor.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative typology and organisational recommendations
Population: Athletes across sport | level: all | sex: all | age: all, with specific attention to children
Design: International consensus statement | n: NA
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: Cross-sport consensus applied to a boxing club
LIMITATIONS: Consensus, 2016 vintage; implementation evidence is thin (see B3-043); does not resolve jurisdictional legal duties
PPBF implication: Defines the categories the PPBF safeguarding SOP must cover. SHADOW may route and timestamp a report and must never triage, assess credibility, or decide an outcome.
Source: Mountjoy M, et al. IOC consensus statement: harassment and abuse (non-accidental violence) in sport. Br J Sports Med. 2016. (PMID 27118273; doi 10.1136/bjsports-2016-096121)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Large European prevalence surveys of adults recalling childhood sport report high proportions experiencing interpersonal violence inside sport, most commonly psychological.
Effect/estimate: Six countries, inside sport: psychological violence 65%, physical 44%, neglect 37%, non-contact sexual 35%, contact sexual 20%; males 79% vs females 71% across all categories. NL/BE: psychological 38%, physical 11%, sexual 14%
Population: Adults aged 18-30 who participated in organised sport before age 18, six European countries; separately Netherlands and Belgium | level: organised youth sport, all levels | sex: 49.3% male / 50% female in the six-country sample | age: recalled experiences before age 18
Design: Retrospective self-report prevalence surveys | n: N=10,302 (six countries); >4,000 (NL/BE)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: European youth sport; US legal and reporting context differs; boxing not disaggregated
LIMITATIONS: Retrospective recall; broad instrument thresholds substantially inflate figures relative to legal definitions of abuse; the two studies use different instruments, hence the large discrepancy — do NOT average them
PPBF implication: Establishes that safeguarding is a baseline operational risk in youth sport, not an exceptional event. Justifies routine, low-friction reporting routes for athletes and parents in the app.
Source: Hartill M, et al. Child Abuse Negl. 2023. | Vertommen T, et al. Child Abuse Negl. 2016. (PMID 37931542; doi 10.1016/j.chiabu.2023.106513 | PMID 26516053; doi 10.1016/j.chiabu.2015.10.006)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Sport federations frequently have safeguarding policy without implemented practice, and a culture of silence is a documented organisational failure mode.
Effect/estimate: Qualitative: few or no measures taken by most federations; conflict between visibility and invisibility of the issue
Population: Ten largest Swedish child/youth sport federations | level: national federation level | sex: NA | age: child and youth sport

Population: Surgical patients, eight hospitals across eight countries | level: NA | sex: mixed | age: >=16 years

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of dropout in youth soccer reported an annual weighted mean dropout rate of 23.9%, with meta-regression indicating rates stable from ages 10-19 and higher rates for girls (26.8%) than boys (21.4%).
Effect/estimate: 23.9% annual weighted mean dropout; girls 26.8%, boys 21.4%
Population: Youth soccer players from five countries | level: Organised club youth soccer, mixed levels | sex: both (sex-stratified) | age: 10-18 years (meta-regression to 19)
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis with mixed-effects meta-regression; 12 studies identified, results based on 10 included articles | n: 724,036 youths
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT - soccer to boxing is unvalidated
LIMITATIONS: Sport-specific to soccer; dropout definitions vary across the included studies; registration-based rather than attendance-based in most sources; no combat-sport data
PPBF implication: Supplies the ONLY defensible external order-of-magnitude reference for annual youth-sport attrition, but must be labelled as soccer. PPBF must not adopt 23.9% as a boxing target or benchmark; it is a comparator with an explicit population label (KPI B4-K034).
Source: Percept Mot Skills, 2015. A systematic review and meta-analysis of dropout rates in youth soccer. (PMID 26595205; doi:10.2466/10.PMS.121c23x0)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A retrospective cohort of Australian youth swimmers used Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with Cox regression on registration data and reported a median sustained participation of 4 years (95% CI 3.93-4.06), with 15.9% still participating at 10 years, and identified age group as associated with dropout.
Effect/estimate: Median sustained participation 4 years (95% CI 3.93-4.06); 15.9% participating at 10 years; hazard ratio for dropout markedly higher for 10-year-olds vs 15-year-olds
Population: New South Wales registered youth swimmers | level: Club and competitive swimming | sex: both (9,400 female, 7,761 male) | age: 10-15 years
Design: Retrospective cohort using registration and competition data; Kaplan-Meier plus Cox proportional hazards | n: 17,161 swimmers (registration analysis)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT - method transfers, the numbers do not
LIMITATIONS: Swimming-specific; registration-based exposure (not attendance); retrospective; a national registry has far more complete follow-up than a single gym will have
PPBF implication: Direct methodological precedent for the retention analysis plan: KM plus Cox on club registration/attendance data is an established approach in youth sport. PPBF should adopt the method and generate its own numbers, not import the swimming figures.
Source: Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2020. Sink or Swim? A survival analysis of sport dropout in Australian youth swimmers. (PMID 32668035; doi:10.1111/sms.13771)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A survival analysis of French swimmers (n=160,861 under age 21) using Kaplan-Meier curves reported dropout peaks at 13.16 years for girls and 17.50 years for boys, and a large gradient by performance level - at age 13 the top 10% of female swimmers had a dropout rate of 8.7% versus 78.1% for the bottom 10%.
Effect/estimate: Dropout peak at 13.16 y (girls) and 17.50 y (boys); age 13 dropout 8.7% top decile vs 78.1% bottom decile (female)
Population: French registered swimmers | level: Registered competitive swimming across performance levels | sex: both (sex-stratified) | age: under 21 years
Design: Registry cohort with chi-squared tests and Kaplan-Meier survival curves | n: 160,861 swimmers
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Swimming-specific; performance-level stratification reflects a selection system that a community boxing gym does not operate; registry data cannot distinguish quitting from switching sports
PPBF implication: Supports stratifying PPBF retention curves by age band and by ability/lane, and warns that a program which visibly sorts athletes by performance may accelerate dropout among the lowest-performing - directly relevant to how PPBF designs its development lanes.
Source: Front Sports Act Living, 2025. A survival analysis of dropout among French swimmers. (PMID 40110418; doi:10.3389/fspor.2025.1509306)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A registry study of 1,898 male handball players completing U20 eligibility in Hungary (2013-2023) using logistic regression and survival analysis found youth-to-senior dropout associated with structural and organisational factors including competition reform exposure, homegrown status, late-adolescent club mobility and team competitive strength - not only individual-level factors.
Effect/estimate: Associations reported for birth cohort, competition reform exposure, homegrown status, club mobility and team strength; specific coefficients not extracted here
Population: Elite youth handball players, Hungary | level: Elite youth to senior transition | sex: male | age: U20 transition
Design: Longitudinal registry cohort; multivariable logistic regression and survival analysis | n: 1,898 players
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT and from an elite population
LIMITATIONS: Elite male handball; a youth-to-senior transition is a different construct from community-gym retention; observational, so associations are not causal
PPBF implication: Justifies including organisational and structural covariates (lane changes, coach changes, schedule changes, fee changes) in the PPBF dropout hazard model, not only athlete characteristics.
Source: Front Sports Act Living, 2026. The achievement-dropout paradox: structural and performance predictors of youth-to-senior transition attrition in elite handball. (PMID 42358508; doi:10.3389/fspor.2026.1868532)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 prospective cohort studies in amateur boxing reported pooled competition injury incidence of 54.7 per 1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8 per 1000 minutes of exposure (95% CI 4.2-10.9), and training injury incidence of 1.3 per 1000 hours (95% CI 0.2-7.0), with head and neck the most commonly injured region in competition (median 72%, range 46-100%).
Effect/estimate: Competition 54.7/1000 athlete-exposures (95% CI 33.8-88.4) and 6.8/1000 min (95% CI 4.2-10.9); training 1.3/1000 h (95% CI 0.2-7.0)
Population: Amateur boxers | level: Amateur competition and training | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract; amateur boxing cohorts are predominantly male | age: Not specified in the abstract; predominantly adult amateur
Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies; random-effects models | n: 17 studies
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but competition-population specific
LIMITATIONS: Very wide confidence intervals, especially for training; heterogeneous injury definitions and denominators across studies; competition populations, not community youth non-contact programs; the training estimate spans an order of magnitude
PPBF implication: Establishes that athlete-exposures, exposure-minutes and exposure-hours are all in legitimate use as boxing injury denominators - and that they are not interchangeable. PPBF must fix ONE denominator per safety KPI and state it (KPIs B4-K040 to B4-K043). The wide CIs mean no external rate can serve as a PPBF safety target.
Source: J Sci Med Sport, 2022. Epidemiology of injuries in amateur boxing: A systematic review and meta-analysis. (PMID 36195527; doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2022.09.165)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A second systematic review and meta-analysis of 21st-century boxing epidemiology calculated injury incidence rates per 1000 boxers, per 1000 competition exposures, per 1000 minutes of competition and per 1000 minutes of training, with subgroup meta-analyses by boxing type - illustrating that a single 'boxing injury rate' does not exist independent of its denominator.
Effect/estimate: Multiple incidence rates reported across four different denominators; sample-size weighted means with 95% CIs
Population: Organised boxing worldwide | level: Amateur and professional | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract | age: not specified in the abstract
Design: PRISMA systematic review with single-arm random-effects meta-analyses; Level of evidence 3 | n: Studies published January 2000 - November 2021 (count not extracted)
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC
LIMITATIONS: Level 3 evidence; heterogeneity across boxing types; no youth community-program subgroup
PPBF implication: Reinforces that PPBF's dashboard must display the exposure denominator next to every safety rate, and must never compare a PPBF rate to an external rate computed on a different denominator.
Source: Orthop J Sports Med, 2023. Incidence Rates and Pathology Types of Boxing-Specific Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Epidemiology Studies in the 21st Century. (PMID 37025124; doi:10.1177/23259671221127669)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 5-year prospective surveillance study of the Great Britain amateur boxing squad (66 boxers, 2005-2009) found hand injuries were the most common by location overall, more injuries occurred during training than during competition, and reported a total competition injury rate of 828 per 1000 hours.
Effect/estimate: Total competition injury rate 828 per 1000 hours; more total injuries in training than competition; hand the most-injured location
Population: Great Britain elite amateur boxing squad | level: Elite amateur (national squad) | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract | age: elite squad athletes; not specified
Design: Longitudinal prospective injury surveillance, medically diagnosed injuries | n: 66 boxers over 5 years
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but ELITE population
LIMITATIONS: Single elite squad; small n; medically diagnosed definition (a national squad has medical staff a community gym does not, which inflates capture relative to a community setting); the per-1000-hour competition rate is not comparable to per-athlete-exposure rates
PPBF implication: Training exposure, not just competition, must be captured in PPBF's safety denominators - most injury volume in this elite cohort occurred in training. Ascertainment differences between a medically staffed squad and a community gym mean PPBF's rate will not be comparable to this figure.
Source: Br J Sports Med, 2015. Boxing injury epidemiology in the Great Britain team: a 5-year surveillance study of medically diagnosed injury incidence and outcome. (PMID 26192194; doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-094755)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A one-year prospective cohort of 33 amateur and 14 professional boxers in Victoria, Australia measured training and competition exposure and recorded 21 injuries, of which most were to the head region (71%), with concussion the most common single injury (33%), and calculated an overall rate of 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing.
Effect/estimate: 2.0 injuries per 1000 hours of boxing; 71% head region (the reported CI in the abstract spans an implausible negative lower bound, indicating an unreliable interval); 33% concussion
Population: Registered amateur and professional boxers, Victoria, Australia | level: Amateur and professional | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract | age: not specified; adult registered boxers
Design: Prospective cohort with one-year follow-up and measured exposure | n: 47 boxers; 21 injuries
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC, small volunteer sample
LIMITATIONS: Very small sample (21 injuries total); volunteer participants; adult registered boxers, not youth; the reported confidence interval for the head-region proportion is not usable as printed; 2004-2005 data predates several rule changes
PPBF implication: Illustrates that small-cohort boxing injury estimates are extremely imprecise. PPBF must set a minimum-exposure floor before publishing any injury rate (KPI B4-K043 sets 10 incidents and 5000 athlete-sessions) and report raw counts below it.
Source: Br J Sports Med, 2006. A prospective cohort study of injury in amateur and professional boxing. (PMID 16807306; doi:10.1136/bjsm.2006.025924)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The International Olympic Committee consensus statement on methods for recording and reporting epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport (2020), including the STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance, provides the standard for injury definitions, exposure denominators and reporting, developed by an expert working group through an open survey and a three-day consensus meeting.
Effect/estimate: Methodological recommendations; no effect estimate
Population: All sports injury and illness surveillance | level: all levels | sex: all | age: all
Design: Expert consensus statement with reporting-checklist extension | n: n/a (consensus)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL STANDARD - applies across sports including boxing
LIMITATIONS: Consensus rather than trial evidence; written primarily for research surveillance rather than community-club operational reporting, so PPBF will need to adapt rather than adopt wholesale
PPBF implication: PPBF should adopt IOC-consistent injury definitions and exposure denominators so its safety data is interpretable and comparable. This is the authoritative source for KPI B4-K040 to B4-K043 denominator design.
Source: Br J Sports Med, 2020. International Olympic Committee consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020 (including STROBE Extension for Sport Injury and Illness Surveillance). (PMID 32071062; doi:10.1136/bjsports-2019-101969)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A cross-sectional observational study of AIBA competitions, comparing World Series Boxing (no head guards) with head-guarded AIBA competitions and comparing the 2009/2011 world championships (head guards) with 2013 (no head guards), found the number of stoppages due to head blows was significantly decreased without head guards, alongside a notable increase in cuts.
Effect/estimate: Significant decrease in head-blow stoppages without head guards; increase in cuts
Population: Elite amateur boxers in AIBA competition | level: Elite international amateur | sex: not disaggregated in the abstract | age: senior elite
Design: Cross-sectional observational study with prospective data collection by ringside physicians | n: Not extracted; measured as stoppages per 10,000 rounds and per 1000 hours
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but ELITE COMPETITION - does not transfer to gym sparring or youth
LIMITATIONS: Observational and confounded by concurrent rule and population changes; stoppage counts are a proxy for brain injury, not a direct measure; elite adult competition only; head guards remain mandatory in many youth and national contexts
PPBF implication: Stoppage counts are shaped by rules and equipment, not only by athlete or coach behaviour. This is a core reason KPI B4-K045 must be framed as a vigilance indicator and never benchmarked downward. PPBF must follow its own sanctioning body's current head-guard rule; nothing here authorises a local deviation.
Source: Clin J Sport Med, 2017. Use of Head Guards in AIBA Boxing Tournaments - A Cross-Sectional Observational Study. (PMID 27116592; doi:10.1097/JSM.0000000000000322)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A review of 29,357 Olympic boxing bouts from 1952 to 2011 found that rule changes altered the rates of health-relevant verdicts - for example an increase in the RSC-Injury rate (0.72% to 2.42%) following the standing-count rule, and changes in RSC-Injury and RSC-Head rates following subsequent rule modifications.
Effect/estimate: RSC-Injury rate rose from 0.72% to 2.42% after the standing-count rule; further changes in RSC-Head and RSC-Injury rates after later rule changes
Population: Olympic boxing competitors | level: Olympic/elite amateur | sex: predominantly male over most of the period | age: senior elite
Design: Retrospective analysis of competition records across 59 years | n: 29,357 bouts
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC, elite competition
LIMITATIONS: Web-sourced retrospective records; ecological analysis with no individual-level data; confounded by concurrent changes in officiating, scoring and population; verdict recording practice itself changed over the period
PPBF implication: Bout verdict rates are a property of the rule environment, not a measure of coaching quality or athlete development. This is direct evidence against any win-rate or verdict-based performance metric (KPIs B4-K061, B4-K113).
Source: Br J Sports Med, 2013. Amateur boxing in the last 59 years. Impact of rules changes on the type of verdicts recorded and implications on boxers' health. (PMID 23314931; doi:10.1136/bjsports-2012-091771)

text_content:
[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] An exploratory observational cohort of seven competitive boxers used instrumented mouthguards and the SCAT5 symptom scale before, immediately after and 48 hours after sparring, and found no group-level difference in symptom scores pre- to post-sparring; the authors describe the acute dose-response relationship between head impact exposure and concussion as unresolved.
Effect/estimate: No group-level pre-post symptom difference; authors recommend individual-specific and cumulative approaches
Population: Competitive boxers | level: Competitive amateur | sex: not specified in the abstract | age: adult competitive
Design: Exploratory observational cohort with instrumented mouthguards and repeated symptom measurement | n: 7 boxers
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but n=7
LIMITATIONS: Seven participants; exploratory qualitative analysis of impact metrics; no control condition; self-reported symptoms are under-reported in competitive settings; a null result at n=7 is uninformative about a true effect
PPBF implication: There is NO validated head-impact or symptom threshold PPBF could implement. KPI B4-K046 reports symptom-flag rates descriptively and routes every flag to a qualified human; SHADOW must never compute a safe-exposure threshold. TBD - PPBF cannot resolve this and must not attempt to.
Source: J Sci Med Sport, 2026. Exploring the link between acute symptom changes and repetitive head impacts in boxing sparring. (PMID 41672855; doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2026.01.018)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Instrumented mouthguards worn by 22 male US Military Academy cadets during a compulsory introductory boxing course captured 809 video-verified impacts across 205 analysed player-bouts, averaging 3.9 impacts per player-bout.
Effect/estimate: Mean 3.9 video-verified impacts per player-bout
Population: US Military Academy cadets in an introductory boxing course | level: Novice/introductory | sex: male | age: mean 19.9 (SD 1.1) years
Design: Observational instrumented-mouthguard study with video verification; preliminary dataset | n: 22 subjects; 205 player-bouts; 809 verified impacts
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but young-adult male military cadets, not youth community athletes
LIMITATIONS: Preliminary dataset; all male; young-adult military population under compulsory participation; impact counts are not injury outcomes; sensor data quality in boxing is a documented problem
PPBF implication: Head-impact exposure is measurable in principle, but instrumenting youth athletes raises consent, cost and data-governance questions PPBF has not resolved. PPBF's practical exposure proxy remains logged sparring rounds and contact minutes (KPIs B4-K041, B4-K042).
Source: Mil Med, 2023. Measurement of Head Kinematics Using Instrumented Mouthguards During Introductory Boxing Courses in U.S. Military Academy Cadets. (PMID 37948285; doi:10.1093/milmed/usad249)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A prospective controlled study of 82 collegiate amateur boxers in a 7-day single-elimination tournament, with 30 matched non-boxing controls, administered a computerised battery before the tournament and within two hours of each bout, testing simple and choice reaction time, working memory and learning across 142 tested bouts.
Effect/estimate: Effect direction and magnitude not extracted from the abstract text available; design and measures verified
Population: Collegiate amateur boxers with matched non-boxing controls | level: Collegiate amateur | sex: not specified in the abstract | age: collegiate; not specified
Design: Prospective controlled study with repeated computerised cognitive testing | n: 82 boxers (159 bouts, 142 tested) and 30 controls
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC, collegiate adult
LIMITATIONS: Participants had no history of recent concussion or prior brain injury, so results do not generalise to athletes with injury history; 2004 study using a computerised battery of that era; acute testing only, no long-term follow-up; tournament format concentrates exposure atypically
PPBF implication: Repeated same-period bout exposure is a recognised research concern in amateur boxing. PPBF should record bout density per athlete as a monitored exposure variable, with any competition-scheduling decision made by a qualified coach and physician under the sanctioning body's rules - never by SHADOW.
Source: Neurology, 2004. A prospective controlled study of cognitive function during an amateur boxing tournament. (PMID 15136671; doi:10.1212/wnl.62.9.1497)

text_content:
[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR identified 16 documents using NON-CONTACT boxing exercise as an intervention, reporting reductions in symptoms of anxiety, depression, PTSD and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and concluded that the evidence is preliminary.
Effect/estimate: Reported symptom reductions across several conditions; the authors characterise the evidence as preliminary
Population: Mixed clinical and general populations in the included documents | level: Non-competitive; non-contact boxing exercise | sex: mixed | age: predominantly adult
Design: Scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of academic and grey literature | n: 16 documents
Boxing-specific: yes (non-contact boxing exercise specifically) | transfer status: BOXING-SPECIFIC but NON-CONTACT and largely adult clinical populations
LIMITATIONS: Scoping review, so no pooled effect estimate and no formal risk-of-bias synthesis; includes grey literature; the interventions are non-contact boxing-style exercise, which is a different exposure from competitive boxing training; mostly adult, not youth
PPBF implication: PPBF may honestly describe non-contact boxing-style exercise as having preliminary mental-health evidence in adult populations. It must NOT claim mental-health outcomes for its youth contact program, and must not present this as validation of PPBF's own effect (KPI B4-K085).
Source: Am J Lifestyle Med, 2022. Boxing as an Intervention in Mental Health: A Scoping Review. (PMID 37426738; doi:10.1177/15598276221124095)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The England Boxing rule book applies protective medical suspensions where a boxer receives a knockout or where a sparring session is stopped because a boxer received blows to the head, requires return via the England Boxing Concussion Protocol with separate annexes for under-18s and over-19s, prohibits a boxer serving a medical suspension from boxing, and sets age-graded participation rules including that a child under 10 may join a club and take classes but may not box competitively, take a skills bout, or spar, with round durations and weight-difference limits specified by age category.
Effect/estimate: Rules, not estimates: medical suspension following KO or head-blow sparring stoppage; concussion protocol by age band; under-10 sparring and competition prohibition; 2 kg weight-difference limit in the youngest categories
Population: Amateur boxers registered with England Boxing | level: All amateur levels including youth | sex: all | age: 10 years upward, with age-banded categories
Design: Governing-body rulebook (not a study) | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - England Boxing rules do not apply in the United States
LIMITATIONS: Applies only within England Boxing's jurisdiction; rulebook editions change annually, so the specific edition must be cited; PPBF operates under USA Boxing rules and must not apply England Boxing provisions as if they were its own
PPBF implication: Confirms that (i) sparring incidents, not only bouts, trigger protective suspensions in at least one major jurisdiction, and (ii) age-graded contact restriction is a rulebook matter. PPBF must encode its OWN sanctioning body's current rules, and KPI B4-K047 must be parameterised by jurisdiction rather than hard-coded.
Source: England Boxing Technical and Competition Rules (2025 and 2026 editions) and England Boxing Rule Book (2019, 2022/23, 2023/24 editions), sections on medical suspensions, concussion protocol annexes B1/B2, and age categories. (n/a - governing-body rulebook)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] USA Boxing rules require the ringside doctor to complete and sign a Restriction Affidavit after a bout resulting in knockout or technical knockout, recommending prescribed rest days or protective restrictive measures, with the data recorded in the USA Boxing database; the rulebook sets age divisions (for example Junior 15-16, Youth 17-18, Elite 19-40), sets minimum bout counts for entry to certain advancing competitions, and prohibits exhibition bouts.
Effect/estimate: Rules, not estimates: mandatory Restriction Affidavit after KO/TKO with prescribed rest days set by the ringside doctor; division age bands; bout-count minimums for certain advancing competitions; exhibition bouts prohibited
Population: Amateur boxers registered with USA Boxing | level: All USA Boxing amateur levels | sex: all | age: Age-banded divisions from Junior through Elite and Masters
Design: Governing-body rulebook (not a study) | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: yes | transfer status: JURISDICTION-SPECIFIC - USA Boxing
LIMITATIONS: Rulebook editions are revised annually (editions dated January 2024 and January 2025 were both retrieved); PPBF must work from the current edition, and local boxing committees and state commissions may add requirements
PPBF implication: The rest period after a KO/TKO is set by the ringside physician on a per-case affidavit, not by a fixed formula. SHADOW must therefore store and enforce the physician's recorded restriction (KPI B4-K047) and must never compute, shorten or infer one. Verdict codes for KPI B4-K061 should follow the USA Boxing passbook vocabulary.
Source: USA Boxing National Rule Book (editions effective January 1, 2024 and January 1, 2025), sections on Restriction Affidavits after KO/TKO, age divisions, competition entry requirements, and the prohibition on exhibition bouts. (n/a - governing-body rulebook)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A cohort of preprofessional ballet (n=85) and contemporary (n=60) dancers completing weekly health-problem questionnaires under three injury definitions - time loss, medical attention, and any complaint - was designed specifically to describe how the choice of definition changes estimated injury prevalence, incidence and severity.
Effect/estimate: Injury burden estimates differ by definition; percent agreement between registration methods was assessed
Population: Preprofessional ballet and contemporary dancers | level: Preprofessional full-time training | sex: predominantly female (77/85 and 58/60) | age: ballet median 15 (range 11-19); contemporary median 19 (range 17-30)
Design: Prospective cohort with weekly self-report (modified OSTRC health-problem questionnaire) plus physiotherapist injury reports | n: 145 dancers
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL - the finding is about measurement, and transfers across sports
LIMITATIONS: Dance population, predominantly female; the specific magnitudes are dance-specific and are not transferable, only the methodological point is
PPBF implication: PPBF must FIX and PUBLISH its injury definition before computing any safety rate (KPI B4-K043), and must break the trend series if the definition ever changes. Comparing a PPBF rate to any external rate computed under a different definition is invalid.
Source: J Orthop Sports Phys Ther, 2018. The Influence of Injury Definition on Injury Burden in Preprofessional Ballet and Contemporary Dancers. (PMID 29237356; doi:10.2519/jospt.2018.7542)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] An analysis using two oncology phase II trials as worked examples plus simulation showed that informative censoring biases the Kaplan-Meier estimate, with the magnitude of bias depending primarily on the proportion of patients informatively censored and secondarily on the hazard ratio between censored and continuing patients.
Effect/estimate: Bias magnitude driven mainly by the proportion informatively censored, secondarily by the hazard ratio between groups
Population: Clinical trial participants (methodological demonstration) | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Methodological paper with worked trial examples and simulation study | n: Two trials plus simulations
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL - applies to any survival analysis including sport retention
LIMITATIONS: Oncology context; the principle transfers but the specific magnitudes do not
PPBF implication: PPBF retention analysis has a direct informative-censoring risk: athletes who stop attending but are never marked as exited are effectively censored at a moment correlated with their hazard. This is why the analysis plan requires an explicit exit-event table and a sensitivity analysis on censoring assumptions.
Source: J Clin Oncol, 2014. Impact of informative censoring on the Kaplan-Meier estimate of progression-free survival in phase II clinical trials. (PMID 25113767; doi:10.1200/JCO.2014.55.6340)

Effect/estimate: No effect estimate; methodological requirement

Effect/estimate: Systematic responder/non-responder differences in characteristics and in some association estimates
Population: Adult disaster-cohort survivors and Dutch adolescents respectively | level: n/a | sex: both | age: adults; and adolescents from mean age 11.09 (SD 0.56) to 19.1 (SD 0.60)
Design: Longitudinal cohort non-response analyses | n: 67,670 adults; 2,230 adolescents at baseline
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL - transfers to exit surveys and satisfaction surveys

Effect/estimate: Power determined by expected event count via an equivalent two-sample formulation
Population: n/a (methodological) | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Methodological paper with simulation validation | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL
LIMITATIONS: Approximation; performance at very small event counts needs checking in PPBF's own setting
PPBF implication: PPBF's covariate-adjusted dropout models are limited by the number of DROPOUT EVENTS, not the roster size. The analysis plan therefore specifies an events-per-variable rule and restricts the covariate set until enough events accumulate.
Source: Stat Med, 2004. A simple approach to power and sample size calculations in logistic regression and Cox regression models. (PMID 15160408; doi:10.1002/sim.1753)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Fine-Gray proportional subdistribution hazards model and the associated competing-risks literature establish that when more than one type of event can end follow-up, treating competing events as censored misstates the cumulative incidence of the event of interest, and that cause-specific and subdistribution approaches answer different questions.
Effect/estimate: Method, not an effect estimate: subdistribution hazard model for competing risks; cumulative incidence function rather than 1 minus Kaplan-Meier
Population: n/a (methodological) | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Foundational statistical method paper plus epidemiological methods reviews and reporting recommendations | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL - applies directly to sport retention with multiple exit types
LIMITATIONS: Requires enough events per cause; interpretation of subdistribution hazard ratios is frequently misreported, which is why reporting recommendations exist
PPBF implication: Central to the retention plan: aging out, transferring to another club and dropping out are competing events. The worked synthetic example demonstrates that treating them as censoring overstated dropout cumulative incidence by roughly 8 percentage points at day 540 in that simulation. PPBF must report cause-specific cumulative incidence (KPI B4-K036).
Source: J Am Stat Assoc, 1999. A Proportional Hazards Model for the Subdistribution of a Competing Risk. Supporting: Am J Epidemiol, 2009. Competing Risk Regression Models for Epidemiologic Data. Int J Epidemiol, 2012. Competing risks in epidemiology: possibilities and pitfalls. Stat Med, 2017. Practical recommendations for reporting Fine-Gray model analyses. (doi:10.1080/01621459.1999.10474144; doi:10.1093/aje/kwp107; doi:10.1093/ije/dyr213; doi:10.1002/sim.7501)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Multiple imputation by chained equations is an established approach for handling missing covariate data, with published guidance on its practical use, its assumptions, and when it is and is not appropriate in clinical research.
Effect/estimate: Method, not an effect estimate
Population: n/a (methodological) | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Methodological guidance papers and software documentation | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL
LIMITATIONS: Assumes missing at random; will NOT fix the missing-not-at-random exit-reason problem, only missing covariates; unstable at very small sample sizes

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Concept-mapping work with 142 youth soccer players, 37 coaches and 57 parents produced the Fun Integration Theory, identifying 4 fundamental tenets, 11 fun-dimensions and 81 fun-determinants, and reported that children cite fun as the primary reason for participation and its absence as the leading reason for youth sport attrition. Separate prospective work in team sport links enjoyment and behavioural intention to subsequent organised participation and dropout.
Effect/estimate: 11 fun-dimensions and 81 fun-determinants identified; enjoyment and behavioural intention predict participation and dropout in the prospective work
Population: Youth soccer players, their coaches and parents; and adolescents in team sport | level: Organised youth soccer across competition levels | sex: both (stratified by sex in the concept mapping) | age: youth soccer players; adolescents
Design: Mixed-method concept mapping (FUN MAPS); and prospective observational studies of enjoyment and intention predicting participation | n: 142 players, 37 coaches, 57 parents in the concept mapping
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM OTHER SPORT - soccer and general team sport to boxing is unvalidated
LIMITATIONS: Concept mapping produces a framework, not an effect size or a threshold; soccer-specific; self-reported; boxing has a different affective and risk profile from soccer and the fun-determinants may not map across
PPBF implication: Justifies measuring athlete-reported enjoyment as a leading indicator of retention (KPI B4-K071) rather than relying on attendance alone. Supplies NO numeric target - the construct is measurable, the threshold is not established.

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A cohort study using the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (n=4,241, waves 3 to 9) found continued sport participation associated with lower odds of school absence (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.26-0.74), higher numeracy (B=20.21, 95% CI 14.56-25.86) and literacy (B=9.42, 95% CI 2.82-16.02) scores, higher end-of-school academic performance and higher odds of university study (OR 1.78). A smaller US longitudinal study (n=271) found sport participation at year one predicted English and mathematics achievement at year two controlling for prior achievement, explaining approximately 7% additional variance.
Effect/estimate: Australia: absence OR 0.44 (0.26-0.74); numeracy B=20.21 (14.56-25.86); literacy B=9.42 (2.82-16.02); university OR 1.78. US: ~7% additional variance explained
Population: Nationally representative Australian children; and US Mid-Atlantic high-school students | level: General sport participation, not elite | sex: both | age: 4-5 years to 20-21 years (Australia); high school (US)
Design: Longitudinal cohort with latent class analysis (Australia); longitudinal study with controls for prior achievement and SES (US) | n: 4,241 (Australia); 271 (US)
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM GENERAL SPORT - not boxing, and not causal
LIMITATIONS: OBSERVATIONAL: children who continue in sport differ systematically from those who do not (self-selection on family resources, health, prior ability), so these associations cannot be read as effects of a program; neither study is boxing; the US study is small and single-region; residual confounding is likely substantial
PPBF implication: PPBF may state that sport participation is ASSOCIATED with academic outcomes in general populations. It must NOT claim its own program improves academic outcomes without externally measured, consented outcome data and a comparison group. KPI B4-K085 encodes this as a hard gate on external claims. Correlation is not causation and self-selection is the dominant confound.
Source: J Phys Act Health, 2023. Sport Participation for Academic Success: Evidence From the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children. Supporting: Am J Health Behav, 2017. Sport Participation and Academic Achievement: A Longitudinal Study. (PMID 38141604; doi:10.1123/jpah.2023-0506. Supporting: PMID 28452695; doi:10.5993/AJHB.41.2.9)

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport, built from a qualitative meta-study, and a scoping review of facilitative coaching behaviours both position life-skill transfer as something coaches must deliberately structure rather than an automatic byproduct of participation.
Effect/estimate: Theoretical model and behaviour taxonomy; no effect size
Population: Youth sport participants and coaches across studies | level: youth sport generally | sex: mixed | age: youth and adolescent
Design: Grounded theory from a qualitative meta-study; scoping review | n: Synthesis across primary qualitative studies
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM GENERAL YOUTH SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Qualitative synthesis; no quantified effect; no boxing-specific validation; transfer measurement instruments remain contested
PPBF implication: If PPBF intends life-skill outcomes, the coaching that produces them must be designed and delivered deliberately, and the outcome must be measured externally. Coach-observed gym behaviour is not evidence of transfer (KPI B4-K085).
Source: Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol, 2016. A grounded theory of positive youth development through sport based on results from a qualitative meta-study. Supporting: Int Rev Sport Exerc Psychol, 2021. [CONTESTED PRACTICE] Widely circulated health-club retention figures originate from trade-association industry surveys rather than peer-reviewed research. A commonly quoted 71.4% annual retention figure is attributed to IHRSA Profiles of Success reporting 2015 data from a self-selected sample of member clubs, and a corresponding 28.6% annual attrition figure is attributed to the same source; more recent trade reporting attributes a 66.4% annual retention figure to a 2025 Health and Fitness Association benchmarking report using 2024 data. Trade commentary itself notes that member clubs in these surveys tend to be better-performing than the industry as a whole.
Effect/estimate: 71.4% annual retention (2015 data) and 28.6% annual attrition, attributed to IHRSA Profiles of Success; 66.4% annual retention (2024 data), attributed to the HFA 2025 benchmarking report
Population: Commercial health clubs, predominantly adult paying members, US and international | level: n/a - commercial fitness membership | sex: mixed adult | age: predominantly adult
Design: Trade-association industry survey of self-selected member organisations; methodology not peer-reviewed and not fully public | n: Reported as ~90 companies / 4,865 facilities for the 2016 Profiles of Success edition and ~175 companies / 17,000+ facilities for the 2025 HFA report, per secondary trade sources
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: NOT TRANSFERABLE - a paying adult gym membership is a fundamentally different construct from a youth nonprofit sport program
LIMITATIONS: LOW AUTHORITY: self-selected respondent base, vendor and trade-association sourcing, methodology not peer-reviewed, definitions of retention vary between operators, figures accessed through secondary reporting rather than the primary paywalled reports. Membership churn measures a billing relationship, not participation in a developmental youth program.
PPBF implication: PPBF must NOT benchmark youth program retention against commercial gym churn. This row exists so the temptation is documented and refused: KPI B4-K011 notes the commercial billing-status convention only to reject it, and no PPBF retention KPI carries a commercial benchmark. Evidence pool (a) is recorded as LOW authority throughout the dictionary.
Source: Figures attributed to IHRSA Profiles of Success (2016 edition, 2015 data) and to the Health and Fitness Association 2025 Fitness Industry Benchmarking Report (2024 data), as reported by fitness-industry trade publications. (n/a - no DOI; industry report, primary sources paywalled)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of barriers to voluntary sport participation for children identifies cost among the reported barriers, and a parent-reported study of 218 young people with disabilities found non-participation in organised physical activity significantly predicted by the barrier that no available activities were enjoyable to the child and by lack of child motivation and happiness during activity.
Effect/estimate: Cost identified among barriers in the review; in the disability study, enjoyment-related barriers and child motivation significantly predicted non-participation
Population: Children generally; and young people with neurodevelopmental, physical and medical conditions | level: Community and organised youth sport | sex: mixed | age: children and young people
Design: Systematic review; and cross-sectional parent-report survey | n: Systematic review (study count not extracted); 218 parent respondents in the disability study
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM GENERAL YOUTH SPORT
LIMITATIONS: Barriers evidence is largely cross-sectional and parent-reported; the disability study is a specific population; neither quantifies how much cost reduction changes participation
PPBF implication: Supports collecting fee-assistance and barrier status at intake and stratifying retention by it (KPIs B4-K080, B4-K081), and supports treating enjoyment as a retention driver rather than assuming cost is the only barrier.
Source: BMC Pediatr, 2018. Barriers to voluntary participation in sport for children: a systematic review. Supporting: Front Psychol, 2020. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The Aspen Institute's Project Play State of Play reports compile US youth sport participation and cost trends, drawing on the federal National Survey of Children's Health and on Sports and Fitness Industry Association survey data. Reported figures include organised sport participation of 55% of youth in 2023 (up from 54% in 2022) per the National Survey of Children's Health, a stated federal Healthy People 2030 goal of 63% participation by 2030, and a reported 46% increase in the cost of youth sports since 2019 per Project Play research.
Effect/estimate: 55% organised sport participation in 2023 (NSCH); 63% by 2030 federal goal; 46% cost increase since 2019 (Project Play research)
Population: US youth ages 6-17 | level: Organised and casual youth sport | sex: both | age: 6-17 years
Design: Compilation of federal survey data (National Survey of Children's Health, administered through the US Census Bureau) and industry survey data (SFIA), plus Project Play's own parent surveys | n: National survey samples; specific ns not extracted
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: NATIONAL POPULATION DATA - not a club-level benchmark
LIMITATIONS: Mixed authority: the National Survey of Children's Health is a federal parent-report survey (higher authority) while SFIA data is industry survey data and Project Play is an advocacy organisation (lower authority). Reports note a roughly two-year lag in the best federal participation data. A national participation RATE is not a club RETENTION benchmark and the two must never be conflated.
PPBF implication: Useful for context on the population PPBF serves and for equity framing, and it is the correct source family for evidence pool (b) participation context. It supplies NO retention benchmark. Any PPBF use must carry the population label and the advocacy/industry sourcing caveat (KPIs B4-K080, B4-K081, B4-K082).
Source: Aspen Institute Project Play, State of Play reports (2022 through 2025 editions), compiling National Survey of Children's Health and Sports and Fitness Industry Association data. (n/a - no DOI)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of 26 studies covering 3,994 participants across 14 combat sports found weight loss practices highly prevalent, with many athletes beginning competitive weight loss as teenagers two to three times per year and typically losing under 5% of body weight in the 7-14 days before competition, and reported that the influence of scientific practitioners on athletes' practices is negligible. Related work documents concerning weight-cutting behaviours specifically in young combat sport athletes, and a cluster analysis of 164 Italian boxers found 88% used weight loss strategies, with more severe practices concentrated among professionals, higher-level athletes and females.
Effect/estimate: Weight loss typically under 5% body mass over 7-14 days pre-competition, 2-3 times per season, often initiated in the teenage years; 88% of surveyed Italian boxers used weight loss strategies
Population: Combat sport athletes across 14 sports; and Italian amateur (88%) and professional (12%) boxers | level: Amateur through professional | sex: both, with sex differences reported in the boxing cluster analysis | age: Adolescent through adult; teenage initiation specifically documented
Design: Systematic review of survey-design studies (PROSPERO CRD42023487196); and a cross-sectional questionnaire study with hierarchical clustering | n: 26 studies, 3,994 participants; 164 boxers in the cluster analysis
Boxing-specific: partly - the cluster analysis is boxing-specific; the systematic review covers combat sports including boxing | transfer status: COMBAT-SPORT SPECIFIC, with boxing-specific supporting evidence
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported survey designs throughout, subject to recall and social-desirability bias; prevalence varies widely across the included sports and countries; the reviews describe practice, not safety thresholds
PPBF implication: Weight-making behaviour starts young in combat sports and is largely unguided by qualified practitioners. PPBF must therefore treat weight-management flags as a SAFETY ROUTING function to a qualified human (KPI B4-K064), must not operate youth weight cutting, and SHADOW is prohibited from any dietary, weight-loss or target-weight output. This is a medical and safeguarding matter owned by a qualified clinician, the head coach and the guardian.
Source: Nutrients, 2024. The Practice of Weight Loss in Combat Sports Athletes: A Systematic Review. Supporting: Int J Environ Res Public Health, 2020. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The public-management and statistics literature documents that performance measurement systems produce distortion and gaming: an empirical examination of performance improvement and dysfunction, a Royal Statistical Society working-party paper on performance indicators, and an analysis of ambulance-service response-time targets all document target-induced behavioural distortion rather than genuine improvement.
Effect/estimate: Documented distortion effects including threshold effects around published targets; specific magnitudes vary by setting
Population: Public-sector and human-service organisations | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Empirical analyses of administrative performance data and expert working-party analysis | n: Varies by study
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM PUBLIC SECTOR - the mechanism is general to any published target
LIMITATIONS: Public-sector settings differ from a small nonprofit; the mechanism generalises but the magnitude in PPBF's context is unknown
PPBF implication: This is the evidential basis for the gaming_risk, perverse_incentive and mitigation columns being mandatory in the KPI dictionary, and for the explicit no-target rules on the coach override rate (B4-K103), head-blow stoppage rate (B4-K045) and competition participation (B4-K060). Publishing a target changes behaviour toward the target, not toward the underlying goal.
Source: J Public Adm Res Theory, 2009. Performance Improvement and Performance Dysfunction: An Empirical Examination of Distortionary Impacts. Supporting: J R Stat Soc Ser A, 2004. Performance Indicators: Good, Bad, and Ugly. J R Stat Soc Ser A, 2008. Hitting and Missing Targets by Ambulance Services for Emergency Calls: Effects of Different Systems of Performance Measurement. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The nonprofit management literature documents that performance and outcome measurement in human-service nonprofits is methodologically contested, frequently driven by funder accountability demands rather than by measurement validity, and that outcome measurement systems vary widely in quality and use.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate; a body of evidence on measurement practice and its drivers
Population: Nonprofit human-service organisations | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Peer-reviewed nonprofit-management research and reviews | n: Varies
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM NONPROFIT SECTOR - directly applicable to PPBF as a nonprofit
LIMITATIONS: Largely US-focused; descriptive rather than prescriptive; does not supply comparable cost or outcome benchmarks
PPBF implication: Cost-per-participant and similar efficiency ratios are not comparable across organisations without identical cost-allocation policies (KPI B4-K095). It also explains the structural pressure toward vanity metrics in grant reporting, which the dashboard honesty spec is designed to resist.

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A systematic review of burnout in sport establishes it as a recognised construct in the sport psychology literature, and a 6-year prospective longitudinal study following a graduating class from 7th to 12th grade found sports participation and weekly strenuous exercise days declined across that period (from 4.0 to 2.3 days per week of at least 60 minutes of strenuous exercise).
Effect/estimate: Weekly days of at least 60 minutes strenuous exercise fell from 4.0 to 2.3 from 7th to 12th grade (p<0.01); sports participation percentage also declined
Population: Athletes across sports; and a US school cohort followed from 7th to 12th grade | level: school and club sport | sex: both | age: adolescent, 7th to 12th grade in the longitudinal study
Design: Systematic review; and prospective longitudinal survey study with mixed-effects models | n: n varied from 35 to 77 across waves in the longitudinal study due to new enrollment and attrition
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: TRANSFER FROM GENERAL YOUTH SPORT
LIMITATIONS: The longitudinal study is small (n=35-77 per wave) and single-cohort with its own attrition, which is itself a caution about small-cohort tracking; the burnout review supplies a construct, not a screening threshold; no validated burnout instrument for community youth boxing exists
PPBF implication: Age-related decline in participation is expected and is not by itself evidence of program failure - PPBF's retention curves must be interpreted against this background trend. No validated burnout screening instrument exists for this setting, so SHADOW must not screen for burnout. TBD - PPBF would need to select and validate an instrument before measuring it.
Source: Sport Psychol, 2007. Burnout in Sport: A Systematic Review. Supporting: Sports Health, 2024. Changes in Sports Participation, Specialization, and Burnout From 7th to 12th Grade: Final Results From a 6-Year Longitudinal Study. (doi:10.1123/tsp.21.2.127. Supporting: PMID 38284394; doi:10.1177/19417381231224792)

[INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE] Systematic searching of PubMed and OpenAlex for boxing-specific club retention, dropout, or membership survival evidence returned no study reporting 30-day, 90-day, 180-day or 365-day retention for a community boxing program. The boxing-specific literature located concerns injury epidemiology, head impact exposure, competition verdicts, weight-making practices and non-contact boxing as a mental-health intervention - not participation retention.
Effect/estimate: No estimate exists
Population: Community boxing gyms | level: community/amateur | sex: all | age: youth and adult
Design: Absence of evidence following systematic database searching | n: 0 studies located
Boxing-specific: yes - the gap is boxing-specific | transfer status: NO TRANSFER AVAILABLE - the nearest evidence is youth soccer and swimming, different sports with different participation structures
LIMITATIONS: Absence of evidence in the searched databases is not proof of absence; grey literature, national federation internal data and non-English sources were not searched. OpenAlex querying was additionally curtailed by an API daily-budget limit during this work, so coverage of that index was incomplete.
PPBF implication: THE HEADLINE EVIDENCE GAP OF THIS TRACK. Every retention KPI (B4-K030 to B4-K035) carries benchmark_status = DATA GAP - PPBF MUST ESTABLISH. PPBF's own first cohort becomes its baseline, and PPBF is positioned to generate the first such benchmark if it runs the cohort analysis properly and publishes the method.
Source: No qualifying source located. (INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Methodological literature on cluster randomised and multicentre designs establishes that observations grouped within clusters (classes, coaches, sites) are correlated, that the intraclass correlation coefficient governs the design effect, and that designs with small numbers of clusters require specific analytic treatment.
Effect/estimate: Design effect determined by cluster size and the intraclass correlation; small-cluster designs require adjusted methods
Population: n/a (methodological) | level: n/a | sex: n/a | age: n/a
Design: Statistical methodology papers on cluster design and analysis | n: n/a
Boxing-specific: no | transfer status: METHODOLOGICAL
LIMITATIONS: Written for trial design; PPBF's setting is observational, so the relevance is to standard-error estimation rather than to randomisation
PPBF implication: Athletes are clustered within coaches and classes. The dropout model must use a random effect or standard errors clustered on coach or class; ignoring clustering understates uncertainty and would make coach-level differences look more real than they are - a direct input to the prohibition on coach ranking (KPI B4-K115).
Source: Stat Methods Med Res, 2011. Efficient design of cluster randomized and multicentre trials with unknown intraclass correlation. Supporting: Stat Med, 2020. Design and analysis of three-arm parallel cluster randomized trials with small numbers of clusters. (PMID 21937473. Supporting: PMID 33258219)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Financial cost of organised sport participation influenced participation decisions specifically among lower-income families and among families of girls; time was the dominant influence for parents of 5-12 year olds overall.
Effect/estimate: Cost influenced decisions for lower-income families p=0.01 and for girls p=0.04; 63% of children participated
Population: Parents of children in New South Wales, Australia | level: Community/organised youth sport | sex: Mixed (child sex analysed) | age: 5-17 y
Design: Cross-sectional CATI survey | n: 402 parents
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from general organised youth sport (Australia) to US community boxing — flag
LIMITATIONS: Self-report; single Australian state; 2010 data; parent-reported perceptions not observed behaviour; correlational.
PPBF implication: Justifies a sliding-scale/waiver policy as an access intervention, and justifies measuring fee-barrier separately by household income and athlete sex.
Source: Hardy LL, Kelly B, et al. Parental perceptions of barriers to children's participation in organised sport in Australia. J Paediatr Child Health. 2010. (PMID 20105247 / 10.1111/j.1440-1754.2009.01661.x)

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A universal government sport voucher reached 53% of eligible children in its first year, but registration was lower among children in the most disadvantaged areas, girls, older adolescents, and those speaking a language other than English at home.
Effect/estimate: 53% of eligible children registered; 70% of registrants had attended structured PA sessions
Population: School-enrolled children, New South Wales, Australia | level: Structured physical activity/organised sport | sex: Mixed | age: 4.5-18 y
Design: Cross-sectional population registration data vs Census | n: 671,375 registrants
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from a state-funded universal voucher scheme to a single US nonprofit's fee policy — flag
LIMITATIONS: Reach is not effectiveness; registration data cannot show counterfactual participation; Australian policy context differs from US.
PPBF implication: A price subsidy alone does not reach the most disadvantaged. PPBF must pair any waiver with active outreach and measure uptake BY subgroup, not just count waivers issued.
Source: Foley BC, Owen KB, et al. Physical Activity Behaviors of Children Who Register for the Universal, State-Wide Active Kids Voucher. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2020. (PMID 32781753 / 10.3390/ijerph17165691)

Effect/estimate: Qualitative — no effect size; 91% aware of the program
Population: Parents/carers of children with overweight/obesity, western Sydney, Australia | level: Community sport | sex: Mixed | age: School-aged
Design: Qualitative focus groups, Framework analysis | n: 54 parents
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from Australian voucher context — flag
LIMITATIONS: Convenience sample recruited from a weight-management program; not generalisable; qualitative findings are not prevalence estimates.
PPBF implication: A one-off registration waiver is weaker than a recurring waiver. PPBF should model waiver COST over a full season, not per enrolment event, and consider equipment/travel as separate barrier line items.
Source: Virgona N, Foley BC, et al. 'One hundred dollars is a big help, but to continue, it's a challenge'. Health Promot J Austr. 2021. (PMID 33570224 / 10.1002/hpja.468)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Across five years of a universal voucher program, the proportion of children meeting physical activity guidelines did not rise at population level, indicating that removing a price barrier alone did not shift population participation.
Effect/estimate: Slight decrease in the proportion meeting PA guidelines over the implementation period
Population: Children and adolescents, New South Wales, Australia | level: Sport and active recreation | sex: Mixed | age: 4.5-18 y
Design: Repeated cross-sectional program data triangulated with two population surveys | n: Program registrants 2018-2022 plus population survey samples
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from population-level policy evaluation to organisation-level fee policy — flag; a null population effect does not mean no effect for an individual family
LIMITATIONS: Ecological design; COVID-19 disruption overlaps the period; self-reported PA; cannot attribute the population trend to the program.
PPBF implication: Do not claim in grant applications that fee waivers alone increase physical activity. Claim access, and measure PPBF's own retention and attendance outcomes as the evidence.
Source: Owen KB, Foley BC, et al. Population level effects of the active kids program on children and adolescents' physical activity and sport participation in NSW, Australia. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2025. (PMID 40437604 / 10.1186/s12966-025-01763-2)

text_content:
[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Financial barriers to municipal recreation access for low-income families coexist with informational, physical and social barriers, and subsidy programs alone were judged insufficient without accompanying access design.
Effect/estimate: No quantitative effect estimate — recommendation set
Population: Low-income families with preschool-aged children, Strathcona County, Canada | level: Municipal recreation | sex: Mixed | age: 3-5 y (children)
Design: Triangulation of Photovoice data, framework guidance and targeted critical literature review | n: Not a single enumerated sample — mixed evidence synthesis
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from Canadian municipal recreation to US nonprofit boxing — flag
LIMITATIONS: Small qualitative base; single municipality; recommendations are expert-synthesised rather than trial-tested; preschool age group differs from typical boxing entry age.
PPBF implication: Budget for outreach, transport and information as access line items, not only fee waivers. These are real costs that a fee-only access model hides.
Source: Belon AP, Nieuwendyk L, et al. [VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Club sports participation was associated with substantially higher odds of families spending over $1,000 per year on the sport, in a pediatric sports medicine clinic sample.
Effect/estimate: Club participation adjusted OR 5.88 (95% CI 1.10-31.4) for spending >$1,000/y; female sex adjusted OR 3.47 (95% CI 1.12-10.74)
Population: Parents of pediatric sports medicine patients, USA | level: Club/specialised youth sport | sex: Mixed (female sex analysed) | age: Approx. 10-18 y
Design: Clinic-based cross-sectional survey with logistic regression | n: Survey of parents over a three-month clinic period
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from US clinic-recruited specialised youth sport to community boxing — flag
LIMITATIONS: Clinic sample is injured/care-seeking and not representative; very wide confidence intervals indicate imprecise estimates; self-reported spending; correlation not causation.
PPBF implication: If PPBF adds a competitive/travel tier, model it as a SEPARATE cost centre with its own access policy — competitive tiers are where cost exclusion concentrates.
Source: Allahabadi S, Calthorpe L, et al. Financial and medical burdens of youth sports specialization: survey of pediatric sports patients. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2021. (PMID 33768778 / 10.23736/S0022-4707.21.12304-7)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] School-district policies permitting greater community use of school facilities increased afterschool physical activity program participation without a significant increase in school operating expenses.
Effect/estimate: Increased participation with no significant operating-expense increase; cost per student and cost per building square foot computed
Population: 30 middle schools in one large US school district | level: Afterschool community programs | sex: Mixed (boys and girls counted) | age: Middle school
Design: Observational cost-benefit assessment across 12 months | n: All 30 middle schools in the district
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from US school shared-use to a boxing gym facility strategy — flag; boxing has equipment/space needs a gymnasium may not meet
LIMITATIONS: Single district; 2010-2011 data; observational, not randomised; marginal-cost finding may not hold where a facility is at capacity or requires specialised fit-out.
PPBF implication: Facility is the largest fixed cost in the model. A shared-use or joint-use agreement with a school/municipal partner is the highest-leverage cost strategy PPBF can test — but boxing-specific fit-out (ring, bag mounts, storage) must be priced into the agreement.
Source: Kanters MA, Bocarro JN, et al. Shared Use of School Facilities With Community Organizations and Afterschool Physical Activity Program Participation: A Cost-Benefit Assessment. J Sch Health. 2014. (PMID 24707924 / 10.1111/josh.12148)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Financial vulnerability in charitable nonprofits can be operationalised as the likelihood of cutting service offerings when a financial shock occurs, using four financial ratios (equity balance, revenue concentration, administrative cost ratio, operating margin).
Effect/estimate: Four vulnerability criteria defined and applied; no single effect size
Population: US charitable nonprofits filing tax returns | level: N/A (organisational) | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Conceptual framework applied to a national sample of tax returns | n: 4,730 US charitable nonprofits (1983 sample)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — PPBF is a US nonprofit; sport-sector specificity untested here
LIMITATIONS: 1983 data; ratios are proxies not outcomes; the framework predates the modern nonprofit reporting regime; subsequent tests find mixed predictive utility (see B5-010).
PPBF implication: Adopt these four ratios as PPBF's standing board financial-health dashboard; they are computable directly from Form 990 and internal ledgers.
Source: Tuckman HP, Chang CF. A Methodology for Measuring the Financial Vulnerability of Charitable Nonprofit Organizations. Nonprofit Volunt Sect Q. 1991;20(4). (10.1177/089976409102000407)
