text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Empirical testing of the Tuckman-Chang vulnerability measures in nonprofit arts organisations found they do not have utility for all subtypes but show promise for predicting closure in some organisations.
Effect/estimate: Mixed predictive utility by subtype; no single pooled effect size
Population: US nonprofit arts organisations | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Empirical test of published ratio measures against organisational closure | n: Population of nonprofit arts organisations (see paper)
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from arts nonprofits to a sport nonprofit — flag; subsector matters and this is the paper's own finding
LIMITATIONS: Arts subsector only; the paper's core finding is precisely that transferability across subsectors is limited — do not assume sport behaves like arts.
PPBF implication: Use the ratios as monitoring signals, not as a predictive model. Do not build an automated SHADOW alert that declares PPBF 'at risk' from these ratios alone.
Source: Hager MA. Financial Vulnerability among Arts Organizations: A Test of the Tuckman-Chang Measures. Nonprofit Volunt Sect Q. 2001;30(2). (10.1177/0899764001302010)

text_content:
[CONTESTED PRACTICE] Whether revenue diversification improves nonprofit financial health is contested in the literature: a meta-analysis synthesising the empirical studies exists, and separate work argues concentration can carry rewards as well as risks.
Effect/estimate: Direction and magnitude vary by study and by financial-health outcome — no single agreed estimate
Population: US nonprofits (multiple subsectors across studies) | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Meta-analysis (Hung & Hager) and conceptual/empirical counter-argument (Frumkin & Keating) | n: Meta-analysis pools multiple primary studies; see paper for k
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to US nonprofit finance; sport-club-specific findings are separate (see B5-013, B5-014)
LIMITATIONS: Primary studies use heterogeneous definitions of both diversification and financial health; most rely on Form 990 data with known reporting-quality limits; the outcome measured (volatility vs survival vs efficiency) changes the answer.
PPBF implication: Do NOT encode 'more diversified = healthier' as a scoring rule in SHADOW. Report the concentration index as a descriptive risk indicator with an explicit note that its interpretation is contested.
Source: Hung C, Hager MA. The Impact of Revenue Diversification on Nonprofit Financial Health: A Meta-analysis. Nonprofit Volunt Sect Q. 2019. AND Frumkin P, Keating EK. Diversification Reconsidered: The Risks and Rewards of Revenue Concentration. J Soc Entrep. 2011;2(2). (10.1177/0899764018807080 ; 10.1080/19420676.2011.614630)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In UK charities, greater financial vulnerability was associated with dependence on GRANT funding specifically, rather than with income concentration as such; the authors characterise the usual concentration-vulnerability association as a specification error.
Effect/estimate: Vulnerability associated with grant dependence, not concentration per se
Population: UK registered charities | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Panel modelling of income composition against short-term volatility and long-term survival, nested specification tests | n: UK charity register panel — see paper
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from UK charity regulation/funding environment to US nonprofit — flag; UK grant landscape differs materially from US
LIMITATIONS: UK-specific funding structures; register data; observational — grant-dependent charities may differ systematically in mission and size.
PPBF implication: Track grant dependence as its own risk metric alongside overall concentration. A PPBF budget that is 'diversified' but grant-heavy may still be fragile.
Source: Green E, Ritchie F. Financial Resilience, Income Dependence and Organisational Survival in UK Charities. Voluntas. 2021. (10.1007/s11266-020-00311-9)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a large national survey of nonprofit sport clubs, human, financial, infrastructure and cultural resources predicted the severity of organisational problems in recruiting and retaining members, volunteers and coaches, and in club finances; a Herfindahl revenue-concentration index was among the financial resource measures used.
Effect/estimate: Significant regression effects of human, financial and infrastructure resources on problem severity — see paper for coefficients
Population: Nonprofit sport clubs, Germany | level: Community/grassroots sport clubs | sex: N/A (club level; board gender composition analysed) | age: N/A
Design: Cross-sectional nationwide online survey with regression | n: n = 19,345 clubs
Boxing-specific: No — multi-sport club sample | transfer status: Transfer from German voluntary sport-club system to a US 501(c)(3) — flag; German clubs operate under a distinct Verein legal and subsidy regime
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported problem severity; cross-sectional so no causal direction; German institutional context (municipal subsidy, membership-fee norms) differs sharply from the US.
PPBF implication: This is the closest large-sample analogue to PPBF's situation. It supports treating volunteer/coach supply and finance as a COUPLED risk, not two separate registers.
Source: Wicker P, Breuer C. Understanding the Importance of Organizational Resources to Explain Organizational Problems: Evidence from Nonprofit Sport Clubs in Germany. Voluntas. 2013. (10.1007/s11266-012-9272-2)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In nonprofit sport clubs, financial and volunteer problems were interrelated; clubs relying on sponsorship income reported larger financial AND volunteer problems, while public subsidies were associated with increased volunteer problems only.
Effect/estimate: Sponsorship reliance associated with larger financial and volunteer problems; subsidies associated with increased volunteer problems; internal revenues not significant
Population: Sport clubs, Germany | level: Community sport clubs | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Bivariate probit model on survey data | n: German sport club survey — see paper
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from German sport clubs — flag
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional; self-reported problems; reverse causation plausible (struggling clubs may chase sponsorship); German subsidy context.
PPBF implication: Chasing sponsorship and grants is not free — it consumes volunteer and staff capacity. Budget the ADMINISTRATIVE cost of each funding stream, and treat 'volunteer hours consumed by fundraising' as a tracked metric.
Source: Coates D, Wicker P. A Bivariate Probit Examination of Financial and Volunteer Problems of Non-Profit Sport Clubs. Int J Sport Finance. 2014;9(3). (10.1177/155862351400900304)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] The financial and economic condition of the surrounding community significantly affected the human, infrastructure and financial resource situation of local nonprofit sport clubs.
Effect/estimate: Significant community-level effects on club resources — see paper for coefficients
Population: Nonprofit sport clubs (n=19,345) nested in communities (n=3,153), Germany | level: Community sport | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Multilevel analysis combining club survey with community secondary data | n: 19,345 clubs; 3,153 communities
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from German municipalities to a Pennsylvania borough — flag
LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional multilevel design; German municipal finance system channels resources to clubs in ways with no direct US equivalent.
PPBF implication: PPBF's revenue ceiling is partly set by the local economy, not by management quality. Board reporting should include local economic context so that a revenue shortfall is not misattributed to staff performance.
Source: Wicker P, Breuer C. How the Economic and Financial Situation of the Community Affects Sport Clubs' Resources: Evidence from Multi-Level Models. Int J Financ Stud. 2015;3(1):31. (10.3390/ijfs3010031)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Revenue diversification among nonprofit sport clubs was significantly determined by the club's organisational mission, with different missions associated with different funding sources.
Effect/estimate: Significant mission effects on diversification level — see paper for coefficients
Population: Nonprofit sport clubs, Germany | level: Community sport | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Panel regression on nationwide club survey | n: Nationwide German sport-club panel — see paper
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from German sport clubs — flag
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported mission categories; German context; diversification measured at a point in time.
PPBF implication: PPBF's access-first mission structurally constrains which revenue mixes are achievable. A fee-maximising mix would conflict with the mission; the board should state the acceptable mix explicitly rather than leaving it implicit.
Source: Wicker P, Feiler S. Organizational Mission and Revenue Diversification among Non-profit Sports Clubs. Int J Financ Stud. 2013;1(4):119. (10.3390/ijfs1040119)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Using Form 990 data for all filing 501(c)(3) organisations 1998-2003, four commonly used financial indicators converged into a single financial-health construct; accounting and revenue variables were less clearly related to financial health than the literature suggests, while environmental variables (macroeconomic conditions, community median household income, revenue share in the policy area) were strong predictors.
Effect/estimate: Environmental variables strong predictors; accounting/revenue variables weaker than expected
Population: US 501(c)(3) organisations, human services and higher education subsectors | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Panel analysis of IRS Form 990 data | n: All filing 501(c)(3) organisations in two subsectors, 1998-2003
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to US nonprofits; sport subsector not among the two analysed — flag
LIMITATIONS: Two subsectors only; pre-2008 period; Form 990 self-reported data with known allocation inconsistencies; correlational.
PPBF implication: Reinforces B5-015: report local median household income alongside PPBF's own ratios. It also cautions against over-weighting internal accounting ratios in any SHADOW health score.
Source: Prentice CR. Understanding Nonprofit Financial Health. Nonprofit Volunt Sect Q. 2016. (10.1177/0899764015601243)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a survey experiment, donors preferred the organisation with lower overhead, but describing higher overhead as building long-term organisational capacity increased the proportion choosing the higher-overhead organisation; omitting the word 'overhead' increased it further.
Effect/estimate: Directional shifts in choice proportions by framing condition — see paper for magnitudes
Population: Survey-experiment participants (donor decision scenario), US | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: Adults
Design: Randomised survey experiment | n: See paper
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Transfer from hypothetical donor-choice experiment to real giving behaviour — flag; stated choice is not revealed giving
LIMITATIONS: Hypothetical scenario, not actual donations; single experiment; framing effects can be fragile across populations.
PPBF implication: PPBF should not starve its administrative and coach-development budget to protect an overhead ratio. Where overhead is reported, pair it with a capacity explanation — the evidence says framing matters.
Source: Qu H, Daniel JL. Is 'Overhead' A Tainted Word? A Survey Experiment Exploring Framing Effects of Nonprofit Overhead on Donor Decision. Nonprofit Volunt Sect Q. 2021. (10.1177/0899764020959475)

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A meta-analysis examined whether government support crowds out or crowds in charitable donations, synthesising the empirical literature on this relationship.
Effect/estimate: Direction and size of crowding effect vary across studies — consult the paper before quoting any pooled value
Population: Nonprofit organisations across studies (predominantly US/Europe) | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Meta-analysis | n: Pooled primary studies — see paper for k
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to nonprofit fundraising strategy; not sport-specific
LIMITATIONS: Primary studies use heterogeneous designs and definitions; publication bias is a standing concern in this literature; I have not verified a specific pooled coefficient and therefore do not state one.
PPBF implication: Do not assume a new government grant is purely additive to PPBF's donation base, and do not assume it displaces giving either. Measure PPBF's own donation trend before and after any large public award.
Source: de Wit A, Bekkers R. Government Support and Charitable Donations: A Meta-Analysis of the Crowding-out Hypothesis. J Public Adm Res Theory. 2017. (10.1093/jopart/muw044)

Population: US parents of children participating regularly in one or more sports | level: All levels of youth sport, mixed | sex: Mixed | age: 6-18 y
Design: Nationally representative online parent survey | n: 1,848 youth sports parents, all 50 states + DC, surveyed Nov-Dec 2024

PPBF implication: This is a DEMAND-side benchmark (what families pay across all sports), NOT a supply-side cost. It is useful for positioning PPBF's fee as low-cost relative to the market, and must never be used as PPBF's own cost per athlete.
Source: Aspen Institute Project Play. National Youth Sports Parent Survey — family spending on youth sports rises 46% over five years. 2025. ()

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] A 501(c)(3) generally avoids private-foundation classification by meeting a public support test — the 509(a)(1)/170(b)(1)(A)(vi) test at one-third public support (with a 10% facts-and-circumstances alternative) or the 509(a)(2) test — computed over a five-year measuring period and reported on Form 990 Schedule A, with consequences applying from the sixth year.
Effect/estimate: One-third (33⅓%) public support threshold; 10% facts-and-circumstances alternative; 5-year computation period
Population: US 501(c)(3) public charities | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary regulatory requirement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — binding on PPBF
LIMITATIONS: Which test applies (509(a)(1) vs 509(a)(2)) depends on the organisation's revenue composition and materially changes how program-service fee revenue is treated; this is a determination for PPBF's CPA/counsel, not a modelling choice.
PPBF implication: CRITICAL INTERACTION WITH THE FINANCE MODEL: a strategy that shifts PPBF toward fee revenue and away from broad public support can jeopardise public-charity status. The revenue mix is a compliance variable, not only a sustainability variable. Route the test determination to PPBF's CPA before changing the fee/donation balance.
Source: Internal Revenue Service. Exempt organizations annual reporting requirements — Form 990 Schedules A and B: public charity support test. ()

Population: US tax-exempt organisations | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary regulatory requirement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — binding on PPBF

Source: Internal Revenue Service. Unrelated business income tax. ()

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Under IRC section 513(i), a qualified sponsorship payment is excluded from unrelated business taxable income, but a payment becomes taxable advertising income where the sponsor receives a substantial return benefit such as qualitative or comparative claims, price information, or an inducement to purchase.
Effect/estimate: Acknowledgement = excluded; advertising = taxable UBI; exclusive-provider arrangements treated separately
Population: US tax-exempt organisations receiving corporate support | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary statutory and regulatory requirement (IRC 513(i); Treas. Reg. 1.513-4) | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — binding on PPBF
LIMITATIONS: The acknowledgement/advertising line is fact-specific; a banner naming a sponsor differs from one making product claims. Contract wording matters.
PPBF implication: Draft PPBF's sponsorship agreements as acknowledgements. Any sponsor asking for comparative claims, pricing, or a call to action converts that revenue into taxable advertising — a legal review item, not a sales decision.
Source: Internal Revenue Service. Advertising or qualified sponsorship payments? ; 26 CFR 1.513-4. ()

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] 501(c)(3) status prohibits private inurement to insiders and more than incidental private benefit; IRC section 4958 imposes excise taxes on excess benefit transactions — a first-tier tax on the disqualified person, an additional tier if not corrected, and a tax on organisation managers who knowingly participate, subject to a per-transaction cap.
Effect/estimate: Tiered excise taxes on the disqualified person and on knowing managers, with a statutory cap on the manager-level tax per transaction
Population: US 501(c)(3) organisations and their insiders | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary statutory requirement (IRC 4958) | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — binding on PPBF
LIMITATIONS: Specific rates and the manager-tax cap should be confirmed against the current Code and regulations before any compensation decision; a rebuttable presumption of reasonableness procedure exists and its requirements are technical.
PPBF implication: HIGH RELEVANCE TO A FOUNDER-LED ORGANISATION. Any payment to a founder, board member, family member or related business — including coaching stipends and facility rental from a related party — must go through a documented conflict-of-interest and comparability process. This is the compliance face of the founder-dependence failure mode.
Source: Congressional Research Service. The Prohibitions on Private Inurement & Benefit by Tax-Exempt Organizations and Intermediate Sanctions (R48873). IRS. An Introduction to I.R.C. 4958 (Intermediate Sanctions). ()

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Under 2 CFR 200.414, a non-federal entity without a negotiated indirect cost rate may elect a de minimis indirect cost rate; the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision raised that rate to 15% of modified total direct costs, effective for awards from 1 October 2024.
Effect/estimate: De minimis rate 15% of modified total direct costs (MTDC), up from the prior 10%; effective for awards issued on or after 1 Oct 2024
Population: Non-federal recipients of US federal awards | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary regulatory requirement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — applies if PPBF receives federal awards or federal pass-through funds
LIMITATIONS: MTDC has a specific definition that excludes certain cost categories; some programs have statutory indirect-cost caps that override the de minimis rate; confirm per award.
PPBF implication: If PPBF pursues federal or federal pass-through funding, elect the de minimis rate rather than absorbing administrative cost. Under-recovering indirect cost is a common and avoidable way small nonprofits subsidise grants out of unrestricted funds.
Source: 2 CFR 200.414 — Indirect costs (Uniform Guidance, 2024 revision). ()

[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] Under 2 CFR 200.501, a non-federal entity that expends $1,000,000 or more in federal awards in its fiscal year must have a single or program-specific audit; the threshold was raised to $1,000,000 in the 2024 Uniform Guidance revision.
Effect/estimate: $1,000,000 federal expenditure threshold (raised from $750,000)
Population: Non-federal recipients of US federal awards | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary regulatory requirement | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — applies if PPBF's federal expenditure reaches the threshold
LIMITATIONS: The trigger is federal awards EXPENDED in the year, not awarded; pass-through funds count; effective-date detail matters for the transition year.
PPBF implication: Far above PPBF's illustrative scale, but it defines the ceiling on how much federal money the organisation can absorb before a materially more expensive audit regime applies. Budget the audit cost before accepting an award that crosses it.
Source: 2 CFR 200.501 — Audit requirements (Uniform Guidance, 2024 revision). ()

Effect/estimate: Functional expense analysis + allocation-method disclosure + liquidity/availability disclosure; net asset classes reduced to two (with and without donor restrictions)
Population: US not-for-profit entities reporting under US GAAP | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Primary accounting standard | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct — applies to PPBF's audited or reviewed GAAP financial statements
LIMITATIONS: Applies to GAAP financial statements; an organisation on a cash or modified-cash basis has different presentation, though funders may still require GAAP.

[CONTESTED PRACTICE] A commonly cited nonprofit operating-reserve benchmark is a minimum of 25% of the annual operating expense budget, equivalent to roughly three months of operating expenses; this is a practice recommendation from sector bodies, not an empirically validated optimum.
Effect/estimate: 25% of annual operating expenses ≈ 3 months
Population: US nonprofit organisations | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Sector practice guidance (Nonprofit Operating Reserves Initiative workgroup; National Council of Nonprofits) | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to US nonprofits; a seasonal youth sport program with lumpy enrolment cycles may need a different target
LIMITATIONS: This is a widely repeated practice heuristic, not a finding from a controlled study; the appropriate reserve depends on the organisation's own revenue volatility, funder concentration and fixed-cost rigidity. Treat any single number as a starting point for a board policy discussion.
PPBF implication: The model uses a 3-month reserve target as a LABELLED ASSUMPTION. PPBF's board should adopt a written reserve policy and set the target from PPBF's own measured revenue volatility once data exists.
Source: National Council of Nonprofits. Operating reserves for nonprofits. Nonprofit Operating Reserves Initiative Workgroup. Nonprofit Operating Reserves — An Introduction. ()

Population: Adults in direct-contact roles with children in Pennsylvania | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: Adults (staff/volunteers)

Boxing-specific: No — applies to all Pennsylvania youth-serving organisations including boxing gyms | transfer status: Direct — binding on PPBF
LIMITATIONS: Requirements differ for volunteers vs employees and for those with PA residency history under 10 years (FBI fingerprint clearance); exact fees and intervals must be confirmed against current PA DHS guidance. This is a safeguarding requirement first and a budget line second.

text_content:
[VERIFIED EVIDENCE] In a 35-year prospective cohort of men, self-reported serious amateur boxing was associated with roughly twofold odds of cognitive impairment and with earlier onset of dementia.
Effect/estimate: Cognitive impairment OR 2.27 (95% CI 1.18-4.38); amnestic impairment OR 2.78 (95% CI 1.37-5.65); onset advanced by 4.8 years (95% CI 0.9-8.8)
Population: Adult men, Caerphilly Prospective Study, Wales | level: Amateur boxing (self-reported 'serious') | sex: Male only | age: 45-59 y at baseline, followed 35 years
Design: Prospective cohort | n: 1,123 men
Boxing-specific: YES — amateur boxing | transfer status: Boxing-specific but male-only, historical cohort, older rule era
LIMITATIONS: Self-reported boxing exposure with no dose measure; men only; historical amateur boxing rules and headguard/medical practice differ from current; observational — residual confounding by socioeconomic and lifestyle factors is plausible; correlation not causation.
PPBF implication: FINANCE RELEVANCE ONLY: head-injury exposure is a material factor in insurability, medical-cost budgeting and governance. It does NOT belong in SHADOW as a participation-clearance rule. Medical eligibility, sparring clearance and any return-to-play decision are owned by qualified medical professionals and the Head Coach under governing-body rules — never by this model or by SHADOW.
Source: Gallacher J, Pickering J, et al. Amateur Boxing and Dementia: Cognitive Impairment Within the 35-Year Caerphilly Cohort Study. Clin J Sport Med. 2021. (PMID 35470341 / 10.1097/JSM.0000000000000976)

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] In a coached sport program, coaching and facility costs are step-fixed rather than smoothly variable — they jump when a supervision-ratio or capacity threshold is crossed — so cost per participant does not decline monotonically with enrolment but sawtooths.
Effect/estimate: Visible step discontinuities at each supervision-ratio and facility-capacity threshold
Population: Coached community sport programs | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Structural consequence demonstrated in the accompanying model | n: Rosters 5-600 modelled
Boxing-specific: Model is boxing-parameterised; the structure is general to coached sport | transfer status: Structural/analytical, not empirical
LIMITATIONS: The location of the steps depends entirely on the supervision ratio and facility capacity assumed, both of which are PPBF safety and facility decisions, not model outputs.
PPBF implication: Enrolment growth just past a step is the worst place to sit financially. PPBF should plan intake in blocks aligned to supervision capacity rather than accepting athletes continuously, and should know where its own steps are.

Effect/estimate: breakeven_enrolment returns NaN for both configurations across the modelled range; required contributed revenue at 100 athletes is roughly $178k (paid staff) and $109k (volunteer-led) under the placeholder assumptions
Population: Illustrative community boxing program | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Deterministic scenario model with fully declared assumption inputs | n: 6 rosters x 2 configurations

PPBF implication: The operationally decisive planning number for a low-fee access-first program is the annual contributed revenue required for solvency, not a break-even roster size. Build the fundraising plan around that figure once PPBF's real costs are known.

[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] In one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis at a 100-athlete roster, coaching-labour parameters (athletes per paid coach, and cost per assistant coach) dominated the swing in annual surplus by a wide margin over price, collection rate, grants and every other tested parameter.
Effect/estimate: Supervision ratio produced roughly a $43k swing and cost per assistant coach roughly $28k, versus roughly $18k for facility base cost and roughly $18k for the membership fee, under the placeholder assumptions
Population: Illustrative community boxing program | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: One-at-a-time ±25% sensitivity analysis across 12 parameters | n: 12 parameters, roster 100
Boxing-specific: Parameterised for boxing; placeholders | transfer status: Not empirical
LIMITATIONS: OAT sensitivity ignores interactions and does not give an outcome distribution; the ranking depends on the base values chosen. It answers 'which assumption most deserves measurement effort', not 'what will happen'.
PPBF implication: PPBF's first data-collection priority is its true coaching cost structure and its actual supervision ratio in practice. IMPORTANT: the supervision ratio must be set on safety and governing-body grounds by the Head Coach and board — the fact that it dominates the economics is a reason to measure it accurately, never a reason to raise it.
Source: PPBF B5 finance model, fig_sensitivity_tornado.png and finance_sensitivity_computed.csv, 2026-08-07. ()

[STRONG EVIDENCE-SUPPORTED INFERENCE] Founder dependence is a recognised organisational risk for small nonprofits, and it has a specific financial-compliance dimension: transactions between the organisation and a founder or related party are exactly the transactions IRC section 4958 governs.
Effect/estimate: No effect estimate — a risk-structure claim
Population: Small US nonprofit organisations | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Inference linking verified statutory requirements to the small-nonprofit governance context | n: N/A
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to PPBF's context
LIMITATIONS: 'Founder syndrome' as a construct is widely discussed in practitioner literature but I did not verify a peer-reviewed effect estimate for it; the statutory element (section 4958) IS verified. Do not present the behavioural claim as measured.
PPBF implication: Two concrete controls: a written conflict-of-interest policy with annual disclosure, and a documented compensation-comparability process for any related-party payment. Also: a succession plan and a second person with financial-system access.
Source: Congressional Research Service R48873 (private inurement and intermediate sanctions); IRS EO CPE text on IRC 4958. ()

Effect/estimate: No agreed estimate — see B5-011 and B5-012
Population: US and UK nonprofits | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Contested across a meta-analysis, panel studies and a specification-error argument | n: Multiple large samples across studies
Boxing-specific: No | transfer status: Direct to nonprofit finance; sport-club evidence is separate
LIMITATIONS: The disagreement is genuine and unresolved; presenting either position as settled would misrepresent the literature.
PPBF implication: Report BOTH the concentration index and the grant-dependence share, and flag any single funder above a board-set share of total revenue. Do not let SHADOW score 'diversified' as automatically 'healthy'.

text_content:
[HYPOTHESIS REQUIRING TESTING] Facility cost is the largest single fixed line in the illustrative model and is the least controllable in the short run, making a lease increase, loss of a shared-use arrangement, or a required capital repair the highest-magnitude single-event financial risk to a program of this shape.
Effect/estimate: Facility base cost ranked third in the ±25% sensitivity swing, behind only the two coaching-labour parameters
Population: Illustrative community boxing program | level: N/A | sex: N/A | age: N/A
Design: Structural observation from the model's fixed-cost composition and sensitivity ranking | n: Model scenarios
Boxing-specific: Parameterised for boxing; placeholders | transfer status: Not empirical
LIMITATIONS: Depends entirely on the assumed facility cost. A program in donated or shared-use space has a completely different risk profile — which is itself the point.
PPBF implication: Know the lease renewal date, the escalation clause and the notice period, and hold them in the risk register. Evidence on shared-use arrangements (B5-008) suggests a partner facility is the highest-leverage cost strategy available.
